Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 1–2 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Qurtubi said: It is Medinan by consensus (ijma'). Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah that he said: "Al-Ma'idah is Medinan."

Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, who said: "I performed Hajj and entered upon Aisha, and she said to me: 'O Jubayr, do you recite al-Ma'idah?' I said: 'Yes.' She said: 'Indeed, it is the last surah to be revealed. Whatever you find in it that is permitted, make it permitted, and whatever you find in it that is forbidden, make it forbidden.'"

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Abdullah ibn Umar, who said: "The last surah to be revealed was al-Ma'idah and al-Fath." Ahmad also narrated from him, who said: "Surah al-Ma'idah was revealed upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was riding his mount, and it could not bear him, so he dismounted from it." Ibn Kathir said: "Ahmad alone narrated it." I say: Its chain includes Ibn Lahi'ah.

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Muhammad ibn Nasr in Kitab al-Salah, al-Tabarani, Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Asma bint Yazid something similar. Ibn Abi Shaybah in his Musnad, al-Baghawi in his Mu'jam, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-Nubuwwah narrated from Umm Amr bint Isa, from her paternal uncle, something similar as well. Abu Ubayd narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi something similar.

It is also added that it was revealed during the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjat al-Wada') between Makkah and Madinah. Ibn Jarir narrated this addition from al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Abu Ubayd narrated from Damrah ibn Habib and Atiyyah ibn Qays, who both said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Al-Ma'idah is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, so make permitted its permitted things and make forbidden its forbidden things."

Abu Dawud and al-Nahhas, both in their works on abrogation (al-Naskh), narrated from Abu Maysarah Amr ibn Shurahbil, who said: "Nothing from al-Ma'idah has been abrogated." Likewise, Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated it from him. Likewise, Abd ibn Humayd and Abu Dawud in his work on abrogation narrated it, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated it from al-Sha'bi. Likewise, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud in his work on abrogation, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated it from al-Hasan al-Basri.

Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud in his work on abrogation, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Sha'bi, who said: "Nothing from al-Ma'idah has been abrogated except this verse: ﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah or the sacred month or the sacrificial animals or the garlands﴾."

Abu Dawud in his work on abrogation, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim (who graded it sahih) narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Two verses have been abrogated from this surah: the verse of the garlands, and His saying: ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 42]." Abd ibn Humayd in his Musnad narrated from Ibn Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited in his sermon Surah al-Ma'idah and Surah al-Tawbah.

al-Naqqash mentioned, from Abu Salamah, that he said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from al-Hudaybiyah, he said: 'O Ali, did you realize that Surah al-Ma'idah was revealed to me? And what a beneficial thing it is!'" Ibn al-Arabi said: "This is a fabricated hadith (hadith mawdu'), and it is not permissible for a Muslim to believe it." Ibn Atiyyah said: "In my view, this does not resemble the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ)."

* *

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

﴿O you who have believed, fulfill the contracts. Lawful for you are the animals of grazing livestock, except what is recited to you [in prohibition], not making lawful hunting while you are in the state of ihram. Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah or the sacred month or the sacrificial animals or the garlands or those coming to the Sacred House seeking bounty from their Lord and His approval. And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt. And let not the animosity of a people [in having] obstructed you from al-Masjid al-Haram lead you to transgress. And cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

This verse, with which Allah opened this surah, up to His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills﴾, contains such eloquence that human faculties fall short of it, while it includes several rulings. Among them: fulfilling contracts; the permissibility of grazing livestock; the exception of what will be recited (as prohibited); the prohibition of hunting for the one in ihram; and the permissibility of hunting for one who is not in ihram. Al-Naqqash related that the companions of the philosopher al-Kindi said to him: "O sage, compose for us something like this Qur'an." He said: "Yes, I will compose something like part of it." So he secluded himself for many days, then came out and said: "By Allah, no one can do this, nor can anyone bear it. I opened the mushaf and Surah al-Ma'idah came out. I looked, and behold, it has spoken of fulfilling (covenants) and forbidden breaking them, and it permitted in a general way, then made an exception after an exception, then informed of His power and wisdom in two lines. No one can produce this."

His saying ﴿Fulfill the contracts﴾: It is said awfa and wafa are two dialects (lughatan), and a poet combined both, saying:

"As for Ibn Tawf, he fulfilled his covenant,
just as the riders of the swift she-camels (of the stars) fulfilled [their journey]."

Al-'Uqud (the contracts) means al-'uhud (covenants). The root of al-'uqud is tying (al-rubut); its singular is 'aqd. It is said: "I tied the rope (aqadtu al-habl) and the pledge (al-'ahd)." It is used for physical things and for abstract meanings. When it is used for abstract meanings, as here, it conveys that it is very firm and strongly secured. It is said: the contracts are those which Allah established upon His servants and obligated them to through rulings. It is also said: they are the contracts which people make among themselves in transactions. The more preferred view is that the verse includes both together, and there is no basis for restricting it to some over others. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: fulfill the covenant of Allah upon you and your covenants with one another. End of quote. The contract that must be fulfilled is that which agrees with the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah. If it contradicts them, it is rejected; fulfilling it is not obligatory and it is not permissible.

His saying ﴿Lawful for you are the animals of grazing livestock﴾: The address is to those who have believed. Bahimah (animal) is the name for every four-legged creature. It was so named because of its lack of clarity (ibham) in terms of its deficiency in speech, understanding, and intellect. From it comes "a locked door" (bab mubham), i.e., closed; "a dark night" (layl bahim); and buhmah, for a brave man who does not know from where he will be attacked; and "an ambiguous ring" (halqah mubhamah), whose two ends are not known. Al-an'am (grazing livestock) is the name for camels, cattle, and sheep. They were so named because of the gentleness in their walking. It was also said: bahimat al-an'am refers to their wild counterparts, such as gazelles, wild cattle, wild donkeys, and other such animals. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari related this from a group of people, and others related it from al-Suddi, al-Rabi', Qatadah, and al-Dahhak.

Ibn Atiyyah said: This is a good view, because al-an'am are the eight pairs, and whatever is added to them from the rest of the animals is also called an'am together with them. Predatory animals like the lion, and every animal with fangs outside the boundary of an'am, are excluded. So bahimat al-an'am is the grazing four-legged animal. It was also said: bahimat al-an'am is whatever is not game (sayd), because game is called wild (wahsh), not bahimah. It was also said: bahimat al-an'am refers to the fetuses that come out at slaughter from the bellies of livestock, so they are eaten without slaughtering (dhakah). According to the first view, namely restricting al-an'am to camels, cattle, and sheep, the idafah (construct) is explanatory (bayaniyyah). What is permitted that lies outside them is added by analogy (qiyas), and even by the texts in the Book and Sunnah, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it unless it is carrion﴾ [al-An'am: 145], and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every fanged predator and every clawed bird is forbidden," for its implication indicates that whatever else is excluded is permitted. Likewise are all the texts specific to a category, as found in the purified books of the Sunnah.

His saying ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ is an exception from His saying ﴿Lawful for you are the animals of grazing livestock﴾. That is: except the implication of what is recited to you, for it is not lawful. What is recited is what Allah explicitly prohibited, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] and so on, and it is joined by what the Sunnah explicitly prohibited. This exception may mean: except what is recited to you now; and it may mean: in the future, which would indicate the permissibility of delaying clarification (ta'khir al-bayan) beyond the time of need; and it may include both meanings together.

His saying ﴿other than those who hunt game﴾: The Basrans held that His saying ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ is an exception from bahimat al-an'am, and His saying ﴿other than those who hunt game﴾ is another exception from it also. So both exceptions are from bahimat al-an'am, and the sense is: "Lawful for you are the animals of grazing livestock, except what is recited to you, except game while you are in ihram." It was said: the first exception is from bahimat al-an'am, and the second exception is from the first exception. This was refuted on the grounds that it would imply permitting hunting while in the state of ihram, since it is excepted from what is forbidden and so would be permitted. Al-Farra' permitted that ﴿except what is recited﴾ be in the nominative position as a substitute (badal), but the Basrans do not permit it except with an indefinite noun and what is close to it among general categories. He said: The accusative of ﴿other than those who hunt game﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal) of His saying ﴿fulfill the contracts﴾. Al-Akhfash said likewise. Others said it is a state of the kaf and mim in ﴿lakum﴾ (for you). The sense: lawful for you are the animals of grazing livestock, other than those who hunt game; that is, hunting on land and eating its game.

The meaning of their not making it lawful is affirming its prohibition in action and belief, ﴿while you are in the state of ihram﴾; that is, while you are muhrimun (in the state of ihram). The clause ﴿while you are in the state of ihram﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state of the pronoun in "muhilli" (those making lawful). The meaning of this restriction is clear according to those who restrict bahimat al-an'am to wild land animals that are lawful to eat. It is as if He said: Lawful for you is the game of the land except while in the state of ihram. As for the view of those who make the idafah explanatory, the meaning is: Lawful for you is a bahimah that is the an'am, at the time the game is forbidden to you by your entering into ihram, because you are in need of that. So the purpose of this restriction is to favor them by permitting what is other than what is forbidden to them in that state. By "those in ihram" (al-hurum) is meant the one who is in ihram for Hajj, for 'Umrah, or for both. He is called muhrim because game, perfume, and women become forbidden to him. Likewise the reason the sacred (haram) is called haram and the ihram is called ihram. Al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿hurum﴾ with a sukun on the ra', and this is a Tamimi dialect: they say rusul as rusl and kutub as kutb, and similar.

His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills﴾: From the rulings that differ from what the Arabs used to practice. He is the Owner of all; He does what He wills and ordains what He wills, with none to repel His judgment.

His saying ﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah﴾: al-Sha'a'ir (the rites) is the plural of sha'irah, on the pattern of fa'ilah. Ibn Faris said: It is also said for the singular: shi'ar, which is better. From it comes ish'ar (marking) for the sacrificial animal, and al-mash'ar (the landmarks) is plural mash'ar; these are the places marked with signs. It was said: what is meant here is all the rites of Hajj. It was also said: al-Safa and al-Marwah, the sacrificial animal, and the building. The meaning according to these two views: do not make these matters lawful (do not violate them), by committing any violation of them, or by coming between them and one who intends to perform them.

Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the prohibition against violating the rites of Allah immediately after mentioning the prohibition on hunting while in the state of ihram. It has been said that the meaning of "rites" (sha'a'ir) here is the obligations (fara'id) of Allah, and from this usage comes ﴿And whoever honours the rites of Allah﴾. It has also been said that they are the sacred things (hurumat) of Allah. There is no obstacle to understanding it as encompassing all of these, taking into account the generality of the wording and not only the specific occasion of revelation, nor only what the context indicates.

His saying ﴿nor the sacred month﴾ refers to the category, so it includes all the sacred months, which are four: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram, and Rajab. That is, do not violate them by fighting in them. It has also been said that what is meant here is only the month of the Hajj.

His saying "nor the sacrificial animals (al-hady)" refers to what is brought as an offering to the House of Allah, whether a camel, a cow, or a sheep. The singular is hadiyyah. Allah, glorified is He, forbade them to violate the sanctity of the sacrificial animals by taking them from their owners or by preventing them from reaching the place to which they are offered. He joined the sacrificial animals to the rites, although they are already included under them, in order to draw attention to their special status and to emphasise the seriousness of their matter.

His saying "nor the garlands (qala'id)" is the plural of qala'idah, which is what is hung around the neck of the sacrificial animal, such as a sandal or the like. Violating them means seizing them by force. The prohibition on violating the garlands is a reinforcement of the prohibition on violating the sacrificial animals. It has also been said that the meaning of "garlands" is the animals that have been garlanded, and that their being joined to the sacrificial animals is to add emphasis on the sacrificial animals. The first view is preferable. It has also been said that the meaning of "garlands" is what people used to hang around themselves as a guarantee of safety for them, so it is an elision: that is, "and for the owners of the garlands."

His saying ﴿nor those who make for the Sacred House﴾: that is, those who intend it, from the expression "I aimed at such-and-such" (ammamtu kadha), meaning I intended it. Al-A'mash recited "nor those who make for the Sacred House" with the genitive construction (idafah). The meaning is: do not prevent anyone who intends the Sacred House for the Hajj or the 'Umrah, or in order to dwell in it. It has also been said that the occasion of revelation of this verse was that the polytheists used to perform the Hajj, the 'Umrah, and offer sacrifices, and the Muslims wished to raid them. So it was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah﴾ to the end of the verse. In that case it is abrogated (mansukh) by His saying ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾, and His saying ﴿So let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram after this year of theirs﴾, and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "No polytheist shall perform the Hajj after this year." Others said: the verse is decisive (muhkam), and it concerns the Muslims.

His saying ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord and approval﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) relating to the hidden pronoun in (ammin, "those who make for"). The majority of the exegetes said: its meaning is that they seek bounty and profits in trade, and they seek along with that the approval of Allah. It has also been said that some of them sought trade, and some of them sought, through the Hajj, the approval of Allah. This seeking of approval would be according to their belief and their assumption, according to the one who holds that the verse concerns the polytheists. It has also been said that the meaning of "bounty" here is reward, not profits in trade.

His saying ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾ is an explicit statement of what the qualification ﴿while you are in ihram﴾ implies. He permitted them to hunt after He had forbidden it to them, because the cause for which it was forbidden had ceased, and that cause was the state of ihram.

His saying ﴿And do not let the hatred of a people commit you to transgression﴾: Ibn Faris said: jarama, ajrama and la jarama have the sense of your saying "there is no doubt and no escape," and their origin is from jarama, meaning he earned. It has been said that the meaning is: "let not ... move you," as said by al-Kisa'i and Tha'lab, and it transitively takes two objects. One says: "Such-and-such moved me to your hatred," that is, it impelled me to it. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed you struck Abu 'Uyaynah with a blow,
which Fazarah impelled, after it, to become angry."

That is, you made them angry. Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Farra' said: the meaning of (p. 351) "let not ... commit you" is: let not the hatred of a people earn for you that you transgress from truth to falsehood and from justice to injustice. The noun jarimah means one who earns, and from this is the saying of the poet:

"A predator perching on the summit of a cliff,
which sees in the bones what it has gathered a marrow-fat."

Its meaning is "earner of sustenance," and as-salib means fat. From this is the saying of another:

"O you who complain of 'Ukl, and what they earned
of killing and bereavement among the tribes."

That is, what they earned. The meaning in the verse is: let not the hatred of a people move you to aggression against them, or let not their hatred earn for you that you transgress against the truth into falsehood. It is said: jarama yajrumu jarman, meaning he cut off. 'Ali ibn 'Isa al-Rummani said: this is the origin, so jarama in the sense of "impelled to a thing" is because it cuts him off from others, and jarama in the sense of "earned" is because it cuts him off to earning. La jarama in the sense of "truly" is because truth is decisive.

Al-Khalil said: the meaning of ﴿Truly, for them is the Fire﴾ [an-Nahl 16:62] is: it is indeed true that for them is the Fire. Al-Kisa'i said: jarama and ajrama are two dialects with one meaning, that is, "he earned." Ibn Mas'ud recited "la yujrimannakum" with a damma on the yā' (ya), and the meaning is: "let not ... earn for you." The Basrans do not recognise ajrama; they say only jarama. Ash-shana'an means hatred, and it is read with a fatha and with a sukun on the nun. One says: shanaytu ar-rajul, ashnu'uhu, shana'an, mash'natan, and shana'an, all of these when you hate him. Here shana'an is in construction with the object: that is, the hatred of a people from among you, not the hatred of a people toward you.

His saying "because they barred you" (an sadduukum) with a fatha on the hamzah is an object of cause: that is, "because they barred you." Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read it with a kasrah on the hamzah in the conditional form, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd. Al-A'mash read "an yasuddakum" (if they bar you). The meaning according to the conditional reading is: let not their hatred move you to transgress against them if they bar you from al-Masjid al-Haram. An-Nahhas said: as for "in sadduukum" with a kasrah on in, the eminent scholars of grammar, Hadith, and analysis forbid this reading for several reasons. Among them: the verse was revealed in the year of the Conquest, in the eighth year, and the polytheists had barred the believers in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, in the sixth year. So the barring occurred before the verse, and if it is read with a kasrah it cannot refer to anything except after it, as you say: "Do not give such-and-such anything if he fights you." This applies only to the future, whereas with a fatha it refers to the past. How excellent this statement is! Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubaydah rejected shana'an with a sukun on the nun, because the verbal nouns (masadir) in this pattern come with a vowel. Others disagreed with them and said: this is not a verbal noun, but an active participle on the pattern of kaslan and ghadban.

When He forbade them from transgression, He commanded them to cooperate in righteousness and piety, whatever the case. It has been said: birr (righteousness) and taqwa (piety) are two words with one meaning, and it was repeated for emphasis. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: birr encompasses what is obligatory and what is recommended, while taqwa is specific to what is obligatory. Al-Mawardi said: in righteousness is the approval of people, and in piety is the approval of Allah, so whoever combines the two has completed his happiness. Then Allah, glorified is He, forbade them to cooperate in sin and transgression. Sin (ithm) is every act or statement that makes its doer or speaker liable for sin, and transgression ('udwan) is oppression against people in what involves injustice. So no kind of thing that causes sin, and no kind of injustice to people (among whom is the self) is left out, but it falls under this prohibition, because these two categories apply to everything in which their meanings are found. Then He commanded His servants to be pious and threatened whoever opposed what He commanded by abandoning it, or opposed what He forbade by doing it, with His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is severe in penalty﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman have related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Fulfil the contracts﴾, that he said: "Whatever Allah has made lawful, whatever He has made unlawful, whatever He has obligated, and whatever He has set as limits in the whole Qur'an: do not betray and do not break them." 'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah that he said: "They are the pacts of the Jahiliyyah, the alliance."

Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: "It has been mentioned to us that the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: 'Fulfil the pact of the Jahiliyyah, and do not create a pact in Islam.'" 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Hasan regarding His saying ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of grazing livestock﴾ that he said: "The camels, the cattle, and the sheep."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Umar regarding His saying ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of grazing livestock﴾ that he said: "What is in their bellies." I said: "If it comes out dead, may I eat it?" He said: "Yes."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ that he said: "The carrion, the blood, the flesh of swine, and what has been dedicated to other than Allah," to the end of the verse. This is what Allah has forbidden of the beasts of grazing livestock.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Do not violate the rites of Allah﴾ that he said: "The polytheists used to perform the Hajj to the Sacred House, offer sacrificial gifts, glorify the sanctity of the holy places, and slaughter during their Hajj. The Muslims wished to raid them, so Allah said: ﴿Do not violate the rites of Allah﴾." Regarding His saying "nor the sacred month," he means: do not consider fighting in it lawful. ﴿Nor those who make for the Sacred House﴾, he means: whoever heads toward the Sacred House. The believers and the polytheists used to perform the Hajj together, so Allah forbade the believers to prevent anyone who performs the Hajj to the House or to molest him, whether believer or unbeliever. Then Allah revealed after this verse: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are unclean, so let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram after this year of theirs﴾ [at-Tawbah 9:28]. Regarding His saying ﴿seeking bounty﴾, he means that they please Allah by their Hajj. ﴿And let not...commit you﴾ means: let not ... move you. ﴿The hatred of a people﴾ means: the enmity of a people. ﴿And cooperate in righteousness and piety﴾: he said: "Righteousness is what you are commanded, and piety is what you are forbidden." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding the verse that he said: "The rites of Allah are what Allah has forbidden you to violate while you are in ihram. The sacrificial animal is what has not been garlanded, and the garlands are the garlanded sacrificial animals. ﴿Nor those who make for the Sacred House﴾ means: whoever sets out as a pilgrim."

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding His saying ﴿Do not violate the rites of Allah﴾ that he said: "The rituals of the Hajj."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zayd ibn Aslam that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was at al-Hudaybiyyah with his Companions when the polytheists had barred them from the House, and this was very grievous to them. Some polytheists from the people of the East passed by them, intending 'Umrah. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Let us bar these, just as our companions barred us.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And let not...commit you﴾," the verse.

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and al-Bukhari in his History related from Wabisah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Righteousness is what the heart is at rest with and the soul is at ease with, and sin is what stirs in the heart and wavers in the breast, even if people give you fatwas and give you fatwas." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, Muslim, at-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi related from an-Nawwas ibn Sam'an that he said: "I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about righteousness and sin, and he said: 'Righteousness is good character, and sin is what stirs in your soul and you dislike that people should see it.'"

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Hibban, at-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Umamah that a man asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about sin, and he said: "What stirs in your soul, leave it." He said: "Then what is faith?" He said: "He whose evil deed distresses him and whose good deed pleases him, he is a believer."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 1–2 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Qurtubi said: It is Medinan by consensus (ijma'). Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah that he said: "Al-Ma'idah is Medinan."

Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, who said: "I performed Hajj and entered upon Aisha, and she said to me: 'O Jubayr, do you recite al-Ma'idah?' I said: 'Yes.' She said: 'Indeed, it is the last surah to be revealed. Whatever you find in it that is permitted, make it permitted, and whatever you find in it that is forbidden, make it forbidden.'"

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Abdullah ibn Umar, who said: "The last surah to be revealed was al-Ma'idah and al-Fath." Ahmad also narrated from him, who said: "Surah al-Ma'idah was revealed upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was riding his mount, and it could not bear him, so he dismounted from it." Ibn Kathir said: "Ahmad alone narrated it." I say: Its chain includes Ibn Lahi'ah.

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Muhammad ibn Nasr in Kitab al-Salah, al-Tabarani, Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Asma bint Yazid something similar. Ibn Abi Shaybah in his Musnad, al-Baghawi in his Mu'jam, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-Nubuwwah narrated from Umm Amr bint Isa, from her paternal uncle, something similar as well. Abu Ubayd narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi something similar.

It is also added that it was revealed during the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjat al-Wada') between Makkah and Madinah. Ibn Jarir narrated this addition from al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Abu Ubayd narrated from Damrah ibn Habib and Atiyyah ibn Qays, who both said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Al-Ma'idah is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, so make permitted its permitted things and make forbidden its forbidden things."

Abu Dawud and al-Nahhas, both in their works on abrogation (al-Naskh), narrated from Abu Maysarah Amr ibn Shurahbil, who said: "Nothing from al-Ma'idah has been abrogated." Likewise, Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated it from him. Likewise, Abd ibn Humayd and Abu Dawud in his work on abrogation narrated it, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated it from al-Sha'bi. Likewise, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud in his work on abrogation, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated it from al-Hasan al-Basri.

Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud in his work on abrogation, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Sha'bi, who said: "Nothing from al-Ma'idah has been abrogated except this verse: ﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah or the sacred month or the sacrificial animals or the garlands﴾."

Abu Dawud in his work on abrogation, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim (who graded it sahih) narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Two verses have been abrogated from this surah: the verse of the garlands, and His saying: ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 42]." Abd ibn Humayd in his Musnad narrated from Ibn Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited in his sermon Surah al-Ma'idah and Surah al-Tawbah.

al-Naqqash mentioned, from Abu Salamah, that he said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from al-Hudaybiyah, he said: 'O Ali, did you realize that Surah al-Ma'idah was revealed to me? And what a beneficial thing it is!'" Ibn al-Arabi said: "This is a fabricated hadith (hadith mawdu'), and it is not permissible for a Muslim to believe it." Ibn Atiyyah said: "In my view, this does not resemble the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ)."

* *

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

﴿O you who have believed, fulfill the contracts. Lawful for you are the animals of grazing livestock, except what is recited to you [in prohibition], not making lawful hunting while you are in the state of ihram. Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah or the sacred month or the sacrificial animals or the garlands or those coming to the Sacred House seeking bounty from their Lord and His approval. And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt. And let not the animosity of a people [in having] obstructed you from al-Masjid al-Haram lead you to transgress. And cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

This verse, with which Allah opened this surah, up to His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills﴾, contains such eloquence that human faculties fall short of it, while it includes several rulings. Among them: fulfilling contracts; the permissibility of grazing livestock; the exception of what will be recited (as prohibited); the prohibition of hunting for the one in ihram; and the permissibility of hunting for one who is not in ihram. Al-Naqqash related that the companions of the philosopher al-Kindi said to him: "O sage, compose for us something like this Qur'an." He said: "Yes, I will compose something like part of it." So he secluded himself for many days, then came out and said: "By Allah, no one can do this, nor can anyone bear it. I opened the mushaf and Surah al-Ma'idah came out. I looked, and behold, it has spoken of fulfilling (covenants) and forbidden breaking them, and it permitted in a general way, then made an exception after an exception, then informed of His power and wisdom in two lines. No one can produce this."

His saying ﴿Fulfill the contracts﴾: It is said awfa and wafa are two dialects (lughatan), and a poet combined both, saying:

"As for Ibn Tawf, he fulfilled his covenant,
just as the riders of the swift she-camels (of the stars) fulfilled [their journey]."

Al-'Uqud (the contracts) means al-'uhud (covenants). The root of al-'uqud is tying (al-rubut); its singular is 'aqd. It is said: "I tied the rope (aqadtu al-habl) and the pledge (al-'ahd)." It is used for physical things and for abstract meanings. When it is used for abstract meanings, as here, it conveys that it is very firm and strongly secured. It is said: the contracts are those which Allah established upon His servants and obligated them to through rulings. It is also said: they are the contracts which people make among themselves in transactions. The more preferred view is that the verse includes both together, and there is no basis for restricting it to some over others. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: fulfill the covenant of Allah upon you and your covenants with one another. End of quote. The contract that must be fulfilled is that which agrees with the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah. If it contradicts them, it is rejected; fulfilling it is not obligatory and it is not permissible.

His saying ﴿Lawful for you are the animals of grazing livestock﴾: The address is to those who have believed. Bahimah (animal) is the name for every four-legged creature. It was so named because of its lack of clarity (ibham) in terms of its deficiency in speech, understanding, and intellect. From it comes "a locked door" (bab mubham), i.e., closed; "a dark night" (layl bahim); and buhmah, for a brave man who does not know from where he will be attacked; and "an ambiguous ring" (halqah mubhamah), whose two ends are not known. Al-an'am (grazing livestock) is the name for camels, cattle, and sheep. They were so named because of the gentleness in their walking. It was also said: bahimat al-an'am refers to their wild counterparts, such as gazelles, wild cattle, wild donkeys, and other such animals. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari related this from a group of people, and others related it from al-Suddi, al-Rabi', Qatadah, and al-Dahhak.

Ibn Atiyyah said: This is a good view, because al-an'am are the eight pairs, and whatever is added to them from the rest of the animals is also called an'am together with them. Predatory animals like the lion, and every animal with fangs outside the boundary of an'am, are excluded. So bahimat al-an'am is the grazing four-legged animal. It was also said: bahimat al-an'am is whatever is not game (sayd), because game is called wild (wahsh), not bahimah. It was also said: bahimat al-an'am refers to the fetuses that come out at slaughter from the bellies of livestock, so they are eaten without slaughtering (dhakah). According to the first view, namely restricting al-an'am to camels, cattle, and sheep, the idafah (construct) is explanatory (bayaniyyah). What is permitted that lies outside them is added by analogy (qiyas), and even by the texts in the Book and Sunnah, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it unless it is carrion﴾ [al-An'am: 145], and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every fanged predator and every clawed bird is forbidden," for its implication indicates that whatever else is excluded is permitted. Likewise are all the texts specific to a category, as found in the purified books of the Sunnah.

His saying ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ is an exception from His saying ﴿Lawful for you are the animals of grazing livestock﴾. That is: except the implication of what is recited to you, for it is not lawful. What is recited is what Allah explicitly prohibited, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] and so on, and it is joined by what the Sunnah explicitly prohibited. This exception may mean: except what is recited to you now; and it may mean: in the future, which would indicate the permissibility of delaying clarification (ta'khir al-bayan) beyond the time of need; and it may include both meanings together.

His saying ﴿other than those who hunt game﴾: The Basrans held that His saying ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ is an exception from bahimat al-an'am, and His saying ﴿other than those who hunt game﴾ is another exception from it also. So both exceptions are from bahimat al-an'am, and the sense is: "Lawful for you are the animals of grazing livestock, except what is recited to you, except game while you are in ihram." It was said: the first exception is from bahimat al-an'am, and the second exception is from the first exception. This was refuted on the grounds that it would imply permitting hunting while in the state of ihram, since it is excepted from what is forbidden and so would be permitted. Al-Farra' permitted that ﴿except what is recited﴾ be in the nominative position as a substitute (badal), but the Basrans do not permit it except with an indefinite noun and what is close to it among general categories. He said: The accusative of ﴿other than those who hunt game﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal) of His saying ﴿fulfill the contracts﴾. Al-Akhfash said likewise. Others said it is a state of the kaf and mim in ﴿lakum﴾ (for you). The sense: lawful for you are the animals of grazing livestock, other than those who hunt game; that is, hunting on land and eating its game.

The meaning of their not making it lawful is affirming its prohibition in action and belief, ﴿while you are in the state of ihram﴾; that is, while you are muhrimun (in the state of ihram). The clause ﴿while you are in the state of ihram﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state of the pronoun in "muhilli" (those making lawful). The meaning of this restriction is clear according to those who restrict bahimat al-an'am to wild land animals that are lawful to eat. It is as if He said: Lawful for you is the game of the land except while in the state of ihram. As for the view of those who make the idafah explanatory, the meaning is: Lawful for you is a bahimah that is the an'am, at the time the game is forbidden to you by your entering into ihram, because you are in need of that. So the purpose of this restriction is to favor them by permitting what is other than what is forbidden to them in that state. By "those in ihram" (al-hurum) is meant the one who is in ihram for Hajj, for 'Umrah, or for both. He is called muhrim because game, perfume, and women become forbidden to him. Likewise the reason the sacred (haram) is called haram and the ihram is called ihram. Al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿hurum﴾ with a sukun on the ra', and this is a Tamimi dialect: they say rusul as rusl and kutub as kutb, and similar.

His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills﴾: From the rulings that differ from what the Arabs used to practice. He is the Owner of all; He does what He wills and ordains what He wills, with none to repel His judgment.

His saying ﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah﴾: al-Sha'a'ir (the rites) is the plural of sha'irah, on the pattern of fa'ilah. Ibn Faris said: It is also said for the singular: shi'ar, which is better. From it comes ish'ar (marking) for the sacrificial animal, and al-mash'ar (the landmarks) is plural mash'ar; these are the places marked with signs. It was said: what is meant here is all the rites of Hajj. It was also said: al-Safa and al-Marwah, the sacrificial animal, and the building. The meaning according to these two views: do not make these matters lawful (do not violate them), by committing any violation of them, or by coming between them and one who intends to perform them.

Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the prohibition against violating the rites of Allah immediately after mentioning the prohibition on hunting while in the state of ihram. It has been said that the meaning of "rites" (sha'a'ir) here is the obligations (fara'id) of Allah, and from this usage comes ﴿And whoever honours the rites of Allah﴾. It has also been said that they are the sacred things (hurumat) of Allah. There is no obstacle to understanding it as encompassing all of these, taking into account the generality of the wording and not only the specific occasion of revelation, nor only what the context indicates.

His saying ﴿nor the sacred month﴾ refers to the category, so it includes all the sacred months, which are four: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram, and Rajab. That is, do not violate them by fighting in them. It has also been said that what is meant here is only the month of the Hajj.

His saying "nor the sacrificial animals (al-hady)" refers to what is brought as an offering to the House of Allah, whether a camel, a cow, or a sheep. The singular is hadiyyah. Allah, glorified is He, forbade them to violate the sanctity of the sacrificial animals by taking them from their owners or by preventing them from reaching the place to which they are offered. He joined the sacrificial animals to the rites, although they are already included under them, in order to draw attention to their special status and to emphasise the seriousness of their matter.

His saying "nor the garlands (qala'id)" is the plural of qala'idah, which is what is hung around the neck of the sacrificial animal, such as a sandal or the like. Violating them means seizing them by force. The prohibition on violating the garlands is a reinforcement of the prohibition on violating the sacrificial animals. It has also been said that the meaning of "garlands" is the animals that have been garlanded, and that their being joined to the sacrificial animals is to add emphasis on the sacrificial animals. The first view is preferable. It has also been said that the meaning of "garlands" is what people used to hang around themselves as a guarantee of safety for them, so it is an elision: that is, "and for the owners of the garlands."

His saying ﴿nor those who make for the Sacred House﴾: that is, those who intend it, from the expression "I aimed at such-and-such" (ammamtu kadha), meaning I intended it. Al-A'mash recited "nor those who make for the Sacred House" with the genitive construction (idafah). The meaning is: do not prevent anyone who intends the Sacred House for the Hajj or the 'Umrah, or in order to dwell in it. It has also been said that the occasion of revelation of this verse was that the polytheists used to perform the Hajj, the 'Umrah, and offer sacrifices, and the Muslims wished to raid them. So it was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah﴾ to the end of the verse. In that case it is abrogated (mansukh) by His saying ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾, and His saying ﴿So let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram after this year of theirs﴾, and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "No polytheist shall perform the Hajj after this year." Others said: the verse is decisive (muhkam), and it concerns the Muslims.

His saying ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord and approval﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) relating to the hidden pronoun in (ammin, "those who make for"). The majority of the exegetes said: its meaning is that they seek bounty and profits in trade, and they seek along with that the approval of Allah. It has also been said that some of them sought trade, and some of them sought, through the Hajj, the approval of Allah. This seeking of approval would be according to their belief and their assumption, according to the one who holds that the verse concerns the polytheists. It has also been said that the meaning of "bounty" here is reward, not profits in trade.

His saying ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾ is an explicit statement of what the qualification ﴿while you are in ihram﴾ implies. He permitted them to hunt after He had forbidden it to them, because the cause for which it was forbidden had ceased, and that cause was the state of ihram.

His saying ﴿And do not let the hatred of a people commit you to transgression﴾: Ibn Faris said: jarama, ajrama and la jarama have the sense of your saying "there is no doubt and no escape," and their origin is from jarama, meaning he earned. It has been said that the meaning is: "let not ... move you," as said by al-Kisa'i and Tha'lab, and it transitively takes two objects. One says: "Such-and-such moved me to your hatred," that is, it impelled me to it. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed you struck Abu 'Uyaynah with a blow,
which Fazarah impelled, after it, to become angry."

That is, you made them angry. Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Farra' said: the meaning of (p. 351) "let not ... commit you" is: let not the hatred of a people earn for you that you transgress from truth to falsehood and from justice to injustice. The noun jarimah means one who earns, and from this is the saying of the poet:

"A predator perching on the summit of a cliff,
which sees in the bones what it has gathered a marrow-fat."

Its meaning is "earner of sustenance," and as-salib means fat. From this is the saying of another:

"O you who complain of 'Ukl, and what they earned
of killing and bereavement among the tribes."

That is, what they earned. The meaning in the verse is: let not the hatred of a people move you to aggression against them, or let not their hatred earn for you that you transgress against the truth into falsehood. It is said: jarama yajrumu jarman, meaning he cut off. 'Ali ibn 'Isa al-Rummani said: this is the origin, so jarama in the sense of "impelled to a thing" is because it cuts him off from others, and jarama in the sense of "earned" is because it cuts him off to earning. La jarama in the sense of "truly" is because truth is decisive.

Al-Khalil said: the meaning of ﴿Truly, for them is the Fire﴾ [an-Nahl 16:62] is: it is indeed true that for them is the Fire. Al-Kisa'i said: jarama and ajrama are two dialects with one meaning, that is, "he earned." Ibn Mas'ud recited "la yujrimannakum" with a damma on the yā' (ya), and the meaning is: "let not ... earn for you." The Basrans do not recognise ajrama; they say only jarama. Ash-shana'an means hatred, and it is read with a fatha and with a sukun on the nun. One says: shanaytu ar-rajul, ashnu'uhu, shana'an, mash'natan, and shana'an, all of these when you hate him. Here shana'an is in construction with the object: that is, the hatred of a people from among you, not the hatred of a people toward you.

His saying "because they barred you" (an sadduukum) with a fatha on the hamzah is an object of cause: that is, "because they barred you." Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read it with a kasrah on the hamzah in the conditional form, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd. Al-A'mash read "an yasuddakum" (if they bar you). The meaning according to the conditional reading is: let not their hatred move you to transgress against them if they bar you from al-Masjid al-Haram. An-Nahhas said: as for "in sadduukum" with a kasrah on in, the eminent scholars of grammar, Hadith, and analysis forbid this reading for several reasons. Among them: the verse was revealed in the year of the Conquest, in the eighth year, and the polytheists had barred the believers in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, in the sixth year. So the barring occurred before the verse, and if it is read with a kasrah it cannot refer to anything except after it, as you say: "Do not give such-and-such anything if he fights you." This applies only to the future, whereas with a fatha it refers to the past. How excellent this statement is! Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubaydah rejected shana'an with a sukun on the nun, because the verbal nouns (masadir) in this pattern come with a vowel. Others disagreed with them and said: this is not a verbal noun, but an active participle on the pattern of kaslan and ghadban.

When He forbade them from transgression, He commanded them to cooperate in righteousness and piety, whatever the case. It has been said: birr (righteousness) and taqwa (piety) are two words with one meaning, and it was repeated for emphasis. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: birr encompasses what is obligatory and what is recommended, while taqwa is specific to what is obligatory. Al-Mawardi said: in righteousness is the approval of people, and in piety is the approval of Allah, so whoever combines the two has completed his happiness. Then Allah, glorified is He, forbade them to cooperate in sin and transgression. Sin (ithm) is every act or statement that makes its doer or speaker liable for sin, and transgression ('udwan) is oppression against people in what involves injustice. So no kind of thing that causes sin, and no kind of injustice to people (among whom is the self) is left out, but it falls under this prohibition, because these two categories apply to everything in which their meanings are found. Then He commanded His servants to be pious and threatened whoever opposed what He commanded by abandoning it, or opposed what He forbade by doing it, with His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is severe in penalty﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman have related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Fulfil the contracts﴾, that he said: "Whatever Allah has made lawful, whatever He has made unlawful, whatever He has obligated, and whatever He has set as limits in the whole Qur'an: do not betray and do not break them." 'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah that he said: "They are the pacts of the Jahiliyyah, the alliance."

Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: "It has been mentioned to us that the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: 'Fulfil the pact of the Jahiliyyah, and do not create a pact in Islam.'" 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Hasan regarding His saying ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of grazing livestock﴾ that he said: "The camels, the cattle, and the sheep."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Umar regarding His saying ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of grazing livestock﴾ that he said: "What is in their bellies." I said: "If it comes out dead, may I eat it?" He said: "Yes."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ that he said: "The carrion, the blood, the flesh of swine, and what has been dedicated to other than Allah," to the end of the verse. This is what Allah has forbidden of the beasts of grazing livestock.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Do not violate the rites of Allah﴾ that he said: "The polytheists used to perform the Hajj to the Sacred House, offer sacrificial gifts, glorify the sanctity of the holy places, and slaughter during their Hajj. The Muslims wished to raid them, so Allah said: ﴿Do not violate the rites of Allah﴾." Regarding His saying "nor the sacred month," he means: do not consider fighting in it lawful. ﴿Nor those who make for the Sacred House﴾, he means: whoever heads toward the Sacred House. The believers and the polytheists used to perform the Hajj together, so Allah forbade the believers to prevent anyone who performs the Hajj to the House or to molest him, whether believer or unbeliever. Then Allah revealed after this verse: ﴿Indeed, the polytheists are unclean, so let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram after this year of theirs﴾ [at-Tawbah 9:28]. Regarding His saying ﴿seeking bounty﴾, he means that they please Allah by their Hajj. ﴿And let not...commit you﴾ means: let not ... move you. ﴿The hatred of a people﴾ means: the enmity of a people. ﴿And cooperate in righteousness and piety﴾: he said: "Righteousness is what you are commanded, and piety is what you are forbidden." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding the verse that he said: "The rites of Allah are what Allah has forbidden you to violate while you are in ihram. The sacrificial animal is what has not been garlanded, and the garlands are the garlanded sacrificial animals. ﴿Nor those who make for the Sacred House﴾ means: whoever sets out as a pilgrim."

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding His saying ﴿Do not violate the rites of Allah﴾ that he said: "The rituals of the Hajj."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zayd ibn Aslam that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was at al-Hudaybiyyah with his Companions when the polytheists had barred them from the House, and this was very grievous to them. Some polytheists from the people of the East passed by them, intending 'Umrah. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Let us bar these, just as our companions barred us.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And let not...commit you﴾," the verse.

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and al-Bukhari in his History related from Wabisah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Righteousness is what the heart is at rest with and the soul is at ease with, and sin is what stirs in the heart and wavers in the breast, even if people give you fatwas and give you fatwas." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, Muslim, at-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi related from an-Nawwas ibn Sam'an that he said: "I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about righteousness and sin, and he said: 'Righteousness is good character, and sin is what stirs in your soul and you dislike that people should see it.'"

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Hibban, at-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Umamah that a man asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about sin, and he said: "What stirs in your soul, leave it." He said: "Then what is faith?" He said: "He whose evil deed distresses him and whose good deed pleases him, he is a believer."

This is a commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verse 3 (part 1 of 2):

This begins the discussion of the prohibited things that He (glorified is He) pointed to with His words: ﴿except what is recited to you﴾. Carrion (al-maytah) has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah, and likewise blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah. What is mentioned here regarding the prohibition of blood in general is restricted to blood that is poured forth (masfuh), as was mentioned before, by applying the unrestricted (mutlaq) to the restricted (muqayyad). The Sunnah has also specified carrion by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Two kinds of carrion and two kinds of blood have been made lawful for us. As for the two kinds of carrion, they are fish and locusts; as for the two kinds of blood, they are the liver and the spleen." It was narrated by al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni, and al-Bayhaqi, and its chain contains some criticism. It is strengthened by the hadith: "Its water is pure and its carrion is lawful," which is in Ahmad, the authors of the Sunan, and others, and a group of scholars declared it sound, including Ibn Khuzaymah and Ibn Hibban. We have extensively discussed it in our commentary on al-Muntaqa.

Ihlal (dedication) is raising the voice for other than Allah, such as saying the name of al-Lat and al-'Uzza and the like. There is no need here to repeat what we have already set forth, for in it is what the reader does not need anything else for.

(And the strangled animal, al-Munkhaniqah) is the one that dies by strangulation, which is the restriction of breath, whether that is by its own action, such as putting its head into a rope or between two pieces of wood, or by the action of a human or something else. The people of the Jahiliyyah used to strangle the sheep, and when it died they would eat it.

(And the beaten to death, al-Mawqudhah) is the one that is struck with a stone or a stick until it dies without slaughter. It is said: waqadahu yaqidhuhu waqdan, so he is waqidh, and al-waqdh is the severity of striking; and so-and-so is waqidh, i.e., badly beaten. The people of the Jahiliyyah used to do that, striking the livestock with wood for their gods until they died, and then they would eat them. From this is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"A she-camel that kicks the young camel with her leg, a leaping one, tearing the forelegs' nails."

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Scholars, past and present, have disagreed regarding hunting with the bunduq (pellet bow), the stone, and the mi'rad. By bunduq he means the pellet bow, and by mi'rad the arrow that has no feathers, or a stick whose head is sharpened. He said: Whoever holds that it is waqidh does not permit it except that which he has reached its slaughter, as is narrated from Ibn 'Umar; this is the view of Malik, Abu Hanifah and his companions, al-Thawri, and al-Shafi'i. The Syrians differed with them in this. Al-Awza'i said regarding the mi'rad: eat it whether it pierced or did not pierce. Abu al-Darda', Fudalah ibn 'Ubayd, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, and Makhul held that there was no harm in it.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: This is what al-Awza'i related from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, but what is known from Ibn 'Umar is what Malik related from Nafi', who said: The foundation in this chapter, on which action is based and in which the proof lies, is the hadith of 'Adi ibn Hatim, in which: "What strikes with its width, do not eat it, for it is waqidh." End of quote. I say: The hadith is in the Two Sahihs and others from 'Adi, who said: "I said, O Messenger of Allah, I hunt game with the mi'rad and hit it, and he said: When you shoot with the mi'rad and it pierces, then eat it; but if it strikes with its width, then it is only waqidh, so do not eat it." The Prophet (ﷺ) thus considered piercing and its absence. The truth is that only that which is pierced is lawful, not that which is struck, and so there must be slaughter before death, otherwise it is waqidh.

As for the bundaqi known today, which are iron guns into which gunpowder and lead are placed and are fired, the scholars did not speak about them because their emergence was recent; they did not reach the Yemeni lands until the tenth century after the Hijrah. A group of scholars asked me about hunting with them when the game dies and the hunter could not slaughter it while alive. What appears to me is that it is lawful, because it generally pierces and enters from one side and exits from the other side. The Prophet (ﷺ) said in the sound hadith mentioned earlier: "When you shoot with the mi'rad and it pierces, then eat it," and he considered piercing as a condition for the lawfulness of game.

His words: (And the fallen, al-Mutaraddiyah) are those that fall from a height to a lower place and die, without distinction between falling from a mountain, a well, a pit, or other things. Taraddi is derived from al-radaa, which is destruction, whether it fell by itself or was pushed by another.

His words: (And the gored, al-Nateehah) is on the pattern of fa'ilah in the sense of maf'ulah, and it is the one gored by another, and it dies without slaughter. Some people also said it is fa'ilah in the sense of fa'ilah, because the two animals gore each other and both die. He said "nateehah" and did not say "nateeh," though it is the analogical form of fa'il, because the obligatory deletion of the tā' is specific to what is of this category when it is a qualifier for a mentioned noun; if it is not mentioned, the tā' is retained for transferring it from being an adjective to being a noun. Abu Maysarah recited (al-manTuhah).

His words: ﴿And what the beast of prey has eaten﴾ means what a fanged predator has seized, such as the lion, the leopard, the wolf, the hyena, and the like. What is meant here is what the beast of prey has eaten of it, because what the beast of prey has entirely eaten has been destroyed. Some Arabs restrict the name of "beast" (sab') to the lion. The Arabs, when a beast of prey ate a sheep and then they rescued it from it, would eat it, even if it died without being slaughtered. al-Hasan and Abu Haywah recited (al-sab') with a sukun on the ba', and it is a dialect of the people of Najd. From this is the verse of Hassan regarding 'Utbah ibn Abi Lahab:

"Whoever returns this year to his family—then the eaten of the beast is not one who returns."

Ibn Mas'ud recited (wa-akilatu al-sab'), and Ibn 'Abbas recited (wa-akilu al-sab').

His words: (Except what you have slaughtered, illa ma dhakkaytum) is in the accusative position as an exception that is connected according to the majority, and it refers back to what you have reached its slaughter from the things mentioned previously, and in it there is life. The Madinans said—and this is (p-353) the well-known position of the school of Malik, and it is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i—that if the beast of prey has reached it, except for what has no life remaining in it, then it is not eaten. This is related in the Muwatta' from Zayd ibn Thabit, and Isma'il al-Qadi took this view. On this view, the exception is disconnected, i.e., these things have been made unlawful for you, but what you have slaughtered is what is lawful and not forbidden. The first is preferable. Dhakat in the speech of the Arabs means slaughter, as Qutrub and others said.

The root of dhakat in the language is completeness, i.e., the completion of the full development of strength. Dhaka' is sharpness of the heart, and dhaka' is quickness of insight. Dhakwah is what fire is kindled from, and from it: I kindled the war and the fire, I lit them. Dhaka' is also a name for the sun. What is meant here is: except what you have reached its slaughter in full. Dhakah in the sharia is an expression for the flowing out of blood and the severing of the jugular veins in the slaughtered animal, the nahr (throat-cutting) in the camel that is slaughtered by piercing, and the 'aqr (wounding) in an animal that is not within reach, accompanied by intention for Allah and the mention of His name over it. As for the instrument by which dhakah is effected, the majority held that whatever makes blood flow and severs the jugular veins is an instrument for dhakah, except the tooth and the bone, and the sound hadiths came with this.

His words: ﴿And what is sacrificed on the nusub﴾. Ibn Faris said: al-nusub is a stone that used to be set up and worshipped, and blood of the sacrifices was poured on it; and al-nasa'ib are stones set up around the edge of a well and made into supports. It was also said: nusub is a plural whose singular is nisab, like himar and humur. Talhah recited with a damma on the nun and sukun on the sad; it was narrated from Abu 'Amr with a fatha on the nun and sukun on the sad; and al-Jahdari recited with fatha on both the nun and the sad, taking it as a singular noun like al-jabal and al-jamal, and its plural is ansab like al-ajbal and al-ajmal. Mujahid said: they are stones that were around Makkah upon which they would slaughter. Ibn Jurayj said: The Arabs would slaughter in Makkah and sprinkle with blood what faced the House, cut up the meat and place it on the stones. When Islam came, the Muslims said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We have more right to honor this House with these acts," so Allah revealed: ﴿And what is sacrificed on the nusub﴾. The meaning: the intention in that is to honor the nusub, not that slaughtering upon them is impermissible. For this reason it was said that "ala" here means "li" (for the sake of), i.e., for their sake; Qutrub said this. On this view, it falls under what was dedicated to other than Allah, and it was singled out for mention to emphasize its prohibition and to repel what they supposed of such things, to honor and glorify the House.

His words: ﴿And that you seek decision by the arrows﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it, i.e., and He prohibited for you seeking decision by the arrows. The azlam are the lots of gambling, singular zalam. The poet said:

"He spent the night dealing with them, a young man like the zalam, not a shepherd of camels or sheep, nor a butcher upon meat and fat."

Another said:

"If Judhaymah's leaders have been killed, then their women strike with the arrows."

The arrows for the Arabs are of three types: one on which is written "do," another on which is written "do not," and a third that is blank with nothing on it. He places them in a bag with him; when he wants to do something he puts his hand in, and they are similar, and he takes out one of them. If the first comes out, he does what he resolved; if the second comes out, he leaves it; if the third comes out, he repeats the drawing until one of the first two comes out.

This act was called istiqsam because they would seek by it the provision and what they wished to do, just as it is said: istasqa, i.e., he asked for the watering. So istiqsam is seeking the share and portion. The total of the arrows of the gambling is ten, and we have already set forth their explanation. They used to strike with them in gambling. It was also said that the azlam are the knucklebones of Persia and Rome with which they gamble, and it was said they are chess. Allah prohibited seeking decision by the arrows because it is an encroachment upon claiming knowledge of the unseen and a form of soothsaying.

His words: (﴿That is fisq﴾) is a reference either to seeking decision by the arrows or to all the prohibited things mentioned here. Fisq is going beyond the limit, and its meaning has already been explained. In this is a severe warning, because fisq is worse than disbelief, not what a group has conventionally defined as an intermediate position between faith and disbelief.

His words: ﴿Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion﴾. The intended day is the day on which this verse was revealed, which is the day of the conquest of Makkah, eight days remaining from Ramadan in the year nine; it was said: the year eight. It was also said: by "the day" is meant the present time and what is connected to it, and no specific day is intended. (Ya'isa) in it has two dialects: yaysa with two ya's, yasan, and aysa, ayasan and iyasah, as al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said; i.e., despair arose in them of nullifying your religion and of returning you to their religion, as they used to claim. (So do not fear them) i.e., do not be afraid of them, that they will overcome you or nullify your religion. (And fear Me) for I am capable of everything; if I help you, no one can overcome you, and if I forsake you, no one other than Me can help you.

His words: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾. I made it complete, not in need of completion, because of its prevalence over all religions and its dominance over them, and because of the completeness of its rulings that Muslims need, of the lawful, the unlawful, and the doubtful, and it fulfilled what the Book and the Sunnah contained of that. What is derived from placing "lakum" (for you) first is not hidden. The majority said: what is meant here by completion is the revelation of most of the obligations and the lawful and unlawful. They said: after that a Qur'an was revealed, such as the verse on usury and the verse on kalalah and the like. The day mentioned here is Friday, and it was the day of 'Arafah after the 'Asr prayer during the Farewell Pilgrimage in the year ten; this is established in the Sahih from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. It was also said: it was revealed on the day of the Greater Hajj.

His words: ﴿And I have completed My favor upon you﴾ by completing the religion which includes the rulings, and by the conquest of Makkah and the subjugation of the disbelievers and their despair of prevailing over you, as I promised you with My words: ﴿And that I may complete My favor upon you﴾.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verse 3 (part 2 of 2):**

His saying: ﴿And I have approved Islam for you as a religion﴾ means: I informed you of My approval of it for you. He, glorified is He, has always been pleased with the community (ummah) of His Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, for Islam. Therefore, if we take the words in their apparent sense, restricting the approval to this day has little benefit. It is also possible that He means: "I have approved for you the Islam in which you are today as a religion that remains until the end of the days of this world." Here "religion" (dinan) is in the accusative of specification (tamyiz), and it may also be the second object (maf'ul thani).

His saying: ﴿So whoever is compelled by hunger﴾ is connected to the mention of the forbidden things, and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraid). That is: whoever is driven by necessity (darurah) ( in hunger ), meaning in famine, to eat carrion and what follows it of the forbidden things. Al-khams means the shrinking of the belly. A man is called khamis and khumsan, and a woman khamisah and khumsanah. From it comes akhmas al-qadam (the arch of the foot). It is used frequently for hunger. Al-A'sha said:

*"You spend the winter nights with your bellies full,*
*while your neighbours' women pass the night hungry and shrunken."*

His saying: ( without inclining to sin ). Al-janaf means inclination, and sin (ithm) means what is forbidden. That is: while the one compelled is in hunger, not inclining towards sin. This is in the sense of "neither rebelling nor transgressing." Everyone who inclines is mutajanif and janaf. Al-Nakha'i, Yahya ibn Wathhab, and al-Sulami read ( mutajannif ). ﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ toward him: He does not hold him accountable for what necessity has driven him to in hunger, provided he does not incline, by eating what He has forbidden to him, towards sin, such as by being a rebel against others or exceeding what necessity has permitted, as was previously stated.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, sent me to my people to invite them to Allah and His Messenger, and to present to them the rites of Islam. While we were thus, they came with a bowl of blood, gathered around it, and began eating it. They said: 'Come, O Suddi, and eat.' I said: 'Woe to you! I have only come to you from one who forbids you this, by what Allah has revealed to him.' They said: 'And what is that?' So I recited to them this verse: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿and that over which the name of other than Allah has been invoked﴾, he said: "that which is sacrificed to the idols (taghut)." ( And the strangled ) he said: "the one that is choked until it dies." ( And the struck down ) he said: "the sheep that is struck by another sheep." ﴿And what the beast of prey has eaten﴾, he says: "what the beast of prey has taken." ( Except what you slaughter ) he says: "you slaughter from that while there is still life in it, so eat it." ﴿And what is sacrificed on the stone altars﴾, he said: "The nusub are idols (ansab) upon which they used to slaughter and invoke (other than Allah)." ﴿And that you seek decision by arrows﴾, he said: "They are the qidah (arrow shafts) with which they sought decision in matters." ( That is grave disobedience ) meaning: whoever eats all of that is in disobedience (fisq).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "al-raddah are those that fall into a well, and al-mutaraddiyah are those that fall from a mountain."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, concerning His saying ﴿and that you seek decision by arrows﴾, that he said: "white pebbles with which they used to cast lots."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Hasan concerning the verse, that he said: "When they wanted to do a matter or a journey, they would take three arrow shafts. On one of them they wrote: 'Command me,' on another: 'Forbid me,' and they left the third blank between them, having nothing written on it. Then they would shuffle them. If the one marked 'Command me' came out, they would proceed with their matter; if the one marked 'Forbid me' came out, they would desist; and if the blank one came out, they would repeat the drawing."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion﴾, that he said: "They despaired of ever returning to their religion."

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from him concerning the verse, that he said: "He says: the people of Makkah despaired of ever returning to their religion of idol-worship." ( So do not fear them ) in following Muhammad, ( but fear Me ) in worshipping idols and denying Muhammad. When he was standing at Arafat, Jibril descended upon him while he was raising his hands and the Muslims were supplicating Allah. ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾, He says: "your lawful and your unlawful." Nothing lawful or unlawful was revealed after this. ﴿And completed My favour upon you﴾, he said: "My grace (minnah)," so no polytheist performed the pilgrimage with you. ( And I have approved ) he says: "I have chosen" ( ﴿Islam as a religion for you﴾ ). The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, remained after the revelation of this verse eighty-one days, then Allah took him to Himself.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said: "Allah informed His Prophet and the believers that He had perfected faith for them, so they will never need anything added to it, and He has completed it, so it will never be diminished, and He has approved it, so He will never be displeased with it."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Tariq ibn Shihab, who said: "The Jews said to Umar: 'You recite a verse in your Book which, had it been revealed to us, the Jewish community, we would have taken that day as a festival.' He said: 'And which verse is that?' They said: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾. Umar said: 'By Allah, I know the day on which it was revealed to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, and the hour in which it was revealed. It was revealed to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family, in the evening of Arafat, on the day of Friday.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying: ( So whoever is compelled ) meaning to what has been forbidden of what was named at the beginning of this surah ( in hunger ) meaning in famine ( without inclining to sin ), he says: "without deliberately inclining to sin."

This is the opening of al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 4–5 (part 1 of 2):

This is the beginning of the explanation of what Allah has made lawful to them after the explanation of what Allah has forbidden to them. The occasion of revelation of the verse will be mentioned later. His saying: ﴿What has been made lawful for them?﴾ means: what thing has been made lawful for them, or: what is it that has been made lawful for them of foods in general, of game, of the food of the People of the Book, and of their women? His saying: ﴿Say: the good things have been made lawful for you﴾ — the "good things" (al-tayyibat) are what the eater finds delicious and pleasant of what Allah has made lawful for His servants. It has also been said that they are the lawful (al-halal), and the discussion of this has already preceded. It has also been said that the "good things" are the slaughtered animals, because they become good through the dhakah (ritual slaughter). This is a specification of the general term without a specifying evidence, and neither the occasion of revelation nor the context supports that.

His saying: ﴿and what you have taught of the hunting animals﴾ is coordinated with "the good things" by supplying an elided noun to make the meaning sound; that is: the good things have been made lawful for you, and the game of what you have taught of the hunting animals has been made lawful for you. Ibn ʿAbbas and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah read ﴿ʿullimtum﴾ with a damma on the ʿayn and a kasra on the lam; that is: you have been taught concerning the hunting animals and the hunting with them.

Al-Qurtubi said: Some of those who wrote on the rulings of the Qur'an mentioned that the verse indicates that the permission covers what we have taught of the hunting animals, which includes the dog and all hunting birds, and this necessitates the permission of all forms of benefit, so it indicates the permissibility of selling dogs and hunting animals and benefiting from them in all forms of benefit, except what the evidence has specified, namely eating from the hunting animals — i.e., the predators among the dogs and the birds of prey. He said: The community has agreed that if the dog is not black, and it was taught by a Muslim, and did not eat from the game that it caught, and it wounded the game with a wound or by tearing it, and a Muslim sent it while mentioning the name of Allah at its release, then its game is sound and may be eaten without disagreement.

If any of these conditions is violated, disagreement arises. If what is used for hunting is other than a dog, such as a leopard and the like, or the falcon, the hawk and similar birds, then the majority of the community holds that whatever it catches after being trained is a hunting predator that earns (kasib). It is said: "Fulan was wounded (juriha) and ijtarah" when he earned; from it comes al-jarihah (the hunting animal), because it is acquired by means of it; and from it comes "ijtirah al-sayyiʾat" (committing misdeeds). From it is His saying the Exalted: ﴿And He knows what you have earned (jaraḥtum) by day﴾, and His saying: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds (ijtarahu al-sayyiʾat) think...﴾.

His saying: ( mukallibin ) is a circumstantial clause (ḥal). The mukallib is the one who trains dogs for the manner of hunting. The more specific term is "trainer of dogs," although he is also a trainer of all other hunting animals, because hunting with dogs is the most common. He did not suffice with His saying ﴿what you have taught of the hunting animals﴾, although taklib is ta'lim, in order to emphasize what must be included of training. It has been said that the predator is called a "dog," so every predator used for hunting is included. It has also been said that this verse is specifically about dogs. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿUmar that he said: What is hunted with falcons and other birds — whatever you reach its slaughter, it is lawful for you; otherwise, do not eat it.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: Abu Jaʿfar was asked about the falcon: is its game lawful? He said: No, unless you reach its slaughter. Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: ﴿and what you have taught of the hunting animals, trainers﴾ refers to dogs only. If the dog is black, entirely black, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Nakhaʿi disliked its game.

Ahmad said: I do not know anyone who grants a concession for it if it is entirely black, and Ibn Rahawayh said the same.
