As for the general scholars of Medina and Kufa, they hold the permissibility of the game of every trained dog. Those who prohibit the game of the black dog argue with the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The black dog is a devil." Related by Muslim and others. The truth is that the game of everything that falls under the general term of hunting animals is lawful, without distinction between the dog and others, between the black among dogs and others, and between birds and others. This is supported by the fact that the occasion of revelation of the verse was the question of ʿAdi ibn Hatim about the falcon's game, as will come.

His saying: ﴿You teach them of what Allah has taught you﴾ is a clause in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause; that is: of what Allah has taught you, which you have grasped through the reason He created in you, by which you are guided to teaching them and training them until they become capable of holding the game when you release them. His saying: ﴿So eat of what they hold for you﴾: the fa' is for consequence, and the clause follows from what preceded of the permission of the game of what they have been taught from the hunting animals. The min in ﴿of what they hold for you﴾ is partitive, because some of the game is not eaten, such as the skin, the bone, and what the dog ate or the like. This is evidence that it must hold it for its owner; if it eats from it, then it has held it for itself, as in the established hadith in the Sahih.

The majority have held that the game which the predator catches on its own initiative without being released is not lawful to eat. ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah and al-Awza'i said — and it is related from Salman al-Farisi, Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, Abu Hurayrah, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, and it is related from ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Zuhri, Rabiʿah, Malik, and al-Shafiʿi in the old view — that its game may be eaten. Their argument is refuted by His saying: ﴿of what they hold for you﴾, and by the Prophet's ﷺ saying to ʿAdi ibn Hatim: "When you release your trained dog and mention the name of Allah over it, then eat what it holds for you." It is in the two Sahihs and others. In another wording in both: "If it eats, then do not eat, for I fear it held it for itself." As for what Abu Dawud related with a sound chain from the hadith of Abu Thaʿlabah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When your trained dog releases and you mention the name of Allah, then eat, even if it has eaten from it." He also related it with a sound chain from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb from his father from his grandfather. And al-Nasa'i also related it.

Some of the Shafiʿis reconciled these hadiths by saying: if it eats immediately after holding it, then it becomes unlawful, due to the hadith of ʿAdi ibn Hatim; but if it held it and then he waited for its owner, the waiting lengthened, and it became hungry and ate from the game out of its hunger, not because it held it for itself, then this does not affect it and the game is not made unlawful thereby. They applied to this the hadith of Abu Thaʿlabah al-Khushani and the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb. This is a good reconciliation. Others said: if the dog ate from it, it becomes unlawful, due to the hadith of ʿAdi; but if it ate from something else, it does not become unlawful, due to the other two hadiths. It is also said: the hadith of Abu Thaʿlabah is applied to the case where he held it and let it go, then it returned and ate from it.

Many scholars have taken the path of preference (tarjih) and did not take the path of reconciliation, because of its remoteness. They said: the hadith of ʿAdi ibn Hatim is preferred, being in the two Sahihs. I have established this path in my commentary on al-Muntaqa with what increases the reader's insight.

His saying: ﴿and mention the name of Allah over it﴾: the pronoun in "over it" refers to "what you have taught" — that is, invoke His name over it upon releasing it — or to "what they hold for you," that is, invoke His name over it when you wish to slaughter it. The majority have held that invoking the name is obligatory when releasing the hunting animal, and they used this verse as evidence. It is supported by the hadith of ʿAdi ibn Hatim, established in the two Sahihs and others, with the wording: "When you release your dog, mention the name of Allah; and when you shoot your arrow, mention the name of Allah."

Some scholars said: what is meant is invoking the name at the time of eating. Al-Qurtubi said: this is the more apparent. They argued with the narrations that direct to invoking the name, and this is an error. The Prophet ﷺ fixed the invoking of the name at the release of the dog and the release of the arrow, and the prescription of invoking the name at eating is a different ruling and a different question. There is no basis for applying what is in the Book and the Sunnah here to the invocation at eating, and no compulsion to do so. In another wording in the two Sahihs from the hadith of ʿAdi: "If you release your dog and invoke the name, and it seizes, then eat." Some held that invoking the name is a condition; others held it is only a sunnah; and some held that it is a condition for the one who remembers, not for the one who forgets. This is the strongest and most preferred of the opinions.

His saying: ﴿And fear Allah; indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾: that is, His reckoning, may He be glorified, is swift in coming, and everything that is coming is near. His saying: ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you﴾: this sentence emphasizes the first sentence, which is His saying: ﴿The good things have been made lawful for you﴾, and the explanation of the good things has already preceded.

(p-356) His saying: ﴿And the food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you﴾: al-ṭaʿam is a noun for what is eaten, and from it are the slaughtered animals. Most scholars held that it is specified here to the slaughtered animals. In this verse there is evidence that all the food of the People of the Book, without distinction between meat and other things, is lawful to Muslims, even if they do not mention the name of Allah over their slaughter. This verse specifies the general sense of His saying: ﴿And do not eat of what the name of Allah has not been mentioned over﴾ [al-An'am: 121]. The apparent meaning of this is that the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book are lawful, even if the Jew mentions the name of ʿUzayr over his slaughter, or the Christian mentions the name of the Messiah over his slaughter. This was the view of Abu al-Darda', ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Zuhri, Rabiʿah, al-Shaʿbi, and Makhul.

ʿAli, ʿAʾishah and Ibn ʿUmar said: if you hear the People of the Book mention other than Allah, do not eat. This is the view of Tawus and al-Hasan. They held fast to His saying the Exalted: ﴿And do not eat of what the name of Allah has not been mentioned over﴾ [al-An'am: 121], and His saying also indicates it: ﴿and what has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. Malik said: it is disliked but not forbidden. This disagreement applies when we know that the People of the Book mentioned the name of other than Allah over their slaughter. As for when there is no knowledge of this, al-Kiya al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir related a consensus on its lawfulness, on the basis of this verse and what came in the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ eating the roasted sheep that the Jewish woman gave him as a gift, which is in the Sahih; and likewise the bag of fat that some Companions took from Khaybar, and the Prophet ﷺ knew of it, also in the Sahih, and other things. The People of the Book here means the Jews and the Christians.

As for the Magians, the majority held that their slaughtered animals are not eaten and their women are not married, because they are not People of the Book according to the well-known view among scholars. Abu Thawr disagreed on this, and the jurists rejected this from him, to the point that Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: Abu Thawr is like his name, meaning in this issue. He seems to have held fast to what is related from the Prophet ﷺ as a mursal report that he said about the Magians: "Treat them as you treat the People of the Book." This wording is not established. And even if it has a basis, it contains an addition that refutes what he said, namely: "other than those who eat their slaughtered animals or marry their women." Many among the exegetes and jurists who have no expertise in the science of hadith related it with this addition, and neither the basis nor the addition is established. Rather, what is established in the Sahih is that "the Prophet ﷺ took the jizyah from the Magians of Hajar." As for the Banu Taghlib, ʿAli ibn Abi Talib used to forbid their slaughtered animals, because they are Arabs, and he said: They did not hold to anything of Christianity except the drinking of wine. Likewise all the Arab Christianized tribes, such as Tanukh, Judham, Lakhm, ʿAmilah and those like them.

Ibn Kathir said: This is the view of more than one of the early and later scholars. It is related from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab and al-Hasan al-Basri that they saw no harm in the slaughter of the Christians of Banu Taghlib. Al-Qurtubi said: The majority of the community said: the slaughter of every Christian is lawful, whether he is from Banu Taghlib or from others, and likewise the Jews. He said: There is no disagreement among the scholars that what does not need dhakah, such as food, is permissible to eat.

**"And your food is lawful for them"**: that is, the food of the Muslims is lawful for the People of the Book. This indicates that it is permissible for Muslims to feed the People of the Book from their slaughtered animals. This falls under reciprocity and recompense, and it informs the Muslims that what they receive from the People of the Book in the form of food is lawful for them through implicative signification (*dalālah iltizāmiyyah*).

**"And chaste women from among the believing women"**: Scholars have differed on the meaning of *al-muḥṣanāt* here. Some said it means "the chaste," and others said it means "the free women." Al-Sha'bi read it with a kasra on the *ṣād*, and al-Kisa'i also read it that way. This matter has been discussed fully in al-Baqarah and al-Nisa'. *Al-muḥṣanāt* is the subject (*mubtada'*), *min al-mu'mināt* is its qualifier, and the predicate (*khabar*) is omitted, meaning: "lawful for you." The intended meaning is free women, not slave women. This is what the majority said. Ibn Jarir reported from a group of the early generations (*salaf*) that this verse covers every free or slave-woman from the People of the Book.

'Abdullah ibn 'Umar said: "The Christian woman is not lawful." He said: "I know of no greater polytheism than for her to say that her lord is 'Isa." Allah has said: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:221], and so on. This is answered by saying that this verse specifies the People of the Book women from the general category (*'umūm*) of polytheistic women, so the general (*'āmm*) is built upon the specific (*khāṣṣ*).

Those who forbade marrying slave-women from the People of the Book used this verse, because they interpreted it as referring to free women, and also His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So from those whom your right hands possess of your believing young women﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:25]. The conclusion is that under this verse fall free chaste women from the People of the Book according to all the opinions, except the opinion of Ibn 'Umar regarding Christian women. Also included is the free woman who is not chaste, and the chaste slave-woman, according to the view of those who say it is permissible to use the word *mushrik* in both of its meanings. As for those who do not permit that, if they interpret *al-muḥṣanāt* here as free women, they will not permit marrying a slave-woman, whether chaste or not, unless there is another proof. They will permit marrying a free woman, whether chaste or not. If they interpret *al-muḥṣanāt* here as chaste women, they will permit marrying a chaste free woman and a chaste slave-woman, but not a non-chaste one of either kind.

**"When you have given them their wages"**: that is, their dowries (*muhūr*). The answer to *idhā* (when) is omitted, meaning: "then they are lawful." Or it is an adverbial clause (*ẓarf*) modifying the implied predicate of *al-muḥṣanāt*, meaning: "lawful for you."

**"Chaste, not unlawful sexual companions"** (*muḥṣinīn ghayra musāfiḥīn*): *Muḥṣinīn* is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*), meaning: "while you are chaste through marriage." Likewise *ghayra musāfiḥīn* is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in *muḥṣinīn*, or it is a qualifier of *muḥṣinīn*. The meaning is: not openly committing fornication.

**"Nor those who take secret lovers"**: this is conjoined to *ghayra musāfiḥīn* or to *musāfiḥīn*. The *lā* (not) is an extra particle for emphasis. *Al-khidn* applies to both males and females, meaning: they do not take mistresses. Allah has stipulated for men chastity, not openly committing fornication, and not taking secret lovers, just as He stipulated for women that they be chaste.

**"And whoever disbelieves in faith"**, that is, in the laws of Islam, **"his deed has become void"**, that is, it has been invalidated, **"and he, in the Hereafter, is among the losers."** Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *faqad ḥabaṭa* with a fatḥa on the *bā'*. End.

(p-357) Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Abu Rafi': "The Prophet (ﷺ) ordered him to kill the dogs among the people. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is lawful for us of this community which you have ordered to be killed?' The Prophet (ﷺ) was silent, so Allah revealed: ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them﴾, the verse."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ikrimah something similar. He also reported from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that 'Adi ibn Hatim and Zayd ibn al-Muhalhil, both of the Tayy tribe, asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we are a people who hunt with dogs and falcons," so the verse was revealed.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from al-Sha'bi that 'Adi ibn Hatim al-Ta'i came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), asked him, and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And what you have taught of the trained predatory animals, training them as dogs are trained﴾. He said: "These are the trained dogs, the falcon, and the predatory animals, meaning dogs, leopards, falcons, and the like." Ibn Jarir reported from him: "The sign of the trained animal is that it holds its prey and does not eat from it until its owner comes."

He also reported from him: "If the dog eats, then do not eat, for it has only held it for itself." 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from him something similar, adding: "And if the falcon eats, then do not eat, because you can strike the dog but you cannot strike the falcon."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from him regarding His saying: ﴿And the food of those who were given the Scripture﴾: "Their slaughtered animals." And regarding His saying: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾, he said: "Lawful for you when you have given them their wages," meaning their dowries. ﴿Chaste﴾, meaning marrying them with dowry and witnesses. ﴿Not unlawful sexual companions﴾, meaning not openly committing fornication. ﴿Nor those who take secret lovers﴾, meaning they keep fornication secret.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿And chaste women from among the believing women and chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture﴾: "Allah has made lawful for us two kinds of chaste women: a chaste believing woman and a chaste woman from the People of the Book. Our women are forbidden to them, and their women are lawful for us."

Ibn Jarir reported from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "So we marry the women of the People of the Book, but they do not marry our women."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "A Muslim man may marry a Christian woman, but a Christian man may not marry a Muslim woman."

al-Tabarani and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The slaughtered animals of the Jews and Christians were only made lawful because they believe in the Torah and the Gospel."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture﴾, that he said: "The free women." 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from al-Dahhak, who said: "The chaste ones."

This is the opening of al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 4–5 (part 1 of 2):

This is the beginning of the explanation of what Allah has made lawful to them after the explanation of what Allah has forbidden to them. The occasion of revelation of the verse will be mentioned later. His saying: ﴿What has been made lawful for them?﴾ means: what thing has been made lawful for them, or: what is it that has been made lawful for them of foods in general, of game, of the food of the People of the Book, and of their women? His saying: ﴿Say: the good things have been made lawful for you﴾ — the "good things" (al-tayyibat) are what the eater finds delicious and pleasant of what Allah has made lawful for His servants. It has also been said that they are the lawful (al-halal), and the discussion of this has already preceded. It has also been said that the "good things" are the slaughtered animals, because they become good through the dhakah (ritual slaughter). This is a specification of the general term without a specifying evidence, and neither the occasion of revelation nor the context supports that.

His saying: ﴿and what you have taught of the hunting animals﴾ is coordinated with "the good things" by supplying an elided noun to make the meaning sound; that is: the good things have been made lawful for you, and the game of what you have taught of the hunting animals has been made lawful for you. Ibn ʿAbbas and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah read ﴿ʿullimtum﴾ with a damma on the ʿayn and a kasra on the lam; that is: you have been taught concerning the hunting animals and the hunting with them.

Al-Qurtubi said: Some of those who wrote on the rulings of the Qur'an mentioned that the verse indicates that the permission covers what we have taught of the hunting animals, which includes the dog and all hunting birds, and this necessitates the permission of all forms of benefit, so it indicates the permissibility of selling dogs and hunting animals and benefiting from them in all forms of benefit, except what the evidence has specified, namely eating from the hunting animals — i.e., the predators among the dogs and the birds of prey. He said: The community has agreed that if the dog is not black, and it was taught by a Muslim, and did not eat from the game that it caught, and it wounded the game with a wound or by tearing it, and a Muslim sent it while mentioning the name of Allah at its release, then its game is sound and may be eaten without disagreement.

If any of these conditions is violated, disagreement arises. If what is used for hunting is other than a dog, such as a leopard and the like, or the falcon, the hawk and similar birds, then the majority of the community holds that whatever it catches after being trained is a hunting predator that earns (kasib). It is said: "Fulan was wounded (juriha) and ijtarah" when he earned; from it comes al-jarihah (the hunting animal), because it is acquired by means of it; and from it comes "ijtirah al-sayyiʾat" (committing misdeeds). From it is His saying the Exalted: ﴿And He knows what you have earned (jaraḥtum) by day﴾, and His saying: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds (ijtarahu al-sayyiʾat) think...﴾.

His saying: ( mukallibin ) is a circumstantial clause (ḥal). The mukallib is the one who trains dogs for the manner of hunting. The more specific term is "trainer of dogs," although he is also a trainer of all other hunting animals, because hunting with dogs is the most common. He did not suffice with His saying ﴿what you have taught of the hunting animals﴾, although taklib is ta'lim, in order to emphasize what must be included of training. It has been said that the predator is called a "dog," so every predator used for hunting is included. It has also been said that this verse is specifically about dogs. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿUmar that he said: What is hunted with falcons and other birds — whatever you reach its slaughter, it is lawful for you; otherwise, do not eat it.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: Abu Jaʿfar was asked about the falcon: is its game lawful? He said: No, unless you reach its slaughter. Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: ﴿and what you have taught of the hunting animals, trainers﴾ refers to dogs only. If the dog is black, entirely black, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Nakhaʿi disliked its game.

Ahmad said: I do not know anyone who grants a concession for it if it is entirely black, and Ibn Rahawayh said the same. As for the general scholars of Medina and Kufa, they hold the permissibility of the game of every trained dog. Those who prohibit the game of the black dog argue with the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The black dog is a devil." Related by Muslim and others. The truth is that the game of everything that falls under the general term of hunting animals is lawful, without distinction between the dog and others, between the black among dogs and others, and between birds and others. This is supported by the fact that the occasion of revelation of the verse was the question of ʿAdi ibn Hatim about the falcon's game, as will come.

His saying: ﴿You teach them of what Allah has taught you﴾ is a clause in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause; that is: of what Allah has taught you, which you have grasped through the reason He created in you, by which you are guided to teaching them and training them until they become capable of holding the game when you release them. His saying: ﴿So eat of what they hold for you﴾: the fa' is for consequence, and the clause follows from what preceded of the permission of the game of what they have been taught from the hunting animals. The min in ﴿of what they hold for you﴾ is partitive, because some of the game is not eaten, such as the skin, the bone, and what the dog ate or the like. This is evidence that it must hold it for its owner; if it eats from it, then it has held it for itself, as in the established hadith in the Sahih.

The majority have held that the game which the predator catches on its own initiative without being released is not lawful to eat. ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah and al-Awza'i said — and it is related from Salman al-Farisi, Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, Abu Hurayrah, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, and it is related from ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Zuhri, Rabiʿah, Malik, and al-Shafiʿi in the old view — that its game may be eaten. Their argument is refuted by His saying: ﴿of what they hold for you﴾, and by the Prophet's ﷺ saying to ʿAdi ibn Hatim: "When you release your trained dog and mention the name of Allah over it, then eat what it holds for you." It is in the two Sahihs and others. In another wording in both: "If it eats, then do not eat, for I fear it held it for itself." As for what Abu Dawud related with a sound chain from the hadith of Abu Thaʿlabah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When your trained dog releases and you mention the name of Allah, then eat, even if it has eaten from it." He also related it with a sound chain from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb from his father from his grandfather. And al-Nasa'i also related it.

Some of the Shafiʿis reconciled these hadiths by saying: if it eats immediately after holding it, then it becomes unlawful, due to the hadith of ʿAdi ibn Hatim; but if it held it and then he waited for its owner, the waiting lengthened, and it became hungry and ate from the game out of its hunger, not because it held it for itself, then this does not affect it and the game is not made unlawful thereby. They applied to this the hadith of Abu Thaʿlabah al-Khushani and the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb. This is a good reconciliation. Others said: if the dog ate from it, it becomes unlawful, due to the hadith of ʿAdi; but if it ate from something else, it does not become unlawful, due to the other two hadiths. It is also said: the hadith of Abu Thaʿlabah is applied to the case where he held it and let it go, then it returned and ate from it.

Many scholars have taken the path of preference (tarjih) and did not take the path of reconciliation, because of its remoteness. They said: the hadith of ʿAdi ibn Hatim is preferred, being in the two Sahihs. I have established this path in my commentary on al-Muntaqa with what increases the reader's insight.

His saying: ﴿and mention the name of Allah over it﴾: the pronoun in "over it" refers to "what you have taught" — that is, invoke His name over it upon releasing it — or to "what they hold for you," that is, invoke His name over it when you wish to slaughter it. The majority have held that invoking the name is obligatory when releasing the hunting animal, and they used this verse as evidence. It is supported by the hadith of ʿAdi ibn Hatim, established in the two Sahihs and others, with the wording: "When you release your dog, mention the name of Allah; and when you shoot your arrow, mention the name of Allah."

Some scholars said: what is meant is invoking the name at the time of eating. Al-Qurtubi said: this is the more apparent. They argued with the narrations that direct to invoking the name, and this is an error. The Prophet ﷺ fixed the invoking of the name at the release of the dog and the release of the arrow, and the prescription of invoking the name at eating is a different ruling and a different question. There is no basis for applying what is in the Book and the Sunnah here to the invocation at eating, and no compulsion to do so. In another wording in the two Sahihs from the hadith of ʿAdi: "If you release your dog and invoke the name, and it seizes, then eat." Some held that invoking the name is a condition; others held it is only a sunnah; and some held that it is a condition for the one who remembers, not for the one who forgets. This is the strongest and most preferred of the opinions.

His saying: ﴿And fear Allah; indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾: that is, His reckoning, may He be glorified, is swift in coming, and everything that is coming is near. His saying: ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you﴾: this sentence emphasizes the first sentence, which is His saying: ﴿The good things have been made lawful for you﴾, and the explanation of the good things has already preceded.

Likewise *ghayra musāfiḥīn* is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in *muḥṣinīn*, or it is a qualifier of *muḥṣinīn*. The meaning is: not openly committing fornication.

**"Nor those who take secret lovers"**: this is conjoined to *ghayra musāfiḥīn* or to *musāfiḥīn*. The *lā* (not) is an extra particle for emphasis. *Al-khidn* applies to both males and females, meaning: they do not take mistresses. Allah has stipulated for men chastity, not openly committing fornication, and not taking secret lovers, just as He stipulated for women that they be chaste.

**"And whoever disbelieves in faith"**, that is, in the laws of Islam, **"his deed has become void"**, that is, it has been invalidated, **"and he, in the Hereafter, is among the losers."** Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *faqad ḥabaṭa* with a fatḥa on the *bā'*. End.

(p-357) Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Abu Rafi': "The Prophet (ﷺ) ordered him to kill the dogs among the people. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is lawful for us of this community which you have ordered to be killed?' The Prophet (ﷺ) was silent, so Allah revealed: ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them﴾, the verse."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ikrimah something similar. He also reported from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that 'Adi ibn Hatim and Zayd ibn al-Muhalhil, both of the Tayy tribe, asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we are a people who hunt with dogs and falcons," so the verse was revealed.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from al-Sha'bi that 'Adi ibn Hatim al-Ta'i came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), asked him, and he mentioned something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And what you have taught of the trained predatory animals, training them as dogs are trained﴾. He said: "These are the trained dogs, the falcon, and the predatory animals, meaning dogs, leopards, falcons, and the like." Ibn Jarir reported from him: "The sign of the trained animal is that it holds its prey and does not eat from it until its owner comes."

He also reported from him: "If the dog eats, then do not eat, for it has only held it for itself." 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from him something similar, adding: "And if the falcon eats, then do not eat, because you can strike the dog but you cannot strike the falcon."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from him regarding His saying: ﴿And the food of those who were given the Scripture﴾: "Their slaughtered animals." And regarding His saying: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾, he said: "Lawful for you when you have given them their wages," meaning their dowries. ﴿Chaste﴾, meaning marrying them with dowry and witnesses. ﴿Not unlawful sexual companions﴾, meaning not openly committing fornication. ﴿Nor those who take secret lovers﴾, meaning they keep fornication secret.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿And chaste women from among the believing women and chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture﴾: "Allah has made lawful for us two kinds of chaste women: a chaste believing woman and a chaste woman from the People of the Book. Our women are forbidden to them, and their women are lawful for us."

Ibn Jarir reported from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "So we marry the women of the People of the Book, but they do not marry our women."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "A Muslim man may marry a Christian woman, but a Christian man may not marry a Muslim woman."

al-Tabarani and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The slaughtered animals of the Jews and Christians were only made lawful because they believe in the Torah and the Gospel."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture﴾, that he said: "The free women." 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from al-Dahhak, who said: "The chaste ones."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verse 6:**

His words, "when you stand (ﷺ)" [﴿إذا قُمْتُمْ﴾]: "when you intend to stand," using the effect for the cause, as in His words: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 98]. The scholars differed regarding this command when one intends to stand for prayer. One group said: it is general for every standing for prayer, whether the one standing is in a state of purity or is in a state of minor impurity (hadath). So he should perform wudu' (ablution) whenever he stands for prayer. This is related from 'Ali and 'Ikrimah. Ibn Sirin said: the caliphs used to perform wudu' for every prayer. Another group said: this command is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), but this view is weak, because the address is to the believers and the command is directed to them. Another group said: the command is for recommendation (nadb), seeking merit. Others said: performing wudu' for every prayer was an obligation upon them by this verse, then it was abrogated (naskh) at the Conquest of Makkah. A group said: this command is specific to one who is in a state of minor impurity. Others said: the meaning is "when you rise from sleep to prayer," so the address includes everyone who rises from sleep. Muslim, Ahmad and the authors of the Sunan related from Buraydah, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to perform wudu' for every prayer. But when the Day of the Conquest came, he performed wudu', wiped over his leather socks (khuff), and prayed the prayers with one wudu'. 'Umar said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, you did something you had not been doing.' He said: 'I did it deliberately, O 'Umar.'" This is narrated through many chains with wordings that agree in meaning. Al-Bukhari, Ahmad and the authors of the Sunan related from 'Amr ibn 'Amir al-Ansari, who said: I heard Anas ibn Malik say: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to perform wudu' for every prayer." He said: I said: "And how did you used to do it?" He said: "We would pray the prayers with one wudu' as long as we did not become impure (lit. did not break wudu')." From what has been mentioned, it is established that wudu' is obligatory only upon one who is in a state of minor impurity. This is the view of the majority of scholars, and it is the truth.

His words: ﴿wash your faces﴾. The word "wajh" (face) linguistically is derived from "muwajahah" (facing). It is a limb comprising parts, and it has length and breadth. Its limit in length is from the beginning of the surface of the forehead to the end of the two jaws (lihyan), and in breadth from ear to ear. Evidence has come for passing the fingers through the beard (takhlil al-lihyah), and the scholars differed concerning washing what hangs down beyond the face (istirsal). The discussion of that is extended in its proper places. The scholars also differed: is rubbing (dalk) with the hand required in washing, or is it sufficient to let water flow over? The disagreement on this is well known, and the reference is the Arabic language. If it is established in the language that rubbing is included in the meaning of "washing" (ghasl), then it is required; otherwise it is not. In Shams al-'Ulum it is said: "He washed the thing (ghasala al-shay') with washing when he let water flow over it and rubbed it," end of quote. As for rinsing the mouth (madmadah) and sniffing water into the nose (istinshaq): if the word "wajh" does not include the inside of the mouth and nose, then washing them has been established by authentic Sunnah. The disagreement over whether they are obligatory or not is well known, and we have clarified what the truth is in our writings.

His words: ﴿and your hands to the elbows﴾. The particle "ila" (to) denotes the limit (ghayah). As for whether what comes after it enters into what comes before it, this is a matter of disagreement. Sibawayh and a group held that what follows it enters into what precedes it if it is of the same kind as what precedes it, and otherwise it does not. It was also said that here it means "ma'a" (with). A people held that it indicates the limit absolutely. As for entry or non-entry, it is a matter that depends on the evidence. The majority held that the elbows are washed, and they cited what al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi related through the chain of al-Qasim ibn Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Aqil, from his grandfather, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed wudu', he turned the water around his two elbows." But this al-Qasim is abandoned (matruk) and his grandfather is weak.

His words: (and wipe over your heads). It was said: the "ba'" is extra (za'idah), and the meaning is "wipe your heads." This requires generalizing the wiping to the entire head. It was also said: it is for partiality (tab'idh), and this requires that wiping part of it suffices. Those who held the generality argued with His words, exalted is He, regarding tayammum: ﴿wipe your faces﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], and wiping part of the face does not suffice by consensus. It was also said: it is for attachment (ilsaq), i.e., press your hands onto your heads. In any case, the purified Sunnah has come with what indicates that wiping part of the head suffices, as we have clarified in our writings. This is thus evidence for the sought ruling, not open to the possibility that the verse is open to, even on the assumption that it is open to possibility. There is no doubt that whoever commands another to wipe his head is one who complies by doing what truly fits the designation of wiping. Nothing in the language of the Arabs requires that in such an act the whole head must be wiped. The same applies to all transitive verbs, such as "hit Zayd," "stab him," or "stone him." The Arabic meaning is realized by the blow, stab, or stoning landing on one of his limbs, and no speaker of the language, or one who knows it, says that one is not a striker unless the blow lands on every part of Zayd. The same is true of stabbing, stoning and all other acts. So understand this, until it becomes clear to you which of the opinions on wiping the head is correct. If you say: this would apply to washing the face, hands and feet too. I say: it would apply, were it not for the explanation from the Sunnah concerning the face, and the limitation by the limit (ghayah) for the hands and feet, unlike the head, for the Sunnah has come with wiping all of it and wiping part of it.

His words: ﴿and your feet to the ankles﴾. Nafi' read "arjulakum" in the accusative (nasb). This is also the reading of al-Hasan al-Basri and al-A'mash. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hamzah read it in the genitive (jarr). The accusative reading indicates that washing both feet is obligatory, since they are coordinated with the face (mu'attafah 'ala al-wajh). To this the majority of scholars went. The genitive reading indicates that it is permissible to limit oneself to wiping both feet, since they are coordinated with the head (mu'attafah 'ala al-ra's). To this Ibn Jarir al-Tabari went, and it is related from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn al-'Arabi said: the community has agreed on the obligation of washing them, and I know of no one who rejected that except al-Tabari among the jurists of the Muslims, and the Rafidah among others. Al-Tabari relied on the genitive reading. Al-Qurtubi said: It has been related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Wudu' is two washings and two wipings." He said: 'Ikrimah used to wipe his feet, and he said: "There is no washing for the two feet; only wiping was revealed concerning them." 'Amir al-Sha'bi said: "Jibril descended with wiping." He said: Qatadah said: "Allah prescribed two wipings and two washings." He said: Ibn Jarir al-Tabari went to the view that their obligation is an option between washing and wiping, and he made the two readings like two narrations. al-Nahhas strengthened this view. But it has been established in the purified Sunnah, by authentic hadiths, from his action (ﷺ) and his statement, that the feet are washed only. And it is established from him that he said: "Woe to the heels from the Fire," and this is in the Two Sahihs and others. This indicates the obligation of washing both feet and that wiping them does not suffice, because the nature of wiping is that it reaches what it reaches and misses what it misses. If it were sufficient, he would not have said: "Woe to the heels from the Fire."

It is also established from him that, after he performed wudu' and washed his feet, he said: "This is a wudu' with which Allah does not accept prayer except with it." And it is established in Sahih Muslim and elsewhere that a man performed wudu' and left a spot on his foot the size of a fingernail, and he said to him: "Go back and perform your wudu' well."

As for wiping over the two leather socks (khuffayn), it is established by mutawatir hadiths. His words: (to the ankles), the discussion concerning it is like the discussion of his words: (to the elbows). It has been said regarding the reason for using the plural of "elbows" (marafiq) and the dual of "ankles" (ka'bayn): since each person has two ankles, but in each hand there is only one elbow, the ankles were put in the dual to alert that each foot has two ankles, unlike the elbows, which were put in the plural because, since each hand has one elbow, it was not imagined that there was another. Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned the meaning of this.

al-Kawashi said: He made "ka'bayn" dual and "marafiq" plural to negate the illusion that each of the two feet has two ankles, whereas in each foot there is one ankle having two ends on either side of the foot. Unlike the elbow, which is further from the illusion, end of quote.

Among the obligatory parts of wudu', the intention (niyyah) and saying the basmalah (tasmiyah) remain. They are not mentioned in this verse. Rather, the Sunnah has come with them. It was also said: there is in this verse what indicates the intention, because when He said: ﴿when you stand to prayer, wash your faces﴾, the sense of the speech is: "wash your faces for it," and that is the valid intention.

His words: ﴿And if you are in janabah (major impurity), then purify yourselves﴾. That is: bathe with water. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn Mas'ud went to the view that one in janabah does not perform tayammum (dry ablution with earth) at all, but abstains from prayer until he finds water, relying on this verse. The majority went to the obligation of tayammum for janabah when water is absent. This verse is for one who has water. Moreover, purification (tahhur) is more general than what is attained by water or by what substitutes for it when it is absent, which is earth. It has been authentically reported from 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud that they returned to what the majority said, because of the authentic hadiths regarding the tayammum of one in janabah when water is absent. The explanation of janabah has already been mentioned in (the chapter on) women.

His words: ﴿And if you are sick, or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself (al-gha.it)﴾ [al-Nisa': 43]. The explanation of this has already been given in full in surah al-Nisa'. Likewise, the discussion of touching women, tayammum, and "al-sa'id" has already been given. The "min" in his words "minhu" (from it) denotes the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah). It was also said: it denotes partiality. It was said: the reason for repeating this here is to complete the discussion on the types of purification. ﴿Allah does not want to place upon you any difficulty﴾, that is: He does not want, by commanding you to purify with water or with earth, to constrict you in religion. From the same root is His words: ﴿and He has not placed upon you in religion any difficulty﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. Then He said: ﴿but He wants to purify you﴾ from sins; it was also said: from minor and major impurity (hadath). ﴿and to complete His favor upon you﴾, that is: by granting you dispensation in tayammum when water is absent, or by what He has legislated for you of the laws through which He presents you to reward. ﴿that you may be grateful﴾ for His favor upon you, so that by gratitude you deserve the reward of the grateful.

Malik, al-Shafi'i, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Zayd ibn Aslam regarding His words: ﴿When you stand to prayer﴾ that he said: "you stand from the beds," meaning sleep. Ibn Jarir related the same from al-Suddi. Ibn Jarir also related from him that he said: "when you stand while you are not in a state of purity." Ibn Abi Shaybah related from al-Hasan regarding His words: ﴿wash your faces﴾ that he said: "That washing is rubbing (dalk)." Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir related from Anas that it was said to him: "al-Hajjaj addressed us and said: 'Wash your faces and your hands, wipe your heads and your feet,' and that nothing of the son of Adam is closer to filth than his two feet, so wash their bellies, their backs and their heels." Anas said: "Allah spoke the truth and al-Hajjaj lied. Allah said: (and wipe your heads and your feet)." And Anas, when he wiped his two feet, would moisten them.

Sa'id ibn Mansur related from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla who said: "The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) agreed on washing the two feet." 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿difficulty﴾ that he said: "constriction." 'Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His words: ﴿and to complete His favor upon you﴾ that he said: "The completion of the favor is entering Paradise. He does not complete His favor upon a servant who has not entered Paradise."

(نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ) It is said: it is Islam.

Al-mithaq (the covenant) means the pact. It is said that what is meant here is the covenant He took from the children of Adam, as He said: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam...﴾ [al-A'raf 7:172], up to the end of the verse. Mujahid and others said: "Even though we do not remember it, God has informed us of it." It is also said that the address is to the Jews, and that the covenant is what He took from them in the Torah. The majority of the exegetes (mufassirun) among the early generations (al-salaf) and those after them held that it is the covenant that the Prophet (ﷺ) took from them on the night of al-'Aqabah, which is hearing and obeying in ease and in hardship. God attributed it to Himself because it was by His command and permission, as He said: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you pledge allegiance only to God﴾ [al-Fath 48:10]. The Pledge of al-'Aqabah is mentioned in the books of biography (kutub al-siyar), and this is connected to His saying: (Fulfill the contracts) [al-Ma'idah 5:1].

His saying: ﴿when you said, "We hear and we obey"﴾ means: at the time you said this statement. This is related to (wathaqakum), or to an omitted element that came as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: existing at this time. (Dhat al-suduri) refers to what the breasts conceal, because it is specific to them and no one knows it. For this reason it is called dhat, which here carries the meaning of "possessor." If He, glorified is He, knows it, then how much more so what is apparent and manifest.

His saying: ﴿O you who believe, be persistent in standing firm (qawwamin) for God﴾. Its explanation has already been given in al-Nisa'. The intensive form in (qawwamin) indicates that they are commanded to uphold it in the most complete manner, (lillah), that is, for His sake, magnifying His command and hoping for His reward.

Al-qist is justice. The discussion of His saying (yajrimannakum) has already been given in full. That is: let the hatred of a people not drive you to abandon justice and to conceal testimony. (I'dilu huwa) means: justice, which is implied by His saying "be just." (Is closer to piety), which you were commanded about more than once; that is, it is closer to your being mindful of God, or closer to your being mindful of the Fire.

His saying: ﴿For them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾. This sentence is in the accusative position, being the second object of (wa'ada), meaning: He promised them that they would have forgiveness, or He promised them forgiveness, so the sentence took the place of a single noun and served in its stead. Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

"We found the righteous, for them is a reward, and gardens, and a spring called Salsabil."

(As-hab al-Jahim) means: those who are involved with it. (Idh hamma qawmun) is a temporal clause (zarf) related to (udhkuru), or to (ni'mah), or to an omitted element that came as a circumstantial clause from it: (an yabsutu), meaning: that they would stretch out. (Fakaffa) is conjoined to (hamma). The cause of the revelation of this verse will come later, and the meaning becomes clear through it. Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿when you said, "We hear and we obey"﴾: that is, when God sent the Prophet (ﷺ) and revealed the Book to him, they said, "We believe in the Prophet and the Book, and we affirm what is in the Torah." So God reminded them of His covenant, which they had affirmed against themselves, and commanded them to fulfill it.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid, who said: "The blessings (ni'am) are the favors (al-ala')." (And His covenant which He made with you) he said: it is the covenant He made with the children of Adam in the loins of Adam, peace be upon him. Ibn Jarir reported from 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir regarding His saying ﴿O you who believe, be persistent in standing firm for God, as witnesses in justice﴾, up to the end of the verse, he said: it was revealed concerning the Jews of Khaybar. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went to them seeking their ruling concerning blood money (diyah), and they resolved to kill him. That is His saying: ﴿And do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just﴾, up to the end of the verse.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that "the Prophet (ﷺ) stopped at a place, and the people scattered among the 'idah (thorny trees) seeking shade beneath them. The Prophet (ﷺ) hung his sword on a tree. A Bedouin came to his sword, took it and drew it, then turned toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: 'Who will protect you from me?' He said: 'God.' The Bedouin said, twice or three times: 'Who will protect you from me?' and the Prophet (ﷺ) kept saying: 'God.' So the Bedouin sheathed the sword. The Prophet (ﷺ) called his companions and informed them of the Bedouin's deed, while he was sitting beside him, and he did not punish him."

Ma'mar said: Qatadah used to mention something similar to this, and he would mention that a group of the Arabs wanted to assassinate the Prophet (ﷺ), so they sent this Bedouin. He interpreted ﴿Remember the favor of God upon you when a people resolved to stretch out their hands against you﴾, up to the end of the verse. Al-Hakim reported it with a similar wording and declared it sound (sahih), and he mentioned that the man's name was Ghawrath ibn al-Harith, and that "when the Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'God,' the sword fell from his hand. The Prophet (ﷺ) picked it up and said: 'Who will protect you from me?' He said: 'Be the best of takers.' He said: 'Then he testified that there is no god but God.'"

Ibn Ishaq and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il also reported it from him (p-360). Ibn Nu'aym in al-Dala'il reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the Banu al-Nadir resolved to drop a stone upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and those with him, so Gabriel came and informed him of what they had planned, so he stood up with those who were with him. Then this verse was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, remember the favor of God upon you when a people resolved...﴾, up to the end of the verse. Something similar to this was narrated through other chains from others. The story of the Bedouin, who is Ghawrath mentioned above, is established in the Sahih.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 5, verses 12–14:**

His statement: ﴿And Allah had already taken a covenant from the Children of Israel﴾ is a new sentence (kalam mustaʾnaf) that includes mention of some of the betrayal that came from the Children of Israel. The covenant that Allah took from them has already been explained. The exegetes differed over the manner in which these *nuqaba'* (chiefs, sing. *naqib*) were sent, after they agreed (ijma', the scholarly consensus) that the *naqib* is the leader of the people, knowledgeable about their affairs, who investigates those affairs and their interests. The *niqab* is the great man who holds this position among the people. It is also said that the *naqib* of a people is their witness and guarantor.

The *naqib* originally means a path through a mountain, and the leader of a people was named after it because he is a path to knowing their affairs. The *naqib* is higher in rank than the *arif* (overseer). It was said that the purpose of sending these chiefs was that they were sent as trustees to observe the tyrants (*al-jabbarin*) and to examine their strength and their power. They set out to test the condition of those who were there and to report back. They observed from the tyrants a great strength and thought that they had no means of confronting them. So they agreed among themselves to conceal this from the Children of Israel and to inform Musa (Moses) about it. When they returned to the Children of Israel, ten of them betrayed the agreement and informed their relatives, so the news spread until the matter of the military campaign was abandoned, and they said: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 360]. It was also said that each of these chiefs was a guarantor over his tribe, that they would believe and fear Allah, and this is the meaning of sending them. The mention of some of what a group of the early generations (al-salaf) said about this will come later.

His statement: ﴿And Allah said, "Indeed I am with you"﴾, meaning He said this to the Children of Israel. It was also said that He said it to the chiefs. The meaning is: I am with you through support and help. The *lam* in His statement ﴿If you establish prayer﴾ is the *lam* that prepares for an omitted oath (al-muwatti'ah lil-qasam), and its answer is *la-ukaffiranna* (لَأُكَفِّرَنَّ), which takes the place of the answer to the condition. *Ta'zir* means honoring and revering. Abu Ubaydah recited:

*"How many a noble man among them, generous, and how many a lion who is honored in the gathering."*

That is, he is exalted and revered. *Ta'zir* is also used for striking and repelling. It is said: "*Azzartu* so-and-so" when you disciplined him and turned him away from wrongdoing. So His statement *wa-azzartumuhum* (وعَزَّرْتُمُوهم) means: you honored them according to the first meaning, or you repelled their enemies from them and protected them according to the second meaning. His statement ﴿and lend Allah a goodly loan﴾ means: you spend in the ways of good. *Qardan* (قَرْضًا) is a verbal noun with its extra letters removed, like His statement ﴿and caused it to grow a goodly growth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37], or it is a second object of *aqradtum* (أقْرَضْتُمْ). The *hasan* (goodly) is said to be what the soul is content with, or what is sought for the sake of Allah's face, or the lawful.

His statement: ﴿Then whoever disbelieves after that﴾ means: after the covenant or after the stated condition, ﴿has certainly strayed from the sound way﴾, meaning: he erred from the middle of the path.

His statement: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant﴾. The *ba'* (ب) is causal and *ma* is extra. That is: because of their breaking their covenant, ﴿We cursed them﴾ (la'annahum, لَعَنّاهم), meaning: We drove them away and removed them far. ﴿And We made their hearts hard﴾, meaning: solid, not understanding good or comprehending it. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited *qasiyyatan* (قَسِيَّةً) with a doubled *ya'* and without an *alif*, and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i and Yahya ibn Wathhab. It is said: "a *qasiyy* dirham," with the *sin* light and the *ya'* doubled, that is, counterfeit. Abu Ubayd mentioned this. Al-Asma'i and Abu Ubaydah said: a *qasiyy* dirham seems to be an arabized form of *qasin* (قاسٍ, hard). Al-A'mash recited *qasiyyah* (قَسِيَةً) with a light *ya'*. The rest recited *qasiyah* (قاسِيَةً).

﴿They distort words from their places﴾. This sentence is a new sentence explaining their condition, or it is a circumstantial clause (hal). That is: they replace it with other than it, or they interpret it in a way other than its proper interpretation. Al-Sulami and al-Nakha'i recited *al-kalam* (الكَلامَ). His statement: ﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them﴾, meaning: O Muhammad, you will not cease to come upon treachery from them. *Al-kha'inah* means betrayal. It is also said that it is an adjective for an omitted noun, and the estimate is "a treacherous group." It may also be used for emphasis, as in *allamah* and *nassabah*, when you intend to emphasize describing him with betrayal. It is also said that *khaʾinah* means disobedience.

His statement: *"except a few of them"* (إلّا قَلِيلًا مِنهم) is an exception from the pronoun in *minhum*. ﴿So pardon them and overlook﴾. It was said: this has been abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword. It was also said: it is specific to those with whom there is a treaty.

His statement: ﴿And from those who said, "We are Christians," We took their covenant﴾, meaning: concerning monotheism and belief in Muhammad (ﷺ) and what he brought. Al-Akhfash said: it is like your saying: "I took from Zayd his garment and his dirham," so the position of *alladhina* comes after *akhadhna*. The Kufans held the opposite view. It was also said that the pronoun in *mithaqahum* refers to the Children of Israel. Ibn Ishaq mentioned the names of these tribes, and their names are mentioned in the Fourth Book of the Torah (the Book of Numbers). There is a disagreement between it and what Ibn Ishaq mentioned.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas concerning His statement *"and you honored them"* (وعَزَّرْتُمُوهم) that he said: you helped them. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid concerning His statement *"and you honored them"* that he said: you supported them. Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas concerning His statement ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant﴾ that he said: it is a covenant that Allah took from the People of the Torah, and they broke it. Ibn Jarir also reported from him concerning His statement ﴿They distort words from their places﴾, meaning: the limits of Allah. They say: "If Muhammad orders you to do what you are upon, then accept it, and if he opposes you, then beware." Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him concerning His statement ﴿But they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of﴾ that he said: they forgot the Book.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid concerning His statement ﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them﴾ that he said: they are Jews like those who planned against the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day he entered their orchard. Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatadah concerning His statement ﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them﴾ that he said: it is lying and wickedness. And concerning His statement ﴿So pardon them and overlook﴾ he said: He was not commanded at that time to fight them, so Allah commanded him to pardon them and overlook. Then this was abrogated in *Bara'ah* (Surah al-Tawbah), where He said: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29], the verse. Abu Ubayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i concerning His statement ﴿So We caused among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection﴾ that he said: some of them incited others against one another through disputes and argument over the religion.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 15–16:

The alif and lam in "al-Kitab" (the Book) are for the genus (lil-jins), and the address is to the Jews and the Christians. ﴿Indeed there has come to you Our Messenger﴾, i.e., Muhammad (ﷺ), while ﴿he makes clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Book﴾ revealed to you, which is the Torah and the Gospel: such as the verse of stoning (al-rajm) and the story of the People of the Sabbath who were transformed into apes. ( ﴿And he pardons much﴾ ) of what you conceal, so he leaves its explanation, because it does not contain any legal rulings that must be explained. As for what is not of this kind, there is no benefit connected to explaining it except merely exposing you. It was also said that the meaning is: he pardons much, meaning he overlooks it and does not inform you of it. It was also said: he pardons much of you, so he does not hold you accountable for what proceeds from them. The clause is in the accusative position (mahall nasb), conjoined (ʿatf) to the circumstantial clause, namely his saying: ( ﴿he makes clear to you﴾ ).

His saying: ﴿There has come to you from Allah a light﴾ is a resumptive clause (jumla mustaʾnafa) containing a statement that Muhammad's (ﷺ) mission has included benefits beyond the mere making clear mentioned before. Al-Zajjaj said: the light is Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said: it is Islam. "The clear Book" is the Qur'an, for it is the clarifier. The pronoun in his saying ( ﴿by which He guides﴾ ) refers to the Book, or to him and to the light, since the two are like a single thing. ( ﴿Whoever follows His pleasure﴾ ), i.e., what Allah is pleased with. ( ﴿The paths of peace﴾ ) are the ways of safety from punishment, leading to peace, free from every calamity. It was also said that by "peace" is meant Islam. ﴿And brings them out of darkness﴾ (of disbelief) ( ﴿into light﴾ ) (of Islam), ﴿and guides them to a straight path﴾, to a way by which they arrive at the truth, with no crookedness in it and no fear.

Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah, regarding his saying ( ﴿Our Messenger﴾ ), that he said: it is Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn Jarir also reported from Ikrimah, who said: "The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) was approached by the Jews asking him about stoning, and he said: 'Which of you is the most knowledgeable?' They pointed to Ibn Suriya, and he adjured him by Him who revealed the Torah to Musa and who raised the Mount over them with the covenants that were taken from them, until he was seized with trembling. He said: 'When it became widespread among us, we would flog a hundred lashes and shave the heads, so he (the Prophet) ruled for them with stoning, and this verse was revealed.'" Ibn al-Mundhir reported similarly from Ibn Jurayj. ʿAbd ibn Humayd reported from Qatadah, regarding his saying ( ﴿and pardons much﴾ ), that he said: "of many sins." Ibn Jarir reported from al-Suddi, who said: ( ﴿the paths of peace﴾ ) are the way of Allah which He legislated for His servants, called them to, and sent His messengers with: and it is Islam.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 17–18:

The separative pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl) in His saying (هو المَسِيحُ, "He is the Messiah") indicates restriction (al-ḥaṣr). It has been said: some sects of the Christians have said this. And it has been said: none of them said it, but their saying "Indeed Allah is the Messiah" necessitates that it be Him and not other than Him. What has preceded at the end of Surat al-Nisa' suffices and is enough, so there is no need for repetition.

His saying: ﴿Say: "Who then has any power against Allah at all"﴾. The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach. Al-mulk (dominion) means control, preservation and power, from their saying: "I held power over so-and-so's affair" (malaktu ʿalā fulānin amrahu), i.e., I had power over him. That is: who is able to prevent ﴿if He had wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother, and everyone on earth, all together﴾? And if no one is able to prevent that, then there is no god but Allah, and no lord other than Him, and no truly worshipped one besides Him. Had the Messiah been a god, as the Christians claim, he would have had some share of the affair, and he would have been able to defend himself at least minimally; yet he was not able to defend his mother from death when it descended upon her. Her being singled out for mention, although she is included in the generality of "everyone on earth," is because defending her would be more fitting and more due from him than defending others. So if he was not able to defend her, he is more incapable of defending anyone else. The mention of "everyone on earth" serves to indicate the comprehensiveness of His power, and that when He wills something there is no opponent to His command and no partner in His decree. ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾, i.e., what is between the two kinds of creatures.

His saying: (يَخْلُقُ ما يَشاءُ, "He creates what He wills") is a resumptive clause (jumla mustaʾnafa) brought to explain that He, glory be to Him, is the Creator of creation according to His will, and that He is able over everything, nothing being difficult for Him.

His saying: ﴿And the Jews and the Christians said: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved."﴾ The Jews attributed to themselves what they attributed to ʿUzayr, when they said: (عُزَيْرٌ ابْنُ اللَّهِ, "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah") [al-Tawba: 30]. The Christians attributed to themselves what they attributed to the Messiah, when they said: (المَسِيحُ ابْنُ اللَّهِ, "The Messiah is the son of Allah") [al-Tawba: 30]. It has been said that it is by elision of a modifier: i.e., "We are the followers of the sons of Allah." Thus they claimed for themselves that they are the beloved of Allah merely by false assertion and vain wishes. So Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to respond to them, and He said: ﴿Say: "Why then does He punish you for your sins?"﴾ i.e., if you were as you claim, then why does He punish you for the sins you commit, by killing, transformation, and by the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, as you yourselves admit when you say: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few countable days﴾? For the son is of the same kind as his father; what is impossible for the father does not proceed from him, yet you sin. And the beloved does not punish his beloved, yet you are punished. This indicates that you are lying in this claim. This proof is what the dialecticians call the proof by reductio (burhan al-khalf).

His saying: ﴿Rather, you are human beings from among those He has created﴾ is a conjunction with an implied element indicated by the speech; i.e., "Then you are not so." ﴿Rather, you are human beings from among those He has created﴾, i.e., of the same kind as those whom Allah the Exalted has created, whom He will call to account for good and evil, and will recompense every doer according to his deed. ﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, and to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ of existing things. (وإلَيْهِ المَصِيرُ, "And to Him is the return") i.e., you will return to Him when you pass from the abode of this world to the abode of the Hereafter.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il have related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Nuʿman ibn Adaʾ, Bahri ibn ʿAmr and Shas ibn ʿAdi came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and they spoke with him, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, spoke with them, called them to Allah and warned them of His vengeance. They said: 'What do you frighten us with, O Muhammad? ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved﴾, like the saying of the Christians.' So Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿And the Jews and the Christians said﴾ to the end of the verse."

Ahmad in his Musnad related from Anas, who said: "The Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, passed by with a group of his companions, and there was a child on the road. When his mother saw the people she feared for her son that he would be trampled, so she came running and saying: 'My son, my son!' She ran and took him. The people said: 'O Messenger of Allah, would this woman ever throw her son into the Fire?' The Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: 'No, by Allah, Allah does not throw His beloved into the Fire.'" Its isnad in the Musnad is thus: "Ibn Abi ʿAdi narrated to us, from Humayd, from Anas," and he mentioned it.

The meaning of the verse points to the meaning of this hadith. For this reason some of the Sufi shaykhs said to some of the jurists: "Where do you find in the Qur'an that the beloved does not punish his beloved?" He did not answer him, so the Sufi recited this verse.

Ahmad in al-Zuhd related from al-Hasan that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "No, by Allah, Allah does not punish His beloved, but He may test him in this world."

Ibn Jarir related from al-Suddi, concerning His saying: ﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾, that he said: "He guides whom He wills among you in this world, and so He forgives him; and He causes to die whom He wills among you upon his disbelief, and so He punishes him."
