The intended meaning of "the People of the Book" is the Jews and the Christians. The Messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿Allah makes clear to you﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). What is made clear is what Allah has prescribed for His servants, and its object is omitted because it is known; the sending of messengers is for precisely this purpose. Al-fatrah (the interval between messengers) originally means stillness. It is said that "fatara al-shay'" means it became still, and it is also said that it means a cessation. This is the view of Abu 'Ali al-FARISI and others. From the same root: "fatara al-ma'" means the water ceased from its former state of coldness to warmth, and "fatara al-rajul 'an 'amalihi" means the man ceased from the earnestness he had in it. "Imra'ah fatirat al-taraf" means a woman whose glance has lost its sharpness. The meaning is that the messengers ceased for a period of time before his sending (ﷺ), and scholars differed about the length of that interval (p-٣٦٣), which will be explained later.

His saying ﴿lest you should say: "No bearer of good tidings and no warner came to us"﴾ gives the reason for the coming of the Messenger with clarification during a period of interval. That is, [it is] lest you make this statement, offering excuses for your negligence. The *min* in His saying "min bashīr" (no bearer of good tidings) is extra (zā'idah), for emphasis in negating the coming. The *fā'* in His saying "fa-qad jā'akum" (then there has indeed come to you) is the eloquent *fā'* (al-fā' al-faṣīḥah), like the poet's saying:

*"Fa-qad ji'nā Khurāsānā"*
(So we have come to Khurasan)

That is: do not offer excuses, for there has come to you a bearer of good tidings and a warner, and he is Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿And Allah is over all things Competent﴾. Among the things He is able to do is His sending His Messenger after an interval between messengers.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi, in *al-Dala'il*, transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited the Jews to Islam, and he encouraged them towards it and warned them, but they refused. Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah and 'Uqbah ibn Wahb said to them: 'O assembly of Jews, fear Allah! By Allah, you know that he is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). You used to mention him to us before his mission and describe him to us by his attributes.' Rafi' ibn Harmalah and Wahb ibn Yahudha said: 'We did not say this to you, and Allah has not sent down any Book after Moses, nor has He sent any bearer of good tidings or any warner after him.' So Allah sent down: ﴿O People of the Book, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you [the truth] after an interval between messengers﴾," the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Qatadah, concerning the verse, that he said: "He is Muhammad (ﷺ), who came with the truth by which Allah distinguished between truth and falsehood. In it is clarification, admonition, light, guidance and protection for whoever holds to it." He said: "The interval between 'Isa and Muhammad was six hundred years and whatever Allah willed of that."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from him that he said: "It was five hundred and sixty years." Al-Kalbi said: "Five hundred and forty years."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Jarir, who said: "It was five hundred years."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Dahhak, who said: "It was four hundred and thirty-some years."

Ibn Sa'd, in *Kitab al-Tabaqat*, transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Between Moses and 'Isa there were one thousand nine hundred years, and there was no interval between them, for a thousand prophets were sent between them from the Children of Israel, besides those sent from other than them. Between the birth of 'Isa and Muhammad (ﷺ) there were five hundred and sixty-nine years, and in its beginning three prophets were sent, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿When We sent to them two, and they denied them, so We reinforced [them] with a third﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:14]. The one with whom they were reinforced was Shim'un, who was one of the disciples (al-Hawariyyun). The period in which Allah did not send a messenger was four hundred and thirty-four years." Other than what we have mentioned has also been said.

These verses contain a statement from God, glorified is He, that the forefathers of the Jews who lived in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ) rebelled against Moses and disobeyed him, just as these people rebelled against our Prophet (ﷺ) and disobeyed him. This is also a consolation to him (ﷺ).

It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Kathir that he recited "Ya qawmu adhkuru" (﴿O my people, remember﴾) with a *damma* on the *mim*, and he recited similarly in similar places. Its estimated reading is: "O people, remember the favour of God upon you when He made among you prophets," meaning at the time of this making. Attaching the remembrance to a time, while what is intended is the events that occurred in it, is for emphasis, because the command to remember a time is a command to remember what happened in it by way of priority. God, glorified is He, reminded them of His favour by making prophets among them, even though He made prophets from other peoples too, because of the great number of prophets He sent from among them.

His words, "and made you kings" (﴿وَجَعَلَكُم مُّلُوكًا﴾), mean "and made from among you kings." The preposition was omitted because it is evident that the meaning of the sentence depends on it. It may be said that since the office of prophethood is of great rank and high station, it is not attributed to anyone other than its holder, so He said of it, "when He made among you prophets." But since the office of kingship may be attributed to others than its holder, as one says of the relatives of a king, "We are the kings," He said of it, "and made you kings." It was also said that the meaning of "kings" is that they came to possess their own affairs after they had been subjects of Pharaoh, so they were all kings in this sense. It was also said that it means He made them people of dwellings, into which no one enters except by permission. Other things have been said too. The apparent meaning is that the verse intends true kingship, and if it had another meaning, there would be little point in citing it as a favour. If it is objected that He made others kings as well, the answer is that kings were numerous among them as prophets were numerous, and this is the basis of the favour.

His words, "and gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds" (﴿وَآتَاكُم مَّا لَمْ يُؤْتِ أَحَدًا مِّنَ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾), mean: what He gave them of the manna and quails, the rock and the cloud, the great number of prophets, the great number of kings, and other things. "The worlds" means the peoples of their time. It was also said that the address here is to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), but this is a deviation from the apparent meaning without a valid reason. The correct view is that held by the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun): that these are the words of Moses to his people, addressing them thus as a preparation and introduction to what follows of his command to them to enter the Holy Land. The Holy Land has been disputed as to its identification. Qatadah said it is Syria; Mujahid said it is Mount Sinai (al-Tur) and what surrounds it; Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and others said it is Ariha (Jericho); al-Zajjaj said it is Damascus, Palestine and part of Jordan. Qatadah's view encompasses the views mentioned after it. "Muqaddasah" means purified, and it was also said blessed. "Which God has prescribed for you" means He apportioned it and destined it for them in His eternal knowledge and made it a dwelling for them. "And do not turn back on your heels" means do not turn back from My command and abandon obedience to Me and what I have obligated you to do, namely fighting the tyrants, out of cowardice and weakness, "so that you will turn back" (﴿فَتَنقَلِبُوا﴾) "losers" (﴿خَاسِرِينَ﴾) in the good of this world and the Hereafter because of that.

﴿They said, "O Moses, indeed in it are a people of tyrants."﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: the *jabbar* among human beings is the obstinate one, who compels people to do what he wants. Its root in this view is from *ijbar*, which means coercion, for he compels others to do what he wants; one says *ajbarahu* when he forces him. It was also said that it derives from *jabara al-‘azm* (setting a bone). On this view, the root of *jabbar* is one who mends his own affairs, and then it was used for anyone who draws benefit to himself, whether rightfully or wrongfully. It was also said that the setting of a bone returns to the meaning of compulsion. Al-Farra' said: I have not heard the form *fa‘‘al* from *af‘ala* except in two words: *jabbar* from *ajbara*, and *darrak* from *adraka*.

The intended meaning here is that they were a people of large bodies, tall and arrogant. It was said they were some of the remnant of the people of ‘Ad. It was said they were of the descendants of Esau son of Isaac. It was said they were of the Romans. It is also said that among them was ‘Awj ibn ‘Unuq, famous for excessive height, and that ‘Unuq was a daughter of Adam. It was said his height was three thousand three hundred and thirty-three and a third cubits. Ibn Kathir said: this is something one should be ashamed to mention. Moreover, it contradicts what is established in the two Sahihs, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God created Adam, and his height was sixty cubits. Then creation continued to diminish." Furthermore, they mentioned that this man was a disbeliever, that he was the son of an adulteress, that he refused to board the ark, and that the flood did not reach his knees. This is a lie and a fabrication, for God mentioned that Noah prayed against the disbelievers on earth, saying: ﴿My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers a single dweller﴾ [Nuh: 26]. He also said: ﴿Then We saved him and those with him in the laden ship; then We drowned the rest afterwards﴾ [al-Shu‘ara: 119–120]. And He said: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of God, except for whom He has mercy﴾ [Hud: 43]. If Noah's disbelieving son drowned, how could ‘Awj ibn ‘Unuq remain, being a disbeliever and the son of an adulteress? This is not permissible in reason or in law. Moreover, the existence of a man called ‘Awj ibn ‘Unuq is open to question, and God knows best. End of his words.

I say: nothing has come concerning this man that calls for lengthy discussion about him. This is not the first lie that has become famous among people. We are not obliged to refute the falsehoods that storytellers (qussas) invented and which circulated among those who cannot distinguish the sound from the weak. How many lies, calamities and tales, all of them mere fables, lie buried in the pages of the books of tafsir! Most deserving of blame is the one who has no discernment in the science of narration and no knowledge of it: let him refrain from interpreting the Book of God, and place these follies and absurdities in the places suited to them in the books of the storytellers.

His words, ﴿"If they go out from it, then we will enter."﴾ This is an explicit statement of what is understood from the sentence preceding this one, to clarify that their refusal to enter was for no reason other than this. His words, "Said two men" (﴿قَالَ رَجُلَانِ﴾), are Joshua and Caleb son of Jephunneh, or Caleb son of Fanya, and both were among the twelve chiefs (nuqaba'), as their explanation has already passed.

His words, "from those who fear" (﴿مِنَ الَّذِينَ يَخَافُونَ﴾), mean: who fear God, the Mighty and Majestic. It was also said: from the tyrants, that is, these two men were among the group of people who feared the tyrants. It was also said: from those who feared the weakness and cowardice of the Children of Israel. It was also said that the waw in "yakhafun" belongs to the Children of Israel, meaning: from those whom the Children of Israel feared. Mujahid and Sa‘id ibn Jubayr recited "yukhafun" with a *damma* on the *ya’*, meaning: those whom others feared.

His words, "upon whom God had bestowed favour" (﴿أَنْعَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمَا﴾), are in the nominative position as a second attribute of "two men," with faith and certainty that what they had been promised of victory and triumph would be realised. "Enter upon them through the gate" (﴿ادْخُلُوا عَلَيْهِمُ الْبَابَ﴾) means the gate of the city of the tyrants. "When you have entered it, you will surely be victorious" (﴿فَإِذَا دَخَلْتُمُوهُ فَإِنَّكُمْ غَالِبُونَ﴾). They said this statement to the Children of Israel. The apparent meaning is that they knew this from the report of Moses, or they said it out of confidence in God's promise, or they knew that the hearts of the tyrants had been filled with fear and terror.

"They said," that is, the Children of Israel said to Moses: ﴿"Indeed we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting here."﴾ This statement of theirs was out of weakness and cowardice, or out of obstinacy and audacity against God and His Messenger. They said this out of ignorance of God, the Mighty and Majestic, and of His attributes, and out of disbelief in what is due to Him, or out of contempt for God and His Messenger. It was also said that by "going" they meant intending and resolving. It was also said that by "your Lord" they meant Aaron, who was older than Moses, and Moses used to obey him. "Indeed we are sitting here" means: we will not move from here; we will neither advance with you nor fall back from this place. It was also said that they meant by this not advancing, not not falling back.

Moses said: ﴿"My Lord, I do not possess except myself and my brother. So separate us from the defiant people."﴾ It is possible that "and my brother" is conjoined to "myself," and it is possible that it is conjoined to the pronoun in "I," meaning: I do not possess except myself, and indeed my brother possesses only himself. He said this out of grief and sorrow, and seeking God's help, the Mighty and Majestic. "So separate us" means: distinguish between us, that is himself and his brother, and between the defiant people, and set us apart from them, and do not make us share their punishment. It was also said the meaning is: judge between us and them. It was also said that he only meant in the Hereafter.

‘Ubayd ibn ‘Umayr recited "fa-fruq" with a kasra on the *ra'*. ﴿He said, "Indeed it is forbidden to them for forty years."﴾ "It" means the holy land, and "to them" means these disobedient ones because of their refusal to fight the tyrants. "Forty years" is a time-frame for the prohibition: it is forbidden to them to enter it for this period and no longer. Thus this prohibition does not contradict the earlier statement "which God has prescribed for you," for it is prescribed for whoever remains of them after this period. It was also said that none of those who said "Indeed we will never enter it" entered it, so the setting of this period for the prohibition refers to their descendants. It was also said that "forty years" is a time-frame for His words, "they will wander in the land" (﴿يَتِيهُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾), meaning they will wander for this amount of time, and the prohibition would then be absolute.

The time-limited element is the wandering (*tih*), which in the language means bewilderment. It is said: *tаha yatihu tihan aw tawhan*, when he was bewildered. The meaning is that they were bewildered in the land. It was said that this land in which they wandered was small, about six farsakhs. They would spend the evening where they had risen in the morning, and rise in the morning where they had spent the evening, continuously moving without settling. The people of knowledge disagreed over whether Moses and Aaron were with them. It was said they were not with them, because the wandering was a punishment. It was said they were with them, but God made it easy for them both, as He made the fire cool and safe for Abraham. It has been asked: how can such a thing happen to a group of intelligent people in such a small land for such a long period? Abu ‘Ali said: this may occur by God turning the land on which they were, when they slept, back to the place from which they had started. It may also occur by other causes preventing them from leaving it, by way of a miracle that breaks habit.

‘Abd al-Razzaq, ‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah concerning His words, "and made you kings" (﴿وَجَعَلَكُم مُّلُوكًا﴾), that he said: "their servants made them kings, and they were the first to possess servants." Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ‘Abbas concerning the verse, that he said: "a man among the Children of Israel who had a wife, a servant and a house was called a king." ‘Abd al-Razzaq, ‘Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from him concerning the verse, that he said: "the wife, the servant and the house." al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in Shu‘ab al-Iman related from him also, concerning His words "and made you kings," that he said: "the woman and the servants." ﴿"And gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds"﴾: he said: "those who were among them at that time."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that he said: "When one of the Children of Israel had a servant, a beast and a wife, he was recorded as a king." Ibn Jarir and al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar in al-Mawqifiyyat related from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has a house and a servant is a king."

Abu Dawud in his Marasil related from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning the verse, that he said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "a wife, a dwelling and a servant." Sa‘id ibn Mansur and Ibn Jarir related from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr ibn al-‘As that a man asked him: "Are we not among the poor emigrants?" He said: "Do you have a wife to whom you retreat?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do you have a dwelling in which you live?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then you are among the wealthy." He said: "I have a servant." He said: "Then you are among the kings."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verse 20–28 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abd ibn Humayd narrated, from Mujahid regarding His saying (and He made you kings), that he said: "He made for them wives, servants and houses." ﴿And gave you what He had not given anyone else among the worlds﴾: he said, "The manna and the quails, the stone and the cloud."

Ibn Jarir narrated through the route of Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, that he said: "The manna and the quails, the stone and the cloud." It is established in the sound hadith: "Whoever among you wakes up secure in his body, safe in his dwelling, possessing his food for the day, it is as if the world has been gathered for him with all its parts." Ibn Jarir also narrated from him regarding His saying (Enter the holy land): he said, "It is al-Tur and what surrounds it." He also narrated from him that he said: "It is Ariha (Jericho)."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: "It is what lies between al-'Arish and the Euphrates." Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah, who said: "It is al-Sham (Syria)." Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi regarding His saying ﴿which Allah has prescribed for you﴾, that he said: "The one which Allah commanded you to enter." Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah regarding the verse, who said: "He commanded the people to enter it, just as He commanded us to perform the prayer, the zakat, the hajj and the 'umrah." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas: Musa was commanded to enter the city of the tyrants. He set out with those who were with him until he halted near the city, which is Ariha, and he sent to them twelve spies, one from each tribe, to bring him news of the people. They entered the city and saw a great matter in their appearance, their bodies and their stature. They entered an orchard belonging to one of them, and the owner of the orchard came to pick fruit from his orchard. He began picking fruit and then looked at their traces and followed them. Whenever he came upon one of them, he seized him and placed him in his sleeve among the fruit, until he had gathered all twelve and placed them in his sleeve among the fruit. He went to their king and scattered them before him. The king said: "You have seen our condition and our affair; go and inform your companion." They returned to Musa and informed him of what they had witnessed of their affair. He said: "Keep it hidden from us." But the man began telling his father and his friend, saying: "Keep it hidden from me." Thus it spread through their camp, and only two men did not conceal it from them: Yusha' ibn Nun and Kalib ibn Yufunna, and they are the two about whom Allah revealed ﴿Two men from among those who feared said﴾.

Similar reports have been transmitted which contain exaggeration in describing these people and the greatness of their bodies, and there is no benefit in expounding on that, for most of it is from the fabrications of the storytellers, as we have previously mentioned. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying (so separate) that he said: "Judge." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him that he said: "Distinguish between us and them." Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿it is forbidden to them﴾, that he said: "Forever," and regarding His saying ﴿they will wander in the land﴾, he said: "Forty years."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "They wandered for forty years, and Musa and Harun died in the wandering, and everyone who had passed forty years of age. When the forty years had passed, Yusha' ibn Nun led them forth, and he is the one who took charge of the affair after Musa, and he is the one who conquered it, and he is the one to whom it was said, 'Today is Friday.' They resolved to conquer it, but the sun approached setting, so he feared that if the night of Saturday came they would be forbidden to work. So he called to the sun: 'I am commanded and you are commanded,' and it stood still until he conquered it. He found in it wealth the like of which had never been seen. They brought it near the fire, but it did not come. He said: 'Among you is theft.' So he summoned the heads of the tribes, who were twelve men, and he pledged allegiance to them, and the hand of one man stuck to his hand. He said: 'The stolen goods are with you, so bring it out.' He brought out a calf's head of gold with two eyes of ruby and teeth of pearl, and he placed it with the offerings, and the fire came and consumed them." Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "For them in the wandering were garments that did not wear out and were not soiled."

These verses contain a statement from God, glorified is He, that the forefathers of the Jews who lived in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ) rebelled against Moses and disobeyed him, just as these people rebelled against our Prophet (ﷺ) and disobeyed him. This is also a consolation to him (ﷺ).

It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Kathir that he recited "Ya qawmu adhkuru" (﴿O my people, remember﴾) with a *damma* on the *mim*, and he recited similarly in similar places. Its estimated reading is: "O people, remember the favour of God upon you when He made among you prophets," meaning at the time of this making. Attaching the remembrance to a time, while what is intended is the events that occurred in it, is for emphasis, because the command to remember a time is a command to remember what happened in it by way of priority. God, glorified is He, reminded them of His favour by making prophets among them, even though He made prophets from other peoples too, because of the great number of prophets He sent from among them.

His words, "and made you kings" (﴿وَجَعَلَكُم مُّلُوكًا﴾), mean "and made from among you kings." The preposition was omitted because it is evident that the meaning of the sentence depends on it. It may be said that since the office of prophethood is of great rank and high station, it is not attributed to anyone other than its holder, so He said of it, "when He made among you prophets." But since the office of kingship may be attributed to others than its holder, as one says of the relatives of a king, "We are the kings," He said of it, "and made you kings." It was also said that the meaning of "kings" is that they came to possess their own affairs after they had been subjects of Pharaoh, so they were all kings in this sense. It was also said that it means He made them people of dwellings, into which no one enters except by permission. Other things have been said too. The apparent meaning is that the verse intends true kingship, and if it had another meaning, there would be little point in citing it as a favour. If it is objected that He made others kings as well, the answer is that kings were numerous among them as prophets were numerous, and this is the basis of the favour.

Abu ‘Ali said: this may occur by God turning the land on which they were, when they slept, back to the place from which they had started. It may also occur by other causes preventing them from leaving it, by way of a miracle that breaks habit.

‘Abd al-Razzaq, ‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah concerning His words, "and made you kings" (﴿وَجَعَلَكُم مُّلُوكًا﴾), that he said: "their servants made them kings, and they were the first to possess servants." Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ‘Abbas concerning the verse, that he said: "a man among the Children of Israel who had a wife, a servant and a house was called a king." ‘Abd al-Razzaq, ‘Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from him concerning the verse, that he said: "the wife, the servant and the house." al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in Shu‘ab al-Iman related from him also, concerning His words "and made you kings," that he said: "the woman and the servants." ﴿"And gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds"﴾: he said: "those who were among them at that time."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that he said: "When one of the Children of Israel had a servant, a beast and a wife, he was recorded as a king." Ibn Jarir and al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar in al-Mawqifiyyat related from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has a house and a servant is a king."

Abu Dawud in his Marasil related from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning the verse, that he said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "a wife, a dwelling and a servant." Sa‘id ibn Mansur and Ibn Jarir related from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr ibn al-‘As that a man asked him: "Are we not among the poor emigrants?" He said: "Do you have a wife to whom you retreat?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do you have a dwelling in which you live?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then you are among the wealthy." He said: "I have a servant." He said: "Then you are among the kings."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verse 20–28 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abd ibn Humayd narrated, from Mujahid regarding His saying (and He made you kings), that he said: "He made for them wives, servants and houses." ﴿And gave you what He had not given anyone else among the worlds﴾: he said, "The manna and the quails, the stone and the cloud."

Ibn Jarir narrated through the route of Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, that he said: "The manna and the quails, the stone and the cloud." It is established in the sound hadith: "Whoever among you wakes up secure in his body, safe in his dwelling, possessing his food for the day, it is as if the world has been gathered for him with all its parts." Ibn Jarir also narrated from him regarding His saying (Enter the holy land): he said, "It is al-Tur and what surrounds it." He also narrated from him that he said: "It is Ariha (Jericho)."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: "It is what lies between al-'Arish and the Euphrates." Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah, who said: "It is al-Sham (Syria)." Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi regarding His saying ﴿which Allah has prescribed for you﴾, that he said: "The one which Allah commanded you to enter." Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah regarding the verse, who said: "He commanded the people to enter it, just as He commanded us to perform the prayer, the zakat, the hajj and the 'umrah." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas: Musa was commanded to enter the city of the tyrants. He set out with those who were with him until he halted near the city, which is Ariha, and he sent to them twelve spies, one from each tribe, to bring him news of the people. They entered the city and saw a great matter in their appearance, their bodies and their stature. They entered an orchard belonging to one of them, and the owner of the orchard came to pick fruit from his orchard. He began picking fruit and then looked at their traces and followed them. Whenever he came upon one of them, he seized him and placed him in his sleeve among the fruit, until he had gathered all twelve and placed them in his sleeve among the fruit. He went to their king and scattered them before him. The king said: "You have seen our condition and our affair; go and inform your companion." They returned to Musa and informed him of what they had witnessed of their affair. He said: "Keep it hidden from us." But the man began telling his father and his friend, saying: "Keep it hidden from me." Thus it spread through their camp, and only two men did not conceal it from them: Yusha' ibn Nun and Kalib ibn Yufunna, and they are the two about whom Allah revealed ﴿Two men from among those who feared said﴾.

Similar reports have been transmitted which contain exaggeration in describing these people and the greatness of their bodies, and there is no benefit in expounding on that, for most of it is from the fabrications of the storytellers, as we have previously mentioned. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying (so separate) that he said: "Judge." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him that he said: "Distinguish between us and them." Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿it is forbidden to them﴾, that he said: "Forever," and regarding His saying ﴿they will wander in the land﴾, he said: "Forty years."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "They wandered for forty years, and Musa and Harun died in the wandering, and everyone who had passed forty years of age. When the forty years had passed, Yusha' ibn Nun led them forth, and he is the one who took charge of the affair after Musa, and he is the one who conquered it, and he is the one to whom it was said, 'Today is Friday.' They resolved to conquer it, but the sun approached setting, so he feared that if the night of Saturday came they would be forbidden to work. So he called to the sun: 'I am commanded and you are commanded,' and it stood still until he conquered it. He found in it wealth the like of which had never been seen. They brought it near the fire, but it did not come. He said: 'Among you is theft.' So he summoned the heads of the tribes, who were twelve men, and he pledged allegiance to them, and the hand of one man stuck to his hand. He said: 'The stolen goods are with you, so bring it out.' He brought out a calf's head of gold with two eyes of ruby and teeth of pearl, and he placed it with the offerings, and the fire came and consumed them." Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "For them in the wandering were garments that did not wear out and were not soiled."

These verses contain a statement from God, glorified is He, that the forefathers of the Jews who lived in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ) rebelled against Moses and disobeyed him, just as these people rebelled against our Prophet (ﷺ) and disobeyed him. This is also a consolation to him (ﷺ).

It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Kathir that he recited "Ya qawmu adhkuru" (﴿O my people, remember﴾) with a *damma* on the *mim*, and he recited similarly in similar places. Its estimated reading is: "O people, remember the favour of God upon you when He made among you prophets," meaning at the time of this making. Attaching the remembrance to a time, while what is intended is the events that occurred in it, is for emphasis, because the command to remember a time is a command to remember what happened in it by way of priority. God, glorified is He, reminded them of His favour by making prophets among them, even though He made prophets from other peoples too, because of the great number of prophets He sent from among them.

His words, "and made you kings" (﴿وَجَعَلَكُم مُّلُوكًا﴾), mean "and made from among you kings." The preposition was omitted because it is evident that the meaning of the sentence depends on it. It may be said that since the office of prophethood is of great rank and high station, it is not attributed to anyone other than its holder, so He said of it, "when He made among you prophets." But since the office of kingship may be attributed to others than its holder, as one says of the relatives of a king, "We are the kings," He said of it, "and made you kings." It was also said that the meaning of "kings" is that they came to possess their own affairs after they had been subjects of Pharaoh, so they were all kings in this sense. It was also said that it means He made them people of dwellings, into which no one enters except by permission. Other things have been said too. The apparent meaning is that the verse intends true kingship, and if it had another meaning, there would be little point in citing it as a favour. If it is objected that He made others kings as well, the answer is that kings were numerous among them as prophets were numerous, and this is the basis of the favour.

His words, "and gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds" (﴿وَآتَاكُم مَّا لَمْ يُؤْتِ أَحَدًا مِّنَ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾), mean: what He gave them of the manna and quails, the rock and the cloud, the great number of prophets, the great number of kings, and other things. "The worlds" means the peoples of their time. It was also said that the address here is to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), but this is a deviation from the apparent meaning without a valid reason. The correct view is that held by the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun): that these are the words of Moses to his people, addressing them thus as a preparation and introduction to what follows of his command to them to enter the Holy Land. The Holy Land has been disputed as to its identification. Qatadah said it is Syria; Mujahid said it is Mount Sinai (al-Tur) and what surrounds it; Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and others said it is Ariha (Jericho); al-Zajjaj said it is Damascus, Palestine and part of Jordan. Qatadah's view encompasses the views mentioned after it. "Muqaddasah" means purified, and it was also said blessed. "Which God has prescribed for you" means He apportioned it and destined it for them in His eternal knowledge and made it a dwelling for them. "And do not turn back on your heels" means do not turn back from My command and abandon obedience to Me and what I have obligated you to do, namely fighting the tyrants, out of cowardice and weakness, "so that you will turn back" (﴿فَتَنقَلِبُوا﴾) "losers" (﴿خَاسِرِينَ﴾) in the good of this world and the Hereafter because of that.

﴿They said, "O Moses, indeed in it are a people of tyrants."﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: the *jabbar* among human beings is the obstinate one, who compels people to do what he wants. Its root in this view is from *ijbar*, which means coercion, for he compels others to do what he wants; one says *ajbarahu* when he forces him. It was also said that it derives from *jabara al-‘azm* (setting a bone). On this view, the root of *jabbar* is one who mends his own affairs, and then it was used for anyone who draws benefit to himself, whether rightfully or wrongfully. It was also said that the setting of a bone returns to the meaning of compulsion. Al-Farra' said: I have not heard the form *fa‘‘al* from *af‘ala* except in two words: *jabbar* from *ajbara*, and *darrak* from *adraka*.

The intended meaning here is that they were a people of large bodies, tall and arrogant. It was said they were some of the remnant of the people of ‘Ad. It was said they were of the descendants of Esau son of Isaac. It was said they were of the Romans. It is also said that among them was ‘Awj ibn ‘Unuq, famous for excessive height, and that ‘Unuq was a daughter of Adam. It was said his height was three thousand three hundred and thirty-three and a third cubits. Ibn Kathir said: this is something one should be ashamed to mention. Moreover, it contradicts what is established in the two Sahihs, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God created Adam, and his height was sixty cubits. Then creation continued to diminish." Furthermore, they mentioned that this man was a disbeliever, that he was the son of an adulteress, that he refused to board the ark, and that the flood did not reach his knees. This is a lie and a fabrication, for God mentioned that Noah prayed against the disbelievers on earth, saying: ﴿My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers a single dweller﴾ [Nuh: 26]. He also said: ﴿Then We saved him and those with him in the laden ship; then We drowned the rest afterwards﴾ [al-Shu‘ara: 119–120]. And He said: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of God, except for whom He has mercy﴾ [Hud: 43]. If Noah's disbelieving son drowned, how could ‘Awj ibn ‘Unuq remain, being a disbeliever and the son of an adulteress? This is not permissible in reason or in law. Moreover, the existence of a man called ‘Awj ibn ‘Unuq is open to question, and God knows best. End of his words.

I say: nothing has come concerning this man that calls for lengthy discussion about him. This is not the first lie that has become famous among people. We are not obliged to refute the falsehoods that storytellers (qussas) invented and which circulated among those who cannot distinguish the sound from the weak. How many lies, calamities and tales, all of them mere fables, lie buried in the pages of the books of tafsir! Most deserving of blame is the one who has no discernment in the science of narration and no knowledge of it: let him refrain from interpreting the Book of God, and place these follies and absurdities in the places suited to them in the books of the storytellers.

His words, ﴿"If they go out from it, then we will enter."﴾ This is an explicit statement of what is understood from the sentence preceding this one, to clarify that their refusal to enter was for no reason other than this. His words, "Said two men" (﴿قَالَ رَجُلَانِ﴾), are Joshua and Caleb son of Jephunneh, or Caleb son of Fanya, and both were among the twelve chiefs (nuqaba'), as their explanation has already passed.

His words, "from those who fear" (﴿مِنَ الَّذِينَ يَخَافُونَ﴾), mean: who fear God, the Mighty and Majestic. It was also said: from the tyrants, that is, these two men were among the group of people who feared the tyrants. It was also said: from those who feared the weakness and cowardice of the Children of Israel. It was also said that the waw in "yakhafun" belongs to the Children of Israel, meaning: from those whom the Children of Israel feared. Mujahid and Sa‘id ibn Jubayr recited "yukhafun" with a *damma* on the *ya’*, meaning: those whom others feared.

His words, "upon whom God had bestowed favour" (﴿أَنْعَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمَا﴾), are in the nominative position as a second attribute of "two men," with faith and certainty that what they had been promised of victory and triumph would be realised. "Enter upon them through the gate" (﴿ادْخُلُوا عَلَيْهِمُ الْبَابَ﴾) means the gate of the city of the tyrants. "When you have entered it, you will surely be victorious" (﴿فَإِذَا دَخَلْتُمُوهُ فَإِنَّكُمْ غَالِبُونَ﴾). They said this statement to the Children of Israel. The apparent meaning is that they knew this from the report of Moses, or they said it out of confidence in God's promise, or they knew that the hearts of the tyrants had been filled with fear and terror.

"They said," that is, the Children of Israel said to Moses: ﴿"Indeed we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting here."﴾ This statement of theirs was out of weakness and cowardice, or out of obstinacy and audacity against God and His Messenger. They said this out of ignorance of God, the Mighty and Majestic, and of His attributes, and out of disbelief in what is due to Him, or out of contempt for God and His Messenger. It was also said that by "going" they meant intending and resolving. It was also said that by "your Lord" they meant Aaron, who was older than Moses, and Moses used to obey him. "Indeed we are sitting here" means: we will not move from here; we will neither advance with you nor fall back from this place. It was also said that they meant by this not advancing, not not falling back.

Moses said: ﴿"My Lord, I do not possess except myself and my brother. So separate us from the defiant people."﴾ It is possible that "and my brother" is conjoined to "myself," and it is possible that it is conjoined to the pronoun in "I," meaning: I do not possess except myself, and indeed my brother possesses only himself. He said this out of grief and sorrow, and seeking God's help, the Mighty and Majestic. "So separate us" means: distinguish between us, that is himself and his brother, and between the defiant people, and set us apart from them, and do not make us share their punishment. It was also said the meaning is: judge between us and them. It was also said that he only meant in the Hereafter.

‘Ubayd ibn ‘Umayr recited "fa-fruq" with a kasra on the *ra'*. ﴿He said, "Indeed it is forbidden to them for forty years."﴾ "It" means the holy land, and "to them" means these disobedient ones because of their refusal to fight the tyrants. "Forty years" is a time-frame for the prohibition: it is forbidden to them to enter it for this period and no longer. Thus this prohibition does not contradict the earlier statement "which God has prescribed for you," for it is prescribed for whoever remains of them after this period. It was also said that none of those who said "Indeed we will never enter it" entered it, so the setting of this period for the prohibition refers to their descendants. It was also said that "forty years" is a time-frame for His words, "they will wander in the land" (﴿يَتِيهُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾), meaning they will wander for this amount of time, and the prohibition would then be absolute.

The time-limited element is the wandering (*tih*), which in the language means bewilderment. It is said: *tаha yatihu tihan aw tawhan*, when he was bewildered. The meaning is that they were bewildered in the land. It was said that this land in which they wandered was small, about six farsakhs. They would spend the evening where they had risen in the morning, and rise in the morning where they had spent the evening, continuously moving without settling. The people of knowledge disagreed over whether Moses and Aaron were with them. It was said they were not with them, because the wandering was a punishment. It was said they were with them, but God made it easy for them both, as He made the fire cool and safe for Abraham. It has been asked: how can such a thing happen to a group of intelligent people in such a small land for such a long period? Abu ‘Ali said: this may occur by God turning the land on which they were, when they slept, back to the place from which they had started. It may also occur by other causes preventing them from leaving it, by way of a miracle that breaks habit.

‘Abd al-Razzaq, ‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah concerning His words, "and made you kings" (﴿وَجَعَلَكُم مُّلُوكًا﴾), that he said: "their servants made them kings, and they were the first to possess servants." Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ‘Abbas concerning the verse, that he said: "a man among the Children of Israel who had a wife, a servant and a house was called a king." ‘Abd al-Razzaq, ‘Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from him concerning the verse, that he said: "the wife, the servant and the house." al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in Shu‘ab al-Iman related from him also, concerning His words "and made you kings," that he said: "the woman and the servants." ﴿"And gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds"﴾: he said: "those who were among them at that time."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that he said: "When one of the Children of Israel had a servant, a beast and a wife, he was recorded as a king." Ibn Jarir and al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar in al-Mawqifiyyat related from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has a house and a servant is a king."

Abu Dawud in his Marasil related from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning the verse, that he said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "a wife, a dwelling and a servant." Sa‘id ibn Mansur and Ibn Jarir related from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr ibn al-‘As that a man asked him: "Are we not among the poor emigrants?" He said: "Do you have a wife to whom you retreat?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do you have a dwelling in which you live?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then you are among the wealthy." He said: "I have a servant." He said: "Then you are among the kings."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verse 20–28 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abd ibn Humayd narrated, from Mujahid regarding His saying (and He made you kings), that he said: "He made for them wives, servants and houses." ﴿And gave you what He had not given anyone else among the worlds﴾: he said, "The manna and the quails, the stone and the cloud."

Ibn Jarir narrated through the route of Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, that he said: "The manna and the quails, the stone and the cloud." It is established in the sound hadith: "Whoever among you wakes up secure in his body, safe in his dwelling, possessing his food for the day, it is as if the world has been gathered for him with all its parts." Ibn Jarir also narrated from him regarding His saying (Enter the holy land): he said, "It is al-Tur and what surrounds it." He also narrated from him that he said: "It is Ariha (Jericho)."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: "It is what lies between al-'Arish and the Euphrates." Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah, who said: "It is al-Sham (Syria)." Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah regarding the verse, who said: "He commanded the people to enter it, just as He commanded us to perform the prayer, the zakat, the hajj and the 'umrah." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas: Musa was commanded to enter the city of the tyrants. He set out with those who were with him until he halted near the city, which is Ariha, and he sent to them twelve spies, one from each tribe, to bring him news of the people. They entered the city and saw a great matter in their appearance, their bodies and their stature. They entered an orchard belonging to one of them, and the owner of the orchard came to pick fruit from his orchard. He began picking fruit and then looked at their traces and followed them. Whenever he came upon one of them, he seized him and placed him in his sleeve among the fruit, until he had gathered all twelve and placed them in his sleeve among the fruit. He went to their king and scattered them before him. The king said: "You have seen our condition and our affair; go and inform your companion." Similar reports have been transmitted which contain exaggeration in describing these people and the greatness of their bodies, and there is no benefit in expounding on that, for most of it is from the fabrications of the storytellers, as we have previously mentioned. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying (so separate) that he said: "Judge." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him that he said: "Distinguish between us and them." Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿it is forbidden to them﴾, that he said: "Forever," and regarding His saying ﴿they will wander in the land﴾, he said: "Forty years."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "They wandered for forty years, and Musa and Harun died in the wandering, and everyone who had passed forty years of age. When the forty years had passed, Yusha' ibn Nun led them forth, and he is the one who took charge of the affair after Musa, and he is the one who conquered it, and he is the one to whom it was said, 'Today is Friday.' They resolved to conquer it, but the sun approached setting, so he feared that if the night of Saturday came they would be forbidden to work. So he called to the sun: 'I am commanded and you are commanded,' and it stood still until he conquered it. He found in it wealth the like of which had never been seen. They brought it near the fire, but it did not come. He said: 'Among you is theft.' So he summoned the heads of the tribes, who were twelve men, and he pledged allegiance to them, and the hand of one man stuck to his hand. He said: 'The stolen goods are with you, so bring it out.' He brought out a calf's head of gold with two eyes of ruby and teeth of pearl, and he placed it with the offerings, and the fire came and consumed them." Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "For them in the wandering were garments that did not wear out and were not soiled."

These verses contain a statement from God, glorified is He, that the forefathers of the Jews who lived in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ) rebelled against Moses and disobeyed him, just as these people rebelled against our Prophet (ﷺ) and disobeyed him. This is also a consolation to him (ﷺ).

It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Kathir that he recited "Ya qawmu adhkuru" (﴿O my people, remember﴾) with a *damma* on the *mim*, and he recited similarly in similar places. His words, "and made you kings" (﴿وَجَعَلَكُم مُّلُوكًا﴾), mean "and made from among you kings." The preposition was omitted because it is evident that the meaning of the sentence depends on it. The Holy Land has been disputed as to its identification. Qatadah's view encompasses the views mentioned after it. "Muqaddasah" means purified, and it was also said blessed. "Which God has prescribed for you" means He apportioned it and destined it for them in His eternal knowledge and made it a dwelling for them. "And do not turn back on your heels" means do not turn back from My command and abandon obedience to Me and what I have obligated you to do, namely fighting the tyrants, out of cowardice and weakness, "so that you will turn back" (﴿فَتَنقَلِبُوا﴾) "losers" (﴿خَاسِرِينَ﴾) in the good of this world and the Hereafter because of that.

﴿They said, "O Moses, indeed in it are a people of tyrants."﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: the *jabbar* among human beings is the obstinate one, who compels people to do what he wants. Its root in this view is from *ijbar*, which means coercion, for he compels others to do what he wants; one says *ajbarahu* when he forces him. It was also said that it derives from *jabara al-‘azm* (setting a bone). On this view, the root of *jabbar* is one who mends his own affairs, and then it was used for anyone who draws benefit to himself, whether rightfully or wrongfully. It was also said that the setting of a bone returns to the meaning of compulsion. Al-Farra' said: I have not heard the form *fa‘‘al* from *af‘ala* except in two words: *jabbar* from *ajbara*, and *darrak* from *adraka*.

The intended meaning here is that they were a people of large bodies, tall and arrogant. It was said they were some of the remnant of the people of ‘Ad. It was said they were of the descendants of Esau son of Isaac. It was said they were of the Romans. It is also said that among them was ‘Awj ibn ‘Unuq, famous for excessive height, and that ‘Unuq was a daughter of Adam. It was said his height was three thousand three hundred and thirty-three and a third cubits. Ibn Kathir said: this is something one should be ashamed to mention. Moreover, it contradicts what is established in the two Sahihs, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God created Adam, and his height was sixty cubits. Then creation continued to diminish." Furthermore, they mentioned that this man was a disbeliever, that he was the son of an adulteress, that he refused to board the ark, and that the flood did not reach his knees. This is a lie and a fabrication, for God mentioned that Noah prayed against the disbelievers on earth, saying: ﴿My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers a single dweller﴾ [Nuh: 26]. He also said: ﴿Then We saved him and those with him in the laden ship; then We drowned the rest afterwards﴾ [al-Shu‘ara: 119–120]. And He said: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of God, except for whom He has mercy﴾ [Hud: 43]. If Noah's disbelieving son drowned, how could ‘Awj ibn ‘Unuq remain, being a disbeliever and the son of an adulteress? This is not permissible in reason or in law. Moreover, the existence of a man called ‘Awj ibn ‘Unuq is open to question, and God knows best. End of his words.

I say: nothing has come concerning this man that calls for lengthy discussion about him. This is not the first lie that has become famous among people. We are not obliged to refute the falsehoods that storytellers (qussas) invented and which circulated among those who cannot distinguish the sound from the weak. How many lies, calamities and tales, all of them mere fables, lie buried in the pages of the books of tafsir! Most deserving of blame is the one who has no discernment in the science of narration and no knowledge of it: let him refrain from interpreting the Book of God, and place these follies and absurdities in the places suited to them in the books of the storytellers.

His words, ﴿"If they go out from it, then we will enter."﴾ This is an explicit statement of what is understood from the sentence preceding this one, to clarify that their refusal to enter was for no reason other than this. His words, "Said two men" (﴿قَالَ رَجُلَانِ﴾), are Joshua and Caleb son of Jephunneh, or Caleb son of Fanya, and both were among the twelve chiefs (nuqaba'), as their explanation has already passed.

His words, "from those who fear" (﴿مِنَ الَّذِينَ يَخَافُونَ﴾), mean: who fear God, the Mighty and Majestic. It was also said: from the tyrants, that is, these two men were among the group of people who feared the tyrants. It was also said: from those who feared the weakness and cowardice of the Children of Israel. It was also said that the waw in "yakhafun" belongs to the Children of Israel, meaning: from those whom the Children of Israel feared. Mujahid and Sa‘id ibn Jubayr recited "yukhafun" with a *damma* on the *ya’*, meaning: those whom others feared.

His words, "upon whom God had bestowed favour" (﴿أَنْعَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمَا﴾), are in the nominative position as a second attribute of "two men," with faith and certainty that what they had been promised of victory and triumph would be realised. "Enter upon them through the gate" (﴿ادْخُلُوا عَلَيْهِمُ الْبَابَ﴾) means the gate of the city of the tyrants. "When you have entered it, you will surely be victorious" (﴿فَإِذَا دَخَلْتُمُوهُ فَإِنَّكُمْ غَالِبُونَ﴾). They said this statement to the Children of Israel. The apparent meaning is that they knew this from the report of Moses, or they said it out of confidence in God's promise, or they knew that the hearts of the tyrants had been filled with fear and terror.

"They said," that is, the Children of Israel said to Moses: ﴿"Indeed we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting here."﴾ This statement of theirs was out of weakness and cowardice, or out of obstinacy and audacity against God and His Messenger. They said this out of ignorance of God, the Mighty and Majestic, and of His attributes, and out of disbelief in what is due to Him, or out of contempt for God and His Messenger. It was also said that by "going" they meant intending and resolving. It was also said that by "your Lord" they meant Aaron, who was older than Moses, and Moses used to obey him. "Indeed we are sitting here" means: we will not move from here; we will neither advance with you nor fall back from this place. It was also said that they meant by this not advancing, not not falling back.

Moses said: ﴿"My Lord, I do not possess except myself and my brother. So separate us from the defiant people."﴾ It is possible that "and my brother" is conjoined to "myself," and it is possible that it is conjoined to the pronoun in "I," meaning: I do not possess except myself, and indeed my brother possesses only himself. He said this out of grief and sorrow, and seeking God's help, the Mighty and Majestic. "So separate us" means: distinguish between us, that is himself and his brother, and between the defiant people, and set us apart from them, and do not make us share their punishment. It was also said the meaning is: judge between us and them. It was also said that he only meant in the Hereafter.

‘Ubayd ibn ‘Umayr recited "fa-fruq" with a kasra on the *ra'*. ﴿He said, "Indeed it is forbidden to them for forty years."﴾ "It" means the holy land, and "to them" means these disobedient ones because of their refusal to fight the tyrants. "Forty years" is a time-frame for the prohibition: it is forbidden to them to enter it for this period and no longer. Thus this prohibition does not contradict the earlier statement "which God has prescribed for you," for it is prescribed for whoever remains of them after this period. It was also said that none of those who said "Indeed we will never enter it" entered it, so the setting of this period for the prohibition refers to their descendants. It was also said that "forty years" is a time-frame for His words, "they will wander in the land" (﴿يَتِيهُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾), meaning they will wander for this amount of time, and the prohibition would then be absolute.

The time-limited element is the wandering (*tih*), which in the language means bewilderment. It is said: *tаha yatihu tihan aw tawhan*, when he was bewildered. The meaning is that they were bewildered in the land. It was said that this land in which they wandered was small, about six farsakhs. They would spend the evening where they had risen in the morning, and rise in the morning where they had spent the evening, continuously moving without settling. The people of knowledge disagreed over whether Moses and Aaron were with them. It was said they were not with them, because the wandering was a punishment. It was said they were with them, but God made it easy for them both, as He made the fire cool and safe for Abraham. It has been asked: how can such a thing happen to a group of intelligent people in such a small land for such a long period? Abu ‘Ali said: this may occur by God turning the land on which they were, when they slept, back to the place from which they had started. It may also occur by other causes preventing them from leaving it, by way of a miracle that breaks habit.

‘Abd al-Razzaq, ‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah concerning His words, "and made you kings" (﴿وَجَعَلَكُم مُّلُوكًا﴾), that he said: "their servants made them kings, and they were the first to possess servants." Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ‘Abbas concerning the verse, that he said: "a man among the Children of Israel who had a wife, a servant and a house was called a king." ‘Abd al-Razzaq, ‘Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from him concerning the verse, that he said: "the wife, the servant and the house." al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in Shu‘ab al-Iman related from him also, concerning His words "and made you kings," that he said: "the woman and the servants." ﴿"And gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds"﴾: he said: "those who were among them at that time."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that he said: "When one of the Children of Israel had a servant, a beast and a wife, he was recorded as a king." Ibn Jarir and al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar in al-Mawqifiyyat related from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has a house and a servant is a king."

Abu Dawud in his Marasil related from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning the verse, that he said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "a wife, a dwelling and a servant." Sa‘id ibn Mansur and Ibn Jarir related from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr ibn al-‘As that a man asked him: "Are we not among the poor emigrants?" He said: "Do you have a wife to whom you retreat?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do you have a dwelling in which you live?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then you are among the wealthy." He said: "I have a servant." He said: "Then you are among the kings."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verse 20–28 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abd ibn Humayd narrated, from Mujahid regarding His saying (and He made you kings), that he said: "He made for them wives, servants and houses." ﴿And gave you what He had not given anyone else among the worlds﴾: he said, "The manna and the quails, the stone and the cloud."

Ibn Jarir narrated through the route of Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, that he said: "The manna and the quails, the stone and the cloud." It is established in the sound hadith: "Whoever among you wakes up secure in his body, safe in his dwelling, possessing his food for the day, it is as if the world has been gathered for him with all its parts." Ibn Jarir also narrated from him regarding His saying (Enter the holy land): he said, "It is al-Tur and what surrounds it." He also narrated from him that he said: "It is Ariha (Jericho)."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: "It is what lies between al-'Arish and the Euphrates." Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah, who said: "It is al-Sham (Syria)." Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi regarding His saying ﴿which Allah has prescribed for you﴾, that he said: "The one which Allah commanded you to enter." Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah regarding the verse, who said: "He commanded the people to enter it, just as He commanded us to perform the prayer, the zakat, the hajj and the 'umrah." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas: Musa was commanded to enter the city of the tyrants. He set out with those who were with him until he halted near the city, which is Ariha, and he sent to them twelve spies, one from each tribe, to bring him news of the people. They entered the city and saw a great matter in their appearance, their bodies and their stature. They entered an orchard belonging to one of them, and the owner of the orchard came to pick fruit from his orchard. He began picking fruit and then looked at their traces and followed them. Whenever he came upon one of them, he seized him and placed him in his sleeve among the fruit, until he had gathered all twelve and placed them in his sleeve among the fruit. He went to their king and scattered them before him. The king said: "You have seen our condition and our affair; go and inform your companion." They returned to Musa and informed him of what they had witnessed of their affair. He said: "Keep it hidden from us." But the man began telling his father and his friend, saying: "Keep it hidden from me." Thus it spread through their camp, and only two men did not conceal it from them: Yusha' ibn Nun and Kalib ibn Yufunna, and they are the two about whom Allah revealed ﴿Two men from among those who feared said﴾.

Similar reports have been transmitted which contain exaggeration in describing these people and the greatness of their bodies, and there is no benefit in expounding on that, for most of it is from the fabrications of the storytellers, as we have previously mentioned. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying (so separate) that he said: "Judge." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him that he said: "Distinguish between us and them." Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿it is forbidden to them﴾, that he said: "Forever," and regarding His saying ﴿they will wander in the land﴾, he said: "Forty years."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "They wandered for forty years, and Musa and Harun died in the wandering, and everyone who had passed forty years of age. When the forty years had passed, Yusha' ibn Nun led them forth, and he is the one who took charge of the affair after Musa, and he is the one who conquered it, and he is the one to whom it was said, 'Today is Friday.' They resolved to conquer it, but the sun approached setting, so he feared that if the night of Saturday came they would be forbidden to work. So he called to the sun: 'I am commanded and you are commanded,' and it stood still until he conquered it. He found in it wealth the like of which had never been seen. They brought it near the fire, but it did not come. He said: 'Among you is theft.' So he summoned the heads of the tribes, who were twelve men, and he pledged allegiance to them, and the hand of one man stuck to his hand. He said: 'The stolen goods are with you, so bring it out.' He brought out a calf's head of gold with two eyes of ruby and teeth of pearl, and he placed it with the offerings, and the fire came and consumed them." Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "For them in the wandering were garments that did not wear out and were not soiled."

These verses contain a statement from God, glorified is He, that the forefathers of the Jews who lived in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ) rebelled against Moses and disobeyed him, just as these people rebelled against our Prophet (ﷺ) and disobeyed him. This is also a consolation to him (ﷺ).

It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Kathir that he recited "Ya qawmu adhkuru" (﴿O my people, remember﴾) with a *damma* on the *mim*, and he recited similarly in similar places. Its estimated reading is: "O people, remember the favour of God upon you when He made among you prophets," meaning at the time of this making. Attaching the remembrance to a time, while what is intended is the events that occurred in it, is for emphasis, because the command to remember a time is a command to remember what happened in it by way of priority. God, glorified is He, reminded them of His favour by making prophets among them, even though He made prophets from other peoples too, because of the great number of prophets He sent from among them.

His words, "and made you kings" (﴿وَجَعَلَكُم مُّلُوكًا﴾), mean "and made from among you kings." The preposition was omitted because it is evident that the meaning of the sentence depends on it. It may be said that since the office of prophethood is of great rank and high station, it is not attributed to anyone other than its holder, so He said of it, "when He made among you prophets." But since the office of kingship may be attributed to others than its holder, as one says of the relatives of a king, "We are the kings," He said of it, "and made you kings." It was also said that the meaning of "kings" is that they came to possess their own affairs after they had been subjects of Pharaoh, so they were all kings in this sense. It was also said that it means He made them people of dwellings, into which no one enters except by permission. Other things have been said too. The apparent meaning is that the verse intends true kingship, and if it had another meaning, there would be little point in citing it as a favour. If it is objected that He made others kings as well, the answer is that kings were numerous among them as prophets were numerous, and this is the basis of the favour.

His words, "and gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds" (﴿وَآتَاكُم مَّا لَمْ يُؤْتِ أَحَدًا مِّنَ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾), mean: what He gave them of the manna and quails, the rock and the cloud, the great number of prophets, the great number of kings, and other things. "The worlds" means the peoples of their time. It was also said that the address here is to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), but this is a deviation from the apparent meaning without a valid reason. The correct view is that held by the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun): that these are the words of Moses to his people, addressing them thus as a preparation and introduction to what follows of his command to them to enter the Holy Land. The Holy Land has been disputed as to its identification. Qatadah said it is Syria; Mujahid said it is Mount Sinai (al-Tur) and what surrounds it; Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and others said it is Ariha (Jericho); al-Zajjaj said it is Damascus, Palestine and part of Jordan. Qatadah's view encompasses the views mentioned after it. "Muqaddasah" means purified, and it was also said blessed. "Which God has prescribed for you" means He apportioned it and destined it for them in His eternal knowledge and made it a dwelling for them. "And do not turn back on your heels" means do not turn back from My command and abandon obedience to Me and what I have obligated you to do, namely fighting the tyrants, out of cowardice and weakness, "so that you will turn back" (﴿فَتَنقَلِبُوا﴾) "losers" (﴿خَاسِرِينَ﴾) in the good of this world and the Hereafter because of that.
