So said a group of the early generations (salaf). Qabil's offering was not accepted, so he envied his brother and said: "I will surely kill you."

It was also said that the reason for this offering was that Hawwa' (Eve) would give birth to a male and a female in every pregnancy, except Shith (peace be upon him), whom she bore alone. Adam (peace be upon him) would marry the male of one birth to the female of another birth, and a man could not marry his twin sister. Qabil was born with a beautiful sister named Iqlima, and Habil was born with a sister who was not so beautiful, named Layuda. When Adam wanted to marry them off, Qabil said: "I have a better right to my sister." Adam ordered him otherwise, but he did not obey, and when he was rebuked he did not desist. So they agreed on the offering, and that whoever's offering was accepted would marry her.

His saying ﴿بِالحَقِّ﴾ (with truth) is connected with an omitted element that stands as a qualifier of a verbal noun, meaning "a recitation (tilawa) accompanied by truth"; or it is a qualifier of ﴿نَبَأَ﴾ (the account), meaning "an account accompanied by truth." By one of them is meant Habil, and by the other Qabil. His saying ﴿قالَ لَأَقْتُلَنَّكَ﴾ (He said: "I will surely kill you") is an explanatory resumptive clause, as if it were said: "What then was the situation of the one whose offering was not accepted?" His saying ﴿قالَ إنَّما يَتَقَبَّلُ اللَّهُ مِنَ المُتَّقِينَ﴾ (He said: "God only accepts from the God-fearing") is also a resumptive clause, as if it were said: "What then did the one whose offering was accepted say?" The word ﴿إنَّما﴾ (only) here expresses restriction: God accepts offerings only from the God-fearing, not from others. It is as if he were saying to his brother: "You were brought to this by yourself, not by me, for the non-acceptance of your offering is due to the absence of your piety."

His saying ﴿لَئِنْ بَسَطْتَ إلَيَّ يَدَكَ لِتَقْتُلَنِي﴾ (If you extend your hand to me to kill me) means: if you intend to kill me. The lam is the one that introduces the oath, and ﴿ما أنا بباسِطٍ﴾ (I shall not extend my hand) is the answer to the oath, standing in place of the answer to the condition. This is Habil's submission to being killed, as occurs in the hadith: "When strife occurs, be like the better of the two sons of Adam," and the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse. Mujahid said: "At that time the obligation upon them was that no one should draw a sword, and that no one should resist one who intended to kill him." Al-Qurtubi said: "Our scholars said: that is among the things for which worship by such a law may have been revealed. However, in our law it is permitted to repel such an attack by consensus, and there is disagreement over whether it is obligatory. The more sound view is that it is obligatory, because of what it contains of forbidding evil."

Among the Hashwiyya (a term for certain literalist and uncritical groups) there are people who do not permit the one who is attacked to defend himself, and they argued with the hadith of Abu Dharr. The scholars interpreted it as referring to abstaining from fighting in strife and restraining the hand in cases of doubt, as I have explained in my book al-Tadhkira. This ends the words of al-Qurtubi. The hadith of Abu Dharr referred to is in Muslim and the authors of the Sunan, except al-Nasa'i, and in it: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'O Abu Dharr, what would you do if people kill one another?' I said: 'God and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'Stay in your house and close your door upon yourself.' I said: 'If I am not left alone?' He said: 'Then go to those among whom you belong and be among them.' I said: 'Shall I take up my weapon?' He said: 'Then you would be sharing in what they are doing. But if you fear that the glint of the sword will daze you, then throw the end of your garment over your face, so that he may bear his sin and your sin.'" There are similar hadiths from a number of the Companions: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Abu Hurayra, Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, Abu Bakr, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Waqid, and Abu Musa.

His saying ﴿إنِّي أُرِيدُ أنْ تَبُوءَ بِإثْمِي وإثْمِكَ فَتَكُونَ مِن أصْحابِ النّارِ﴾ (Indeed I want you to bear my sin and your sin, and so be among the companions of the Fire) is a reason given for his refraining from fighting, following the first reason, which is ﴿إنِّي أخافُ اللَّهَ رَبَّ العالَمِينَ﴾ (Indeed I fear God, the Lord of the worlds).

The exegetes differed over the meaning. It was said: Habil meant: "I want you to bear the sin that would have fallen upon me had I been eager to kill you, and your sin that you incurred by killing me." It was also said: the meaning of "my sin" is the sin peculiar to me, for a reason that will come, and it will be cast upon you because of your wronging me, and you will bear your sin in killing me. This agrees with what is established in Sahih Muslim from the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "On the Day of Resurrection the wrongdoer and the wronged will be brought, and some of the wrongdoer's good deeds will be taken and added to the good deeds of the wronged until he is compensated. If he has no good deeds, some of the wronged one's evil deeds will be taken and cast upon him." A similar statement is God's saying: ﴿وَلَيَحْمِلُنَّ أَثْقَالَهُمْ وَأَثْقَالًا مَعَ أَثْقَالِهِمْ﴾ (They will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens) [al-'Ankabut: 13]. It was also said: the meaning is: "I want you not to bear my sin and your sin," as in God's saying: ﴿وَأَلْقَى فِي الْأَرْضِ رَوَاسِيَ أَنْ تَمِيدَ بِكُمْ﴾ (And He cast firm mountains upon the earth lest it shake with you) [al-Nahl: 15], meaning: lest it shake with you. And His saying: ﴿يُبَيِّنُ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ أَنْ تَضِلُّوا﴾ (God makes clear to you lest you go astray) [al-Nisa': 176], meaning: lest you go astray.

Most scholars said that the meaning is: "I want you to bear my sin," that is, the sin of your killing me, "and your sin," which has already become upon you because of your wrongdoings before killing me. Al-Tha'labi said: "This is the view of the majority of the exegetes." It was also said that it is in the form of denial; that is, "Or do I want...," in the manner of God's saying: ﴿وَتِلْكَ نِعْمَةٌ﴾ (And is it a favour) [al-Shu'ara': 22], meaning: "Or is it a favour?" This was said by al-Qushayri, and its justification is that the intention to kill is itself a sin.

Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan was asked: "How can a believer want his brother to sin and to enter the Fire?" He answered: "The intention came after he had extended his hand to kill him." This is very far-fetched, and so is what preceded it. The root of "ba'a" means to return to a place of lodging (mabaa'a), which is a dwelling, as in ﴿وَبَاءُوا بِغَضَبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ (And they returned with wrath from God) [Al 'Imran: 112], meaning: they returned.

His saying ﴿فَطَوَّعَتْ لَهُ نَفْسُهُ قَتْلَ أخِيهِ﴾ (So his soul made the killing of his brother easy for him) means: his soul made the matter easy for him, encouraged him, and presented to him that killing his brother was easy and within his power. It is said: "taṭawwaʿa al-shay'" means it became easy and submissive, and "ṭawwaʿahu fulan lahu" means he made it easy for him. Al-Harawi said: "ṭawwaʿat" and "ṭaawaʿat" are the same; it is said "ṭaʿa lahu kadhā" when one comes to it willingly. The mention of his soul making it easy for him, after what preceded of Qabil's saying ﴿لَأَقْتُلَنَّكَ﴾ (I will surely kill you) and Habil's saying ﴿لِتَقْتُلَنِي﴾ (to kill me), is evidence that this making-easy had not yet occurred at the time of that exchange.

His saying ﴿فَقَتَلَهُ﴾ (so he killed him). Ibn Jarir, Mujahid and others said: It is narrated that he did not know how to kill his brother, so Iblis came to him with a bird or another animal, and began to smash its head between two stones, so that Qabil would imitate him, and he did so. It was also said other than this, which requires verification of the narration.

His saying ﴿فَبَعَثَ اللَّهُ غُرَابًا يَبْحَثُ فِي الْأَرْضِ لِيُرِيَهُ كَيْفَ يُوَارِي سَوْءَةَ أَخِيهِ﴾ (Then God sent a crow scratching in the earth to show him how to cover his brother's corpse). It was said: When he killed his brother, he did not know how to conceal him, since he was the first dead person of the children of Adam. So God sent two crows, brothers, who fought, and one of them killed the other. It then dug a hole for it and covered it with earth. When Qabil saw this, he said: ﴿يَا وَيْلَتَا أَعَجَزْتُ أَنْ أَكُونَ مِثْلَ هَذَا الْغُرَابِ فَأُوَارِيَ سَوْءَةَ أَخِي﴾ (Woe is me! Am I unable to be like this crow and cover my brother's corpse?), and he covered him. The pronoun in ﴿لِيُرِيَهُ﴾ (to show him) refers to the crow, and it was said that it refers to God, may He be exalted. The phrase ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ (how) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial element relating to the pronoun in ﴿يُوَارِي﴾ (covers), and the clause is the second object of ﴿يُرِيَهُ﴾. By ﴿السَّوْءَةِ﴾ (the nakedness/corpse) here is meant his whole body, since it was dead. The word ﴿قالَ﴾ (he said) is a resumptive response to an implied question arising from the flow of the discourse, as if it were said: "What did he say when he saw the crow doing that?" The phrase ﴿يا وَيْلَتَى﴾ (Woe is me!) is an expression of grief and sorrow, and the alif is a substitute for the first-person ya', as if he were calling upon his destruction to come at that moment. The "waylah" is ruin. The speech comes out in the manner of expressing astonishment at his own failure to cover his brother, just as the crow was guided to that. The word ﴿فَأُوَارِيَ﴾ (so that I might cover) is in the accusative as the answer to the interrogative. It was also read with a sukun, as an implied "fa-ana uwari" (so I cover). ﴿فَأَصْبَحَ مِنَ النَّادِمِينَ﴾ (So he became among the regretful) for having killed him. It was said that his regret was not the regret of repentance, but that he regretted losing him, not his killing. It was also said other things.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "He forbade a woman from marrying her twin brother, and from marrying her to anyone other than her brothers. Every pregnancy produced a man and a woman. While they were in this state, he had a beautiful daughter and another son who was ugly and unsightly. The brother of the ugly one said: 'Marry me to your sister and I will marry you to mine.' He said: 'No, I have a better right to my sister.' So they offered an offering. The owner of the flock brought a ram, white-horned, with bright eyes, and the owner of the crop brought a heap of grain. The offering of the owner of the ram was accepted, and the offering of the owner of the crop was not accepted." Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: "Its chain is good," and al-Suyuti said the same in al-Durr al-Manthur.

Ibn Jarir narrated from him: "It was among the practices of the children of Adam that no poor person was given charity, but the offering was made by a man himself. While the two sons of Adam were sitting, they said: 'If we were to offer an offering,' and then they mentioned what each of them had offered."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid concerning ﴿لَئِنْ بَسَطْتَ إلَيَّ يَدَكَ﴾ (If you extend your hand to me) that he said: "It was prescribed for them that if a man intended to kill another, he should leave him and not resist him." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated something similar from Ibn Jurayj.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid concerning God's saying ﴿إنِّي أُرِيدُ أنْ تَبُوءَ بِإثْمِي وإثْمِكَ﴾ that he said: "It means: I want your own sin and my blood to be upon you, so that you bear both of them together." Ibn Jarir narrated from him concerning "my sin" that he said: "By your killing of me," and concerning "your sin" that he said: "By what had proceeded from you before that." He narrated something similar from Qatada and al-Dahhak.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid concerning God's saying ﴿فَطَوَّعَتْ لَهُ نَفْسُهُ قَتْلَ أَخِيهِ﴾ that he said: "It emboldened him to kill his brother." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatada concerning the verse that he said: "His soul adorned it for him."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions concerning God's saying ﴿فَطَوَّعَتْ لَهُ نَفْسُهُ قَتْلَ أَخِيهِ﴾ that: "He sought him in order to kill him, but the youth escaped from him among the mountain peaks. One day he came to him while he was grazing his sheep and asleep, so he lifted a rock and smashed his head with it, and he died. He left him in the open, not knowing how to bury him. So God sent two crows, brothers, who fought, and one of them killed the other. It dug a hole for it and then covered it with earth. When he saw it he said: 'Woe is me! Am I unable to be like this crow?'" It is established in the Two Sahihs and others from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Adam bears a share of its blood, because he was the first to establish killing." There are narrations concerning the manner of his killing of his brother, and God knows best their authenticity.

The connection of this passage with what precedes it is a warning from God that the injustice of the Jews, and their breaking of covenants and pledges, is like the injustice of the son of Adam toward his brother. The disease is ancient and the evil is deep-rooted. Scholars have differed over whether the two sons of Adam mentioned were of his own loins. The majority held that they were, while al-Hasan and al-Dahhak held that they were from the Children of Israel, and said: "They were from the Children of Israel," (p. 366) so that they were cited as an example to show the envy of the Jews. There had been a dispute between them, so they each offered a sacrifice (qurban), and sacrifices were only made among the Children of Israel. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is an error. How could anyone among the Children of Israel be ignorant of the form of burial, so that he would have to follow the example of a crow?"

The majority of the Companions and those after them said: their names were Qabil (Cain) and Habil (Abel). Qabil's offering was a bundle of ears of grain, since he was a farmer, and he chose it from the worst of his crop. Indeed, he found a good ear among them, rubbed it and ate it. Habil's offering was a ram, since he was a herder of sheep, and he took it from the best of his flock. Habil's offering was accepted, so it was raised up to Paradise and continued grazing there until the Sacrificed One (peace be upon him) was ransomed with it. So said a group of the early generations (salaf). Qabil's offering was not accepted, so he envied his brother and said: "I will surely kill you."

It was also said that the reason for this offering was that Hawwa' (Eve) would give birth to a male and a female in every pregnancy, except Shith (peace be upon him), whom she bore alone. Adam (peace be upon him) would marry the male of one birth to the female of another birth, and a man could not marry his twin sister. Qabil was born with a beautiful sister named Iqlima, and Habil was born with a sister who was not so beautiful, named Layuda. When Adam wanted to marry them off, Qabil said: "I have a better right to my sister." Adam ordered him otherwise, but he did not obey, and when he was rebuked he did not desist. So they agreed on the offering, and that whoever's offering was accepted would marry her.

His saying ﴿بِالحَقِّ﴾ (with truth) is connected with an omitted element that stands as a qualifier of a verbal noun, meaning "a recitation (tilawa) accompanied by truth"; or it is a qualifier of ﴿نَبَأَ﴾ (the account), meaning "an account accompanied by truth." By one of them is meant Habil, and by the other Qabil. His saying ﴿قالَ لَأَقْتُلَنَّكَ﴾ (He said: "I will surely kill you") is an explanatory resumptive clause, as if it were said: "What then was the situation of the one whose offering was not accepted?" His saying ﴿قالَ إنَّما يَتَقَبَّلُ اللَّهُ مِنَ المُتَّقِينَ﴾ (He said: "God only accepts from the God-fearing") is also a resumptive clause, as if it were said: "What then did the one whose offering was accepted say?" The word ﴿إنَّما﴾ (only) here expresses restriction: God accepts offerings only from the God-fearing, not from others. It is as if he were saying to his brother: "You were brought to this by yourself, not by me, for the non-acceptance of your offering is due to the absence of your piety."

His saying ﴿لَئِنْ بَسَطْتَ إلَيَّ يَدَكَ لِتَقْتُلَنِي﴾ (If you extend your hand to me to kill me) means: if you intend to kill me. The lam is the one that introduces the oath, and ﴿ما أنا بباسِطٍ﴾ (I shall not extend my hand) is the answer to the oath, standing in place of the answer to the condition. This is Habil's submission to being killed, as occurs in the hadith: "When strife occurs, be like the better of the two sons of Adam," and the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse. Mujahid said: "At that time the obligation upon them was that no one should draw a sword, and that no one should resist one who intended to kill him." Al-Qurtubi said: "Our scholars said: that is among the things for which worship by such a law may have been revealed. However, in our law it is permitted to repel such an attack by consensus, and there is disagreement over whether it is obligatory. The more sound view is that it is obligatory, because of what it contains of forbidding evil."

Among the Hashwiyya (a term for certain literalist and uncritical groups) there are people who do not permit the one who is attacked to defend himself, and they argued with the hadith of Abu Dharr. The scholars interpreted it as referring to abstaining from fighting in strife and restraining the hand in cases of doubt, as I have explained in my book al-Tadhkira. This ends the words of al-Qurtubi. The hadith of Abu Dharr referred to is in Muslim and the authors of the Sunan, except al-Nasa'i, and in it: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'O Abu Dharr, what would you do if people kill one another?' I said: 'God and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'Stay in your house and close your door upon yourself.' I said: 'If I am not left alone?' He said: 'Then go to those among whom you belong and be among them.' I said: 'Shall I take up my weapon?' He said: 'Then you would be sharing in what they are doing. But if you fear that the glint of the sword will daze you, then throw the end of your garment over your face, so that he may bear his sin and your sin.'" There are similar hadiths from a number of the Companions: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Abu Hurayra, Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, Abu Bakr, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Waqid, and Abu Musa.

His saying ﴿إنِّي أُرِيدُ أنْ تَبُوءَ بِإثْمِي وإثْمِكَ فَتَكُونَ مِن أصْحابِ النّارِ﴾ (Indeed I want you to bear my sin and your sin, and so be among the companions of the Fire) is a reason given for his refraining from fighting, following the first reason, which is ﴿إنِّي أخافُ اللَّهَ رَبَّ العالَمِينَ﴾ (Indeed I fear God, the Lord of the worlds).

The exegetes differed over the meaning. It was said: Habil meant: "I want you to bear the sin that would have fallen upon me had I been eager to kill you, and your sin that you incurred by killing me." It was also said: the meaning of "my sin" is the sin peculiar to me, for a reason that will come, and it will be cast upon you because of your wronging me, and you will bear your sin in killing me. This agrees with what is established in Sahih Muslim from the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "On the Day of Resurrection the wrongdoer and the wronged will be brought, and some of the wrongdoer's good deeds will be taken and added to the good deeds of the wronged until he is compensated. If he has no good deeds, some of the wronged one's evil deeds will be taken and cast upon him." A similar statement is God's saying: ﴿وَلَيَحْمِلُنَّ أَثْقَالَهُمْ وَأَثْقَالًا مَعَ أَثْقَالِهِمْ﴾ (They will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens) [al-'Ankabut: 13]. It was also said: the meaning is: "I want you not to bear my sin and your sin," as in God's saying: ﴿وَأَلْقَى فِي الْأَرْضِ رَوَاسِيَ أَنْ تَمِيدَ بِكُمْ﴾ (And He cast firm mountains upon the earth lest it shake with you) [al-Nahl: 15], meaning: lest it shake with you. And His saying: ﴿يُبَيِّنُ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ أَنْ تَضِلُّوا﴾ (God makes clear to you lest you go astray) [al-Nisa': 176], meaning: lest you go astray.

Most scholars said that the meaning is: "I want you to bear my sin," that is, the sin of your killing me, "and your sin," which has already become upon you because of your wrongdoings before killing me. Al-Tha'labi said: "This is the view of the majority of the exegetes." It was also said that it is in the form of denial; that is, "Or do I want...," in the manner of God's saying: ﴿وَتِلْكَ نِعْمَةٌ﴾ (And is it a favour) [al-Shu'ara': 22], meaning: "Or is it a favour?" This was said by al-Qushayri, and its justification is that the intention to kill is itself a sin.

Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan was asked: "How can a believer want his brother to sin and to enter the Fire?" He answered: "The intention came after he had extended his hand to kill him." This is very far-fetched, and so is what preceded it. The root of "ba'a" means to return to a place of lodging (mabaa'a), which is a dwelling, as in ﴿وَبَاءُوا بِغَضَبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ (And they returned with wrath from God) [Al 'Imran: 112], meaning: they returned.

His saying ﴿فَطَوَّعَتْ لَهُ نَفْسُهُ قَتْلَ أخِيهِ﴾ (So his soul made the killing of his brother easy for him) means: his soul made the matter easy for him, encouraged him, and presented to him that killing his brother was easy and within his power. It is said: "taṭawwaʿa al-shay'" means it became easy and submissive, and "ṭawwaʿahu fulan lahu" means he made it easy for him. Al-Harawi said: "ṭawwaʿat" and "ṭaawaʿat" are the same; it is said "ṭaʿa lahu kadhā" when one comes to it willingly. The mention of his soul making it easy for him, after what preceded of Qabil's saying ﴿لَأَقْتُلَنَّكَ﴾ (I will surely kill you) and Habil's saying ﴿لِتَقْتُلَنِي﴾ (to kill me), is evidence that this making-easy had not yet occurred at the time of that exchange.

His saying ﴿فَقَتَلَهُ﴾ (so he killed him). Ibn Jarir, Mujahid and others said: It is narrated that he did not know how to kill his brother, so Iblis came to him with a bird or another animal, and began to smash its head between two stones, so that Qabil would imitate him, and he did so. It was also said other than this, which requires verification of the narration.

His saying ﴿فَبَعَثَ اللَّهُ غُرَابًا يَبْحَثُ فِي الْأَرْضِ لِيُرِيَهُ كَيْفَ يُوَارِي سَوْءَةَ أَخِيهِ﴾ (Then God sent a crow scratching in the earth to show him how to cover his brother's corpse). It was said: When he killed his brother, he did not know how to conceal him, since he was the first dead person of the children of Adam. So God sent two crows, brothers, who fought, and one of them killed the other. It then dug a hole for it and covered it with earth. When Qabil saw this, he said: ﴿يَا وَيْلَتَا أَعَجَزْتُ أَنْ أَكُونَ مِثْلَ هَذَا الْغُرَابِ فَأُوَارِيَ سَوْءَةَ أَخِي﴾ (Woe is me! Am I unable to be like this crow and cover my brother's corpse?), and he covered him. The pronoun in ﴿لِيُرِيَهُ﴾ (to show him) refers to the crow, and it was said that it refers to God, may He be exalted. The phrase ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ (how) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial element relating to the pronoun in ﴿يُوَارِي﴾ (covers), and the clause is the second object of ﴿يُرِيَهُ﴾. By ﴿السَّوْءَةِ﴾ (the nakedness/corpse) here is meant his whole body, since it was dead. The word ﴿قالَ﴾ (he said) is a resumptive response to an implied question arising from the flow of the discourse, as if it were said: "What did he say when he saw the crow doing that?" The phrase ﴿يا وَيْلَتَى﴾ (Woe is me!) is an expression of grief and sorrow, and the alif is a substitute for the first-person ya', as if he were calling upon his destruction to come at that moment. The "waylah" is ruin. The speech comes out in the manner of expressing astonishment at his own failure to cover his brother, just as the crow was guided to that. The word ﴿فَأُوَارِيَ﴾ (so that I might cover) is in the accusative as the answer to the interrogative. It was also read with a sukun, as an implied "fa-ana uwari" (so I cover). ﴿فَأَصْبَحَ مِنَ النَّادِمِينَ﴾ (So he became among the regretful) for having killed him. It was said that his regret was not the regret of repentance, but that he regretted losing him, not his killing. It was also said other things.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "He forbade a woman from marrying her twin brother, and from marrying her to anyone other than her brothers. Every pregnancy produced a man and a woman. While they were in this state, he had a beautiful daughter and another son who was ugly and unsightly. The brother of the ugly one said: 'Marry me to your sister and I will marry you to mine.' He said: 'No, I have a better right to my sister.' So they offered an offering. The owner of the flock brought a ram, white-horned, with bright eyes, and the owner of the crop brought a heap of grain. The offering of the owner of the ram was accepted, and the offering of the owner of the crop was not accepted." Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: "Its chain is good," and al-Suyuti said the same in al-Durr al-Manthur.

Ibn Jarir narrated from him: "It was among the practices of the children of Adam that no poor person was given charity, but the offering was made by a man himself. While the two sons of Adam were sitting, they said: 'If we were to offer an offering,' and then they mentioned what each of them had offered."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid concerning ﴿لَئِنْ بَسَطْتَ إلَيَّ يَدَكَ﴾ (If you extend your hand to me) that he said: "It was prescribed for them that if a man intended to kill another, he should leave him and not resist him." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated something similar from Ibn Jurayj.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid concerning God's saying ﴿إنِّي أُرِيدُ أنْ تَبُوءَ بِإثْمِي وإثْمِكَ﴾ that he said: "It means: I want your own sin and my blood to be upon you, so that you bear both of them together." Ibn Jarir narrated from him concerning "my sin" that he said: "By your killing of me," and concerning "your sin" that he said: "By what had proceeded from you before that." He narrated something similar from Qatada and al-Dahhak.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid concerning God's saying ﴿فَطَوَّعَتْ لَهُ نَفْسُهُ قَتْلَ أَخِيهِ﴾ that he said: "It emboldened him to kill his brother." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatada concerning the verse that he said: "His soul adorned it for him."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions concerning God's saying ﴿فَطَوَّعَتْ لَهُ نَفْسُهُ قَتْلَ أَخِيهِ﴾ that: "He sought him in order to kill him, but the youth escaped from him among the mountain peaks. One day he came to him while he was grazing his sheep and asleep, so he lifted a rock and smashed his head with it, and he died. He left him in the open, not knowing how to bury him. So God sent two crows, brothers, who fought, and one of them killed the other. It dug a hole for it and then covered it with earth. When he saw it he said: 'Woe is me! Am I unable to be like this crow?'" It is established in the Two Sahihs and others from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Adam bears a share of its blood, because he was the first to establish killing." There are narrations concerning the manner of his killing of his brother, and God knows best their authenticity.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 32–34 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, ﴿because of that﴾, means: because of that killer, his crime, and on account of his disobedience. Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian and Qur'anic linguist) said: meaning, because of his offence. He said: it is said, *ajala al-rajulu ʿala ahlihi sharran yaʾjulu ajlan* ("the man committed evil against his family"), when he commits an offence, like *akhadha yaʾkhudhu akhdhan* ("he took"). Abu Jaʿfar (one of the ten canonical reciters) read *min ajli* with a kasra on the nun and the elision of the hamza, and this is a dialect form. In *Sharh al-Durra* (a commentary on a work on the recitations) it is said: Abu Jaʿfar alone read *min ajli dhalika* with a kasra on the hamza, with its vowel transferred to the nun before it. It has been said that *min ajli dhalika* may be connected to *min al-nadimin* ("among the regretful"), so that the pause falls on *min ajli dhalika*, but the first view we have mentioned is preferable. The meaning is that the story of the two sons of Adam is what gave rise to the prescription mentioned, laid upon the Children of Israel. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes.

He singled out the Children of Israel for mention because the context concerns the enumeration of their crimes, and because they were the first nation upon whom the threat concerning the killing of souls was sent down. Severity was applied to them at that time because of their abundant shedding of blood and their killing of the prophets. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the verb it depends on, namely *katabna* ("We prescribed"), conveys restriction (*qasr*): i.e., because of that, and not because of anything else. *Min* here denotes the starting point. ﴿That whoever kills a soul﴾, one soul from among these souls, ﴿without a soul﴾, i.e., without a soul that merits retaliation (*qisas*). Thus excluded from this is one who kills a soul in retaliation for a soul.

His saying, ﴿or corruption in the land﴾: the majority read it in the genitive, as a conjunction (*ʿatf*) upon *nafs* ("soul").

Al-Hasan (al-Basri) read it in the accusative, by postulating a deleted verb indicated by the beginning of the speech, its estimated form being: "or he caused corruption in the land." There is weakness in this. The meaning of the majority reading is: whoever kills a soul without any cause of retaliation or corruption in the land, it is as if he had killed all people.

It is established that every conditional ruling where one of two things is realized, its contradiction is conditioned on the absence of both together; and every ruling conditioned on the realization of both together, its contradiction is conditioned on the absence of one of them, since the contradiction of everything is conditioned on the contradiction of its condition. The exegetes have differed over what this corruption mentioned in this verse is. It has been said that it is polytheism (*shirk*), and it has been said that it is highway robbery (*qatʿ al-tariq*).

The apparent sense of the Qur'anic wording is that it includes whatever truly qualifies as corruption in the land. Polytheism is corruption in the land, highway robbery is corruption in the land, shedding blood, violating the sanctity of the sacred (*hatk al-haram*), and plundering property are corruption in the land, and oppression of God's servants without right is corruption in the land, and demolishing buildings, cutting down trees, and polluting rivers are corruption in the land. From this you know that these types truly qualify as corruption in the land. Likewise, the corruption that will come in His saying, ﴿and they strive in the land to cause corruption﴾, applies to these types. The full discussion of the meaning of corruption will come shortly.

His saying, ﴿it is as if he had killed all people﴾: the exegetes differed in establishing this comparison, that the punishment of one who kills all people is greater than that of one who kills one of them. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: the meaning is that whoever kills a prophet or a just imam, it is as if he killed all people; and whoever preserves him, by strengthening his arm and supporting him, it is as if he gave life to all people. Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) transmitted this from him. It is related from Mujahid that he said: the meaning is that whoever kills a believing soul deliberately, God has made his recompense Hell, and He is angry with him, curses him, and prepares for him a great punishment; so even if he killed all people, it would not add to this. He said: and whoever is spared from killing and does not kill anyone, it is as if he gave life to all people.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted something similar from him. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said, in explaining this verse: he ruined his soul just as if he had killed all people. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted this from him. It is related from al-Hasan that he said: "it is as if he killed all people" in respect of the burden, and "as if he gave life to all people" in respect of the reward. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is that whoever kills a soul incurs the same retribution and retaliation as one who kills all people. "And whoever gives life to it" means: whoever pardons one whose killing is due. Al-Qurtubi transmitted this from him. It is related from al-Hasan that giving life means pardon after having the power to exact retribution, i.e., he gave it life.

It is related from Mujahid that giving life to it is rescuing it from drowning, burning, collapse, or destruction. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted this from him. It has been said: the meaning is that whoever kills a soul, all the believers become his adversaries, because he has wronged them all; ﴿and whoever gives it life, it is as if he gave life to all people﴾, i.e., it becomes obligatory upon all to thank him. It has also been said: the meaning is that whoever deems one person lawful to kill has deemed all lawful, because he has denied the Law. In any case, giving life here is an expression for abstaining from killing and rescuing from destruction, so it is figurative, since its literal meaning is specific to God, mighty and majestic.

The purpose of this comparison on the side of killing is to magnify the gravity of killing and to make its matter weighty in souls, so that those bold and audacious would refrain from it. On the side of giving life, the purpose is to encourage pardoning offenders and rescuing those thrown into destruction.

His saying, ﴿And certainly Our messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾: this is an independent sentence, emphasized by the *lam* that precedes the oath (*al-lam al-mutawwiʾa lil-qasam*), containing the information that the messengers, upon them be prayers and peace, came to the servants with what God had legislated for them of rulings, among which is the matter of killing. The *thumma* in His saying, ﴿Then indeed many of them﴾, is for rank-based delay (*al-tarakhi al-rutbi*) and for rational astonishment (*al-istibʿad al-ʿaqli*). The reference in the phrase ﴿that﴾ is to what was mentioned that God prescribed upon the Children of Israel; i.e., indeed many of them, after that prescription, ﴿in the land are transgressors﴾, in killing.

His saying, ﴿Indeed the recompense of those who wage war against God and His Messenger﴾: the people have differed concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse. The majority held that it was revealed concerning the ʿUrayniyyin (a group who attacked the herds of the Prophet, ﷺ). Malik, al-Shafiʿi, Abu Thawr, and the people of opinion (*ahl al-ra'y*) said: it was revealed concerning those among the Muslims who went out to commit highway robbery and strive in the land with corruption.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: the statement of Malik is correct. Abu Thawr argued for this view, saying: His saying in this verse, ﴿except those who repent before you gain power over them﴾, indicates that it was revealed concerning people other than the polytheists, because they have agreed that when polytheists fall into our hands and then embrace Islam, their blood becomes forbidden; so this shows that the verse was revealed concerning the people of Islam. End of quotation.

This is also indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven for them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38], and by His saying, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace: "Islam demolishes what came before it," transmitted by Muslim and others. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, in his exegesis, related from some scholars that this verse, namely the verse of waging war, abrogated (*naskh*) the action of the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, concerning the ʿUrayniyyin, and the matter stopped at these prescribed penalties (*hudud*).

It is related from Muhammad ibn Sirin that he said: this was before the hudud were revealed; he meant the Prophet's action against the ʿUrayniyyin, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace. A group of scholars said this. Another group held that the Prophet's action against the ʿUrayniyyin was abrogated by the Prophet's prohibition of mutilation (*muthla*), and whoever holds this must establish that the abrogating text came later. The sequence of narrations concerning the occasion of revelation will come. The truth is that this verse encompasses polytheists and others who commit what it includes, and the specific occasion does not restrict it; rather, the consideration is the generality of the wording. Al-Qurtubi said in his exegesis: there is no disagreement among the scholars that the ruling of this verse applies to warring Muslims, even if it was revealed concerning apostates or Jews. End of quotation.

The meaning of his saying *mutarattib* ("applies") is: established. It has been said: the intended sense of "waging war against God" mentioned in the verse is waging war against the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and waging war against the Muslims in his time and after his time, by way of expression (*ʿibara*) and not by way of indication (*dalala*) or analogy (*qiyas*); because the revelation of the text is not by way of direct address (*khitab al-mushafaha*) so that its ruling would be restricted to those who were obligated at the time of revelation, and extending the address to others would then require another proof. It has also been said: waging war against the Muslims was made into waging war against God and His Messenger in order to magnify their fighting and to exalt the harm done to them, because God, glorified is He, cannot be warred against or overcome. The better view is that waging war against God, glorified is He, should be interpreted as disobedience to Him and violation of His laws, while waging war against the Messenger is taken in its literal sense, and the ruling for his community is his ruling, and they are his followers.

Striving in the land to cause corruption is applied to various kinds of evil, as we have mentioned shortly before. Ibn Kathir said in his exegesis: many of the early scholars, among them Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, said: clipping dirhams and dinars is among the acts of corruption in the land. God, exalted is He, has said: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and livestock; and God does not love corruption﴾ [al-Baqara: 205]. End of quotation.

Once what we have established of the generality of the verse, and of the meaning of waging war and striving in the land to cause corruption, is settled for you, know that this applies to everyone who commits such acts, whether Muslim or disbeliever, in Egypt or outside Egypt, in every small and great matter, and whether trivial or grave. The ruling of God in this regard is what is stated in this verse: execution or crucifixion, or cutting off of hands and feet on opposite sides, or banishment from the land. However, this is not the ruling for whoever commits any sin whatsoever; rather, it applies to one whose offence is aggression against the lives and property of people, excluding those for which a different ruling has come in the Book of God or the Sunna of His Messenger, such as theft and what requires retaliation. For we know that in his time, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, there were people who committed sins and transgressions other than these, and this ruling mentioned in this verse was not applied to them by the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace.

By this you recognize the weakness of what is related from Mujahid in explaining the "waging war" mentioned in this verse, that it means adultery and theft. The reason is that these two offences have a ruling other than this ruling in the Book of God and in the Sunna of His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace.

Once you know what the apparent meaning of this verse is, according to the usage of the Arabic language, by which we have been commanded to interpret the Book of God and the Sunna of His Messenger, beware of being deceived by any of the transmitted details and the reported doctrines, unless there comes to you a proof necessitating the restriction of this generality or the specification of this meaning understood from Arabic usage. Then you may act upon it and place it in its proper position. As for what lies beyond that:

*"Leave aside a plunder that was cried out about in its sacred enclosures, and bring a tale other than the tale of the riding camels."*

Nevertheless, we shall mention among these doctrines what you will hear. Know that the scholars have differed concerning who deserves the name of "one who wages war." Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, Mujahid, ʿAta, al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, al-Dahhak, and Abu Thawr said: whoever draws a weapon within the dome of Islam (*qubbat al-Islam*), terrorizes the road, and is then seized and overpowered, the imam of the Muslims has the choice regarding him: if he wishes, he kills him; if he wishes, he crucifies him; if he wishes, he cuts off his hand and foot. Malik also held this view, and he explicitly stated that the one who wages war, according to him, is one who attacks people in a city, or in the open country, or overpowers them over their persons and property, without a blood feud, vendetta, or enmity.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: Malik's position on this question is reported in differing ways: once he affirmed the crime of hirabah (armed highway robbery, ḥirābah) within a city (miṣr), and once he denied that. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, other than what preceded, that he said regarding highwaymen (quṭṭāʿ al-ṭarīq): if they kill and take property, they are killed and crucified; if they kill and do not take property, they are killed and not crucified; if they take property and do not kill, their hands and feet are cut off from opposite sides; and if they terrorize the road and take no property, they are banished from the land.

It is also reported from Abu Mijlaz, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi and ʿAtaʾ, with some variation in the reports from some of them. Ibn Kathir reported this from the majority (al-jumhur), and he also said: "Likewise it is reported from many of the early authorities (salaf) and the imams."

Abu Hanifa said: if he kills, he is killed; if he takes property without killing, his hand and foot are cut off from opposite sides; and if he takes property and kills, the ruler (al-sultan) has the choice: if he wishes, he cuts off his hands and feet, and if he wishes, he does not cut them and kills him and crucifies him. Abu Yusuf said: killing covers everything, and the view of al-Awzaʿi is similar to this. Al-Shafiʿi said: if he takes property, his right hand is cut off and cauterized (ḥusima), then his left foot is cut off and cauterized and he is released; because this crime exceeds theft by being hirabah. If he kills, he is killed; and if he takes property and kills, he is killed and crucified. It is reported from him that he said: he is crucified for three days. Ahmad said: if he kills, he is killed; and if he takes property, his hand and foot are cut off, like the view of al-Shafiʿi.

I know of no evidence for these detailed distinctions, neither from the Book of Allah nor from the Sunnah of His Messenger, except what Ibn Jarir reported in his tafsir, and he alone narrated it. He said: "ʿAli ibn Sahl narrated to us, al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib: that ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan wrote to Anas ibn Malik asking him about this verse, and he wrote back informing him that this verse was revealed concerning those men of ʿUrayna, who were from Bajila. Anas said: they apostatized from Islam, killed the herdsman, drove off the camels, terrorized the road and committed unlawful sexual intercourse (farj al-ḥarām). Anas said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked Jibril about the judgment regarding those who wage war, and he said: whoever steals and terrorizes the road, cut off his hand for his theft and his foot for his terrorizing; whoever kills, kill him; and whoever kills and terrorizes the road and makes lawful the unlawful sexual intercourse, crucify him." Along with this there is severe objectionable content (nakarah shadidah), and it is not known how sound it is. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir, after mentioning some of the details we have mentioned, the following: "What supports this distinction is the hadith that Ibn Jarir narrated in his tafsir, if its chain is sound," and then he mentioned it.

His words: ﴿and they strive in the land to cause corruption﴾ — this is either in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), or as an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) by interpretation; meaning: ﴿causing corruption﴾.

His words: (or they be crucified) — its apparent meaning is that they are crucified alive until they die, since it is one of the types among which Allah gave the choice. Some said: crucifixion happens only after killing, and it is not permissible to crucify someone before killing him, so that he is prevented from prayer, eating and drinking. It is answered that this is a punishment which Allah, glorified is He, prescribed in His Book for His servants.

His words: ﴿or their hands and feet be cut off from opposite sides﴾ — its apparent meaning is the cutting of one of the two hands and one of the two feet from opposite sides, whether the hand cut is the right or the left, and likewise the feet; and it is not required except that the cutting be from opposite sides, either the right hand with the left foot, or the left hand with the right foot. It was also said: what is meant by this is cutting the right hand and the left foot only.

His words: ﴿or they be banished from the land﴾ — the exegetes differed about its meaning. al-Suddi said: it is that they are pursued with horse and foot until they are seized and the prescribed punishment (ḥadd) is established on them, or they flee out of the abode of Islam. This is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, Anas, Malik, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas and al-Zuhri; al-Rummani related it from them in his book. It is reported from al-Shafiʿi that they are taken out from one town to another so that the prescribed punishments may be established on them, and al-Layth ibn Saʿd said likewise. It is reported from Malik that he is banished from the town in which he committed the crime to another and imprisoned there, like the adulterer; and Ibn Jarir and al-Qurtubi preferred this. The Kufans said: their banishment is their imprisonment, so he is banished from the breadth of the world to its narrowness. The apparent meaning of the verse is that he is driven out of the land in which he committed what he committed, without imprisonment or anything else. Banishment may also carry the sense of destruction (al-ihlak), but that is not intended here.

His words: ﴿That is a disgrace for them in this world﴾ — the reference is to the rulings mentioned earlier; khizy means humiliation and disgrace. His words: ﴿except those who repent before you gain power over them; then know that Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ — Allah, glorified is He, excepted those who repent before they come under one's power from the general scope of those punished with the earlier penalties. The apparent meaning is that there is no distinction between bloodshed and property and other sins that entail fixed, defined penalties, so the penitent before capture is not required to answer for any of that; and this is the practice of the Companions.

Some scholars held that retaliation (qiṣaṣ) and all other rights of human beings are not dropped by repentance before capture; the first view is the correct one. As for repentance after capture, the penalty mentioned in the verse is not dropped by it, as the mention of the condition ﴿before you gain power over them﴾ indicates. al-Qurtubi said: The scholars agreed that the ruler is the guardian of one who wages war; so if a combatant kills a man's brother and comes to him in the state of hirabah, the matter of hirabah offers the blood-seeker no recourse, and the pardon of the blood-guardian is not permissible. Ibn Jarir reported from al-Dahhak, concerning His words ﴿because of that We prescribed for the Children of Israel﴾, that he said: because of the son of Adam who killed his brother unjustly.

Ibn Jarir also reported from al-Hasan that it was said to him regarding this verse, meaning His words ﴿it is as if he had slain mankind entirely﴾: "Is it for us as it was for the Children of Israel?" He said: "Yes, by Him besides whom there is no god." Abu Dawud and al-Nasai reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿Indeed, the penalty of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾ that he said: it was revealed concerning the polytheists; whoever of them repents before he is overpowered, there is no path against him. This verse does not shield a Muslim man from the legal punishment if he kills, or causes corruption in the land, or wages war against Allah and His Messenger.

Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir reported from him regarding this verse that he said: some people of the People of the Book had a covenant and pact with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but they broke the covenant and caused corruption in the land, so Allah gave His Prophet the choice concerning them: if he wished he could kill, if he wished he could crucify, and if he wished he could cut off their hands and feet from opposite sides. As for banishment, it means striking out in the land; so if he comes repentant and enters Islam, it is accepted from him and he is not held to account for what preceded. Abu Dawud and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas that this verse was revealed concerning the Harurites (al-Ḥarūriyya).

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Anas that some men from ʿUkl came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), embraced Islam, and found Madina unhealthy; so the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered them to go to the camels of the charity (ṣadaqa), drink from their urine and milk; they killed its herdsman and drove the camels off. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent a party (qafa) in pursuit of them; they were brought back, and he cut off their hands and feet, branded (samala) their eyes, did not cauterize them, and left them until they died. Then Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, the penalty of those who wage war...﴾ the verse. In Muslim, from Anas, he said: the Prophet (ﷺ) only branded the eyes of those people because they had branded the eyes of the herdsmen.

Al-Shafiʿi in al-Umm, ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: if the combatant goes out, takes property and does not kill, he is cut off from opposite sides; if he goes out and kills without taking property, he is killed; if he goes out, takes property and kills, he is killed and crucified; and if he goes out, terrorizes the road, takes no property and does not kill, he is banished. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him regarding the verse that he said: whoever draws the sword within the dome of Islam (qubbat al-Islam) and corrupts the road, and is overpowered and captured, the imam of the Muslims has the choice concerning him: if he wishes he may kill him, if he wishes he may crucify him, and if he wishes he may cut off his hand and foot. He said: ﴿or be banished from the land﴾ means they flee and leave the abode of Islam for the abode of war. Ibn Jarir also reported from him that he said: its banishment is that he be pursued. He also reported similarly from Anas.

Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Shaʿbi that he said: Haritha ibn Badr al-Taymi, a man of Basra, had caused corruption in the land and waged war; he spoke to men of Quraysh asking them to seek security for him from ʿAli, but they refused. Then Saʿid ibn Qays al-Hamdani came to ʿAli and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, what is the penalty of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive in the land to cause corruption?" He said: ﴿that they be killed, or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off from opposite sides, or be banished from the land﴾; then he said: ﴿except those who repent before you gain power over them﴾. Saʿid said: "Even if it is Haritha ibn Badr?" He said: "Even if it is Haritha ibn Badr." Then he said: "This is Haritha ibn Badr; he has come repentant, so he is secure." He said: "Yes." So he brought him to him, he pledged allegiance to him, ʿAli accepted that from him and wrote him a letter of safe conduct (amān).

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 32–34 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, ﴿because of that﴾, means: because of that killer, his crime, and on account of his disobedience. Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian and Qur'anic linguist) said: meaning, because of his offence. He said: it is said, *ajala al-rajulu ʿala ahlihi sharran yaʾjulu ajlan* ("the man committed evil against his family"), when he commits an offence, like *akhadha yaʾkhudhu akhdhan* ("he took"). Abu Jaʿfar (one of the ten canonical reciters) read *min ajli* with a kasra on the nun and the elision of the hamza, and this is a dialect form. In *Sharh al-Durra* (a commentary on a work on the recitations) it is said: Abu Jaʿfar alone read *min ajli dhalika* with a kasra on the hamza, with its vowel transferred to the nun before it. It has been said that *min ajli dhalika* may be connected to *min al-nadimin* ("among the regretful"), so that the pause falls on *min ajli dhalika*, but the first view we have mentioned is preferable. The meaning is that the story of the two sons of Adam is what gave rise to the prescription mentioned, laid upon the Children of Israel. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes.

He singled out the Children of Israel for mention because the context concerns the enumeration of their crimes, and because they were the first nation upon whom the threat concerning the killing of souls was sent down. Severity was applied to them at that time because of their abundant shedding of blood and their killing of the prophets. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the verb it depends on, namely *katabna* ("We prescribed"), conveys restriction (*qasr*): i.e., because of that, and not because of anything else. *Min* here denotes the starting point. ﴿That whoever kills a soul﴾, one soul from among these souls, ﴿without a soul﴾, i.e., without a soul that merits retaliation (*qisas*). Thus excluded from this is one who kills a soul in retaliation for a soul.

His saying, ﴿or corruption in the land﴾: the majority read it in the genitive, as a conjunction (*ʿatf*) upon *nafs* ("soul").

Al-Hasan (al-Basri) read it in the accusative, by postulating a deleted verb indicated by the beginning of the speech, its estimated form being: "or he caused corruption in the land." There is weakness in this. The meaning of the majority reading is: whoever kills a soul without any cause of retaliation or corruption in the land, it is as if he had killed all people.

It is established that every conditional ruling where one of two things is realized, its contradiction is conditioned on the absence of both together; and every ruling conditioned on the realization of both together, its contradiction is conditioned on the absence of one of them, since the contradiction of everything is conditioned on the contradiction of its condition. The exegetes have differed over what this corruption mentioned in this verse is. It has been said that it is polytheism (*shirk*), and it has been said that it is highway robbery (*qatʿ al-tariq*).

The apparent sense of the Qur'anic wording is that it includes whatever truly qualifies as corruption in the land. Polytheism is corruption in the land, highway robbery is corruption in the land, shedding blood, violating the sanctity of the sacred (*hatk al-haram*), and plundering property are corruption in the land, and oppression of God's servants without right is corruption in the land, and demolishing buildings, cutting down trees, and polluting rivers are corruption in the land. From this you know that these types truly qualify as corruption in the land. Likewise, the corruption that will come in His saying, ﴿and they strive in the land to cause corruption﴾, applies to these types. The full discussion of the meaning of corruption will come shortly.

His saying, ﴿it is as if he had killed all people﴾: the exegetes differed in establishing this comparison, that the punishment of one who kills all people is greater than that of one who kills one of them. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: the meaning is that whoever kills a prophet or a just imam, it is as if he killed all people; and whoever preserves him, by strengthening his arm and supporting him, it is as if he gave life to all people. Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) transmitted this from him. It is related from Mujahid that he said: the meaning is that whoever kills a believing soul deliberately, God has made his recompense Hell, and He is angry with him, curses him, and prepares for him a great punishment; so even if he killed all people, it would not add to this. He said: and whoever is spared from killing and does not kill anyone, it is as if he gave life to all people.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted something similar from him. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said, in explaining this verse: he ruined his soul just as if he had killed all people. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted this from him. It is related from al-Hasan that he said: "it is as if he killed all people" in respect of the burden, and "as if he gave life to all people" in respect of the reward. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is that whoever kills a soul incurs the same retribution and retaliation as one who kills all people. "And whoever gives life to it" means: whoever pardons one whose killing is due. Al-Qurtubi transmitted this from him. It is related from al-Hasan that giving life means pardon after having the power to exact retribution, i.e., he gave it life.

It is related from Mujahid that giving life to it is rescuing it from drowning, burning, collapse, or destruction. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted this from him. It has been said: the meaning is that whoever kills a soul, all the believers become his adversaries, because he has wronged them all; ﴿and whoever gives it life, it is as if he gave life to all people﴾, i.e., it becomes obligatory upon all to thank him. It has also been said: the meaning is that whoever deems one person lawful to kill has deemed all lawful, because he has denied the Law. In any case, giving life here is an expression for abstaining from killing and rescuing from destruction, so it is figurative, since its literal meaning is specific to God, mighty and majestic.

The purpose of this comparison on the side of killing is to magnify the gravity of killing and to make its matter weighty in souls, so that those bold and audacious would refrain from it. On the side of giving life, the purpose is to encourage pardoning offenders and rescuing those thrown into destruction.

His saying, ﴿And certainly Our messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾: this is an independent sentence, emphasized by the *lam* that precedes the oath (*al-lam al-mutawwiʾa lil-qasam*), containing the information that the messengers, upon them be prayers and peace, came to the servants with what God had legislated for them of rulings, among which is the matter of killing. The *thumma* in His saying, ﴿Then indeed many of them﴾, is for rank-based delay (*al-tarakhi al-rutbi*) and for rational astonishment (*al-istibʿad al-ʿaqli*). The reference in the phrase ﴿that﴾ is to what was mentioned that God prescribed upon the Children of Israel; i.e., indeed many of them, after that prescription, ﴿in the land are transgressors﴾, in killing.

His saying, ﴿Indeed the recompense of those who wage war against God and His Messenger﴾: the people have differed concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse. The majority held that it was revealed concerning the ʿUrayniyyin (a group who attacked the herds of the Prophet, ﷺ). Malik, al-Shafiʿi, Abu Thawr, and the people of opinion (*ahl al-ra'y*) said: it was revealed concerning those among the Muslims who went out to commit highway robbery and strive in the land with corruption.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: the statement of Malik is correct. Abu Thawr argued for this view, saying: His saying in this verse, ﴿except those who repent before you gain power over them﴾, indicates that it was revealed concerning people other than the polytheists, because they have agreed that when polytheists fall into our hands and then embrace Islam, their blood becomes forbidden; so this shows that the verse was revealed concerning the people of Islam. End of quotation.

This is also indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven for them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38], and by His saying, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace: "Islam demolishes what came before it," transmitted by Muslim and others. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, in his exegesis, related from some scholars that this verse, namely the verse of waging war, abrogated (*naskh*) the action of the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, concerning the ʿUrayniyyin, and the matter stopped at these prescribed penalties (*hudud*).

It is related from Muhammad ibn Sirin that he said: this was before the hudud were revealed; he meant the Prophet's action against the ʿUrayniyyin, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace. A group of scholars said this. Another group held that the Prophet's action against the ʿUrayniyyin was abrogated by the Prophet's prohibition of mutilation (*muthla*), and whoever holds this must establish that the abrogating text came later. The sequence of narrations concerning the occasion of revelation will come. The truth is that this verse encompasses polytheists and others who commit what it includes, and the specific occasion does not restrict it; rather, the consideration is the generality of the wording. Al-Qurtubi said in his exegesis: there is no disagreement among the scholars that the ruling of this verse applies to warring Muslims, even if it was revealed concerning apostates or Jews. End of quotation.

The meaning of his saying *mutarattib* ("applies") is: established. It has been said: the intended sense of "waging war against God" mentioned in the verse is waging war against the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and waging war against the Muslims in his time and after his time, by way of expression (*ʿibara*) and not by way of indication (*dalala*) or analogy (*qiyas*); because the revelation of the text is not by way of direct address (*khitab al-mushafaha*) so that its ruling would be restricted to those who were obligated at the time of revelation, and extending the address to others would then require another proof. The better view is that waging war against God, glorified is He, should be interpreted as disobedience to Him and violation of His laws, while waging war against the Messenger is taken in its literal sense, and the ruling for his community is his ruling, and they are his followers.

Striving in the land to cause corruption is applied to various kinds of evil, as we have mentioned shortly before. Ibn Kathir said in his exegesis: many of the early scholars, among them Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, said: clipping dirhams and dinars is among the acts of corruption in the land. God, exalted is He, has said: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and livestock; and God does not love corruption﴾ [al-Baqara: 205]. End of quotation.

Once what we have established of the generality of the verse, and of the meaning of waging war and striving in the land to cause corruption, is settled for you, know that this applies to everyone who commits such acts, whether Muslim or disbeliever, in Egypt or outside Egypt, in every small and great matter, and whether trivial or grave. The ruling of God in this regard is what is stated in this verse: execution or crucifixion, or cutting off of hands and feet on opposite sides, or banishment from the land. However, this is not the ruling for whoever commits any sin whatsoever; rather, it applies to one whose offence is aggression against the lives and property of people, excluding those for which a different ruling has come in the Book of God or the Sunna of His Messenger, such as theft and what requires retaliation. For we know that in his time, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, there were people who committed sins and transgressions other than these, and this ruling mentioned in this verse was not applied to them by the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace.

By this you recognize the weakness of what is related from Mujahid in explaining the "waging war" mentioned in this verse, that it means adultery and theft. The reason is that these two offences have a ruling other than this ruling in the Book of God and in the Sunna of His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace.

Nevertheless, we shall mention among these doctrines what you will hear. Know that the scholars have differed concerning who deserves the name of "one who wages war." Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, Mujahid, ʿAta, al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, al-Dahhak, and Abu Thawr said: whoever draws a weapon within the dome of Islam (*qubbat al-Islam*), terrorizes the road, and is then seized and overpowered, the imam of the Muslims has the choice regarding him: if he wishes, he kills him; if he wishes, he crucifies him; if he wishes, he cuts off his hand and foot.
