Ibn al-Mundhir said: Malik's position on this question is reported in differing ways: once he affirmed the crime of hirabah (armed highway robbery, ḥirābah) within a city (miṣr), and once he denied that. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, other than what preceded, that he said regarding highwaymen (quṭṭāʿ al-ṭarīq): if they kill and take property, they are killed and crucified; if they kill and do not take property, they are killed and not crucified; if they take property and do not kill, their hands and feet are cut off from opposite sides; and if they terrorize the road and take no property, they are banished from the land.

It is also reported from Abu Mijlaz, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi and ʿAtaʾ, with some variation in the reports from some of them. Ibn Kathir reported this from the majority (al-jumhur), and he also said: "Likewise it is reported from many of the early authorities (salaf) and the imams."

Abu Hanifa said: if he kills, he is killed; if he takes property without killing, his hand and foot are cut off from opposite sides; and if he takes property and kills, the ruler (al-sultan) has the choice: if he wishes, he cuts off his hands and feet, and if he wishes, he does not cut them and kills him and crucifies him. Abu Yusuf said: killing covers everything, and the view of al-Awzaʿi is similar to this. Al-Shafiʿi said: if he takes property, his right hand is cut off and cauterized (ḥusima), then his left foot is cut off and cauterized and he is released; because this crime exceeds theft by being hirabah. If he kills, he is killed; and if he takes property and kills, he is killed and crucified. It is reported from him that he said: he is crucified for three days. Ahmad said: if he kills, he is killed; and if he takes property, his hand and foot are cut off, like the view of al-Shafiʿi.

I know of no evidence for these detailed distinctions, neither from the Book of Allah nor from the Sunnah of His Messenger, except what Ibn Jarir reported in his tafsir, and he alone narrated it. He said: "ʿAli ibn Sahl narrated to us, al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib: that ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan wrote to Anas ibn Malik asking him about this verse, and he wrote back informing him that this verse was revealed concerning those men of ʿUrayna, who were from Bajila. Anas said: they apostatized from Islam, killed the herdsman, drove off the camels, terrorized the road and committed unlawful sexual intercourse (farj al-ḥarām). Anas said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked Jibril about the judgment regarding those who wage war, and he said: whoever steals and terrorizes the road, cut off his hand for his theft and his foot for his terrorizing; whoever kills, kill him; and whoever kills and terrorizes the road and makes lawful the unlawful sexual intercourse, crucify him." Along with this there is severe objectionable content (nakarah shadidah), and it is not known how sound it is. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir, after mentioning some of the details we have mentioned, the following: "What supports this distinction is the hadith that Ibn Jarir narrated in his tafsir, if its chain is sound," and then he mentioned it.

His words: ﴿and they strive in the land to cause corruption﴾ — this is either in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), or as an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) by interpretation; meaning: ﴿causing corruption﴾.

His words: (or they be crucified) — its apparent meaning is that they are crucified alive until they die, since it is one of the types among which Allah gave the choice. Some said: crucifixion happens only after killing, and it is not permissible to crucify someone before killing him, so that he is prevented from prayer, eating and drinking. It is answered that this is a punishment which Allah, glorified is He, prescribed in His Book for His servants.

His words: ﴿or their hands and feet be cut off from opposite sides﴾ — its apparent meaning is the cutting of one of the two hands and one of the two feet from opposite sides, whether the hand cut is the right or the left, and likewise the feet; and it is not required except that the cutting be from opposite sides, either the right hand with the left foot, or the left hand with the right foot. It was also said: what is meant by this is cutting the right hand and the left foot only.

His words: ﴿or they be banished from the land﴾ — the exegetes differed about its meaning. al-Suddi said: it is that they are pursued with horse and foot until they are seized and the prescribed punishment (ḥadd) is established on them, or they flee out of the abode of Islam. This is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, Anas, Malik, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas and al-Zuhri; al-Rummani related it from them in his book. It is reported from al-Shafiʿi that they are taken out from one town to another so that the prescribed punishments may be established on them, and al-Layth ibn Saʿd said likewise. It is reported from Malik that he is banished from the town in which he committed the crime to another and imprisoned there, like the adulterer; and Ibn Jarir and al-Qurtubi preferred this. The Kufans said: their banishment is their imprisonment, so he is banished from the breadth of the world to its narrowness. The apparent meaning of the verse is that he is driven out of the land in which he committed what he committed, without imprisonment or anything else. Banishment may also carry the sense of destruction (al-ihlak), but that is not intended here.

His words: ﴿That is a disgrace for them in this world﴾ — the reference is to the rulings mentioned earlier; khizy means humiliation and disgrace. His words: ﴿except those who repent before you gain power over them; then know that Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ — Allah, glorified is He, excepted those who repent before they come under one's power from the general scope of those punished with the earlier penalties. The apparent meaning is that there is no distinction between bloodshed and property and other sins that entail fixed, defined penalties, so the penitent before capture is not required to answer for any of that; and this is the practice of the Companions.

Some scholars held that retaliation (qiṣaṣ) and all other rights of human beings are not dropped by repentance before capture; the first view is the correct one. As for repentance after capture, the penalty mentioned in the verse is not dropped by it, as the mention of the condition ﴿before you gain power over them﴾ indicates. al-Qurtubi said: The scholars agreed that the ruler is the guardian of one who wages war; so if a combatant kills a man's brother and comes to him in the state of hirabah, the matter of hirabah offers the blood-seeker no recourse, and the pardon of the blood-guardian is not permissible. Ibn Jarir reported from al-Dahhak, concerning His words ﴿because of that We prescribed for the Children of Israel﴾, that he said: because of the son of Adam who killed his brother unjustly.

Ibn Jarir also reported from al-Hasan that it was said to him regarding this verse, meaning His words ﴿it is as if he had slain mankind entirely﴾: "Is it for us as it was for the Children of Israel?" He said: "Yes, by Him besides whom there is no god." Abu Dawud and al-Nasai reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿Indeed, the penalty of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾ that he said: it was revealed concerning the polytheists; whoever of them repents before he is overpowered, there is no path against him. This verse does not shield a Muslim man from the legal punishment if he kills, or causes corruption in the land, or wages war against Allah and His Messenger.

Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir reported from him regarding this verse that he said: some people of the People of the Book had a covenant and pact with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but they broke the covenant and caused corruption in the land, so Allah gave His Prophet the choice concerning them: if he wished he could kill, if he wished he could crucify, and if he wished he could cut off their hands and feet from opposite sides. As for banishment, it means striking out in the land; so if he comes repentant and enters Islam, it is accepted from him and he is not held to account for what preceded. Abu Dawud and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas that this verse was revealed concerning the Harurites (al-Ḥarūriyya).

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Anas that some men from ʿUkl came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), embraced Islam, and found Madina unhealthy; so the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered them to go to the camels of the charity (ṣadaqa), drink from their urine and milk; they killed its herdsman and drove the camels off. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent a party (qafa) in pursuit of them; they were brought back, and he cut off their hands and feet, branded (samala) their eyes, did not cauterize them, and left them until they died. Then Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, the penalty of those who wage war...﴾ the verse. In Muslim, from Anas, he said: the Prophet (ﷺ) only branded the eyes of those people because they had branded the eyes of the herdsmen.

Al-Shafiʿi in al-Umm, ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: if the combatant goes out, takes property and does not kill, he is cut off from opposite sides; if he goes out and kills without taking property, he is killed; if he goes out, takes property and kills, he is killed and crucified; and if he goes out, terrorizes the road, takes no property and does not kill, he is banished. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him regarding the verse that he said: whoever draws the sword within the dome of Islam (qubbat al-Islam) and corrupts the road, and is overpowered and captured, the imam of the Muslims has the choice concerning him: if he wishes he may kill him, if he wishes he may crucify him, and if he wishes he may cut off his hand and foot. He said: ﴿or be banished from the land﴾ means they flee and leave the abode of Islam for the abode of war. Ibn Jarir also reported from him that he said: its banishment is that he be pursued. He also reported similarly from Anas.

Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Shaʿbi that he said: Haritha ibn Badr al-Taymi, a man of Basra, had caused corruption in the land and waged war; he spoke to men of Quraysh asking them to seek security for him from ʿAli, but they refused. Then Saʿid ibn Qays al-Hamdani came to ʿAli and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, what is the penalty of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive in the land to cause corruption?" He said: ﴿that they be killed, or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off from opposite sides, or be banished from the land﴾; then he said: ﴿except those who repent before you gain power over them﴾. Saʿid said: "Even if it is Haritha ibn Badr?" He said: "Even if it is Haritha ibn Badr." Then he said: "This is Haritha ibn Badr; he has come repentant, so he is secure." He said: "Yes." So he brought him to him, he pledged allegiance to him, ʿAli accepted that from him and wrote him a letter of safe conduct (amān).

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 32–34 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, ﴿because of that﴾, means: because of that killer, his crime, and on account of his disobedience. Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian and Qur'anic linguist) said: meaning, because of his offence. He said: it is said, *ajala al-rajulu ʿala ahlihi sharran yaʾjulu ajlan* ("the man committed evil against his family"), when he commits an offence, like *akhadha yaʾkhudhu akhdhan* ("he took"). Abu Jaʿfar (one of the ten canonical reciters) read *min ajli* with a kasra on the nun and the elision of the hamza, and this is a dialect form. In *Sharh al-Durra* (a commentary on a work on the recitations) it is said: Abu Jaʿfar alone read *min ajli dhalika* with a kasra on the hamza, with its vowel transferred to the nun before it. It has been said that *min ajli dhalika* may be connected to *min al-nadimin* ("among the regretful"), so that the pause falls on *min ajli dhalika*, but the first view we have mentioned is preferable. The meaning is that the story of the two sons of Adam is what gave rise to the prescription mentioned, laid upon the Children of Israel. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes.

He singled out the Children of Israel for mention because the context concerns the enumeration of their crimes, and because they were the first nation upon whom the threat concerning the killing of souls was sent down. Severity was applied to them at that time because of their abundant shedding of blood and their killing of the prophets. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the verb it depends on, namely *katabna* ("We prescribed"), conveys restriction (*qasr*): i.e., because of that, and not because of anything else. *Min* here denotes the starting point. ﴿That whoever kills a soul﴾, one soul from among these souls, ﴿without a soul﴾, i.e., without a soul that merits retaliation (*qisas*). Thus excluded from this is one who kills a soul in retaliation for a soul.

His saying, ﴿or corruption in the land﴾: the majority read it in the genitive, as a conjunction (*ʿatf*) upon *nafs* ("soul").

Al-Hasan (al-Basri) read it in the accusative, by postulating a deleted verb indicated by the beginning of the speech, its estimated form being: "or he caused corruption in the land." There is weakness in this. The meaning of the majority reading is: whoever kills a soul without any cause of retaliation or corruption in the land, it is as if he had killed all people.

It is established that every conditional ruling where one of two things is realized, its contradiction is conditioned on the absence of both together; and every ruling conditioned on the realization of both together, its contradiction is conditioned on the absence of one of them, since the contradiction of everything is conditioned on the contradiction of its condition. The exegetes have differed over what this corruption mentioned in this verse is. It has been said that it is polytheism (*shirk*), and it has been said that it is highway robbery (*qatʿ al-tariq*).

The apparent sense of the Qur'anic wording is that it includes whatever truly qualifies as corruption in the land. Polytheism is corruption in the land, highway robbery is corruption in the land, shedding blood, violating the sanctity of the sacred (*hatk al-haram*), and plundering property are corruption in the land, and oppression of God's servants without right is corruption in the land, and demolishing buildings, cutting down trees, and polluting rivers are corruption in the land. From this you know that these types truly qualify as corruption in the land. Likewise, the corruption that will come in His saying, ﴿and they strive in the land to cause corruption﴾, applies to these types. The full discussion of the meaning of corruption will come shortly.

His saying, ﴿it is as if he had killed all people﴾: the exegetes differed in establishing this comparison, that the punishment of one who kills all people is greater than that of one who kills one of them. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: the meaning is that whoever kills a prophet or a just imam, it is as if he killed all people; and whoever preserves him, by strengthening his arm and supporting him, it is as if he gave life to all people. Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) transmitted this from him. It is related from Mujahid that he said: the meaning is that whoever kills a believing soul deliberately, God has made his recompense Hell, and He is angry with him, curses him, and prepares for him a great punishment; so even if he killed all people, it would not add to this. He said: and whoever is spared from killing and does not kill anyone, it is as if he gave life to all people.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted something similar from him. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said, in explaining this verse: he ruined his soul just as if he had killed all people. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted this from him. It is related from al-Hasan that he said: "it is as if he killed all people" in respect of the burden, and "as if he gave life to all people" in respect of the reward. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is that whoever kills a soul incurs the same retribution and retaliation as one who kills all people. "And whoever gives life to it" means: whoever pardons one whose killing is due. Al-Qurtubi transmitted this from him. It is related from al-Hasan that giving life means pardon after having the power to exact retribution, i.e., he gave it life.

It is related from Mujahid that giving life to it is rescuing it from drowning, burning, collapse, or destruction. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted this from him. It has been said: the meaning is that whoever kills a soul, all the believers become his adversaries, because he has wronged them all; ﴿and whoever gives it life, it is as if he gave life to all people﴾, i.e., it becomes obligatory upon all to thank him. It has also been said: the meaning is that whoever deems one person lawful to kill has deemed all lawful, because he has denied the Law. In any case, giving life here is an expression for abstaining from killing and rescuing from destruction, so it is figurative, since its literal meaning is specific to God, mighty and majestic.

The purpose of this comparison on the side of killing is to magnify the gravity of killing and to make its matter weighty in souls, so that those bold and audacious would refrain from it. On the side of giving life, the purpose is to encourage pardoning offenders and rescuing those thrown into destruction.

His saying, ﴿And certainly Our messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾: this is an independent sentence, emphasized by the *lam* that precedes the oath (*al-lam al-mutawwiʾa lil-qasam*), containing the information that the messengers, upon them be prayers and peace, came to the servants with what God had legislated for them of rulings, among which is the matter of killing. The *thumma* in His saying, ﴿Then indeed many of them﴾, is for rank-based delay (*al-tarakhi al-rutbi*) and for rational astonishment (*al-istibʿad al-ʿaqli*). The reference in the phrase ﴿that﴾ is to what was mentioned that God prescribed upon the Children of Israel; i.e., indeed many of them, after that prescription, ﴿in the land are transgressors﴾, in killing.

His saying, ﴿Indeed the recompense of those who wage war against God and His Messenger﴾: the people have differed concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse. The majority held that it was revealed concerning the ʿUrayniyyin (a group who attacked the herds of the Prophet, ﷺ). Malik, al-Shafiʿi, Abu Thawr, and the people of opinion (*ahl al-ra'y*) said: it was revealed concerning those among the Muslims who went out to commit highway robbery and strive in the land with corruption.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: the statement of Malik is correct. Abu Thawr argued for this view, saying: His saying in this verse, ﴿except those who repent before you gain power over them﴾, indicates that it was revealed concerning people other than the polytheists, because they have agreed that when polytheists fall into our hands and then embrace Islam, their blood becomes forbidden; so this shows that the verse was revealed concerning the people of Islam. End of quotation.

This is also indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven for them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38], and by His saying, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace: "Islam demolishes what came before it," transmitted by Muslim and others. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, in his exegesis, related from some scholars that this verse, namely the verse of waging war, abrogated (*naskh*) the action of the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, concerning the ʿUrayniyyin, and the matter stopped at these prescribed penalties (*hudud*).

It is related from Muhammad ibn Sirin that he said: this was before the hudud were revealed; he meant the Prophet's action against the ʿUrayniyyin, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace. A group of scholars said this. Another group held that the Prophet's action against the ʿUrayniyyin was abrogated by the Prophet's prohibition of mutilation (*muthla*), and whoever holds this must establish that the abrogating text came later. The sequence of narrations concerning the occasion of revelation will come. The truth is that this verse encompasses polytheists and others who commit what it includes, and the specific occasion does not restrict it; rather, the consideration is the generality of the wording. Al-Qurtubi said in his exegesis: there is no disagreement among the scholars that the ruling of this verse applies to warring Muslims, even if it was revealed concerning apostates or Jews. End of quotation.

The meaning of his saying *mutarattib* ("applies") is: established. It has been said: the intended sense of "waging war against God" mentioned in the verse is waging war against the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and waging war against the Muslims in his time and after his time, by way of expression (*ʿibara*) and not by way of indication (*dalala*) or analogy (*qiyas*); because the revelation of the text is not by way of direct address (*khitab al-mushafaha*) so that its ruling would be restricted to those who were obligated at the time of revelation, and extending the address to others would then require another proof. It has also been said: waging war against the Muslims was made into waging war against God and His Messenger in order to magnify their fighting and to exalt the harm done to them, because God, glorified is He, cannot be warred against or overcome. The better view is that waging war against God, glorified is He, should be interpreted as disobedience to Him and violation of His laws, while waging war against the Messenger is taken in its literal sense, and the ruling for his community is his ruling, and they are his followers.

Striving in the land to cause corruption is applied to various kinds of evil, as we have mentioned shortly before. Ibn Kathir said in his exegesis: many of the early scholars, among them Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, said: clipping dirhams and dinars is among the acts of corruption in the land. God, exalted is He, has said: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and livestock; and God does not love corruption﴾ [al-Baqara: 205]. End of quotation.

Once what we have established of the generality of the verse, and of the meaning of waging war and striving in the land to cause corruption, is settled for you, know that this applies to everyone who commits such acts, whether Muslim or disbeliever, in Egypt or outside Egypt, in every small and great matter, and whether trivial or grave. The ruling of God in this regard is what is stated in this verse: execution or crucifixion, or cutting off of hands and feet on opposite sides, or banishment from the land. However, this is not the ruling for whoever commits any sin whatsoever; rather, it applies to one whose offence is aggression against the lives and property of people, excluding those for which a different ruling has come in the Book of God or the Sunna of His Messenger, such as theft and what requires retaliation. For we know that in his time, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, there were people who committed sins and transgressions other than these, and this ruling mentioned in this verse was not applied to them by the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace.

By this you recognize the weakness of what is related from Mujahid in explaining the "waging war" mentioned in this verse, that it means adultery and theft. The reason is that these two offences have a ruling other than this ruling in the Book of God and in the Sunna of His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace.

Once you know what the apparent meaning of this verse is, according to the usage of the Arabic language, by which we have been commanded to interpret the Book of God and the Sunna of His Messenger, beware of being deceived by any of the transmitted details and the reported doctrines, unless there comes to you a proof necessitating the restriction of this generality or the specification of this meaning understood from Arabic usage. Then you may act upon it and place it in its proper position. As for what lies beyond that:

*"Leave aside a plunder that was cried out about in its sacred enclosures, and bring a tale other than the tale of the riding camels."*

Nevertheless, we shall mention among these doctrines what you will hear. Know that the scholars have differed concerning who deserves the name of "one who wages war." Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, Mujahid, ʿAta, al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, al-Dahhak, and Abu Thawr said: whoever draws a weapon within the dome of Islam (*qubbat al-Islam*), terrorizes the road, and is then seized and overpowered, the imam of the Muslims has the choice regarding him: if he wishes, he kills him; if he wishes, he crucifies him; if he wishes, he cuts off his hand and foot. Malik also held this view, and he explicitly stated that the one who wages war, according to him, is one who attacks people in a city, or in the open country, or overpowers them over their persons and property, without a blood feud, vendetta, or enmity.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: Malik's position on this question is reported in differing ways: once he affirmed the crime of hirabah (armed highway robbery, ḥirābah) within a city (miṣr), and once he denied that. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, other than what preceded, that he said regarding highwaymen (quṭṭāʿ al-ṭarīq): if they kill and take property, they are killed and crucified; if they kill and do not take property, they are killed and not crucified; if they take property and do not kill, their hands and feet are cut off from opposite sides; and if they terrorize the road and take no property, they are banished from the land.

It is also reported from Abu Mijlaz, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi and ʿAtaʾ, with some variation in the reports from some of them. Ibn Kathir reported this from the majority (al-jumhur), and he also said: "Likewise it is reported from many of the early authorities (salaf) and the imams."

Abu Hanifa said: if he kills, he is killed; if he takes property without killing, his hand and foot are cut off from opposite sides; and if he takes property and kills, the ruler (al-sultan) has the choice: if he wishes, he cuts off his hands and feet, and if he wishes, he does not cut them and kills him and crucifies him. Abu Yusuf said: killing covers everything, and the view of al-Awzaʿi is similar to this. Al-Shafiʿi said: if he takes property, his right hand is cut off and cauterized (ḥusima), then his left foot is cut off and cauterized and he is released; because this crime exceeds theft by being hirabah. If he kills, he is killed; and if he takes property and kills, he is killed and crucified. It is reported from him that he said: he is crucified for three days. Ahmad said: if he kills, he is killed; and if he takes property, his hand and foot are cut off, like the view of al-Shafiʿi.

I know of no evidence for these detailed distinctions, neither from the Book of Allah nor from the Sunnah of His Messenger, except what Ibn Jarir reported in his tafsir, and he alone narrated it. He said: "ʿAli ibn Sahl narrated to us, al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib: that ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan wrote to Anas ibn Malik asking him about this verse, and he wrote back informing him that this verse was revealed concerning those men of ʿUrayna, who were from Bajila. Anas said: they apostatized from Islam, killed the herdsman, drove off the camels, terrorized the road and committed unlawful sexual intercourse (farj al-ḥarām). Anas said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked Jibril about the judgment regarding those who wage war, and he said: whoever steals and terrorizes the road, cut off his hand for his theft and his foot for his terrorizing; whoever kills, kill him; and whoever kills and terrorizes the road and makes lawful the unlawful sexual intercourse, crucify him." Along with this there is severe objectionable content (nakarah shadidah), and it is not known how sound it is. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir, after mentioning some of the details we have mentioned, the following: "What supports this distinction is the hadith that Ibn Jarir narrated in his tafsir, if its chain is sound," and then he mentioned it.

His words: ﴿and they strive in the land to cause corruption﴾ — this is either in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), or as an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) by interpretation; meaning: ﴿causing corruption﴾.

His words: (or they be crucified) — its apparent meaning is that they are crucified alive until they die, since it is one of the types among which Allah gave the choice. Some said: crucifixion happens only after killing, and it is not permissible to crucify someone before killing him, so that he is prevented from prayer, eating and drinking. It is answered that this is a punishment which Allah, glorified is He, prescribed in His Book for His servants.

His words: ﴿or their hands and feet be cut off from opposite sides﴾ — its apparent meaning is the cutting of one of the two hands and one of the two feet from opposite sides, whether the hand cut is the right or the left, and likewise the feet; and it is not required except that the cutting be from opposite sides, either the right hand with the left foot, or the left hand with the right foot. It was also said: what is meant by this is cutting the right hand and the left foot only.

His words: ﴿or they be banished from the land﴾ — the exegetes differed about its meaning. al-Suddi said: it is that they are pursued with horse and foot until they are seized and the prescribed punishment (ḥadd) is established on them, or they flee out of the abode of Islam. This is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, Anas, Malik, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas and al-Zuhri; al-Rummani related it from them in his book. It is reported from al-Shafiʿi that they are taken out from one town to another so that the prescribed punishments may be established on them, and al-Layth ibn Saʿd said likewise. It is reported from Malik that he is banished from the town in which he committed the crime to another and imprisoned there, like the adulterer; and Ibn Jarir and al-Qurtubi preferred this. The Kufans said: their banishment is their imprisonment, so he is banished from the breadth of the world to its narrowness. The apparent meaning of the verse is that he is driven out of the land in which he committed what he committed, without imprisonment or anything else. Banishment may also carry the sense of destruction (al-ihlak), but that is not intended here.

His words: ﴿That is a disgrace for them in this world﴾ — the reference is to the rulings mentioned earlier; khizy means humiliation and disgrace. His words: ﴿except those who repent before you gain power over them; then know that Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ — Allah, glorified is He, excepted those who repent before they come under one's power from the general scope of those punished with the earlier penalties. The apparent meaning is that there is no distinction between bloodshed and property and other sins that entail fixed, defined penalties, so the penitent before capture is not required to answer for any of that; and this is the practice of the Companions.

Some scholars held that retaliation (qiṣaṣ) and all other rights of human beings are not dropped by repentance before capture; the first view is the correct one. As for repentance after capture, the penalty mentioned in the verse is not dropped by it, as the mention of the condition ﴿before you gain power over them﴾ indicates. al-Qurtubi said: The scholars agreed that the ruler is the guardian of one who wages war; so if a combatant kills a man's brother and comes to him in the state of hirabah, the matter of hirabah offers the blood-seeker no recourse, and the pardon of the blood-guardian is not permissible. Ibn Jarir reported from al-Dahhak, concerning His words ﴿because of that We prescribed for the Children of Israel﴾, that he said: because of the son of Adam who killed his brother unjustly.

Ibn Jarir also reported from al-Hasan that it was said to him regarding this verse, meaning His words ﴿it is as if he had slain mankind entirely﴾: "Is it for us as it was for the Children of Israel?" He said: "Yes, by Him besides whom there is no god." Abu Dawud and al-Nasai reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿Indeed, the penalty of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾ that he said: it was revealed concerning the polytheists; whoever of them repents before he is overpowered, there is no path against him. This verse does not shield a Muslim man from the legal punishment if he kills, or causes corruption in the land, or wages war against Allah and His Messenger.

Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir reported from him regarding this verse that he said: some people of the People of the Book had a covenant and pact with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but they broke the covenant and caused corruption in the land, so Allah gave His Prophet the choice concerning them: if he wished he could kill, if he wished he could crucify, and if he wished he could cut off their hands and feet from opposite sides. As for banishment, it means striking out in the land; so if he comes repentant and enters Islam, it is accepted from him and he is not held to account for what preceded. Abu Dawud and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas that this verse was revealed concerning the Harurites (al-Ḥarūriyya).

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others reported from Anas that some men from ʿUkl came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), embraced Islam, and found Madina unhealthy; so the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered them to go to the camels of the charity (ṣadaqa), drink from their urine and milk; they killed its herdsman and drove the camels off. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent a party (qafa) in pursuit of them; they were brought back, and he cut off their hands and feet, branded (samala) their eyes, did not cauterize them, and left them until they died. Then Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, the penalty of those who wage war...﴾ the verse. In Muslim, from Anas, he said: the Prophet (ﷺ) only branded the eyes of those people because they had branded the eyes of the herdsmen.

Al-Shafiʿi in al-Umm, ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse that he said: if the combatant goes out, takes property and does not kill, he is cut off from opposite sides; if he goes out and kills without taking property, he is killed; if he goes out, takes property and kills, he is killed and crucified; and if he goes out, terrorizes the road, takes no property and does not kill, he is banished. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him regarding the verse that he said: whoever draws the sword within the dome of Islam (qubbat al-Islam) and corrupts the road, and is overpowered and captured, the imam of the Muslims has the choice concerning him: if he wishes he may kill him, if he wishes he may crucify him, and if he wishes he may cut off his hand and foot. He said: ﴿or be banished from the land﴾ means they flee and leave the abode of Islam for the abode of war. Ibn Jarir also reported from him that he said: its banishment is that he be pursued. He also reported similarly from Anas.

Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Shaʿbi that he said: Haritha ibn Badr al-Taymi, a man of Basra, had caused corruption in the land and waged war; he spoke to men of Quraysh asking them to seek security for him from ʿAli, but they refused. Then Saʿid ibn Qays al-Hamdani came to ʿAli and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, what is the penalty of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive in the land to cause corruption?" He said: ﴿that they be killed, or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off from opposite sides, or be banished from the land﴾; then he said: ﴿except those who repent before you gain power over them﴾. Saʿid said: "Even if it is Haritha ibn Badr?" He said: "Even if it is Haritha ibn Badr." Then he said: "This is Haritha ibn Badr; he has come repentant, so he is secure." He said: "Yes." So he brought him to him, he pledged allegiance to him, ʿAli accepted that from him and wrote him a letter of safe conduct (amān).

(ابْتَغُوا) seek/ask (اطْلُبُوا). (إلَيْهِ) toward Him, not toward anything else. (الوَسِيلَةَ) is on the pattern fa'ila, from "tawassaltu ilayhi," meaning "I drew near to him."

ʿAntara said:

*Indeed, men have a means (wasila) to you; if they seize you, then adorn yourself with kohl and dye.*

Another said:

*When the slanderers are heedless, we return to our union, and playful dalliance (al-tasabbi) returns between us, and the means (al-wasa'il).*

So al-wasila is the nearness to God that should be sought. This was said by Abu Wa'il, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAta', and ʿAbdullah ibn Kathir. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: "What these imams have said there is no disagreement among the exegetes about." Then ask God for me al-wasila, for it is a station in Paradise that is not fitting except for one of God's servants, and I hope that I am he. Whoever asks God for al-wasila for me, intercession will be due for him." There are other hadiths on this subject.

It has also been said that al-wasila is taqwa, because it is the foundation of the matter and all good, so the second clause would then explain the first.

The apparent meaning is that al-wasila, which is nearness, applies to taqwa and to other qualities of good by which servants draw near to their Lord. ﴿وجاهِدُوا في سَبِيلِهِ﴾ (And strive in His way) — whoever does not accept His religion. (﴿لَعَلَّكم تُفْلِحُونَ﴾ — so that you may prosper.)

His saying ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ (Indeed, those who disbelieved) is an independent statement, brought to rebuke the disbelievers and to encourage the believers to obey God's commands. ﴿لَوْ أنَّ لَهم ما في الأرْضِ﴾ (If they had whatever is on the earth) of its wealth and resources. It has been said that the meaning is for each one of them, so as to be more terrifying, though the apparent sense of the plural pronoun is otherwise. ﴿جَمِيعًا﴾ (all of it) is an emphasis.

His saying ﴿ومِثْلَهُ﴾ (and the like of it) is conjoined to ﴿ما في الأرْضِ﴾, and ﴿مَعَهُ﴾ (with it) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). ﴿لِيَفْتَدُوا بِهِ﴾ (so as to ransom themselves with it): so that they make it a ransom for themselves. The pronoun is singular, either because it refers back to what was mentioned, or because it stands in the place of a demonstrative, meaning "to ransom themselves with that." ﴿مِن عَذابِ يَوْمِ القِيامَةِ﴾ (from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection) is connected to the verb mentioned. ﴿ما تُقُبِّلَ مِنهم﴾ (it would not be accepted from them), that is, that ransom. This is the answer to ("if," لَوْ).

His saying ﴿يُرِيدُونَ أنْ يَخْرُجُوا مِنَ النّارِ﴾ (They wish to leave the Fire) is an explanatory resumptive clause (istiʾnaf bayani), as if it were said: "What is their condition in this painful punishment?" So it is answered: "They wish to leave the Fire."

It is also read as ﴿إنْ يُخْرَجُوا﴾ (if they are brought out), from akhraja. This reading is weakened by ﴿وما هم بِخارِجِينَ مِنها﴾ (but they will not emerge from it). He said: "He means the poor." I said to Jabir: "God says: ﴿يُرِيدُونَ أنْ يَخْرُجُوا مِنَ النّارِ وما هم بِخارِجِينَ مِنها﴾." He said: "Recite the beginning of the verse: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَوْ أنَّ لَهم ما في الأرْضِ جَمِيعًا ومِثْلَهُ مَعَهُ لِيَفْتَدُوا بِهِ﴾. Indeed, they are those who disbelieved."

Glory be to God, how strange is a man who does not distinguish between the most authentic of the authentic and the most false of lies attributed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He ventures to speak about what he does not know and does not understand what it is. The position of this clause, namely His saying ﴿وما هم بِخارِجِينَ مِنها﴾, is accusative as a circumstantial clause. It has also been said that it is a parenthetical clause (jumla iʿtirāḍiyya).

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿وابْتَغُوا إلَيْهِ الوَسِيلَةَ﴾, that he said: "al-wasila is nearness (al-qurba)."

al-Hakim related it and declared it sound, from Hudhayfa, the same. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿وابْتَغُوا إلَيْهِ الوَسِيلَةَ﴾, that he said: "Draw near to God by obeying Him and acting by what pleases Him."

Muslim, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Jabir ibn ʿAbdullah that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A people will come out of the Fire and enter Paradise." He said: "He means the poor." I said to Jabir: "God says: ﴿يُرِيدُونَ أنْ يَخْرُجُوا مِنَ النّارِ وما هم بِخارِجِينَ مِنها﴾." He said: "Recite the beginning of the verse: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَوْ أنَّ لَهم ما في الأرْضِ جَمِيعًا ومِثْلَهُ مَعَهُ لِيَفْتَدُوا بِهِ﴾. Indeed, they are those who disbelieved."

Ibn Jarir related from ʿIkrima that Nafiʿ ibn al-Azraq said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "You claim that a people will come out of the Fire, and God the Exalted has said: ﴿وما هم بِخارِجِينَ مِنها﴾." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Woe to you! Read what comes before it. This is for the disbelievers."

al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf, after mentioning this: "It is among the things fabricated by the Mujbira. Glory be to God, how strange is a man who does not distinguish between the most authentic of the authentic and the most false of lies attributed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He ventures to speak about what he does not know and does not understand what it is. The hadiths have been transmitted in such a manner (tawatur) that it is hidden from no one who has even a little familiarity with the science of narration that the sinful among the monotheists will come out of the Fire. Whoever denies this is not fit for debate, for he has denied something that is among the necessary matters of the Sharia. O God, forgive us."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 38–40:

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the ruling for the one who takes property openly, who is the robber (al-muharib), He followed it with mention of the one who takes property secretly, who is the thief (al-sariq). He mentioned the female thief along with the male thief for the sake of added clarification, because the Qur'an generally confines itself to men when legislating rulings. The grammarians (a'immat al-nahw) have differed over the predicate of "al-sariq wa-al-sariqah": is it omitted (muqaddar) or is it "fa-aqta'u" (so cut off)? Sibawayh went to the first view and said its implied form is: "What is enjoined upon you, or what is recited to you, is the thief, male and female," meaning their ruling. Al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj went to the second view. The entry of the fa' is because the subject contains the meaning of a condition, since the meaning is: "The one who stole and the one who stole (female)." It has been read as "wa-al-sariqa wa-al-sariqata" in the accusative, on the assumption of "uqta'u" (cut off). Sibawayh preferred this reading and said: "The preferred form in Arabic speech is the accusative, as you say, 'Zayd, strike him' (zaydan idribhu), but the common readers (al-'ammah) refused anything but the nominative," meaning the common body of readers. "Al-sariqah" with a kasra on the ra' is the name of the stolen item, while the verbal noun from "saraqa yasriqu sarqan" is, as al-Jawhari said, taking a thing secretly from the eyes; from it comes "istaraqa al-sam'" (he eavesdropped) and "sarraqahu al-nazar" (he stole a glance at him).

His saying: "fa-aqta'u" (so cut off). Qat' means separation and removal. The plural "aydi" (hands) is used to avoid combining two duals. The purified Sunnah has clarified that the place of cutting is the wrist (al-rusgh). Some people said it is cut from the elbow (al-mirfaq), and the Kharijites said from the shoulder (al-mankib).

Theft must be of at least a quarter of a dinar or more, and it must be from a protected place (hirz), as the sound hadiths report. The majority held the quarter dinar as the standard, while some set the threshold at ten dirhams. The majority also held the requirement of a protected place, and al-Hasan al-Basri said that if one gathers garments in a house, the hand is cut. The jurists (a'immat al-fiqh) and the commentators of hadith have extensively discussed the topic of theft, to a degree that prolonging it here would bring little benefit.

His saying: "jaza'an bima kasaba" (as a recompense for what they earned). It is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu); that is, "cut off for the recompense," or it is an emphatic verbal noun for an omitted verb; that is, "so He requited them with recompense." The ba' is causal (sababiyyah), and ma is verbal (masdariyyah); that is, "because of their earning," or relative (mawsulah); that is, "a recompense for what they earned of the theft."

His saying: "nakalan" (as an exemplary punishment) is a substitute for "jaza'an." It was also said that it is a cause (illah) of the recompense, and the recompense is a cause of the cutting. One says "nakkaltu bihi" when you do to him what should deter him from that act.

His saying: "fa-inna Allaha yatubu 'alayhi" (then indeed Allah relents toward him). However, the wording is general, so it includes the thief and others among the sinners, and the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause.

Ata' and a group have used this to argue that the cutting falls away through repentance. This argument is not sound, because this conditional sentence only establishes the mere acceptance of repentance, that Allah relents toward whoever repents. There is nothing in it indicating that there is no cutting for the one who repents. In the time of prophethood, whoever became liable to a prescribed punishment would come to the Prophet (ﷺ), repentant of the sin he had committed, seeking purification through the punishment, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would apply the penalty to him.

It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "he said to the thief after cutting him: 'Repent to Allah,' then said: 'Allah has accepted your repentance.'" Al-Daraqutni recorded it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah. Ahmad and others recorded that this verse was revealed concerning the woman who used to steal goods, when she said to the Prophet (ﷺ) after her cutting: "Is there any repentance for me?" The Sunnah contains what indicates that once prescribed penalties (hudud) have been brought before the rulers (a'immah), they become obligatory and it is impermissible to waive them.

His saying: "Alam ta'lam anna Allaha lahu mulku as-samawati wa-al-ard" (Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth). This interrogation is for denial together with the affirmation of knowledge, and it serves as a heading for His saying: "He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills"; that is, whoever has dominion over the heavens and the earth is capable of this punishment, which is left to His will, and of this forgiveness, which is left to it as well.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Qatadah concerning His saying: "jaza'an bima kasaba nakalan min Allah" (a recompense for what they earned, an exemplary punishment from Allah) that he said: "Do not show them pity in it, for it is the command of Allah which He has commanded."

He said: It has been related to us that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab used to say: "Be harsh with the corrupt, and make them (feel the consequence) hand by hand and foot by foot." 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Mujahid concerning His saying: "faman taba min ba'di zulmihi wa-aslaha fa-inna Allaha yatubu 'alayhi" (whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, then indeed Allah relents toward him) that he said: "The prescribed punishment is its expiation (kaffarah)."

The hadiths concerning the threshold of theft and all other details related to this prescribed punishment are mentioned in the books of hadith, so we will not lengthen the discussion of them.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 41–44 (part 1 of 3)**

His saying: ﴿Let them not grieve you﴾ (*la yahzunka*). Nafi' read it with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *zay* (*yuhzinka*). The rest read it with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *zay* (*yahzunka*). *Al-huzn* is the opposite of *al-surur* (joy). One says *hazina al-rajul* (with a *kasra*), so he is *hazin* or *hazeen* (grieved), and *ahzanahu ghayruhu* or *hazanahu* (someone else grieved him). Al-Yazidi said: *hazanahu* is the dialect of Quraysh and *ahzanahu* is the dialect of Tamim, and both have been read. In the verse there is a prohibition to the Prophet (ﷺ) against being deeply affected by the swiftness of the disbelievers in their disbelief, because Allah, glorified is He, had promised him in more than one place victory over them. *Al-musara'ah ila al-shay'* is falling into a thing quickly.

What is meant here is their falling into disbelief quickly when an opportunity presents itself. He chose the particle *fi* over *ila* to indicate their settling into it. The *min* in His saying ﴿from those who say﴾ (*min alladhina qalu*) is explanatory (*bayaniyyah*), and the clause explains who the ones hastening to disbelief are. The *ba'* in ﴿with their mouths﴾ (*bi-afwahihim*) is connected to *qalu* and not to *amanna*. Those who said "We believe" with their mouths while their hearts did not believe are the hypocrites. ﴿And from those who are Jews﴾ (*wa-min alladhina hadu*) means the Jews. It is coordinated with *min alladhina qalu amanna*, and this is the completion of the statement. The meaning is that those hastening to disbelief are a group of hypocrites and a group of Jews.

His saying: ﴿They are listeners to falsehood﴾ (*sammaʻuna lil-kadhib*) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are listeners to falsehood. It refers either to both groups or to those who hasten. The *lam* in *lil-kadhib* is for emphasis, or it implies that listening carries the meaning of accepting. It has been said that *sammaʻuna* is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿from those who are Jews﴾, meaning: and from those who are Jews are a people who are *sammaʻuna lil-kadhib*, that is, receptive to the lies of their leaders who distort the Torah. His saying ﴿listeners for another people﴾ (*sammaʻuna li-qawmin akharin*) is a second predicate, and the *lam* in it is like the *lam* in *lil-kadhib*. It has also been said that the *lam* is causal in both places, meaning: they listen to the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the sake of lying about him, and they listen on behalf of another people whom they sent as spies to them, so that they might convey to them what they heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿who have not come to you﴾ (*lam ya'tukum*) is an attribute of *qawm* (people), meaning they did not attend your assembly. They were a group of Jews who did not attend the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) out of arrogance and rebelliousness. It has also been said they were a group of hypocrites who avoided the gatherings of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Al-Farra' said: it is permissible to say *sammaʻeen*, as in His saying: ﴿cursed, wherever they are found﴾ [al-Ahzab: 61].

His saying: ﴿They distort words from their places﴾ (*yuharrifuna al-kalima min ba'di mawadi'ihi*) is among the attributes of the aforementioned people. That is, they turn it away from its places where Allah placed it, and they interpret it other than its true interpretation (*ta'wil*). The distorters are the Jews. It has been said that this clause is the predicate of an omitted subject. It has been said that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *lam ya'tukum*. It has been said that it is a resumed clause (*mustanafah*) with no place in the grammatical structure, for the purpose of enumerating their faults and blemishes.

The meaning of *min ba'di mawadi'ihi* is "after its being placed in its places," or "after its being placed in its places in which Allah placed it," in terms of its wording, or in terms of its meaning.

His saying: ﴿They say: If you are given this, take it﴾ (*yaqulun in utitum hadha fakhudhuhu*) is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*) from the pronoun in *yuharrifuna*, or a resumed clause, or an attribute of *qawm*, or the predicate of an omitted subject. The reference of their words *hadha* ("this") is to the distorted speech. That is: if you are given from Muhammad this speech which we have distorted, then take it and act upon it. And if it is not given to you, but he brings you something other than it, then beware of accepting it and acting upon it.

His saying: ﴿And whoever Allah wills to test﴾ (*wa-man yurid Allahu fitnatahu*), that is, His misguidance, ﴿you will not be able to avail him anything from Allah﴾ (*fa-lan tamlika lahu min Allahi shay'an*), that is, you cannot ward that off from him, nor can you benefit him or guide him. (p-373) This clause is resumed, confirming what precedes it. Its apparent meaning is general, and those whom the context concerns are included in it first and foremost. The reference of His saying *ulaika* ("those") is to those already mentioned: those who said "We believe" with their mouths, and the Jews. It is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿those whom Allah did not intend to purify their hearts﴾, that is, He did not intend to purify them from the filth of disbelief and hypocrisy as He purified the hearts of the believers. ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾ (*lahum fi al-dunya khizy*), through the exposure of the hypocrites' hypocrisy, through the imposition of the poll tax (*jizyah*) on the disbelievers, and through the exposure of their distortion and concealment of what Allah revealed in the Torah.

His saying: ﴿listeners to falsehood﴾ (*sammaʻuna lil-kadhib*) is repeated for emphasis of its ugliness, and so that it serves as an introduction to what follows, which is ﴿devourers of unlawful gain﴾ (*akkaluna lil-suht*). These two are among the predicates of that omitted subject mentioned earlier. *Al-suht* (with a *damma* on the *sin* and a sukun on the *ha'*) is unlawful wealth. Its root meaning is destruction and severity, from *sahatahu*, meaning "he destroyed him." From it comes His saying ﴿lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾ [Ta-Ha: 61]. From it is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*"The bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left of wealth only the stripped or the shaved."*

It is said to the barber: *ushḥat*, that is, uproot. The unlawful is called *suht* because it destroys acts of worship, that is, it removes them and uproots them. Al-Farra' said: its origin is the bite of hunger. It has also been said it is bribery. The first is preferable. Bribery falls within the unlawful first and foremost. A group has explained it as a specific kind of unlawful, such as a gift to one who fulfils a need, or the payment of a soothsayer (*hulwan al-kahin*). But generalization is more correct.

His saying: ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them﴾ (*fa-in ja'uka fa-hkum baynahum aw a'rid 'anhum*) contains an option given to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) between judging between them and turning away from them.

This has been used as evidence that the rulers of the Muslims have the choice between the two matters. The scholars have agreed that it is obligatory for the rulers of the Muslims to judge between a Muslim and a protected non-Muslim (*dhimmi*) when they bring their dispute to them. They differed concerning the People of the Covenant (*ahl al-dhimma*) when they bring disputes among themselves. Some people held that there is a choice, while others held that it is obligatory. They said: this verse is abrogated (*mansukhah*, i.e., superseded by a later ruling) by His saying: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Zuhri, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and al-Suddi said this, and it is the sound position in the view of al-Shafi'i. Al-Qurtubi reported it from most of the scholars.

His saying: ﴿And if you turn away from them, they will not harm you at all﴾ (*wa-in tu'rid 'anhum fa-lan yadurruka shay'an*), that is: if you choose to turn away from judging between them, then they have no way over you, because Allah is your protector and your helper against them. And if you choose to judge between them, ﴿then judge between them with justice﴾ (*fa-hkum baynahum bi-l-qist*), that is, with the justice which Allah commanded you and revealed to you.

His saying: ﴿And how would they make you judge while they have the Torah in which is the judgment of Allah?﴾ (*wa-kayfa yuhakkimunaka wa-'indahumu al-tawrat fiha hukmu Allah*) contains an expression of wonder directed at him (ﷺ) concerning their asking him to judge, even though they do not believe in him or in what he brought. Moreover, what they ask him to judge is present with them in the Torah, such as stoning and the like. They only come to him (ﷺ) and ask him to judge out of hope that it would agree with their distortion and the alteration they made to the Torah.

His saying: ﴿then they turn away﴾ (*thumma yatawallawna*) is coordinated with *yuhakkimunaka*. ﴿After that﴾ (*min ba'di dhalika*) means after their asking you to judge. The clause of His saying ﴿And those are not believers﴾ (*wa-ma ulaika bi-l-mu'minin*) serves to establish the content of what precedes it.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, We revealed the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾ (*inna anzalna al-tawrat fiha hudan wa-nur*) is a resumed statement (*isti'naf*) containing the glorification of the Torah and the magnifying of its status, and that in it is guidance and light. It explains the laws, gives glad tidings of Muhammad (ﷺ), and makes following him obligatory.

His saying: ﴿by which the prophets judged﴾ (*yahkumu biha al-nabiyyun*). They are the prophets of the Children of Israel. The clause is either resumed or circumstantial. ﴿Who submitted﴾ (*alladhina aslamu*) is a praising attribute of the prophets. In it is a humbling of the Jews contemporary with him (ﷺ), by stating that their prophets were following the religion of Islam, which Muhammad (ﷺ) followed. It has been said: what is meant by "the prophets" is Muhammad (ﷺ), and he was referred to with the plural form as a mark of honor.

His saying: ﴿for those who are Jews﴾ (*lilladhina hadu*) is connected to *yahkumu*. The meaning is: the prophets judge by it for those who are Jews, against them.

﴿And the rabbis﴾ (*al-rabbaniyyun*) are the wise scholars, and its explanation has already preceded. ﴿And the rabbis﴾ (*al-ahbar*) are the scholars, derived from *al-tahbir*, which is embellishment, since they embellish knowledge, that is, they make it good. Al-Jawhari said: *al-habr* (with a *fatha* or a *kasra*) is the singular of *ahbar* (scholars) of the Jews, and the *kasra* is more eloquent. Al-Farra' said it is with a *kasra*, and Abu 'Ubayda said it is with a *fatha*.

His saying: ﴿by what they were entrusted with of the Book of Allah﴾ (*bi-ma istuhfizu min kitab Allah*). The *ba'* is causal, and *istuhfizu* means they were commanded to preserve. That is, the prophets commanded them to preserve the Torah from alteration and change. The prepositional phrase is connected to *yahkumu*, meaning they judge by it because of this entrusting.

His saying: ﴿and they were witnesses over it﴾ (*wa-kanu 'alayhi shuhada'*) means over the Book of Allah. *Al-shuhada'* are the watchers. They protect it from alteration and change through this vigilance. The address in His saying ﴿so do not fear the people﴾ (*fa-la takhshu al-nas*) is to the leaders of the Jews, and likewise in His saying ﴿and do not exchange My verses for a small price﴾ (*wa-la tashtaru bi-ayati thaman qalilan*). *Al-ishtira'* is exchange, and its verification has already preceded.

His saying: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾ (*wa-man lam yahkum bi-ma anzala Allahu fa-ulaika humu al-kafirun*). The word *man* ("whoever") is one of the forms of generality, and so it indicates that this is not restricted to a specific group, but applies to everyone who holds judicial authority. It has been said that it is restricted to the People of the Book. It has been said that it applies to disbelievers absolutely, because a Muslim does not become a disbeliever by committing a major sin. It has been said that it is to be understood as meaning that judging by other than what Allah revealed happened out of contempt, or out of considering it lawful, or out of denial. The reference of *ulaika* ("those") is to *man*, and the plural is in accordance with its meaning. Likewise the plural pronoun in His saying *humu al-kafirun* ("they are the disbelievers").

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿Let not grieve you those who hasten into disbelief﴾, that he said: they are the Jews. ﴿From those who say "We believe" with their mouths while their hearts have not believed﴾: he said they are the hypocrites.

Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 5, verses 41–44 (part 2 of 3):

Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ṭabarānī, Abū al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him (Ibn ʿAbbās) that he said: God revealed ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾ (al-ẓālimūn, "the wrongdoers"; al-fāsiqūn, "the defiantly disobedient"). God revealed it concerning two groups of the Jews. One of them had overpowered the other in the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam). They reached an agreement that whoever of the powerful group killed one of the weak group, the blood-money for him would be fifty wasq (a unit of dry measure), and whoever of the weak group killed one of the powerful group, the blood-money would be a hundred wasq. They continued in this state until the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to Madinah. Both groups were humbled by the arrival of the Messenger of God, and the Messenger of God at that time had not yet prevailed over them. Then the weak group killed a man from the powerful group, and the powerful group sent to the weak group: "Send us a hundred wasq." The weak group said: "Has this ever happened between two tribes whose religion is one, whose lineage is one, and whose land is one, and whose blood-money for some is half the blood-money of others? We only gave you this out of oppression by you against us and out of fear of you. But now that Muhammad (ﷺ) has come, we will not give you that." So fighting would break out between them. Then they agreed to make the Messenger of God (ﷺ) the arbiter between them. The powerful group reflected and said: "By God, Muhammad will not give them (the weak group) double what we give them (the powerful group)." And they spoke truly; they had only given us this out of oppression and subjugation of them. So send someone to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to find out his opinion. If he gives you what you want, you will accept his ruling; but if he does not give you what you want, beware of him and do not let him judge between you. So they sent some hypocrites to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to test his opinion. When they came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), God informed His Messenger of their entire affair and what they intended. Then God revealed ﴿O Messenger, let not those hasten to disbelief grieve you﴾ up to His words ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾. Then he said: By God, it was concerning them that it was revealed, and it was them that He meant.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Abū Dāwūd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalāʾil narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "The first person stoned (marjūm) by the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from among the Jews was a man and a woman from them who committed adultery. Some of them said to others: 'Come, let us go to this Prophet, for he is a prophet sent with leniency. If he gives us a ruling short of stoning, we will accept it and argue with it before God, and we will say: a ruling from one of Your prophets.' They came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was sitting in the mosque with his Companions, and they said: 'O Abū al-Qāsim, what do you say about a man and a woman from among them who committed adultery?' He did not speak to them until he came to their house of study (bayt midrāsihim), and stood at the door, and said: 'I adjure you by God who revealed the Torah to Moses: what do you find in the Torah concerning one who commits adultery when he is married (aḥṣana)?' They said: 'They are blackened (yuḥammam) and paraded (yujabbah) and flogged.' Tajbiyah means that the two adulterers are placed on a donkey, their backs facing each other, and they are paraded around. A young man among them remained silent. When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw that he was silent, he pressed him insistently with the oath. So he said: 'O God, since You have made us swear, yes, we find stoning in the Torah.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'What was the first thing with which you departed from the command of God?' He said: 'A man of noble kinship with one of our kings committed adultery, so they suspended the stoning for him. Then a man from ordinary people committed adultery, and they wanted to stone him, but his people stood between him and it, and said: "By God, you will not stone our companion until you bring your companion and stone him." So they agreed on this punishment among themselves.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed I judge by what is in the Torah.' So he ordered that the two be stoned, and they were stoned."

al-Zuhrī said: "It has reached us that this verse was revealed concerning them: ﴿Indeed We revealed the Torah, in which is guidance and light; by it the prophets who submitted judge﴾." So the Prophet (ﷺ) was among them. Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan narrated it through another chain from Abū Hurayrah, and in it he mentioned that the young man was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣūriyā.

Aḥmad, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasāʾī narrated something similar to the hadith of Abū Hurayrah from the hadith of al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib.

al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others narrated from the hadith of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar: "The Jews came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and mentioned to him that a man and a woman from among them had committed adultery. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: 'What do you find in the Torah?' They said: 'We expose them and they are flogged.' ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām said: 'You have lied; indeed in it is the verse of stoning.' So they brought the Torah and unrolled it, and one of them placed his hand over the verse of stoning and read what came before it and what came after it. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām said: 'Lift your hand.' He lifted his hand, and there was the verse of stoning. They said: 'He has spoken truly.' So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered that the two be stoned, and they were stoned."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh concerning His words ﴿And among those who are Jews are listeners to falsehood﴾, he said: "They are the Jews of Madinah." ﴿Listeners for other people who have not come to you﴾, he said: "They are the Jews of Fadak." (Tuḥarrifūn al-kalim, "they distort the words"), he said: "The Jews of Fadak say to the Jews of Madinah: 'If you are given this' (the flogging), ﴿then take it; but if you are not given it, then beware﴾ (of accepting the stoning)."

Abū Dāwūd, Ibn Mājah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him: "A man of the people of Fadak committed adultery. The people of Fadak wrote to some Jews in Madinah: 'Ask Muhammad,' and he mentioned the story."

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His words (ʾAkkālūna lil-suḥt, "devourers of the forbidden gain"): "They took bribes in judgment and gave judgments based on falsehood."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Firyābī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: "Suḥt is bribery in religion." Sufyān said: "He means in judgment."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Abū al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqī in Shuʿab al-Īmān also narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: "Whoever intercedes for a man to ward off an injustice from him, or to return a right to him, and is then given a gift and accepts it, that is suḥt." It was said to him: "O Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, we used to consider suḥt to be bribery in judgment." He said: "That is disbelief (kufr)." Then he recited ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾. Something similar to this has been reported from him through several routes.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "The bribe of rulers is forbidden, and it is the suḥt that God mentioned in His Book."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from Zayd ibn Thābit, who said: "Suḥt is bribery."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib that he was asked about suḥt, and he said: "It is bribes (al-rishā)." It was said to him: "In judgment?" He said: "That is disbelief (kufr)."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarīr narrated from ʿUmar, who said: "There are two doors of suḥt that people consume: the bribe in judgment, and the mahr of a prostitute."

It is firmly established from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning the prohibition of bribery what is well known. Abū Dāwūd in his Nāsikh (book on abrogating and abrogated texts), Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Ḥākim (who declared it ṣaḥīḥ), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "Two verses of Surah al-Māʾidah were abrogated (nusikhatā): the verse of the garlands (al-qalāʾid), and His words ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them﴾. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had the choice: if he wished, he would judge between them, and if he wished, he would turn away from them, returning them to their own judgments. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿And judge between them by what God has revealed and do not follow their desires﴾." He said: "So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was ordered to judge between them by what is in our Book." Abū ʿUbaydah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar concerning the later verse from him. ʿAbd al-Razzāq narrated something similar from ʿIkrimah.

Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ṭabarānī, Abū al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, "from Ibn ʿAbbās that the verses of Surah al-Māʾidah in which He said ﴿judge between them or turn away from them﴾ up to His words (al-muqsiṭīn, "the just") were revealed only concerning blood-money among the Banū al-Naḍīr and Qurayẓah. That was because the slain of the Banū al-Naḍīr had nobility, so they were paid full blood-money, while the Banū Qurayẓah were paid half the blood-money. They brought this dispute before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and God revealed this concerning them. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) brought them to the truth in this matter, and made the blood-money equal." Something similar from him was narrated by Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Abū al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Ḥākim (who declared it ṣaḥīḥ) and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from him concerning His words ﴿And with them is the Torah, in which is the judgment of God﴾, meaning the limits (ḥudūd) of God, so God informed him of His ruling in the Torah. He said: (And We prescribed for them in it) up to His words (and wounds are subject to retaliation). ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from al-Ḥasan concerning His words ﴿by it the prophets who submitted judge﴾, meaning the Prophet (ﷺ), (for those who are Jews), meaning the Jews.

Ibn Jarīr narrated from ʿIkrimah, who said: "Those who submitted, the Prophet and the prophets before him, judge by what is in it of the truth." Ibn Jarīr narrated from al-Ḥasan, who said: "al-Rabbāniyyūn and al-Aḥbār are the jurists and the scholars." He also narrated from Mujāhid, who said: "al-Rabbāniyyūn are the scholars and jurists, and they are above the aḥbār." Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from al-Ḥasan, who said: "al-Rabbāniyyūn are the worshippers, and the aḥbār are the scholars." Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "al-Rabbāniyyūn are the jurists and scholars." Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from him, who said: "al-Rabbāniyyūn are the believers, and the aḥbār are the readers (of scripture)."

Ibn Jarīr narrated from al-Suddī concerning (so do not fear the people), meaning that you would conceal what I have revealed, ﴿and do not sell My signs for a small price﴾, meaning in exchange for concealing what I have revealed. Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn Zayd concerning ﴿and do not sell My signs for a small price﴾, who said: "Do not consume suḥt in exchange for My Book."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His words, "And whoever does not judge," that he said: "Whoever denies the ruling of what God has revealed has disbelieved, and whoever acknowledges it but does not judge by it is a wrongdoer and a defiant sinner." al-Firyābī, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who declared it ṣaḥīḥ) and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning His words ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾, that he said: "It is not the disbelief to which they (the extremists) go, nor is it a disbelief that removes one from the religion, but it is less than that disbelief."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ concerning His words ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾, (they are the wrongdoers), (they are the defiant sinners), that he said: "It is disbelief short of disbelief, injustice short of injustice, and defiance short of defiance." Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Abū al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "God revealed ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾, and (the wrongdoers) and (the defiant sinners), only concerning the Jews specifically."

Many of the early generation (al-salaf) have also related something similar to this. Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) transmitted from Hudhayfah that these verses were mentioned in his presence: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - those are the disbelievers﴾, and (the wrongdoers) and (the defiantly disobedient). A man said: "This applies to the Children of Israel." Hudhayfah said: "Yes. Your brothers are the Children of Israel: if you have every sweet thing and they have every bitter thing - no! By Allah, you will surely follow their path step for step (qadda al-shira'k)." Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted something similar from Ibn Abbas.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 41–44 (part 1 of 3)**

His saying: ﴿Let them not grieve you﴾ (*la yahzunka*). Nafi' read it with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *zay* (*yuhzinka*). The rest read it with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *zay* (*yahzunka*). *Al-huzn* is the opposite of *al-surur* (joy). One says *hazina al-rajul* (with a *kasra*), so he is *hazin* or *hazeen* (grieved), and *ahzanahu ghayruhu* or *hazanahu* (someone else grieved him). Al-Yazidi said: *hazanahu* is the dialect of Quraysh and *ahzanahu* is the dialect of Tamim, and both have been read. In the verse there is a prohibition to the Prophet (ﷺ) against being deeply affected by the swiftness of the disbelievers in their disbelief, because Allah, glorified is He, had promised him in more than one place victory over them. *Al-musara'ah ila al-shay'* is falling into a thing quickly.

What is meant here is their falling into disbelief quickly when an opportunity presents itself. He chose the particle *fi* over *ila* to indicate their settling into it. The *min* in His saying ﴿from those who say﴾ (*min alladhina qalu*) is explanatory (*bayaniyyah*), and the clause explains who the ones hastening to disbelief are. The *ba'* in ﴿with their mouths﴾ (*bi-afwahihim*) is connected to *qalu* and not to *amanna*. Those who said "We believe" with their mouths while their hearts did not believe are the hypocrites. ﴿And from those who are Jews﴾ (*wa-min alladhina hadu*) means the Jews. It is coordinated with *min alladhina qalu amanna*, and this is the completion of the statement. The meaning is that those hastening to disbelief are a group of hypocrites and a group of Jews.

His saying: ﴿They are listeners to falsehood﴾ (*sammaʻuna lil-kadhib*) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are listeners to falsehood. It refers either to both groups or to those who hasten. The *lam* in *lil-kadhib* is for emphasis, or it implies that listening carries the meaning of accepting. It has been said that *sammaʻuna* is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿from those who are Jews﴾, meaning: and from those who are Jews are a people who are *sammaʻuna lil-kadhib*, that is, receptive to the lies of their leaders who distort the Torah. His saying ﴿listeners for another people﴾ (*sammaʻuna li-qawmin akharin*) is a second predicate, and the *lam* in it is like the *lam* in *lil-kadhib*. It has also been said that the *lam* is causal in both places, meaning: they listen to the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the sake of lying about him, and they listen on behalf of another people whom they sent as spies to them, so that they might convey to them what they heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿who have not come to you﴾ (*lam ya'tukum*) is an attribute of *qawm* (people), meaning they did not attend your assembly. They were a group of Jews who did not attend the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) out of arrogance and rebelliousness. It has also been said they were a group of hypocrites who avoided the gatherings of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Al-Farra' said: it is permissible to say *sammaʻeen*, as in His saying: ﴿cursed, wherever they are found﴾ [al-Ahzab: 61].

His saying: ﴿They distort words from their places﴾ (*yuharrifuna al-kalima min ba'di mawadi'ihi*) is among the attributes of the aforementioned people. That is, they turn it away from its places where Allah placed it, and they interpret it other than its true interpretation (*ta'wil*). The distorters are the Jews. It has been said that this clause is the predicate of an omitted subject. It has been said that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *lam ya'tukum*.
