We have already presented, in al-Baqarah, in explaining His saying, ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you in cases of killing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178], what is sufficient on this. The scholars differed over whether the law of those before us binds us or not. The majority held that it binds us if it has not been abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by later revelation), and this is the truth. Ibn al-Sabbagh, in al-Shamil, mentioned the consensus (ijma', the agreement of the scholars) of the scholars on relying on this verse according to what it indicates. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: "All the imams have argued from the generality of this noble verse that a man is killed for a woman." End of quote.

We have clarified what is the truth in this matter in our commentary on al-Muntaqa. In this verse there is a rebuke to the Jews and a reproach for their opposing what Allah prescribed for them in the Torah, as He related here, and for their discriminating between souls, as was explained earlier. They used to take retaliation from the Banu al-Nadir on behalf of the Banu Qurayzah, but they did not take retaliation from the Banu Qurayzah on behalf of the Banu al-Nadir.

His saying: (and the eye for the eye). Nafi', Asim, al-A'mash and Hamzah read all of them in the accusative (naṣb), as coordination (ʿaṭf). Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir, Abu ʿAmr and Abu Ja'far read them in the accusative too, in all of them except the wounds, which are in the nominative (raf'). Al-Kisa'i and Abu ʿUbayd read them all in the nominative, as coordination on the position (maḥall), because the soul (nafs), before the entry of the accusative-governing particle upon it, was in the nominative as a beginning (mubtada').

Al-Zajjaj said: it is coordination on the pronoun in "the soul," because the sense is: "the soul is taken for the soul," so the nouns are coordinated on "hiya" (it). Ibn al-Mundhir said: whoever reads in the nominative makes it the beginning of a statement that contains an explanation of the ruling for the Muslims. (p-376) The apparent meaning of the Qur'anic wording is that if an eye is gouged out so that no capacity for perception remains in it, the eye of the offender is gouged out by it. If a nose is cut off entirely, the offender's nose is cut off by it. If an ear is cut off entirely, the offender's ear is cut off by it, and likewise the tooth. But if the offence removed only part of the perception of the eye, or part of the nose, or part of the ear, or part of the tooth, then there is nothing in this verse that establishes retaliation. The scholars differed on this when the measure is known and its reality can be determined, and their discussions are recorded in the books of jurisprudence (furu').

The apparent meaning of His saying: (and the tooth for the tooth) is that there is no distinction between the front teeth, the canines, the molars and the incisors, that some may be taken for others, and that none has preference over another. This is the view of most of the scholars, as Ibn al-Mundhir said. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and those who followed him disagreed on this, and their discussions are recorded in their places. However, what is taken in retaliation from the offender should be a tooth matching the tooth taken from the injured party. If the tooth is gone, then what is nearest to it.

His saying: (and the wounds are subject to retaliation). That is, they are things subject to retaliation. The scholars mentioned that there is no retaliation for wounds that may cause destruction, nor for those whose extent cannot be known in depth, length or width. The imams of jurisprudence have set the compensation (arsh) for each wound at known amounts. This is not the place to explain their words, nor the place to exhaust the explanation of what has a prescribed compensation.

His saying: ﴿Whoever forgoes it, it is an expiation for him﴾. That is: whoever among those entitled to retaliation forgoes retaliation, by pardoning the offender, then it is an expiation for the one who forgoes, by which Allah expiates his sins.

It has been said that the meaning is: it is an expiation for the one who wounded, so he will not be held accountable for his offence in the Hereafter, because the pardon takes the place of exacting the right from him. The first is preferred, because the pronoun in this other explanation would refer to something not mentioned.

His saying: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has sent down, those are the wrongdoers﴾. The separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl) together with the demonstrative and the definite predicate indicates that this wrongdoing coming from them is a great wrongdoing, reaching its utmost extent.

His saying: ﴿And We sent, following in their footsteps, Jesus son of Mary﴾. This begins the explanation of the ruling of the Gospel after the explanation of the ruling of the Torah. That is: We made Jesus son of Mary follow in their footsteps, that is, the footsteps of the prophets among the Children of Israel who submitted. One says qaffaytuhu, like ʿaqqabtuhu, when one follows him. Then one says qaffaytuhu bi-fulan and ʿaqqabtuhu bihi, and it takes the second object with the preposition bi; the first object is omitted, being dispensed with by the adverbial phrase "in their footsteps," because when he followed him upon his footstep, he followed him with him. The accusative of (confirming) is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of Jesus. (And We gave him the Gospel) is coordinated on (We made him follow). The clause (in it is guidance) has the accusative position as a circumstantial state of the Gospel, and (and light) is coordinated on (guidance).

His saying: (and confirming) is coordinated on the position of (in it is guidance). That is: the Gospel was given to Jesus in a state in which it contained guidance and light, and confirmed what was before it of the Torah. It has been said that (confirming) is coordinated on the first (confirming), so it is a state of Jesus that emphasizes and establishes the first state. The first is better, because establishing something new is better than emphasis.

His saying: ﴿And a guidance and admonition for the God-fearing﴾ is coordinated on "confirming," included under its ruling and joined to it. That is: confirming, guiding, and admonishing the God-fearing.

His saying: ﴿Let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has sent down in it﴾. This is a command to the People of the Gospel to judge by what Allah sent down in it, for before the Muhammadan mission it was true. As for after it, they were commanded in more than one place to act by what Allah sent down upon Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, in the Qur'an, which abrogates all the earlier scriptures.

Al-A'mash and Hamzah read the verb yaḥkuma in the accusative, taking the lam as lam of purpose (kay), and the rest read it in the jussive, taking the lam as the lam of command. According to the first reading, the lam is connected to His saying "and We gave him the Gospel," so that its people might judge by what Allah sent down in it. According to the second reading, it is a new independent statement. Makki said: the preferred reading is the jussive, because the community reads it so, and because what follows of threat and warning indicates that it is a binding obligation from Allah upon the People of the Gospel. Al-Nahhas said: "The correct view in my opinion is that they are two good readings, because Allah, glorified is He, did not send down a book except that it be acted upon in what it contains."

His saying: ﴿And We sent down to you the Book﴾ is an address to Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. "The Book" is the Qur'an, and the definite article is for a known referent. (With the truth) is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial state: that is, "accompanied by the truth." It has been said that it is a state of the subject of "We sent down," and it has been said that it is a state of the Prophet's pronoun, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. (Confirming what is before it of the Book) is a state of "the Book." The definite article in "the Book" in His saying ﴿confirming what is before it of the Book﴾ is generic; that is: We sent down to you, O Muhammad, the Qur'an in a state of being accompanied by the truth, and in a state of confirming what is before it of the books of Allah that were sent down, because it contains the call to Allah, the command to good, and the prohibition of evil, as it contains His saying: (and a watcher over it). It is coordinated on "confirming," and the pronoun in "over it" returns to the Book, which the Qur'an confirmed and watched over. Al-muhaymin means the guardian; it has been said: the victorious, the exalted; it has been said: the witness; it has been said: the preserver; it has been said: the trusted.

Al-Mubarrad said: its origin is mu'aymin, with the hamzah replaced by hā', as one says in "araqtu al-ma'" (I poured the water): "haraqtu." Al-Zajjaj and Abu ʿAli al-Farisi held this too. Al-Jawhari said: it is from amina ghayrahu min al-khawf (he made another safe from fear), and its origin is a'man, so it is mu'annim with two hamzahs, the second was changed into yā' because the two hamzahs collided, so it became mu'aymin, then the first was changed into hā', as they say harāqa al-ma' and arāqahu. One says: haymana ʿala al-shay' yuhaymin if he was its keeper, so he is muhaymin over it. This is related from Abu ʿUbayd.

Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin read (muhaymanan) with a fatha on the mim, meaning that Allah, glorified is He, watched over it. According to the reading of the majority, the meaning is: the Qur'an became a witness to the authenticity of the revealed books, and an affirmer of what is in them that was not abrogated, and an abrogator of what contradicts them, and a watcher over them, and a preserver of the foundations of the laws in them, and dominant over them, since it is the reference point for what is firm (muhkam) and abrogated among them, and a trusted authority over them, since it contains what is acted upon in them and what has been abandoned.

His saying: ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has sent down﴾, that is: by what He sent down to you in the Qur'an, because it includes all that Allah legislated for His servants in all the earlier books before it. ﴿And do not follow their desires﴾, that is: the desires of the people of the earlier religions.

His saying: (p-377) ﴿away from the truth that has come to you﴾ is connected to "do not follow," by including in it the sense of "do not deviate" or "do not turn aside," so that the sense is: "turning aside from the truth that has come to you, following their desires." It has been said it is connected to an omitted element: that is, "do not follow their desires, deviating or turning away from the truth."

In it there is a prohibition to him, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, against following the desires of the People of the Book and deviating from the truth that Allah sent down to him. Every religious community desires that the matter be as they are and as their predecessors found it, even if it is false, abrogated, or distorted from the ruling that Allah sent down to the prophets, as happened in the matter of stoning and similar things that they distorted from the books of Allah.

His saying: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way﴾. Al-shir'ah and al-shari'ah originally mean the apparent path by which one reaches water; then the term was used for what Allah legislated for His servants of religion. Al-minhaj is the clear, evident path. Abu al-ʿAbbas Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad said: al-shari'ah is the beginning of the path, and al-minhaj is the path that continues. The meaning of the verse is: He made the Torah for its people, the Gospel for its people, and the Qur'an for its people. This is before the abrogation of the earlier laws by the Qur'an. As for after it, there is no law and no way except what Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, brought.

His saying: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one community﴾, upon one law, one book and one messenger. (But to test you) — that is, but He did not will that unity; rather He willed to test you by the difference of laws. So "to test you" is connected to an omitted element indicated by the context of the speech, which is what we have mentioned. The meaning of (in what He has given you) is: in what He sent down to you of the differing laws, differing according to times and persons.

His saying: (So race to good deeds). That is: since the will has decreed the difference of laws, then race to do what you have been commanded to do and to leave what you have been commanded to leave. Al-istibaq is hastening. ﴿To Allah is your return, all of you﴾, not to anything else. This sentence serves as the reason for what came before it.

His saying: ﴿And that you judge between them by what Allah has sent down, and do not follow their desires﴾ is coordinated on "the Book." That is: We sent down to you the Book and the judgment by what is in it. It has been used as evidence for the abrogation of the choice mentioned earlier in His saying: "or turn away from them." The explanation of "and do not follow their desires" has already been given.

Regarding His words, ﴿And beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾: that is, lest they lead you astray from it and divert you, by means of their desires, which they want you to act upon and prefer. ﴿Then if they turn away, know that Allah only wants to afflict them for some of their sins﴾: that is, if they refuse to accept your judgment by what Allah has revealed to you, then this is because of what Allah has willed of punishing them for some of their sins, and that sin is their turning away from you and their rejection of what you have brought. ﴿And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient﴾: rebellious against accepting the truth and departing from fairness.

As for His words, ﴿Do they then seek the judgment of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance)?﴾: the interrogative (istifham) is for denunciation and reproach, and the fa' (فاء) is for coordination with an implied antecedent, as in its counterparts. The meaning is: Do they turn away from your judgment by what Allah has revealed to you, and turn away from it, and seek the judgment of the Jahiliyyah? The interrogative in ﴿And who is better in judgment than Allah for a people who are certain?﴾ is also for denunciation; that is, none is better in judgment than Allah's according to those who have certainty, not according to the people of ignorance and desires.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ( We prescribed for them therein ): "in the Torah." ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him, he said: "He prescribed this for them in the Torah, and they used to kill a free person for a slave, and they would say: 'It was prescribed for us that a life is for a life.'" Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn ʿUmar regarding His words ﴿Whoever gives it as charity, it is an expiation for him﴾: he said, "It erases from his sins an amount equal to what he gave in charity." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah ( it is an expiation for him ), he said: "For the one who is wounded."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Majah narrated from Abu al-Darda', who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'No Muslim who is afflicted with something in his body and gives it as charity, except that Allah raises him one degree by it and removes from him one sin by it.'" Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas ( and a guardian over it ), he said: "Trustworthy over it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him, he said: "The muhaymin is the trustworthy, and the Qur'an is a trustworthy guardian over every Book before it." Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him regarding His words ( a law and a path ), he said: "A way and a sunnah."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Ka'b ibn Asad, ʿAbd Allah ibn Suriya, and Shas ibn Qays said: 'Come, let us go to Muhammad, perhaps we can tempt him away from his religion.' So they came to him and said: 'O Muhammad, you know that we are the rabbis of the Jews, their nobles and their leaders, and if we follow you, the Jews will follow us, and between us and our people there is a dispute, so we will bring it to you for judgment, and you will rule for us against them, and we will believe in you and affirm you.' He refused that, and Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿And that you judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ up to His words ( for a people who are certain )." ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His words ( Do they then seek the judgment of the Jahiliyyah? ), he said: "The Jews." ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah, who said: "This is about the murder of the Jews."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 5, verses 51–56 (part 1 of 2):

The apparent meaning of his words, ﴿O you who believe, do not take﴾, is that it is addressed to believers in the literal sense. It has also been said that the intended audience is the hypocrites (munafiqun), and that they are described as believers in terms of what they outwardly displayed. (p. 378) They used to befriend the Jews and Christians, so they were forbidden from doing so. The better view is that it is addressed to everyone who is characterised by faith, more general than whether that faith is outward and inward or only outward. This includes the Muslim and the hypocrite. This is supported by his words, ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾. What matters is the generality of the wording. The explanation of the occasion of revelation, which comes later, will clarify the intended meaning. The prohibition against taking them as awliya' (allies, protectors) means that they should not be treated as allies in companionship, close association, and support. His words, ﴿They are allies of one another﴾, give the reason for the prohibition. The meaning is that some Jews are allies of other Jews, and some Christians are allies of other Christians. The "some" here does not refer to one of the two groups of Jews and Christians against the other group, since they are definitively in extreme enmity and hostility. ﴿The Jews say, "The Christians are not upon anything," and the Christians say, "The Jews are not upon anything"﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:113). It has also been said that the meaning is that each of the two groups allies with the other, supports it, and aids it against the enmity toward the Prophet (ﷺ) and against what he brought, even though they are mutually hostile and opposed among themselves.

The reason for prohibiting this, expressed through this clause, is that it implies that this alliance is the habit of these disbelievers, not yours. So do not do what is part of their conduct, lest you become like them. For this reason, he followed this explanatory clause with what amounts to its result, saying: ﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies, then indeed he is of them﴾. That is, he is among them and counted with them. This is a severe warning, since the sin that necessitates disbelief is the one that reaches an extreme beyond which there is no further extreme. His words, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, give the reason for the preceding clause. That is, their falling into disbelief is due to Allah's not guiding those who wrong themselves by doing what necessitates disbelief, such as one who allies with the disbelievers.

His words, ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them﴾: the fa' indicates causation. The address is either to the Messenger (ﷺ) or to everyone suitable for it. That is, what they committed of alliance and what they fell into of disbelief is due to the disease of hypocrisy in their hearts. His words, "hastening" (yusari'una), are in the accusative position, either as the second object if the seeing is of the heart, or as a circumstantial clause (al-hal) if the seeing is visual. He made hastening in their alliance into hastening toward them, for emphasis in describing their eagerness for that, as if they were settled among them and entered into their number.

It has been read as fa-sayaran (with the yā' prefix), and it has been disputed what its subject is. It has been said that it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has been said that it is anyone who is capable of seeing. It has been said that it is the relative pronoun, and its object is "hastening toward them," with the verbal noun particle an omitted. That is, "he sees the people in whose hearts is disease, that they hasten toward them." When it was omitted, the verb became nominative, as in the line of poetry:

"Ah, you who blame me, let me attend the battle."

The disease in the hearts is hypocrisy and doubt about the religion. His words, ﴿They say, "We fear that a calamity will befall us"﴾, form a clause giving the reason for hastening in alliance. That is, this fear is what drives them to hasten. It has also been said that the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "hastening." The "calamity" (da'ira) is what turns of the misfortunes of time. That is, "we fear that the disbelievers will overcome Muhammad (ﷺ), so that the dominion will be theirs and his dominion will be nullified, and some hardship from them will befall us." From this is the poet's saying:

"It turns away from you the decreed fate, and the turning revolutions of time that they turn."

That is, the revolutions of time that turn from people to people. His words, ﴿So perhaps Allah will bring the conquest﴾, are a refutation of them and a dispelling of the fear that had come over them. "Perhaps" (asa) in the speech of Allah is a true promise that does not fail.

The conquest (al-fath) is the victory of the Prophet (ﷺ) over the disbelievers. It includes what happened of killing the fighting men of Banu Qurayzah and taking their children captive, and the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir. It has also been said that it is the conquest of the lands of the polytheists for the Muslims, and that it is the conquest of Mecca. "The command from Him" means everything by which the attack of the Jews and those with them is repelled and their power is broken. It has also been said that it is the disclosure of the matter of the hypocrites, and the Prophet (ﷺ) being informed of what they concealed within themselves, and his command to kill them. It has also been said that it is the jizya (poll tax) that Allah imposed on them. It has also been said that it is the abundance and plenty for the Muslims. Then the hypocrites will ﴿become, over what they concealed within themselves﴾ of hypocrisy, which drove them to alliance, "regretful" (nadimin) over that, because the causes they had imagined were nullified and their opposite was revealed.

His words, "Those who believe say" (yaqulu alladhina amanu): Abu 'Amr, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and the people of Kufa read it with the waw (wa-yaqulu), and the others read it without it (yaqulu). On the first reading, with the verb in the nominative, it is an independent statement presented to explain what occurred from this group. On the reading in the accusative, it is coordinated with "they will become" (fa-yusbihu), and it has also been said that it is coordinated with "comes" (ya'ti). The first is better, because this statement comes only from the believers when the regret of the disbelievers becomes apparent, not when the conquest comes. It has also been said that it is coordinated with "the conquest," as in the poet's saying:

"Wearing a cloak, and my eye is cooled."

As for the reading without the waw, the clause is resumed as an answer to an implied question. The demonstrative in "These" (ahaaulaa') refers to the hypocrites. That is: those who believe say, addressing the Jews and pointing to the hypocrites, ﴿"Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that they were with you?"﴾, in support and aid in fighting. Or some believers say to others, pointing to the hypocrites. This clause explains the statement. "The most emphatic of oaths" (jahd al-aymān) means the strongest of them. It is in the accusative either as a verbal noun (masdar) or as a circumstantial clause (hal). That is, they swore by Allah exerting themselves in the oath.

His words, "Their deeds have failed" (habitat a'maluhum), means that they became void. This is either part of the statement of the believers or a resumed independent clause, in which case the speaker is Allah, the Glorified. The deeds are those they did in alliance, or every deed they performed.

His words, ﴿O you who believe, whoever of you apostatises﴾: Ahl al-Madina and the Syrians read yartaddid with two dāl's, without assimilation (fakk al-idgham), which is the dialect of Tamim. The others read it with assimilation.

This is the beginning of an explanation of the rulings concerning apostates, after explaining that allying with disbelievers is disbelief on the part of a Muslim. That is one kind of apostasy (ridda). The people whom Allah promised to bring are Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and his army of the Companions and the Successors, with whom he fought the people of apostasy. Then, every one who came after them among those who fought apostates throughout all time. Then the Glorified describes these people with these great attributes, containing the utmost praise and the highest commendation: that they love Allah and He loves them, and that they are ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers, striving in the way of Allah, and not fearing the blame of any blamer﴾. (p. 379) "Humble" (adhillah) is the plural of dhalil, not dhalul (tame). "Mighty" (a'izzah) is the plural of 'aziz. That is, they show tenderness, compassion, and humility toward the believers, and show firmness, harshness, and superiority over the disbelievers. They combine striving in the way of Allah with not fearing reproach in religion. Indeed, they are firm and do not care about what the enemies of truth and the party of Satan do, such as disparaging the people of religion, and turning their virtues into vices and their merits into faults, out of envy, hatred, and aversion to the truth and its people.

The demonstrative in "That" (dhalika) refers to the attributes mentioned previously, with which Allah singled them out. "Bounty" (fadl) means kindness and benevolence.

His words, ﴿Your only ally is Allah﴾: when He, the Glorified, finished explaining whom it is not lawful to take as an ally, He explained who is the Ally whose alliance is obligatory. The position of ﴿Those who establish prayer﴾ is nominative, as an attribute of "those who believe," or as an apposition to it, or accusative as an expression of praise. His words, ﴿and they bow in prayer﴾, form a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of the two verbs preceding it. "Bowing" (ruku') here means humility and submission. That is, they establish prayer and give zakat while being humble and submissive, not arrogant. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "give zakat."

The meaning of "bowing" is the one mentioned: that is, they place zakat in its proper places, not arrogant toward the poor, nor exalting themselves over them. It has also been said that on the second meaning, "bowing" refers to the bowing of prayer, but this is rejected because it is not permissible to pay zakat in that state.

﴿And whoever takes Allah and His Messenger and those who believe as allies, then indeed the party of Allah are the victorious﴾. Then the Glorified promised that whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and the believers as allies will be victorious over their enemy. This is a case of putting the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, and putting "the party of Allah" in place of the pronoun for those who ally with Allah, His Messenger, and the believers. "Hizb" means a category of people, from the expression "hazabahu kadha," meaning "it befell him." It is as though the members of a party gather together like the people of a calamity that befalls them. "The party of a man" means his companions. "Hizb" also means a portion of recitation (wird), and in the hadith: "Whoever misses his portion (hizb) of the night." "They formed a party" (tahazzabu) means they gathered together. "Al-ahzab" means groups.

What Allah promised His allies, the allies of His messengers, and the allies of His believing servants of victory over their enemy has indeed come to pass, and to Allah belongs all praise. They overcame the Jews through taking captives, killing, expulsion, and imposing the jizya (poll tax on non-Muslims), until Allah curse them, they became the most humiliated and least powerful of the disbelieving groups. They remained under the weight of the believers, crushing them as they wished and humiliating them as they desired, from the noble mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) until this point.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Ubada ibn al-Walid ibn Ubada ibn al-Samit, who said: "When Banu Qaynuqa fought the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul clung to their affair and stood in their defence. Ubada ibn al-Samit went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), disassociated himself before Allah and His Messenger from their alliance, and he was one of Banu 'Awf ibn al-Khazraj, and he had with them the same alliance that 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul had with them. So he cut himself off from them before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'I disassociate myself before Allah and His Messenger from the alliance and loyalty of these disbelievers.' Concerning him and 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy the verses in al-Ma'idah were revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and Christians as allies﴾ up to His words ﴿indeed, the party of Allah are the victorious﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh reported, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul became Muslim, then said: 'Indeed, between me and Qurayzah and al-Nadir there is an alliance, and I fear the calamities.' So he apostatised as a disbeliever. Ubada ibn al-Samit said: 'I disassociate myself before Allah from the alliance of Qurayzah and al-Nadir, and I take Allah and His Messenger as allies,' and so it was revealed." Ibn Mardawayh also reported, through the chain of Ubada ibn al-Walid ibn Ubada ibn al-Samit, from his father, from his grandfather, something similar. Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir reported, from 'Atiyya ibn Sa'd, who said: "Ubada came and mentioned something similar to what preceded."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Zuhri, who said: When the people of Badr were defeated, the Muslims said to their allies among the Jews, "Embrace Islam before Allah afflicts you with a day like the day of Badr." If we had resolved to gather against you, you would not have had the strength to fight us." 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Hudhayfah, who said: Let each of you beware of becoming a Jew or a Christian without realizing it. He then recited, ﴿And whoever among you allies with them, then indeed he is one of them﴾.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 5, verses 51–56 (part 1 of 2):

The apparent meaning of his words, ﴿O you who believe, do not take﴾, is that it is addressed to believers in the literal sense. It has also been said that the intended audience is the hypocrites (munafiqun), and that they are described as believers in terms of what they outwardly displayed. (p. 378) They used to befriend the Jews and Christians, so they were forbidden from doing so. The better view is that it is addressed to everyone who is characterised by faith, more general than whether that faith is outward and inward or only outward. This includes the Muslim and the hypocrite. This is supported by his words, ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾. What matters is the generality of the wording. The explanation of the occasion of revelation, which comes later, will clarify the intended meaning. The prohibition against taking them as awliya' (allies, protectors) means that they should not be treated as allies in companionship, close association, and support. His words, ﴿They are allies of one another﴾, give the reason for the prohibition. The meaning is that some Jews are allies of other Jews, and some Christians are allies of other Christians. The "some" here does not refer to one of the two groups of Jews and Christians against the other group, since they are definitively in extreme enmity and hostility. ﴿The Jews say, "The Christians are not upon anything," and the Christians say, "The Jews are not upon anything"﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:113). It has also been said that the meaning is that each of the two groups allies with the other, supports it, and aids it against the enmity toward the Prophet (ﷺ) and against what he brought, even though they are mutually hostile and opposed among themselves.

The reason for prohibiting this, expressed through this clause, is that it implies that this alliance is the habit of these disbelievers, not yours. So do not do what is part of their conduct, lest you become like them. For this reason, he followed this explanatory clause with what amounts to its result, saying: ﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies, then indeed he is of them﴾. That is, he is among them and counted with them. This is a severe warning, since the sin that necessitates disbelief is the one that reaches an extreme beyond which there is no further extreme. His words, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, give the reason for the preceding clause. That is, their falling into disbelief is due to Allah's not guiding those who wrong themselves by doing what necessitates disbelief, such as one who allies with the disbelievers.

His words, ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them﴾: the fa' indicates causation. The address is either to the Messenger (ﷺ) or to everyone suitable for it. That is, what they committed of alliance and what they fell into of disbelief is due to the disease of hypocrisy in their hearts. His words, "hastening" (yusari'una), are in the accusative position, either as the second object if the seeing is of the heart, or as a circumstantial clause (al-hal) if the seeing is visual. He made hastening in their alliance into hastening toward them, for emphasis in describing their eagerness for that, as if they were settled among them and entered into their number.

It has been read as fa-sayaran (with the yā' prefix), and it has been disputed what its subject is. It has been said that it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has been said that it is anyone who is capable of seeing. It has been said that it is the relative pronoun, and its object is "hastening toward them," with the verbal noun particle an omitted. That is, "he sees the people in whose hearts is disease, that they hasten toward them." When it was omitted, the verb became nominative, as in the line of poetry:

"Ah, you who blame me, let me attend the battle."

The disease in the hearts is hypocrisy and doubt about the religion. His words, ﴿They say, "We fear that a calamity will befall us"﴾, form a clause giving the reason for hastening in alliance. That is, this fear is what drives them to hasten. It has also been said that the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "hastening." The "calamity" (da'ira) is what turns of the misfortunes of time. That is, "we fear that the disbelievers will overcome Muhammad (ﷺ), so that the dominion will be theirs and his dominion will be nullified, and some hardship from them will befall us." From this is the poet's saying:

"It turns away from you the decreed fate, and the turning revolutions of time that they turn."

That is, the revolutions of time that turn from people to people. His words, ﴿So perhaps Allah will bring the conquest﴾, are a refutation of them and a dispelling of the fear that had come over them. "Perhaps" (asa) in the speech of Allah is a true promise that does not fail.

The conquest (al-fath) is the victory of the Prophet (ﷺ) over the disbelievers. It includes what happened of killing the fighting men of Banu Qurayzah and taking their children captive, and the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir. It has also been said that it is the conquest of the lands of the polytheists for the Muslims, and that it is the conquest of Mecca. "The command from Him" means everything by which the attack of the Jews and those with them is repelled and their power is broken. It has also been said that it is the disclosure of the matter of the hypocrites, and the Prophet (ﷺ) being informed of what they concealed within themselves, and his command to kill them. It has also been said that it is the jizya (poll tax) that Allah imposed on them. It has also been said that it is the abundance and plenty for the Muslims. Then the hypocrites will ﴿become, over what they concealed within themselves﴾ of hypocrisy, which drove them to alliance, "regretful" (nadimin) over that, because the causes they had imagined were nullified and their opposite was revealed.

His words, "Those who believe say" (yaqulu alladhina amanu): Abu 'Amr, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and the people of Kufa read it with the waw (wa-yaqulu), and the others read it without it (yaqulu). On the first reading, with the verb in the nominative, it is an independent statement presented to explain what occurred from this group. On the reading in the accusative, it is coordinated with "they will become" (fa-yusbihu), and it has also been said that it is coordinated with "comes" (ya'ti). The first is better, because this statement comes only from the believers when the regret of the disbelievers becomes apparent, not when the conquest comes. It has also been said that it is coordinated with "the conquest," as in the poet's saying:

"Wearing a cloak, and my eye is cooled."

As for the reading without the waw, the clause is resumed as an answer to an implied question. The demonstrative in "These" (ahaaulaa') refers to the hypocrites. That is: those who believe say, addressing the Jews and pointing to the hypocrites, ﴿"Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that they were with you?"﴾, in support and aid in fighting. Or some believers say to others, pointing to the hypocrites. This clause explains the statement. "The most emphatic of oaths" (jahd al-aymān) means the strongest of them. It is in the accusative either as a verbal noun (masdar) or as a circumstantial clause (hal). That is, they swore by Allah exerting themselves in the oath.

His words, "Their deeds have failed" (habitat a'maluhum), means that they became void. This is either part of the statement of the believers or a resumed independent clause, in which case the speaker is Allah, the Glorified. The deeds are those they did in alliance, or every deed they performed.

His words, ﴿O you who believe, whoever of you apostatises﴾: Ahl al-Madina and the Syrians read yartaddid with two dāl's, without assimilation (fakk al-idgham), which is the dialect of Tamim. The others read it with assimilation.

This is the beginning of an explanation of the rulings concerning apostates, after explaining that allying with disbelievers is disbelief on the part of a Muslim. That is one kind of apostasy (ridda). The people whom Allah promised to bring are Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and his army of the Companions and the Successors, with whom he fought the people of apostasy. Then, every one who came after them among those who fought apostates throughout all time. Then the Glorified describes these people with these great attributes, containing the utmost praise and the highest commendation: that they love Allah and He loves them, and that they are ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers, striving in the way of Allah, and not fearing the blame of any blamer﴾. (p. 379) "Humble" (adhillah) is the plural of dhalil, not dhalul (tame). "Mighty" (a'izzah) is the plural of 'aziz. That is, they show tenderness, compassion, and humility toward the believers, and show firmness, harshness, and superiority over the disbelievers. They combine striving in the way of Allah with not fearing reproach in religion. Indeed, they are firm and do not care about what the enemies of truth and the party of Satan do, such as disparaging the people of religion, and turning their virtues into vices and their merits into faults, out of envy, hatred, and aversion to the truth and its people.

The demonstrative in "That" (dhalika) refers to the attributes mentioned previously, with which Allah singled them out. "Bounty" (fadl) means kindness and benevolence.

His words, ﴿Your only ally is Allah﴾: when He, the Glorified, finished explaining whom it is not lawful to take as an ally, He explained who is the Ally whose alliance is obligatory. The position of ﴿Those who establish prayer﴾ is nominative, as an attribute of "those who believe," or as an apposition to it, or accusative as an expression of praise. His words, ﴿and they bow in prayer﴾, form a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of the two verbs preceding it. "Bowing" (ruku') here means humility and submission. That is, they establish prayer and give zakat while being humble and submissive, not arrogant. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "give zakat."

The meaning of "bowing" is the one mentioned: that is, they place zakat in its proper places, not arrogant toward the poor, nor exalting themselves over them. It has also been said that on the second meaning, "bowing" refers to the bowing of prayer, but this is rejected because it is not permissible to pay zakat in that state.

﴿And whoever takes Allah and His Messenger and those who believe as allies, then indeed the party of Allah are the victorious﴾. Then the Glorified promised that whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and the believers as allies will be victorious over their enemy. This is a case of putting the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, and putting "the party of Allah" in place of the pronoun for those who ally with Allah, His Messenger, and the believers. "Hizb" means a category of people, from the expression "hazabahu kadha," meaning "it befell him." It is as though the members of a party gather together like the people of a calamity that befalls them. "The party of a man" means his companions. "Hizb" also means a portion of recitation (wird), and in the hadith: "Whoever misses his portion (hizb) of the night." "They formed a party" (tahazzabu) means they gathered together. "Al-ahzab" means groups.

What Allah promised His allies, the allies of His messengers, and the allies of His believing servants of victory over their enemy has indeed come to pass, and to Allah belongs all praise. They overcame the Jews through taking captives, killing, expulsion, and imposing the jizya (poll tax on non-Muslims), until Allah curse them, they became the most humiliated and least powerful of the disbelieving groups. They remained under the weight of the believers, crushing them as they wished and humiliating them as they desired, from the noble mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) until this point.

It has been read as fa-sayaran (with the yā' prefix), and it has been disputed what its subject is. It has been said that it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has been said that it is anyone who is capable of seeing. It has been said that it is the relative pronoun, and its object is "hastening toward them," with the verbal noun particle an omitted. That is, "he sees the people in whose hearts is disease, that they hasten toward them." When it was omitted, the verb became nominative, as in the line of poetry:

"Ah, you who blame me, let me attend the battle."

The disease in the hearts is hypocrisy and doubt about the religion. His words, ﴿They say, "We fear that a calamity will befall us"﴾, form a clause giving the reason for hastening in alliance. That is, this fear is what drives them to hasten. It has also been said that the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "hastening." The "calamity" (da'ira) is what turns of the misfortunes of time. That is, "we fear that the disbelievers will overcome Muhammad (ﷺ), so that the dominion will be theirs and his dominion will be nullified, and some hardship from them will befall us." From this is the poet's saying:

"It turns away from you the decreed fate, and the turning revolutions of time that they turn."

That is, the revolutions of time that turn from people to people. His words, ﴿So perhaps Allah will bring the conquest﴾, are a refutation of them and a dispelling of the fear that had come over them. "Perhaps" (asa) in the speech of Allah is a true promise that does not fail.

The conquest (al-fath) is the victory of the Prophet (ﷺ) over the disbelievers. It includes what happened of killing the fighting men of Banu Qurayzah and taking their children captive, and the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir. It has also been said that it is the conquest of the lands of the polytheists for the Muslims, and that it is the conquest of Mecca. "The command from Him" means everything by which the attack of the Jews and those with them is repelled and their power is broken. It has also been said that it is the disclosure of the matter of the hypocrites, and the Prophet (ﷺ) being informed of what they concealed within themselves, and his command to kill them. It has also been said that it is the jizya (poll tax) that Allah imposed on them. It has also been said that it is the abundance and plenty for the Muslims. Then the hypocrites will ﴿become, over what they concealed within themselves﴾ of hypocrisy, which drove them to alliance, "regretful" (nadimin) over that, because the causes they had imagined were nullified and their opposite was revealed.

His words, "Those who believe say" (yaqulu alladhina amanu): Abu 'Amr, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and the people of Kufa read it with the waw (wa-yaqulu), and the others read it without it (yaqulu). On the first reading, with the verb in the nominative, it is an independent statement presented to explain what occurred from this group. On the reading in the accusative, it is coordinated with "they will become" (fa-yusbihu), and it has also been said that it is coordinated with "comes" (ya'ti). The first is better, because this statement comes only from the believers when the regret of the disbelievers becomes apparent, not when the conquest comes. It has also been said that it is coordinated with "the conquest," as in the poet's saying:

"Wearing a cloak, and my eye is cooled."

As for the reading without the waw, the clause is resumed as an answer to an implied question. The demonstrative in "These" (ahaaulaa') refers to the hypocrites. That is: those who believe say, addressing the Jews and pointing to the hypocrites, ﴿"Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that they were with you?"﴾, in support and aid in fighting. Or some believers say to others, pointing to the hypocrites. This clause explains the statement. "The most emphatic of oaths" (jahd al-aymān) means the strongest of them. It is in the accusative either as a verbal noun (masdar) or as a circumstantial clause (hal). That is, they swore by Allah exerting themselves in the oath.

His words, "Their deeds have failed" (habitat a'maluhum), means that they became void. This is either part of the statement of the believers or a resumed independent clause, in which case the speaker is Allah, the Glorified. The deeds are those they did in alliance, or every deed they performed.

His words, ﴿O you who believe, whoever of you apostatises﴾: Ahl al-Madina and the Syrians read yartaddid with two dāl's, without assimilation (fakk al-idgham), which is the dialect of Tamim. The others read it with assimilation.

This is the beginning of an explanation of the rulings concerning apostates, after explaining that allying with disbelievers is disbelief on the part of a Muslim. That is one kind of apostasy (ridda). The people whom Allah promised to bring are Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and his army of the Companions and the Successors, with whom he fought the people of apostasy. Then, every one who came after them among those who fought apostates throughout all time. Then the Glorified describes these people with these great attributes, containing the utmost praise and the highest commendation: that they love Allah and He loves them, and that they are ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers, striving in the way of Allah, and not fearing the blame of any blamer﴾. (p. 379) "Humble" (adhillah) is the plural of dhalil, not dhalul (tame). "Mighty" (a'izzah) is the plural of 'aziz. That is, they show tenderness, compassion, and humility toward the believers, and show firmness, harshness, and superiority over the disbelievers. They combine striving in the way of Allah with not fearing reproach in religion. Indeed, they are firm and do not care about what the enemies of truth and the party of Satan do, such as disparaging the people of religion, and turning their virtues into vices and their merits into faults, out of envy, hatred, and aversion to the truth and its people.

The demonstrative in "That" (dhalika) refers to the attributes mentioned previously, with which Allah singled them out. "Bounty" (fadl) means kindness and benevolence.

His words, ﴿Your only ally is Allah﴾: when He, the Glorified, finished explaining whom it is not lawful to take as an ally, He explained who is the Ally whose alliance is obligatory. The position of ﴿Those who establish prayer﴾ is nominative, as an attribute of "those who believe," or as an apposition to it, or accusative as an expression of praise. His words, ﴿and they bow in prayer﴾, form a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of the two verbs preceding it. "Bowing" (ruku') here means humility and submission. That is, they establish prayer and give zakat while being humble and submissive, not arrogant. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "give zakat."

The meaning of "bowing" is the one mentioned: that is, they place zakat in its proper places, not arrogant toward the poor, nor exalting themselves over them. It has also been said that on the second meaning, "bowing" refers to the bowing of prayer, but this is rejected because it is not permissible to pay zakat in that state.

﴿And whoever takes Allah and His Messenger and those who believe as allies, then indeed the party of Allah are the victorious﴾. Then the Glorified promised that whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and the believers as allies will be victorious over their enemy. This is a case of putting the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, and putting "the party of Allah" in place of the pronoun for those who ally with Allah, His Messenger, and the believers. "Hizb" means a category of people, from the expression "hazabahu kadha," meaning "it befell him." It is as though the members of a party gather together like the people of a calamity that befalls them. "The party of a man" means his companions. "Hizb" also means a portion of recitation (wird), and in the hadith: "Whoever misses his portion (hizb) of the night." "They formed a party" (tahazzabu) means they gathered together. "Al-ahzab" means groups.

What Allah promised His allies, the allies of His messengers, and the allies of His believing servants of victory over their enemy has indeed come to pass, and to Allah belongs all praise. They overcame the Jews through taking captives, killing, expulsion, and imposing the jizya (poll tax on non-Muslims), until Allah curse them, they became the most humiliated and least powerful of the disbelieving groups. They remained under the weight of the believers, crushing them as they wished and humiliating them as they desired, from the noble mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) until this point.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Ubada ibn al-Walid ibn Ubada ibn al-Samit, who said: "When Banu Qaynuqa fought the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul clung to their affair and stood in their defence. Ubada ibn al-Samit went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), disassociated himself before Allah and His Messenger from their alliance, and he was one of Banu 'Awf ibn al-Khazraj, and he had with them the same alliance that 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul had with them. So he cut himself off from them before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'I disassociate myself before Allah and His Messenger from the alliance and loyalty of these disbelievers.' Concerning him and 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy the verses in al-Ma'idah were revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and Christians as allies﴾ up to His words ﴿indeed, the party of Allah are the victorious﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh reported, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul became Muslim, then said: 'Indeed, between me and Qurayzah and al-Nadir there is an alliance, and I fear the calamities.' So he apostatised as a disbeliever. Ubada ibn al-Samit said: 'I disassociate myself before Allah from the alliance of Qurayzah and al-Nadir, and I take Allah and His Messenger as allies,' and so it was revealed." Ibn Mardawayh also reported, through the chain of Ubada ibn al-Walid ibn Ubada ibn al-Samit, from his father, from his grandfather, something similar. Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir reported, from 'Atiyya ibn Sa'd, who said: "Ubada came and mentioned something similar to what preceded."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Zuhri, who said: When the people of Badr were defeated, the Muslims said to their allies among the Jews, "Embrace Islam before Allah afflicts you with a day like the day of Badr." Malik ibn al-Sayf said, "Did you become deluded because you struck a group of Quraysh who had no knowledge of fighting? If we had resolved to gather against you, you would not have had the strength to fight us." Then 'Ubadah spoke, mentioning something similar to what has preceded from him and from 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding this verse, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, that he said: it concerns slaughtered animals. Whoever enters the religion of a people is one of them.

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Hudhayfah, who said: Let each of you beware of becoming a Jew or a Christian without realizing it. He then recited, ﴿And whoever among you allies with them, then indeed he is one of them﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Atiyyah regarding ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, that it refers to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, (﴿they hasten toward them﴾) in their alliance.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Qatadah, who said: Allah revealed this verse, ﴿O you who have believed, whoever of you reverts from his religion﴾, although He knew that some people would apostatize. When Allah took His Prophet (ﷺ), most of the Arabs reverted from Islam, except for three mosques: the people of Madinah, the people of Makkah, and the people of al-Jawathi from 'Abd al-Qays. Those who apostatized said, "We will pray but we will not pay zakat. By Allah, our wealth will not be seized." Abu Bakr was asked about this so that he would overlook them, and it was said to him, "If they gain understanding, they will pay zakat." He said, "By Allah, I will not separate what Allah has joined. Even if they withheld from me a cord (of camel-tying) of what Allah and His Messenger prescribed, I would fight them over it." So Allah sent companies with Abu Bakr, and they fought until they acknowledged the ma'un, which is zakat (ma'un: a Qur'anic term, from 107:7, here understood as zakat). Qatadah said: We used to say that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr and his companions, ﴿Then Allah will bring forth a people He loves and who love Him﴾, up to the end of the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from al-Hasan something similar.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Shurayh ibn 'Ubayd, who said: "When Allah revealed, ﴿O you who have believed, whoever of you reverts from his religion﴾ up to the end of the verse, 'Umar said, 'Me and my people, O Messenger of Allah?' He said, 'No, rather this man and his people,' meaning Abu Musa al-Ash'ari."

Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah in his Musnad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from 'Iyad al-Ash'ari, who said: "When (p-380) ﴿Then Allah will bring forth a people He loves and who love Him﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'They are the people of this man,' and he gestured toward Abu Musa al-Ash'ari."

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Hakim in his collection of the hadith of Shu'bah, al-Bayhaqi and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: "﴿Then Allah will bring forth a people﴾ was recited in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), up to the end of the verse, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'Your people, O Abu Musa, are the people of Yemen.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim in al-Kuna, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated with a sound chain (isnad) from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about His saying, ﴿Then Allah will bring forth a people﴾ up to the end of the verse, and he said, 'These are a people from the people of Yemen, then Kindah, then Sakun, then Tujib.'"

Al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the verse, who said: They are a people from the people of Yemen, then from Kindah, then from Sakun.

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from him, who said: They are the people of al-Qadisiyyah.

Al-Bukhari in his Tarikh narrated from al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymirah, who said: I came to Ibn 'Umar and he welcomed me. Then he recited, ﴿Whoever of you reverts from his religion, then Allah will bring forth a people﴾ up to the end of the verse. Then he struck my shoulder and said, "I swear by Allah, they are indeed from you, the people of Yemen," three times.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Atiyyah ibn Sa'd, who said regarding His saying, ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger﴾: it was revealed concerning 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit.

Al-Khatib in al-Muttafaq wa'l-Muftaraq narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: 'Ali gave away a ring while he was bowing (in prayer). The Prophet (ﷺ) said to the beggar, "Who gave you this ring?" He said, "That one who is bowing." So Allah revealed concerning him, ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger﴾.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: It was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib something similar. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ammar something similar too. Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from him something similar, with a chain containing unknown narrators (majahil).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 5, verses 51–56 (part 1 of 2):

It has also been said that the intended audience is the hypocrites (munafiqun), and that they are described as believers in terms of what they outwardly displayed. (p. 378) They used to befriend the Jews and Christians, so they were forbidden from doing so. The better view is that it is addressed to everyone who is characterised by faith, more general than whether that faith is outward and inward or only outward. This includes the Muslim and the hypocrite. This is supported by his words, ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾. What matters is the generality of the wording. The explanation of the occasion of revelation, which comes later, will clarify the intended meaning. The prohibition against taking them as awliya' (allies, protectors) means that they should not be treated as allies in companionship, close association, and support. His words, ﴿They are allies of one another﴾, give the reason for the prohibition. The meaning is that some Jews are allies of other Jews, and some Christians are allies of other Christians. The "some" here does not refer to one of the two groups of Jews and Christians against the other group, since they are definitively in extreme enmity and hostility. ﴿The Jews say, "The Christians are not upon anything," and the Christians say, "The Jews are not upon anything"﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:113). It has also been said that the meaning is that each of the two groups allies with the other, supports it, and aids it against the enmity toward the Prophet (ﷺ) and against what he brought, even though they are mutually hostile and opposed among themselves.

The reason for prohibiting this, expressed through this clause, is that it implies that this alliance is the habit of these disbelievers, not yours. So do not do what is part of their conduct, lest you become like them. For this reason, he followed this explanatory clause with what amounts to its result, saying: ﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies, then indeed he is of them﴾. That is, he is among them and counted with them. This is a severe warning, since the sin that necessitates disbelief is the one that reaches an extreme beyond which there is no further extreme. His words, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, give the reason for the preceding clause. That is, their falling into disbelief is due to Allah's not guiding those who wrong themselves by doing what necessitates disbelief, such as one who allies with the disbelievers.

His words, ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them﴾: the fa' indicates causation. The address is either to the Messenger (ﷺ) or to everyone suitable for it. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 5, verses 51–56 (part 1 of 2):

The apparent meaning of his words, ﴿O you who believe, do not take﴾, is that it is addressed to believers in the literal sense. It has also been said that the intended audience is the hypocrites (munafiqun), and that they are described as believers in terms of what they outwardly displayed. (p. 378) They used to befriend the Jews and Christians, so they were forbidden from doing so. The better view is that it is addressed to everyone who is characterised by faith, more general than whether that faith is outward and inward or only outward. This includes the Muslim and the hypocrite. This is supported by his words, ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾. What matters is the generality of the wording. The explanation of the occasion of revelation, which comes later, will clarify the intended meaning. The prohibition against taking them as awliya' (allies, protectors) means that they should not be treated as allies in companionship, close association, and support. His words, ﴿They are allies of one another﴾, give the reason for the prohibition. The meaning is that some Jews are allies of other Jews, and some Christians are allies of other Christians. The "some" here does not refer to one of the two groups of Jews and Christians against the other group, since they are definitively in extreme enmity and hostility. ﴿The Jews say, "The Christians are not upon anything," and the Christians say, "The Jews are not upon anything"﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:113). It has also been said that the meaning is that each of the two groups allies with the other, supports it, and aids it against the enmity toward the Prophet (ﷺ) and against what he brought, even though they are mutually hostile and opposed among themselves.

The reason for prohibiting this, expressed through this clause, is that it implies that this alliance is the habit of these disbelievers, not yours. So do not do what is part of their conduct, lest you become like them. For this reason, he followed this explanatory clause with what amounts to its result, saying: ﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies, then indeed he is of them﴾. That is, he is among them and counted with them. This is a severe warning, since the sin that necessitates disbelief is the one that reaches an extreme beyond which there is no further extreme. His words, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, give the reason for the preceding clause. That is, their falling into disbelief is due to Allah's not guiding those who wrong themselves by doing what necessitates disbelief, such as one who allies with the disbelievers.

His words, ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them﴾: the fa' indicates causation. The address is either to the Messenger (ﷺ) or to everyone suitable for it. That is, what they committed of alliance and what they fell into of disbelief is due to the disease of hypocrisy in their hearts. His words, "hastening" (yusari'una), are in the accusative position, either as the second object if the seeing is of the heart, or as a circumstantial clause (al-hal) if the seeing is visual. He made hastening in their alliance into hastening toward them, for emphasis in describing their eagerness for that, as if they were settled among them and entered into their number.

It has been read as fa-sayaran (with the yā' prefix), and it has been disputed what its subject is. It has been said that it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has been said that it is anyone who is capable of seeing. It has been said that it is the relative pronoun, and its object is "hastening toward them," with the verbal noun particle an omitted. That is, "he sees the people in whose hearts is disease, that they hasten toward them." When it was omitted, the verb became nominative, as in the line of poetry:

"Ah, you who blame me, let me attend the battle."

The disease in the hearts is hypocrisy and doubt about the religion. His words, ﴿They say, "We fear that a calamity will befall us"﴾, form a clause giving the reason for hastening in alliance. That is, this fear is what drives them to hasten. It has also been said that the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "hastening." The "calamity" (da'ira) is what turns of the misfortunes of time. That is, "we fear that the disbelievers will overcome Muhammad (ﷺ), so that the dominion will be theirs and his dominion will be nullified, and some hardship from them will befall us." From this is the poet's saying:

"It turns away from you the decreed fate, and the turning revolutions of time that they turn."

That is, the revolutions of time that turn from people to people. His words, ﴿So perhaps Allah will bring the conquest﴾, are a refutation of them and a dispelling of the fear that had come over them. "Perhaps" (asa) in the speech of Allah is a true promise that does not fail.

The conquest (al-fath) is the victory of the Prophet (ﷺ) over the disbelievers. It includes what happened of killing the fighting men of Banu Qurayzah and taking their children captive, and the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir. It has also been said that it is the conquest of the lands of the polytheists for the Muslims, and that it is the conquest of Mecca. "The command from Him" means everything by which the attack of the Jews and those with them is repelled and their power is broken. It has also been said that it is the disclosure of the matter of the hypocrites, and the Prophet (ﷺ) being informed of what they concealed within themselves, and his command to kill them. It has also been said that it is the jizya (poll tax) that Allah imposed on them. It has also been said that it is the abundance and plenty for the Muslims. Then the hypocrites will ﴿become, over what they concealed within themselves﴾ of hypocrisy, which drove them to alliance, "regretful" (nadimin) over that, because the causes they had imagined were nullified and their opposite was revealed.

His words, "Those who believe say" (yaqulu alladhina amanu): Abu 'Amr, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and the people of Kufa read it with the waw (wa-yaqulu), and the others read it without it (yaqulu). On the first reading, with the verb in the nominative, it is an independent statement presented to explain what occurred from this group. On the reading in the accusative, it is coordinated with "they will become" (fa-yusbihu), and it has also been said that it is coordinated with "comes" (ya'ti). The first is better, because this statement comes only from the believers when the regret of the disbelievers becomes apparent, not when the conquest comes. It has also been said that it is coordinated with "the conquest," as in the poet's saying:

"Wearing a cloak, and my eye is cooled."

As for the reading without the waw, the clause is resumed as an answer to an implied question. The demonstrative in "These" (ahaaulaa') refers to the hypocrites. That is: those who believe say, addressing the Jews and pointing to the hypocrites, ﴿"Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that they were with you?"﴾, in support and aid in fighting. Or some believers say to others, pointing to the hypocrites. This clause explains the statement. "The most emphatic of oaths" (jahd al-aymān) means the strongest of them. It is in the accusative either as a verbal noun (masdar) or as a circumstantial clause (hal). That is, they swore by Allah exerting themselves in the oath.

His words, "Their deeds have failed" (habitat a'maluhum), means that they became void. This is either part of the statement of the believers or a resumed independent clause, in which case the speaker is Allah, the Glorified. The deeds are those they did in alliance, or every deed they performed.

His words, ﴿O you who believe, whoever of you apostatises﴾: Ahl al-Madina and the Syrians read yartaddid with two dāl's, without assimilation (fakk al-idgham), which is the dialect of Tamim. The others read it with assimilation.

This is the beginning of an explanation of the rulings concerning apostates, after explaining that allying with disbelievers is disbelief on the part of a Muslim. That is one kind of apostasy (ridda). The people whom Allah promised to bring are Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and his army of the Companions and the Successors, with whom he fought the people of apostasy. Then, every one who came after them among those who fought apostates throughout all time. Then the Glorified describes these people with these great attributes, containing the utmost praise and the highest commendation: that they love Allah and He loves them, and that they are ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers, striving in the way of Allah, and not fearing the blame of any blamer﴾. (p. 379) "Humble" (adhillah) is the plural of dhalil, not dhalul (tame). "Mighty" (a'izzah) is the plural of 'aziz. That is, they show tenderness, compassion, and humility toward the believers, and show firmness, harshness, and superiority over the disbelievers. They combine striving in the way of Allah with not fearing reproach in religion. Indeed, they are firm and do not care about what the enemies of truth and the party of Satan do, such as disparaging the people of religion, and turning their virtues into vices and their merits into faults, out of envy, hatred, and aversion to the truth and its people.

The demonstrative in "That" (dhalika) refers to the attributes mentioned previously, with which Allah singled them out. "Bounty" (fadl) means kindness and benevolence.

His words, ﴿Your only ally is Allah﴾: when He, the Glorified, finished explaining whom it is not lawful to take as an ally, He explained who is the Ally whose alliance is obligatory. The position of ﴿Those who establish prayer﴾ is nominative, as an attribute of "those who believe," or as an apposition to it, or accusative as an expression of praise. His words, ﴿and they bow in prayer﴾, form a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of the two verbs preceding it. "Bowing" (ruku') here means humility and submission. That is, they establish prayer and give zakat while being humble and submissive, not arrogant. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "give zakat."

The meaning of "bowing" is the one mentioned: that is, they place zakat in its proper places, not arrogant toward the poor, nor exalting themselves over them. It has also been said that on the second meaning, "bowing" refers to the bowing of prayer, but this is rejected because it is not permissible to pay zakat in that state.

﴿And whoever takes Allah and His Messenger and those who believe as allies, then indeed the party of Allah are the victorious﴾. Then the Glorified promised that whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and the believers as allies will be victorious over their enemy. This is a case of putting the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, and putting "the party of Allah" in place of the pronoun for those who ally with Allah, His Messenger, and the believers. "Hizb" means a category of people, from the expression "hazabahu kadha," meaning "it befell him." It is as though the members of a party gather together like the people of a calamity that befalls them. "The party of a man" means his companions. "Hizb" also means a portion of recitation (wird), and in the hadith: "Whoever misses his portion (hizb) of the night." "They formed a party" (tahazzabu) means they gathered together. "Al-ahzab" means groups.

What Allah promised His allies, the allies of His messengers, and the allies of His believing servants of victory over their enemy has indeed come to pass, and to Allah belongs all praise. They overcame the Jews through taking captives, killing, expulsion, and imposing the jizya (poll tax on non-Muslims), until Allah curse them, they became the most humiliated and least powerful of the disbelieving groups. They remained under the weight of the believers, crushing them as they wished and humiliating them as they desired, from the noble mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) until this point.
