So do not do what is part of their conduct, lest you become like them. For this reason, he followed this explanatory clause with what amounts to its result, saying: ﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies, then indeed he is of them﴾. That is, he is among them and counted with them. This is a severe warning, since the sin that necessitates disbelief is the one that reaches an extreme beyond which there is no further extreme. His words, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, give the reason for the preceding clause. That is, their falling into disbelief is due to Allah's not guiding those who wrong themselves by doing what necessitates disbelief, such as one who allies with the disbelievers.

His words, ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them﴾: the fa' indicates causation. The address is either to the Messenger (ﷺ) or to everyone suitable for it. That is, what they committed of alliance and what they fell into of disbelief is due to the disease of hypocrisy in their hearts. His words, "hastening" (yusari'una), are in the accusative position, either as the second object if the seeing is of the heart, or as a circumstantial clause (al-hal) if the seeing is visual. He made hastening in their alliance into hastening toward them, for emphasis in describing their eagerness for that, as if they were settled among them and entered into their number.

It has been read as fa-sayaran (with the yā' prefix), and it has been disputed what its subject is. It has been said that it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has been said that it is anyone who is capable of seeing. It has been said that it is the relative pronoun, and its object is "hastening toward them," with the verbal noun particle an omitted. That is, "he sees the people in whose hearts is disease, that they hasten toward them." When it was omitted, the verb became nominative, as in the line of poetry:

"Ah, you who blame me, let me attend the battle."

The disease in the hearts is hypocrisy and doubt about the religion. His words, ﴿They say, "We fear that a calamity will befall us"﴾, form a clause giving the reason for hastening in alliance. That is, this fear is what drives them to hasten. It has also been said that the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "hastening." The "calamity" (da'ira) is what turns of the misfortunes of time. That is, "we fear that the disbelievers will overcome Muhammad (ﷺ), so that the dominion will be theirs and his dominion will be nullified, and some hardship from them will befall us." From this is the poet's saying:

"It turns away from you the decreed fate, and the turning revolutions of time that they turn."

That is, the revolutions of time that turn from people to people. His words, ﴿So perhaps Allah will bring the conquest﴾, are a refutation of them and a dispelling of the fear that had come over them. "Perhaps" (asa) in the speech of Allah is a true promise that does not fail.

The conquest (al-fath) is the victory of the Prophet (ﷺ) over the disbelievers. It includes what happened of killing the fighting men of Banu Qurayzah and taking their children captive, and the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir. It has also been said that it is the conquest of the lands of the polytheists for the Muslims, and that it is the conquest of Mecca. "The command from Him" means everything by which the attack of the Jews and those with them is repelled and their power is broken. It has also been said that it is the disclosure of the matter of the hypocrites, and the Prophet (ﷺ) being informed of what they concealed within themselves, and his command to kill them. It has also been said that it is the jizya (poll tax) that Allah imposed on them. It has also been said that it is the abundance and plenty for the Muslims. Then the hypocrites will ﴿become, over what they concealed within themselves﴾ of hypocrisy, which drove them to alliance, "regretful" (nadimin) over that, because the causes they had imagined were nullified and their opposite was revealed.

His words, "Those who believe say" (yaqulu alladhina amanu): Abu 'Amr, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and the people of Kufa read it with the waw (wa-yaqulu), and the others read it without it (yaqulu). On the first reading, with the verb in the nominative, it is an independent statement presented to explain what occurred from this group. On the reading in the accusative, it is coordinated with "they will become" (fa-yusbihu), and it has also been said that it is coordinated with "comes" (ya'ti). The first is better, because this statement comes only from the believers when the regret of the disbelievers becomes apparent, not when the conquest comes. It has also been said that it is coordinated with "the conquest," as in the poet's saying:

"Wearing a cloak, and my eye is cooled."

As for the reading without the waw, the clause is resumed as an answer to an implied question. The demonstrative in "These" (ahaaulaa') refers to the hypocrites. That is: those who believe say, addressing the Jews and pointing to the hypocrites, ﴿"Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that they were with you?"﴾, in support and aid in fighting. Or some believers say to others, pointing to the hypocrites. This clause explains the statement. "The most emphatic of oaths" (jahd al-aymān) means the strongest of them. It is in the accusative either as a verbal noun (masdar) or as a circumstantial clause (hal). That is, they swore by Allah exerting themselves in the oath.

His words, "Their deeds have failed" (habitat a'maluhum), means that they became void. This is either part of the statement of the believers or a resumed independent clause, in which case the speaker is Allah, the Glorified. The deeds are those they did in alliance, or every deed they performed.

His words, ﴿O you who believe, whoever of you apostatises﴾: Ahl al-Madina and the Syrians read yartaddid with two dāl's, without assimilation (fakk al-idgham), which is the dialect of Tamim. The others read it with assimilation.

This is the beginning of an explanation of the rulings concerning apostates, after explaining that allying with disbelievers is disbelief on the part of a Muslim. That is one kind of apostasy (ridda). The people whom Allah promised to bring are Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and his army of the Companions and the Successors, with whom he fought the people of apostasy. Then, every one who came after them among those who fought apostates throughout all time. Then the Glorified describes these people with these great attributes, containing the utmost praise and the highest commendation: that they love Allah and He loves them, and that they are ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers, striving in the way of Allah, and not fearing the blame of any blamer﴾. (p. 379) "Humble" (adhillah) is the plural of dhalil, not dhalul (tame). "Mighty" (a'izzah) is the plural of 'aziz. That is, they show tenderness, compassion, and humility toward the believers, and show firmness, harshness, and superiority over the disbelievers. They combine striving in the way of Allah with not fearing reproach in religion. Indeed, they are firm and do not care about what the enemies of truth and the party of Satan do, such as disparaging the people of religion, and turning their virtues into vices and their merits into faults, out of envy, hatred, and aversion to the truth and its people.

The demonstrative in "That" (dhalika) refers to the attributes mentioned previously, with which Allah singled them out. "Bounty" (fadl) means kindness and benevolence.

His words, ﴿Your only ally is Allah﴾: when He, the Glorified, finished explaining whom it is not lawful to take as an ally, He explained who is the Ally whose alliance is obligatory. The position of ﴿Those who establish prayer﴾ is nominative, as an attribute of "those who believe," or as an apposition to it, or accusative as an expression of praise. His words, ﴿and they bow in prayer﴾, form a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of the two verbs preceding it. "Bowing" (ruku') here means humility and submission. That is, they establish prayer and give zakat while being humble and submissive, not arrogant. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "give zakat."

The meaning of "bowing" is the one mentioned: that is, they place zakat in its proper places, not arrogant toward the poor, nor exalting themselves over them. It has also been said that on the second meaning, "bowing" refers to the bowing of prayer, but this is rejected because it is not permissible to pay zakat in that state.

﴿And whoever takes Allah and His Messenger and those who believe as allies, then indeed the party of Allah are the victorious﴾. Then the Glorified promised that whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and the believers as allies will be victorious over their enemy. This is a case of putting the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, and putting "the party of Allah" in place of the pronoun for those who ally with Allah, His Messenger, and the believers. "Hizb" means a category of people, from the expression "hazabahu kadha," meaning "it befell him." It is as though the members of a party gather together like the people of a calamity that befalls them. "The party of a man" means his companions. "Hizb" also means a portion of recitation (wird), and in the hadith: "Whoever misses his portion (hizb) of the night." "They formed a party" (tahazzabu) means they gathered together. "Al-ahzab" means groups.

What Allah promised His allies, the allies of His messengers, and the allies of His believing servants of victory over their enemy has indeed come to pass, and to Allah belongs all praise. They overcame the Jews through taking captives, killing, expulsion, and imposing the jizya (poll tax on non-Muslims), until Allah curse them, they became the most humiliated and least powerful of the disbelieving groups. They remained under the weight of the believers, crushing them as they wished and humiliating them as they desired, from the noble mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) until this point.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Ubada ibn al-Walid ibn Ubada ibn al-Samit, who said: "When Banu Qaynuqa fought the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul clung to their affair and stood in their defence. Ubada ibn al-Samit went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), disassociated himself before Allah and His Messenger from their alliance, and he was one of Banu 'Awf ibn al-Khazraj, and he had with them the same alliance that 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul had with them. So he cut himself off from them before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'I disassociate myself before Allah and His Messenger from the alliance and loyalty of these disbelievers.' Concerning him and 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy the verses in al-Ma'idah were revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and Christians as allies﴾ up to His words ﴿indeed, the party of Allah are the victorious﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh reported, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul became Muslim, then said: 'Indeed, between me and Qurayzah and al-Nadir there is an alliance, and I fear the calamities.' So he apostatised as a disbeliever. Ubada ibn al-Samit said: 'I disassociate myself before Allah from the alliance of Qurayzah and al-Nadir, and I take Allah and His Messenger as allies,' and so it was revealed." Ibn Mardawayh also reported, through the chain of Ubada ibn al-Walid ibn Ubada ibn al-Samit, from his father, from his grandfather, something similar. Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir reported, from 'Atiyya ibn Sa'd, who said: "Ubada came and mentioned something similar to what preceded."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Zuhri, who said: When the people of Badr were defeated, the Muslims said to their allies among the Jews, "Embrace Islam before Allah afflicts you with a day like the day of Badr." Malik ibn al-Sayf said, "Did you become deluded because you struck a group of Quraysh who had no knowledge of fighting? If we had resolved to gather against you, you would not have had the strength to fight us." Then 'Ubadah spoke, mentioning something similar to what has preceded from him and from 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding this verse, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, that he said: it concerns slaughtered animals. Whoever enters the religion of a people is one of them.

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Hudhayfah, who said: Let each of you beware of becoming a Jew or a Christian without realizing it. He then recited, ﴿And whoever among you allies with them, then indeed he is one of them﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Atiyyah regarding ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, that it refers to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, (﴿they hasten toward them﴾) in their alliance.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Qatadah, who said: Allah revealed this verse, ﴿O you who have believed, whoever of you reverts from his religion﴾, although He knew that some people would apostatize. When Allah took His Prophet (ﷺ), most of the Arabs reverted from Islam, except for three mosques: the people of Madinah, the people of Makkah, and the people of al-Jawathi from 'Abd al-Qays. Those who apostatized said, "We will pray but we will not pay zakat. By Allah, our wealth will not be seized." Abu Bakr was asked about this so that he would overlook them, and it was said to him, "If they gain understanding, they will pay zakat." He said, "By Allah, I will not separate what Allah has joined. Even if they withheld from me a cord (of camel-tying) of what Allah and His Messenger prescribed, I would fight them over it." So Allah sent companies with Abu Bakr, and they fought until they acknowledged the ma'un, which is zakat (ma'un: a Qur'anic term, from 107:7, here understood as zakat). Qatadah said: We used to say that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr and his companions, ﴿Then Allah will bring forth a people He loves and who love Him﴾, up to the end of the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from al-Hasan something similar.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Shurayh ibn 'Ubayd, who said: "When Allah revealed, ﴿O you who have believed, whoever of you reverts from his religion﴾ up to the end of the verse, 'Umar said, 'Me and my people, O Messenger of Allah?' He said, 'No, rather this man and his people,' meaning Abu Musa al-Ash'ari."

Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah in his Musnad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from 'Iyad al-Ash'ari, who said: "When (p-380) ﴿Then Allah will bring forth a people He loves and who love Him﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'They are the people of this man,' and he gestured toward Abu Musa al-Ash'ari."

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Hakim in his collection of the hadith of Shu'bah, al-Bayhaqi and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: "﴿Then Allah will bring forth a people﴾ was recited in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), up to the end of the verse, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'Your people, O Abu Musa, are the people of Yemen.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim in al-Kuna, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated with a sound chain (isnad) from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about His saying, ﴿Then Allah will bring forth a people﴾ up to the end of the verse, and he said, 'These are a people from the people of Yemen, then Kindah, then Sakun, then Tujib.'"

Al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the verse, who said: They are a people from the people of Yemen, then from Kindah, then from Sakun.

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from him, who said: They are the people of al-Qadisiyyah.

Al-Bukhari in his Tarikh narrated from al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymirah, who said: I came to Ibn 'Umar and he welcomed me. Then he recited, ﴿Whoever of you reverts from his religion, then Allah will bring forth a people﴾ up to the end of the verse. Then he struck my shoulder and said, "I swear by Allah, they are indeed from you, the people of Yemen," three times.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Atiyyah ibn Sa'd, who said regarding His saying, ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger﴾: it was revealed concerning 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit.

Al-Khatib in al-Muttafaq wa'l-Muftaraq narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: 'Ali gave away a ring while he was bowing (in prayer). The Prophet (ﷺ) said to the beggar, "Who gave you this ring?" He said, "That one who is bowing." So Allah revealed concerning him, ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger﴾.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: It was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib something similar. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ammar something similar too. Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from him something similar, with a chain containing unknown narrators (majahil).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 57–63 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as a mockery and a game﴾. This is a prohibition on allying with those who make the religion a mockery and a game. It covers everyone from whom this occurs, whether from the polytheists, the People of the Book, or the people of innovation (ahl al-bida') who ascribe themselves to Islam. The explanation in His saying ﴿from those who were given the Book﴾ to the end of the verse does not preclude others from falling under the prohibition when the stated reason (al-'illa), which is the motive for the prohibition, is found in them.

His saying: (wa-l-kuffar, "and the disbelievers"). Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it in the genitive (bi-l-jarr), on the assumption of the preposition (min), meaning "and of the disbelievers." Al-Kisa'i said: "In the reading of Ubayy it is (wa-min al-kuffar)." The rest read it in the accusative (bi-l-nasb). Al-Nahhas said: "This is clearer and more explicit." Makki said: "Were it not for the consensus of the community (ijma'') on the accusative, I would have chosen the genitive for its strength in i'rab (grammatical inflection) and in meaning." Here "the disbelievers" means the polytheists, and it has been said that it means the hypocrites. ﴿And fear God﴾, by abandoning what He has forbidden you from this and other things, ﴿if you are believers﴾, for faith requires that.

The nida' (ندَاء, call) is calling out with a raised voice. One says nadahu, munadah and nida', meaning he cried out to him. (wa-tanadaw): meaning some of them called out to one another. (Tanadaw) also means they sat in the nadi (assembly). The pronoun in (ittakhadhuha, "they took it") refers to the prayer, meaning they took your prayer as a mockery and a game. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the call (al-munadah), which is implied by (nadaytum, "you called"). It has been said that the Book of God mentions the adhan (call to prayer) only in this passage. As for His saying concerning Friday: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday﴾, it is specific to the Friday call. The scholars have differed over whether the adhan is obligatory or not, and over its wording. This is expounded in its proper places.

His saying: ﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾. That is, that is because they are a people who do not reason, since mockery and play are the habit of people of foolishness, lightness and frivolity.

His saying: ﴿Say: "O People of the Book, do you find fault with us?"﴾. It is said: naqimtu 'ala al-rajul (with kasra, in the past tense) — fa-ana naqim, when you found fault with him.

Al-Kisa'i said: "Naqimtu (with kasra) is a dialectal form, and naqamtu al-amr (with fatha) also, and naqimtu means: when you disliked it. Allah took vengeance on him (intaqama Allahu minhu), that is, punished him. Its noun is al-niqmah, and its plural is niqamat, like kalimah and kalimat. If you wish, you may make the qaf sukun and transfer its vowel to the nun, and the plural is niqam, like ni'mah and ni'am." It has been said the meaning is "they are angered," and it has been said "they disapprove." 'Abd Allah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

"They found no fault with the Banu Umayyah, except that they are forbearing when they are angered."

God the Exalted said: (wa-ma naqamu minhum, "and they found no fault with them"). The meaning in the verse: do you blame, or are angered by, or disapprove of, or dislike in us, except our faith in God and in His revealed Books? And you know that we are upon the truth. ﴿And that most of you are defiantly disobedient﴾, by your abandoning faith and departing from obedience to God's commands.

His saying: (wa-anna aktharakum fasiqun, "and that most of you are defiantly disobedient") is conjoined (ma'tuf) to (an amanna, "that we believed"). That is: you find fault with us only for combining our faith with your rebellion and your departure from faith. In this there is the point that the believers did not combine the two matters mentioned, for the faith is on their part, while the rebellion and the departure are on the part of those who find fault. It has been said that it is on an implied supplement: "and our belief that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has also been said that (an amanna) is in the accusative as a direct object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and the object is omitted, so (wa-anna aktharakum fasiqun) is conjoined to it, a conjunction of cause to cause, and the construction is: "and you find fault with us only because we believed, and because most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said that it is conjoined to an omitted cause, meaning: "because of the scarcity of your fairness, and because most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said that the waw in (wa-anna aktharakum fasiqun) is the one that means "with" (ma'a), meaning: "you find fault with us only for the faith, together with the fact that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said it is in the accusative by a verb omitted, indicated by (hal tanqimun, "do you find fault"), meaning: "and you do not find fault that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said it is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada') with an omitted predicate, meaning: "and your defiance is known," so the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal). It has been read with kasra on (inna) in His saying (wa-inna aktharakum fasiqun), so it is a new independent clause.

His saying: ﴿Say: "Shall I inform you of something worse than that as requital from God?"﴾. God the Exalted showed His Messenger that among them there is what is more deserving of blame: their disbelief, which brings upon them God's curse, His wrath, and their transformation. The meaning: shall I inform you of something worse than your fault-finding against us, or worse than what you wish for us of hardship, or worse than the People of the Book, or worse than their religion? His saying (mathuba, "requital") means a fixed reward. It is specific to good, just as punishment is specific to evil. It is placed here in the position of punishment, in the manner of (fa-bashshirhum bi-'adhabin alim, "so give them good tidings of a painful punishment"). It is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of (bi-sharr, "something worse"). His saying (man la'anahu Allah, "whom God has cursed") is a predicate of an omitted subject, with an omitted genitive construct, meaning: "it is the cursing of whom God has cursed," or "it is the religion of whom God has cursed." It is permissible that it be in the genitive position as an apposition (badal) of (sharr).

His saying: ﴿and He made of them apes and swine﴾. That is, He transformed some of them into apes and some into swine, and they are the Jews, for God transformed the people of the Sabbath into apes, and the disbelievers of the table of 'Isa among them into swine.

His saying: (wa-'abada al-taghut, "and worshipped the taghut"). Hamza read (abada) with a damma on the ba' and (al-taghut) with a kasra on the ta', meaning: He made of them "abudu al-taghut," by annexing "abud" to "al-taghut." The meaning: He made of them those who exaggerate in the worship of the taghut, since fa'ul is among the forms of intensification, like hadhir and fatin, for emphasis in caution and in shrewdness. The rest read (abada) with a fatha on the ba' and (al-taghut) with a fatha on the ta', as a past verb conjoined to a past verb, namely (ghadiba, "was angry") and (la'ana, "cursed"), as if it were said: "and those who worshipped the taghut." Or it is conjoined to (al-qiradah wa-l-khanazir, "the apes and the swine"), meaning: He made of them apes and swine, and He made of them those who worshipped the taghut, following the wording of (min, "of"). Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read (wa-'abadu al-taghut, "and they worshipped the taghut") following its meaning. Ibn 'Abbas read (wa-'ubud, with damma on the 'ayn and the ba'), as if it were the plural of 'abd, as one says saqf and suquf, and it is permissible that it be the plural of 'abid, like raghif and rughuf, or the plural of 'abid, like bazil and buzul. Abu Waqid read (wa-'ubbad), the plural of 'abid, for intensification, like 'amil and 'ummal. The Basrans read (wa-'ubbad), also the plural of 'abid, like qa'im and qiyam, and it is permissible that it be the plural of 'abd. Abu Ja'far al-Raqqashi read (wa-'ubida al-taghut, "and the taghut was worshipped") in the passive, and the implied meaning is: "and the taghut was worshipped among them." 'Awn al-'Uqayli and Ibn Buraydah read (wa-'abida al-taghut) in the singular. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy that they read (wa-'abadat al-taghut), and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read (wa-a'bud al-taghut), like kalb and akhlub.

It has been read (wa-'abda al-taghut), conjoined to the relative (al-mawsul), on the basis of an omitted genitive construct. This is a very weak reading.

Al-taghut: Satan, or the soothsayers, or others, as has been fully mentioned earlier.

His saying: (ula'ika sharrun makanan, "those are worse in place"). The indication is to those described by the attributes mentioned above. Evil is attributed to the place, while it belongs to its people, for emphasis. It is also permissible that the attribution be figurative (majazi).

His saying: (wa-adallu 'an sawa' al-sabil, "and further astray from the right path") is conjoined to (sharr, "worse"). That is: they are further astray from the straight path than others. The comparative form in both places is for absolute increase, or because they are worse and more astray than those who share with them the basic evil and error.

His saying: ﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe,"﴾. That is, when they come to you they show Islam.

His saying: ﴿while they entered with disbelief and they went out with it﴾. These are two circumstantial clauses (jumlatan halliyyatan), meaning: they come to you in a state in which they entered in your presence bearing disbelief, and they left from your presence still bearing it, and what they heard from you had no effect upon them; rather they went out as they had entered. ﴿And God knows best what they were concealing﴾ in your presence of disbelief. In this there is a severe warning. These are the hypocrites. It has been said they are the Jews who said: ﴿Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end﴾ [Al 'Imran: 72].

His saying: ﴿And you see many of them hastening toward sin﴾. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) or to everyone suitable for it. The pronoun in (minhum, "of them") refers to the hypocrites, or to the Jews, or to both groups together. (yusari'una fi l-ithm, "hastening toward sin") is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), on the basis that the seeing is visual (basariyyah), or it is a second object of (tara, "you see"), on the basis that it is a heart-seeing (qalbiyyah). Al-musara'ah (hastening) is hurrying to do something. Al-ithm (sin) is lying, or polytheism, or the forbidden. Al-'udwan (transgression) is oppression that reaches others, or going beyond limits in sins.

Al-suht (unlawful gain) is the forbidden. According to those who explained al-ithm as the forbidden, its repetition is for emphasis. Al-rabbaniyyun are the scholars of the Christians, and al-ahbar are the scholars of the Jews. It has been said that all of them are from among the Jews, because these verses concern them. Then He rebuked their scholars for leaving off forbidding them, and said: ﴿Evil is what they used to produce﴾. This contains an addition beyond His saying (labi'sa ma kanu ya'maluna, "evil is what they used to do"), because ordinary action does not reach the degree of (sun', "crafting") until its doer is trained in it. For this reason the Arabs say: sayf sani' (a crafted sword) when its maker has perfected his work. So sun' is fine work, not action in general. Thus He, glory be to Him, rebuked the elite, namely the scholars who leave off commanding good and forbidding evil, with something more severe and harsh than the rebuke of the doer of sins. So let the scholars open their ears to this verse and clear their hearts for it, for it has brought the healing clarification for them: that restraining themselves from sins while leaving off denouncing their people does not nourish nor relieve hunger. Rather they are in a worse state and greater in burden than the sinners. May God have mercy on a scholar who performs what God has obligated upon him of the duty of commanding good and forbidding evil, for it is the greatest of what God has made obligatory upon him and the most binding of what has been required of him to undertake. O God, make us among Your righteous servants who command good and forbid evil, who do not fear the blame of any blamer in Your cause. Help us in that, strengthen us for it, make it easy for us, and grant us victory over whoever transgresses Your limits and wrongs Your servants. Indeed there is no helper for us besides You, and none whose help is sought but You. O Master of the Day of Judgment, You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut and Suwayd ibn al-Harith had outwardly shown Islam and were hypocrites, and some men among the Muslims were close friends with them. So God revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as a mockery and a game﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And God knows best what they were concealing﴾. (p-٣٨٢) Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿And when you call to prayer, they take it as a mockery and a game﴾, that he said: The caller of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to call to prayer, and when the Muslims stood up for prayer, the Jews and Christians would say: "They have stood up; may they never stand!" And when they saw them bowing and prostrating, they would mock them and laugh at them. He said: A Jewish merchant, when he heard the caller calling the adhan, would say: "May God burn the liar!" He said: While he was like that, his servant girl came in with a flame of fire, and a spark flew from it into the house and burned it down. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, who said: There was a man from the Christians, and he mentioned something similar to the story of the Jewish man.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: A group of Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about which messengers he believed in. He said: "I believe in God, and in what was sent down to Ibrahim (Abraham), Isma'il (Ishmael), Ishaq (Isaac), Ya'qub (Jacob) and the al-Asbat (the tribes), and in what was given to Musa (Moses), 'Isa (Jesus) and the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submissive." When he mentioned 'Isa, they denied his prophethood and said: "We do not believe in 'Isa, nor in anyone who believes in him." So God revealed about them: ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, do you resent us only because we believe in God...﴾ up to His words: (fasiqun, defiant transgressors).

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Malik that he was asked: "Were the apes and swine in existence before they were transformed?" He said: "Yes, and they were among the nations that had been created."

Muslim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about the apes and swine: are they among those whom God transformed? He said: 'God does not destroy a people,' or he said, 'does not transform a people, so as to give them offspring or a descendant (aqibah). The apes and swine existed before that.'"

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, concerning God's words ﴿When they come to you, they say, "We believe"﴾ and the rest of the verse, that he said: "They were some people from among the Jews who used to enter upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and inform him that they were believers, content with what he had brought, while they were holding fast to their misguidance and disbelief. So they would enter with that and leave with that from the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi concerning the verse, that he said: "These were people from among the hypocrites who were Jews. The meaning is: they entered as disbelievers and left as disbelievers."

He said: "Yasna'un (produce) and ya'malun (do) are one and the same. He spoke to these when they did not desist, just as He spoke to those when they committed (the sins)."

Many hadiths have been transmitted on enjoining good (al-amr bi al-ma'ruf) and forbidding evil (al-nahy 'an al-munkar), but there is no need for us to expand on them here.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 57–63 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as a mockery and a game﴾. This is a prohibition on allying with those who make the religion a mockery and a game. It covers everyone from whom this occurs, whether from the polytheists, the People of the Book, or the people of innovation (ahl al-bida') who ascribe themselves to Islam. The explanation in His saying ﴿from those who were given the Book﴾ to the end of the verse does not preclude others from falling under the prohibition when the stated reason (al-'illa), which is the motive for the prohibition, is found in them.

His saying: (wa-l-kuffar, "and the disbelievers"). Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it in the genitive (bi-l-jarr), on the assumption of the preposition (min), meaning "and of the disbelievers." Al-Kisa'i said: "In the reading of Ubayy it is (wa-min al-kuffar)." The rest read it in the accusative (bi-l-nasb). Al-Nahhas said: "This is clearer and more explicit." Makki said: "Were it not for the consensus of the community (ijma'') on the accusative, I would have chosen the genitive for its strength in i'rab (grammatical inflection) and in meaning." Here "the disbelievers" means the polytheists, and it has been said that it means the hypocrites. ﴿And fear God﴾, by abandoning what He has forbidden you from this and other things, ﴿if you are believers﴾, for faith requires that.

The nida' (ندَاء, call) is calling out with a raised voice. One says nadahu, munadah and nida', meaning he cried out to him. (wa-tanadaw): meaning some of them called out to one another. (Tanadaw) also means they sat in the nadi (assembly). The pronoun in (ittakhadhuha, "they took it") refers to the prayer, meaning they took your prayer as a mockery and a game. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the call (al-munadah), which is implied by (nadaytum, "you called"). It has been said that the Book of God mentions the adhan (call to prayer) only in this passage. As for His saying concerning Friday: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday﴾, it is specific to the Friday call. The scholars have differed over whether the adhan is obligatory or not, and over its wording. This is expounded in its proper places.

His saying: ﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾. That is, that is because they are a people who do not reason, since mockery and play are the habit of people of foolishness, lightness and frivolity.

His saying: ﴿Say: "O People of the Book, do you find fault with us?"﴾. It is said: naqimtu 'ala al-rajul (with kasra, in the past tense) — fa-ana naqim, when you found fault with him.

Al-Kisa'i said: "Naqimtu (with kasra) is a dialectal form, and naqamtu al-amr (with fatha) also, and naqimtu means: when you disliked it. Allah took vengeance on him (intaqama Allahu minhu), that is, punished him. Its noun is al-niqmah, and its plural is niqamat, like kalimah and kalimat. If you wish, you may make the qaf sukun and transfer its vowel to the nun, and the plural is niqam, like ni'mah and ni'am." It has been said the meaning is "they are angered," and it has been said "they disapprove." 'Abd Allah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

"They found no fault with the Banu Umayyah, except that they are forbearing when they are angered."

God the Exalted said: (wa-ma naqamu minhum, "and they found no fault with them"). The meaning in the verse: do you blame, or are angered by, or disapprove of, or dislike in us, except our faith in God and in His revealed Books? And you know that we are upon the truth. ﴿And that most of you are defiantly disobedient﴾, by your abandoning faith and departing from obedience to God's commands.

His saying: (wa-anna aktharakum fasiqun, "and that most of you are defiantly disobedient") is conjoined (ma'tuf) to (an amanna, "that we believed"). That is: you find fault with us only for combining our faith with your rebellion and your departure from faith. In this there is the point that the believers did not combine the two matters mentioned, for the faith is on their part, while the rebellion and the departure are on the part of those who find fault. It has been said that it is on an implied supplement: "and our belief that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has also been said that (an amanna) is in the accusative as a direct object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and the object is omitted, so (wa-anna aktharakum fasiqun) is conjoined to it, a conjunction of cause to cause, and the construction is: "and you find fault with us only because we believed, and because most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said that it is conjoined to an omitted cause, meaning: "because of the scarcity of your fairness, and because most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said that the waw in (wa-anna aktharakum fasiqun) is the one that means "with" (ma'a), meaning: "you find fault with us only for the faith, together with the fact that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said it is in the accusative by a verb omitted, indicated by (hal tanqimun, "do you find fault"), meaning: "and you do not find fault that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said it is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada') with an omitted predicate, meaning: "and your defiance is known," so the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal). It has been read with kasra on (inna) in His saying (wa-inna aktharakum fasiqun), so it is a new independent clause.

His saying: ﴿Say: "Shall I inform you of something worse than that as requital from God?"﴾. God the Exalted showed His Messenger that among them there is what is more deserving of blame: their disbelief, which brings upon them God's curse, His wrath, and their transformation. The meaning: shall I inform you of something worse than your fault-finding against us, or worse than what you wish for us of hardship, or worse than the People of the Book, or worse than their religion? His saying (mathuba, "requital") means a fixed reward. It is specific to good, just as punishment is specific to evil. It is placed here in the position of punishment, in the manner of (fa-bashshirhum bi-'adhabin alim, "so give them good tidings of a painful punishment"). It is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of (bi-sharr, "something worse"). His saying (man la'anahu Allah, "whom God has cursed") is a predicate of an omitted subject, with an omitted genitive construct, meaning: "it is the cursing of whom God has cursed," or "it is the religion of whom God has cursed." It is permissible that it be in the genitive position as an apposition (badal) of (sharr).

His saying: ﴿and He made of them apes and swine﴾. That is, He transformed some of them into apes and some into swine, and they are the Jews, for God transformed the people of the Sabbath into apes, and the disbelievers of the table of 'Isa among them into swine.

His saying: (wa-'abada al-taghut, "and worshipped the taghut"). Hamza read (abada) with a damma on the ba' and (al-taghut) with a kasra on the ta', meaning: He made of them "abudu al-taghut," by annexing "abud" to "al-taghut." The meaning: He made of them those who exaggerate in the worship of the taghut, since fa'ul is among the forms of intensification, like hadhir and fatin, for emphasis in caution and in shrewdness. The rest read (abada) with a fatha on the ba' and (al-taghut) with a fatha on the ta', as a past verb conjoined to a past verb, namely (ghadiba, "was angry") and (la'ana, "cursed"), as if it were said: "and those who worshipped the taghut." Or it is conjoined to (al-qiradah wa-l-khanazir, "the apes and the swine"), meaning: He made of them apes and swine, and He made of them those who worshipped the taghut, following the wording of (min, "of"). Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read (wa-'abadu al-taghut, "and they worshipped the taghut") following its meaning. Ibn 'Abbas read (wa-'ubud, with damma on the 'ayn and the ba'), as if it were the plural of 'abd, as one says saqf and suquf, and it is permissible that it be the plural of 'abid, like raghif and rughuf, or the plural of 'abid, like bazil and buzul. Abu Waqid read (wa-'ubbad), the plural of 'abid, for intensification, like 'amil and 'ummal. The Basrans read (wa-'ubbad), also the plural of 'abid, like qa'im and qiyam, and it is permissible that it be the plural of 'abd. Abu Ja'far al-Raqqashi read (wa-'ubida al-taghut, "and the taghut was worshipped") in the passive, and the implied meaning is: "and the taghut was worshipped among them." 'Awn al-'Uqayli and Ibn Buraydah read (wa-'abida al-taghut) in the singular. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy that they read (wa-'abadat al-taghut), and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read (wa-a'bud al-taghut), like kalb and akhlub.

It has been read (wa-'abda al-taghut), conjoined to the relative (al-mawsul), on the basis of an omitted genitive construct. This is a very weak reading.

Al-taghut: Satan, or the soothsayers, or others, as has been fully mentioned earlier.

His saying: (ula'ika sharrun makanan, "those are worse in place"). The indication is to those described by the attributes mentioned above. Evil is attributed to the place, while it belongs to its people, for emphasis. It is also permissible that the attribution be figurative (majazi).

His saying: (wa-adallu 'an sawa' al-sabil, "and further astray from the right path") is conjoined to (sharr, "worse"). That is: they are further astray from the straight path than others. The comparative form in both places is for absolute increase, or because they are worse and more astray than those who share with them the basic evil and error.

His saying: ﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe,"﴾. That is, when they come to you they show Islam.

His saying: ﴿while they entered with disbelief and they went out with it﴾. These are two circumstantial clauses (jumlatan halliyyatan), meaning: they come to you in a state in which they entered in your presence bearing disbelief, and they left from your presence still bearing it, and what they heard from you had no effect upon them; rather they went out as they had entered. ﴿And God knows best what they were concealing﴾ in your presence of disbelief. In this there is a severe warning. These are the hypocrites. It has been said they are the Jews who said: ﴿Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end﴾ [Al 'Imran: 72].

His saying: ﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾. That is, that is because they are a people who do not reason, since mockery and play are the habit of people of foolishness, lightness and frivolity.

His saying: ﴿Say: "O People of the Book, do you find fault with us?"﴾. It is said: naqimtu 'ala al-rajul (with kasra, in the past tense) — fa-ana naqim, when you found fault with him.

Al-Kisa'i said: "Naqimtu (with kasra) is a dialectal form, and naqamtu al-amr (with fatha) also, and naqimtu means: when you disliked it. Allah took vengeance on him (intaqama Allahu minhu), that is, punished him. Its noun is al-niqmah, and its plural is niqamat, like kalimah and kalimat. If you wish, you may make the qaf sukun and transfer its vowel to the nun, and the plural is niqam, like ni'mah and ni'am." It has been said the meaning is "they are angered," and it has been said "they disapprove." 'Abd Allah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

"They found no fault with the Banu Umayyah, except that they are forbearing when they are angered."

God the Exalted said: (wa-ma naqamu minhum, "and they found no fault with them"). The meaning in the verse: do you blame, or are angered by, or disapprove of, or dislike in us, except our faith in God and in His revealed Books? And you know that we are upon the truth. ﴿And that most of you are defiantly disobedient﴾, by your abandoning faith and departing from obedience to God's commands.

His saying: (wa-anna aktharakum fasiqun, "and that most of you are defiantly disobedient") is conjoined (ma'tuf) to (an amanna, "that we believed"). That is: you find fault with us only for combining our faith with your rebellion and your departure from faith. In this there is the point that the believers did not combine the two matters mentioned, for the faith is on their part, while the rebellion and the departure are on the part of those who find fault. It has been said that it is on an implied supplement: "and our belief that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has also been said that (an amanna) is in the accusative as a direct object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and the object is omitted, so (wa-anna aktharakum fasiqun) is conjoined to it, a conjunction of cause to cause, and the construction is: "and you find fault with us only because we believed, and because most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said that it is conjoined to an omitted cause, meaning: "because of the scarcity of your fairness, and because most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said that the waw in (wa-anna aktharakum fasiqun) is the one that means "with" (ma'a), meaning: "you find fault with us only for the faith, together with the fact that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said it is in the accusative by a verb omitted, indicated by (hal tanqimun, "do you find fault"), meaning: "and you do not find fault that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said it is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada') with an omitted predicate, meaning: "and your defiance is known," so the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal). It has been read with kasra on (inna) in His saying (wa-inna aktharakum fasiqun), so it is a new independent clause.

His saying: ﴿Say: "Shall I inform you of something worse than that as requital from God?"﴾. God the Exalted showed His Messenger that among them there is what is more deserving of blame: their disbelief, which brings upon them God's curse, His wrath, and their transformation. The meaning: shall I inform you of something worse than your fault-finding against us, or worse than what you wish for us of hardship, or worse than the People of the Book, or worse than their religion? His saying (mathuba, "requital") means a fixed reward. It is specific to good, just as punishment is specific to evil. It is placed here in the position of punishment, in the manner of (fa-bashshirhum bi-'adhabin alim, "so give them good tidings of a painful punishment"). It is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of (bi-sharr, "something worse"). His saying (man la'anahu Allah, "whom God has cursed") is a predicate of an omitted subject, with an omitted genitive construct, meaning: "it is the cursing of whom God has cursed," or "it is the religion of whom God has cursed." It is permissible that it be in the genitive position as an apposition (badal) of (sharr).

His saying: ﴿and He made of them apes and swine﴾. That is, He transformed some of them into apes and some into swine, and they are the Jews, for God transformed the people of the Sabbath into apes, and the disbelievers of the table of 'Isa among them into swine.

His saying: (wa-'abada al-taghut, "and worshipped the taghut"). Hamza read (abada) with a damma on the ba' and (al-taghut) with a kasra on the ta', meaning: He made of them "abudu al-taghut," by annexing "abud" to "al-taghut." The meaning: He made of them those who exaggerate in the worship of the taghut, since fa'ul is among the forms of intensification, like hadhir and fatin, for emphasis in caution and in shrewdness. The rest read (abada) with a fatha on the ba' and (al-taghut) with a fatha on the ta', as a past verb conjoined to a past verb, namely (ghadiba, "was angry") and (la'ana, "cursed"), as if it were said: "and those who worshipped the taghut." Or it is conjoined to (al-qiradah wa-l-khanazir, "the apes and the swine"), meaning: He made of them apes and swine, and He made of them those who worshipped the taghut, following the wording of (min, "of"). Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read (wa-'abadu al-taghut, "and they worshipped the taghut") following its meaning. Ibn 'Abbas read (wa-'ubud, with damma on the 'ayn and the ba'), as if it were the plural of 'abd, as one says saqf and suquf, and it is permissible that it be the plural of 'abid, like raghif and rughuf, or the plural of 'abid, like bazil and buzul. Abu Waqid read (wa-'ubbad), the plural of 'abid, for intensification, like 'amil and 'ummal. The Basrans read (wa-'ubbad), also the plural of 'abid, like qa'im and qiyam, and it is permissible that it be the plural of 'abd. Abu Ja'far al-Raqqashi read (wa-'ubida al-taghut, "and the taghut was worshipped") in the passive, and the implied meaning is: "and the taghut was worshipped among them." 'Awn al-'Uqayli and Ibn Buraydah read (wa-'abida al-taghut) in the singular. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy that they read (wa-'abadat al-taghut), and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read (wa-a'bud al-taghut), like kalb and akhlub.

It has been read (wa-'abda al-taghut), conjoined to the relative (al-mawsul), on the basis of an omitted genitive construct. This is a very weak reading.

Al-taghut: Satan, or the soothsayers, or others, as has been fully mentioned earlier.

His saying: (ula'ika sharrun makanan, "those are worse in place"). The indication is to those described by the attributes mentioned above. Evil is attributed to the place, while it belongs to its people, for emphasis. It is also permissible that the attribution be figurative (majazi).

His saying: (wa-adallu 'an sawa' al-sabil, "and further astray from the right path") is conjoined to (sharr, "worse"). That is: they are further astray from the straight path than others. The comparative form in both places is for absolute increase, or because they are worse and more astray than those who share with them the basic evil and error.

His saying: ﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe,"﴾. That is, when they come to you they show Islam.

His saying: ﴿while they entered with disbelief and they went out with it﴾. These are two circumstantial clauses (jumlatan halliyyatan), meaning: they come to you in a state in which they entered in your presence bearing disbelief, and they left from your presence still bearing it, and what they heard from you had no effect upon them; rather they went out as they had entered. ﴿And God knows best what they were concealing﴾ in your presence of disbelief. In this there is a severe warning. These are the hypocrites. It has been said they are the Jews who said: ﴿Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end﴾ [Al 'Imran: 72].

His saying: ﴿And you see many of them hastening toward sin﴾. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) or to everyone suitable for it. The pronoun in (minhum, "of them") refers to the hypocrites, or to the Jews, or to both groups together. (yusari'una fi l-ithm, "hastening toward sin") is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), on the basis that the seeing is visual (basariyyah), or it is a second object of (tara, "you see"), on the basis that it is a heart-seeing (qalbiyyah). Al-musara'ah (hastening) is hurrying to do something. Al-ithm (sin) is lying, or polytheism, or the forbidden. Al-'udwan (transgression) is oppression that reaches others, or going beyond limits in sins.

Al-suht (unlawful gain) is the forbidden. According to those who explained al-ithm as the forbidden, its repetition is for emphasis. Al-rabbaniyyun are the scholars of the Christians, and al-ahbar are the scholars of the Jews. It has been said that all of them are from among the Jews, because these verses concern them. Then He rebuked their scholars for leaving off forbidding them, and said: ﴿Evil is what they used to produce﴾. This contains an addition beyond His saying (labi'sa ma kanu ya'maluna, "evil is what they used to do"), because ordinary action does not reach the degree of (sun', "crafting") until its doer is trained in it. For this reason the Arabs say: sayf sani' (a crafted sword) when its maker has perfected his work. So sun' is fine work, not action in general. Thus He, glory be to Him, rebuked the elite, namely the scholars who leave off commanding good and forbidding evil, with something more severe and harsh than the rebuke of the doer of sins. So let the scholars open their ears to this verse and clear their hearts for it, for it has brought the healing clarification for them: that restraining themselves from sins while leaving off denouncing their people does not nourish nor relieve hunger. Rather they are in a worse state and greater in burden than the sinners. May God have mercy on a scholar who performs what God has obligated upon him of the duty of commanding good and forbidding evil, for it is the greatest of what God has made obligatory upon him and the most binding of what has been required of him to undertake. O God, make us among Your righteous servants who command good and forbid evil, who do not fear the blame of any blamer in Your cause. Help us in that, strengthen us for it, make it easy for us, and grant us victory over whoever transgresses Your limits and wrongs Your servants. Indeed there is no helper for us besides You, and none whose help is sought but You. O Master of the Day of Judgment, You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut and Suwayd ibn al-Harith had outwardly shown Islam and were hypocrites, and some men among the Muslims were close friends with them. So God revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as a mockery and a game﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And God knows best what they were concealing﴾. (p-٣٨٢) Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿And when you call to prayer, they take it as a mockery and a game﴾, that he said: The caller of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to call to prayer, and when the Muslims stood up for prayer, the Jews and Christians would say: "They have stood up; may they never stand!" And when they saw them bowing and prostrating, they would mock them and laugh at them. He said: A Jewish merchant, when he heard the caller calling the adhan, would say: "May God burn the liar!" He said: While he was like that, his servant girl came in with a flame of fire, and a spark flew from it into the house and burned it down. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, who said: There was a man from the Christians, and he mentioned something similar to the story of the Jewish man.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: A group of Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about which messengers he believed in. He said: "I believe in God, and in what was sent down to Ibrahim (Abraham), Isma'il (Ishmael), Ishaq (Isaac), Ya'qub (Jacob) and the al-Asbat (the tribes), and in what was given to Musa (Moses), 'Isa (Jesus) and the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submissive." When he mentioned 'Isa, they denied his prophethood and said: "We do not believe in 'Isa, nor in anyone who believes in him." So God revealed about them: ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, do you resent us only because we believe in God...﴾ up to His words: (fasiqun, defiant transgressors).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid, concerning God's words ﴿And He made some of them apes and swine﴾, that he said: "They were transformed from among the Jews."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Malik that he was asked: "Were the apes and swine in existence before they were transformed?" He said: "Yes, and they were among the nations that had been created."

Muslim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about the apes and swine: are they among those whom God transformed? He said: 'God does not destroy a people,' or he said, 'does not transform a people, so as to give them offspring or a descendant (aqibah). The apes and swine existed before that.'"

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, concerning God's words ﴿When they come to you, they say, "We believe"﴾ and the rest of the verse, that he said: "They were some people from among the Jews who used to enter upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and inform him that they were believers, content with what he had brought, while they were holding fast to their misguidance and disbelief. So they would enter with that and leave with that from the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi concerning the verse, that he said: "These were people from among the hypocrites who were Jews. The meaning is: they entered as disbelievers and left as disbelievers."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Zayd, concerning God's words ﴿You see many of them racing toward sin and aggression﴾, that he said: "These are the Jews" (﴿Wretched is what they used to do﴾) up to His words (﴿Wretched is what they used to produce﴾). He said: "Yasna'un (produce) and ya'malun (do) are one and the same. He spoke to these when they did not desist, just as He spoke to those when they committed (the sins)."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning God's words ﴿Why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them?﴾, that he said: "Then why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them? They are the jurists (fuqaha') and the learned ('ulama')."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more severe in rebuke than this verse: ﴿Why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them?﴾" Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated a similar report from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim.

Many hadiths have been transmitted on enjoining good (al-amr bi al-ma'ruf) and forbidding evil (al-nahy 'an al-munkar), but there is no need for us to expand on them here.

His saying: ﴿Do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as a mockery and a game﴾. This is a prohibition on allying with those who make the religion a mockery and a game. It covers everyone from whom this occurs, whether from the polytheists, the People of the Book, or the people of innovation (ahl al-bida') who ascribe themselves to Islam. The explanation in His saying ﴿from those who were given the Book﴾ to the end of the verse does not preclude others from falling under the prohibition when the stated reason (al-'illa), which is the motive for the prohibition, is found in them.

His saying: (wa-l-kuffar, "and the disbelievers"). Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it in the genitive (bi-l-jarr), on the assumption of the preposition (min), meaning "and of the disbelievers." Al-Kisa'i said: "In the reading of Ubayy it is (wa-min al-kuffar)." The rest read it in the accusative (bi-l-nasb). Al-Nahhas said: "This is clearer and more explicit." Makki said: "Were it not for the consensus of the community (ijma'') on the accusative, I would have chosen the genitive for its strength in i'rab (grammatical inflection) and in meaning." Here "the disbelievers" means the polytheists, and it has been said that it means the hypocrites. ﴿And fear God﴾, by abandoning what He has forbidden you from this and other things, ﴿if you are believers﴾, for faith requires that.

The nida' (ندَاء, call) is calling out with a raised voice. One says nadahu, munadah and nida', meaning he cried out to him. (wa-tanadaw): meaning some of them called out to one another. (Tanadaw) also means they sat in the nadi (assembly). The pronoun in (ittakhadhuha, "they took it") refers to the prayer, meaning they took your prayer as a mockery and a game. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the call (al-munadah), which is implied by (nadaytum, "you called"). It has been said that the Book of God mentions the adhan (call to prayer) only in this passage. As for His saying concerning Friday: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday﴾, it is specific to the Friday call. The scholars have differed over whether the adhan is obligatory or not, and over its wording. This is expounded in its proper places.

His saying: ﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾. That is, that is because they are a people who do not reason, since mockery and play are the habit of people of foolishness, lightness and frivolity.

O God, make us among Your righteous servants who command good and forbid evil, who do not fear the blame of any blamer in Your cause. Help us in that, strengthen us for it, make it easy for us, and grant us victory over whoever transgresses Your limits and wrongs Your servants. Indeed there is no helper for us besides You, and none whose help is sought but You. O Master of the Day of Judgment, You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, who said: There was a man from the Christians, and he mentioned something similar to the story of the Jewish man.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 57–63 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as a mockery and a game﴾. This is a prohibition on allying with those who make the religion a mockery and a game. It covers everyone from whom this occurs, whether from the polytheists, the People of the Book, or the people of innovation (ahl al-bida') who ascribe themselves to Islam. The explanation in His saying ﴿from those who were given the Book﴾ to the end of the verse does not preclude others from falling under the prohibition when the stated reason (al-'illa), which is the motive for the prohibition, is found in them.

His saying: (wa-l-kuffar, "and the disbelievers"). Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it in the genitive (bi-l-jarr), on the assumption of the preposition (min), meaning "and of the disbelievers." Al-Kisa'i said: "In the reading of Ubayy it is (wa-min al-kuffar)." The rest read it in the accusative (bi-l-nasb). Al-Nahhas said: "This is clearer and more explicit." Makki said: "Were it not for the consensus of the community (ijma'') on the accusative, I would have chosen the genitive for its strength in i'rab (grammatical inflection) and in meaning." Here "the disbelievers" means the polytheists, and it has been said that it means the hypocrites. ﴿And fear God﴾, by abandoning what He has forbidden you from this and other things, ﴿if you are believers﴾, for faith requires that.

The nida' (ندَاء, call) is calling out with a raised voice. One says nadahu, munadah and nida', meaning he cried out to him. (wa-tanadaw): meaning some of them called out to one another. (Tanadaw) also means they sat in the nadi (assembly). The pronoun in (ittakhadhuha, "they took it") refers to the prayer, meaning they took your prayer as a mockery and a game. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the call (al-munadah), which is implied by (nadaytum, "you called"). It has been said that the Book of God mentions the adhan (call to prayer) only in this passage. As for His saying concerning Friday: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday﴾, it is specific to the Friday call. The scholars have differed over whether the adhan is obligatory or not, and over its wording. This is expounded in its proper places.

His saying: ﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾. That is, that is because they are a people who do not reason, since mockery and play are the habit of people of foolishness, lightness and frivolity.

His saying: ﴿Say: "O People of the Book, do you find fault with us?"﴾. It is said: naqimtu 'ala al-rajul (with kasra, in the past tense) — fa-ana naqim, when you found fault with him.

Al-Kisa'i said: "Naqimtu (with kasra) is a dialectal form, and naqamtu al-amr (with fatha) also, and naqimtu means: when you disliked it. Allah took vengeance on him (intaqama Allahu minhu), that is, punished him. Its noun is al-niqmah, and its plural is niqamat, like kalimah and kalimat. If you wish, you may make the qaf sukun and transfer its vowel to the nun, and the plural is niqam, like ni'mah and ni'am." It has been said the meaning is "they are angered," and it has been said "they disapprove." 'Abd Allah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

"They found no fault with the Banu Umayyah, except that they are forbearing when they are angered."

God the Exalted said: (wa-ma naqamu minhum, "and they found no fault with them"). The meaning in the verse: do you blame, or are angered by, or disapprove of, or dislike in us, except our faith in God and in His revealed Books? And you know that we are upon the truth. ﴿And that most of you are defiantly disobedient﴾, by your abandoning faith and departing from obedience to God's commands.

His saying: (wa-anna aktharakum fasiqun, "and that most of you are defiantly disobedient") is conjoined (ma'tuf) to (an amanna, "that we believed"). That is: you find fault with us only for combining our faith with your rebellion and your departure from faith. In this there is the point that the believers did not combine the two matters mentioned, for the faith is on their part, while the rebellion and the departure are on the part of those who find fault. It has been said that it is on an implied supplement: "and our belief that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has also been said that (an amanna) is in the accusative as a direct object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and the object is omitted, so (wa-anna aktharakum fasiqun) is conjoined to it, a conjunction of cause to cause, and the construction is: "and you find fault with us only because we believed, and because most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said that it is conjoined to an omitted cause, meaning: "because of the scarcity of your fairness, and because most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said that the waw in (wa-anna aktharakum fasiqun) is the one that means "with" (ma'a), meaning: "you find fault with us only for the faith, together with the fact that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said it is in the accusative by a verb omitted, indicated by (hal tanqimun, "do you find fault"), meaning: "and you do not find fault that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said it is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada') with an omitted predicate, meaning: "and your defiance is known," so the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal). It has been read with kasra on (inna) in His saying (wa-inna aktharakum fasiqun), so it is a new independent clause.

His saying: ﴿Say: "Shall I inform you of something worse than that as requital from God?"﴾. God the Exalted showed His Messenger that among them there is what is more deserving of blame: their disbelief, which brings upon them God's curse, His wrath, and their transformation. The meaning: shall I inform you of something worse than your fault-finding against us, or worse than what you wish for us of hardship, or worse than the People of the Book, or worse than their religion? His saying (mathuba, "requital") means a fixed reward. It is specific to good, just as punishment is specific to evil. It is placed here in the position of punishment, in the manner of (fa-bashshirhum bi-'adhabin alim, "so give them good tidings of a painful punishment"). It is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of (bi-sharr, "something worse"). His saying (man la'anahu Allah, "whom God has cursed") is a predicate of an omitted subject, with an omitted genitive construct, meaning: "it is the cursing of whom God has cursed," or "it is the religion of whom God has cursed." It is permissible that it be in the genitive position as an apposition (badal) of (sharr).

His saying: ﴿and He made of them apes and swine﴾. That is, He transformed some of them into apes and some into swine, and they are the Jews, for God transformed the people of the Sabbath into apes, and the disbelievers of the table of 'Isa among them into swine.

His saying: (wa-'abada al-taghut, "and worshipped the taghut"). Hamza read (abada) with a damma on the ba' and (al-taghut) with a kasra on the ta', meaning: He made of them "abudu al-taghut," by annexing "abud" to "al-taghut." The meaning: He made of them those who exaggerate in the worship of the taghut, since fa'ul is among the forms of intensification, like hadhir and fatin, for emphasis in caution and in shrewdness. The rest read (abada) with a fatha on the ba' and (al-taghut) with a fatha on the ta', as a past verb conjoined to a past verb, namely (ghadiba, "was angry") and (la'ana, "cursed"), as if it were said: "and those who worshipped the taghut." Or it is conjoined to (al-qiradah wa-l-khanazir, "the apes and the swine"), meaning: He made of them apes and swine, and He made of them those who worshipped the taghut, following the wording of (min, "of"). Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read (wa-'abadu al-taghut, "and they worshipped the taghut") following its meaning. Ibn 'Abbas read (wa-'ubud, with damma on the 'ayn and the ba'), as if it were the plural of 'abd, as one says saqf and suquf, and it is permissible that it be the plural of 'abid, like raghif and rughuf, or the plural of 'abid, like bazil and buzul. Abu Waqid read (wa-'ubbad), the plural of 'abid, for intensification, like 'amil and 'ummal. The Basrans read (wa-'ubbad), also the plural of 'abid, like qa'im and qiyam, and it is permissible that it be the plural of 'abd. Abu Ja'far al-Raqqashi read (wa-'ubida al-taghut, "and the taghut was worshipped") in the passive, and the implied meaning is: "and the taghut was worshipped among them." 'Awn al-'Uqayli and Ibn Buraydah read (wa-'abida al-taghut) in the singular. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy that they read (wa-'abadat al-taghut), and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read (wa-a'bud al-taghut), like kalb and akhlub.

It has been read (wa-'abda al-taghut), conjoined to the relative (al-mawsul), on the basis of an omitted genitive construct. This is a very weak reading.

Al-taghut: Satan, or the soothsayers, or others, as has been fully mentioned earlier.

His saying: (ula'ika sharrun makanan, "those are worse in place"). The indication is to those described by the attributes mentioned above. Evil is attributed to the place, while it belongs to its people, for emphasis. It is also permissible that the attribution be figurative (majazi).

His saying: (wa-adallu 'an sawa' al-sabil, "and further astray from the right path") is conjoined to (sharr, "worse"). That is: they are further astray from the straight path than others. The comparative form in both places is for absolute increase, or because they are worse and more astray than those who share with them the basic evil and error.

His saying: ﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe,"﴾. That is, when they come to you they show Islam.

His saying: ﴿while they entered with disbelief and they went out with it﴾. These are two circumstantial clauses (jumlatan halliyyatan), meaning: they come to you in a state in which they entered in your presence bearing disbelief, and they left from your presence still bearing it, and what they heard from you had no effect upon them; rather they went out as they had entered. ﴿And God knows best what they were concealing﴾ in your presence of disbelief. In this there is a severe warning. These are the hypocrites. It has been said they are the Jews who said: ﴿Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end﴾ [Al 'Imran: 72].

His saying: ﴿And you see many of them hastening toward sin﴾. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) or to everyone suitable for it. The pronoun in (minhum, "of them") refers to the hypocrites, or to the Jews, or to both groups together. (yusari'una fi l-ithm, "hastening toward sin") is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), on the basis that the seeing is visual (basariyyah), or it is a second object of (tara, "you see"), on the basis that it is a heart-seeing (qalbiyyah). Al-musara'ah (hastening) is hurrying to do something. Al-ithm (sin) is lying, or polytheism, or the forbidden. Al-'udwan (transgression) is oppression that reaches others, or going beyond limits in sins.

Al-suht (unlawful gain) is the forbidden. According to those who explained al-ithm as the forbidden, its repetition is for emphasis. Al-rabbaniyyun are the scholars of the Christians, and al-ahbar are the scholars of the Jews. It has been said that all of them are from among the Jews, because these verses concern them. Then He rebuked their scholars for leaving off forbidding them, and said: ﴿Evil is what they used to produce﴾. This contains an addition beyond His saying (labi'sa ma kanu ya'maluna, "evil is what they used to do"), because ordinary action does not reach the degree of (sun', "crafting") until its doer is trained in it. Indeed there is no helper for us besides You, and none whose help is sought but You. O Master of the Day of Judgment, You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help.

"They found no fault with the Banu Umayyah, except that they are forbearing when they are angered."
