The meaning in the verse: do you blame, or are angered by, or disapprove of, or dislike in us, except our faith in God and in His revealed Books? And you know that we are upon the truth. ﴿And that most of you are defiantly disobedient﴾, by your abandoning faith and departing from obedience to God's commands.

His saying: (wa-anna aktharakum fasiqun, "and that most of you are defiantly disobedient") is conjoined (ma'tuf) to (an amanna, "that we believed"). That is: you find fault with us only for combining our faith with your rebellion and your departure from faith. In this there is the point that the believers did not combine the two matters mentioned, for the faith is on their part, while the rebellion and the departure are on the part of those who find fault. It has been said that it is on an implied supplement: "and our belief that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has also been said that (an amanna) is in the accusative as a direct object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and the object is omitted, so (wa-anna aktharakum fasiqun) is conjoined to it, a conjunction of cause to cause, and the construction is: "and you find fault with us only because we believed, and because most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said that it is conjoined to an omitted cause, meaning: "because of the scarcity of your fairness, and because most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said that the waw in (wa-anna aktharakum fasiqun) is the one that means "with" (ma'a), meaning: "you find fault with us only for the faith, together with the fact that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said it is in the accusative by a verb omitted, indicated by (hal tanqimun, "do you find fault"), meaning: "and you do not find fault that most of you are defiantly disobedient." It has been said it is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada') with an omitted predicate, meaning: "and your defiance is known," so the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal). It has been read with kasra on (inna) in His saying (wa-inna aktharakum fasiqun), so it is a new independent clause.

His saying: ﴿Say: "Shall I inform you of something worse than that as requital from God?"﴾. God the Exalted showed His Messenger that among them there is what is more deserving of blame: their disbelief, which brings upon them God's curse, His wrath, and their transformation. The meaning: shall I inform you of something worse than your fault-finding against us, or worse than what you wish for us of hardship, or worse than the People of the Book, or worse than their religion? His saying (mathuba, "requital") means a fixed reward. It is specific to good, just as punishment is specific to evil. It is placed here in the position of punishment, in the manner of (fa-bashshirhum bi-'adhabin alim, "so give them good tidings of a painful punishment"). It is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of (bi-sharr, "something worse"). His saying (man la'anahu Allah, "whom God has cursed") is a predicate of an omitted subject, with an omitted genitive construct, meaning: "it is the cursing of whom God has cursed," or "it is the religion of whom God has cursed." It is permissible that it be in the genitive position as an apposition (badal) of (sharr).

His saying: ﴿and He made of them apes and swine﴾. That is, He transformed some of them into apes and some into swine, and they are the Jews, for God transformed the people of the Sabbath into apes, and the disbelievers of the table of 'Isa among them into swine.

His saying: (wa-'abada al-taghut, "and worshipped the taghut"). Hamza read (abada) with a damma on the ba' and (al-taghut) with a kasra on the ta', meaning: He made of them "abudu al-taghut," by annexing "abud" to "al-taghut." The meaning: He made of them those who exaggerate in the worship of the taghut, since fa'ul is among the forms of intensification, like hadhir and fatin, for emphasis in caution and in shrewdness. The rest read (abada) with a fatha on the ba' and (al-taghut) with a fatha on the ta', as a past verb conjoined to a past verb, namely (ghadiba, "was angry") and (la'ana, "cursed"), as if it were said: "and those who worshipped the taghut." Or it is conjoined to (al-qiradah wa-l-khanazir, "the apes and the swine"), meaning: He made of them apes and swine, and He made of them those who worshipped the taghut, following the wording of (min, "of"). Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read (wa-'abadu al-taghut, "and they worshipped the taghut") following its meaning. Ibn 'Abbas read (wa-'ubud, with damma on the 'ayn and the ba'), as if it were the plural of 'abd, as one says saqf and suquf, and it is permissible that it be the plural of 'abid, like raghif and rughuf, or the plural of 'abid, like bazil and buzul. Abu Waqid read (wa-'ubbad), the plural of 'abid, for intensification, like 'amil and 'ummal. The Basrans read (wa-'ubbad), also the plural of 'abid, like qa'im and qiyam, and it is permissible that it be the plural of 'abd. Abu Ja'far al-Raqqashi read (wa-'ubida al-taghut, "and the taghut was worshipped") in the passive, and the implied meaning is: "and the taghut was worshipped among them." 'Awn al-'Uqayli and Ibn Buraydah read (wa-'abida al-taghut) in the singular. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy that they read (wa-'abadat al-taghut), and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read (wa-a'bud al-taghut), like kalb and akhlub.

It has been read (wa-'abda al-taghut), conjoined to the relative (al-mawsul), on the basis of an omitted genitive construct. This is a very weak reading.

Al-taghut: Satan, or the soothsayers, or others, as has been fully mentioned earlier.

His saying: (ula'ika sharrun makanan, "those are worse in place"). The indication is to those described by the attributes mentioned above. Evil is attributed to the place, while it belongs to its people, for emphasis. It is also permissible that the attribution be figurative (majazi).

His saying: (wa-adallu 'an sawa' al-sabil, "and further astray from the right path") is conjoined to (sharr, "worse"). That is: they are further astray from the straight path than others. The comparative form in both places is for absolute increase, or because they are worse and more astray than those who share with them the basic evil and error.

His saying: ﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe,"﴾. That is, when they come to you they show Islam.

His saying: ﴿while they entered with disbelief and they went out with it﴾. These are two circumstantial clauses (jumlatan halliyyatan), meaning: they come to you in a state in which they entered in your presence bearing disbelief, and they left from your presence still bearing it, and what they heard from you had no effect upon them; rather they went out as they had entered. ﴿And God knows best what they were concealing﴾ in your presence of disbelief. In this there is a severe warning. These are the hypocrites. It has been said they are the Jews who said: ﴿Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end﴾ [Al 'Imran: 72].

His saying: ﴿And you see many of them hastening toward sin﴾. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) or to everyone suitable for it. The pronoun in (minhum, "of them") refers to the hypocrites, or to the Jews, or to both groups together. (yusari'una fi l-ithm, "hastening toward sin") is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), on the basis that the seeing is visual (basariyyah), or it is a second object of (tara, "you see"), on the basis that it is a heart-seeing (qalbiyyah). Al-musara'ah (hastening) is hurrying to do something. Al-ithm (sin) is lying, or polytheism, or the forbidden. Al-'udwan (transgression) is oppression that reaches others, or going beyond limits in sins.

Al-suht (unlawful gain) is the forbidden. According to those who explained al-ithm as the forbidden, its repetition is for emphasis. Al-rabbaniyyun are the scholars of the Christians, and al-ahbar are the scholars of the Jews. It has been said that all of them are from among the Jews, because these verses concern them. Then He rebuked their scholars for leaving off forbidding them, and said: ﴿Evil is what they used to produce﴾. This contains an addition beyond His saying (labi'sa ma kanu ya'maluna, "evil is what they used to do"), because ordinary action does not reach the degree of (sun', "crafting") until its doer is trained in it. For this reason the Arabs say: sayf sani' (a crafted sword) when its maker has perfected his work. So sun' is fine work, not action in general. Thus He, glory be to Him, rebuked the elite, namely the scholars who leave off commanding good and forbidding evil, with something more severe and harsh than the rebuke of the doer of sins. So let the scholars open their ears to this verse and clear their hearts for it, for it has brought the healing clarification for them: that restraining themselves from sins while leaving off denouncing their people does not nourish nor relieve hunger. Rather they are in a worse state and greater in burden than the sinners. May God have mercy on a scholar who performs what God has obligated upon him of the duty of commanding good and forbidding evil, for it is the greatest of what God has made obligatory upon him and the most binding of what has been required of him to undertake. O God, make us among Your righteous servants who command good and forbid evil, who do not fear the blame of any blamer in Your cause. Help us in that, strengthen us for it, make it easy for us, and grant us victory over whoever transgresses Your limits and wrongs Your servants. Indeed there is no helper for us besides You, and none whose help is sought but You. O Master of the Day of Judgment, You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut and Suwayd ibn al-Harith had outwardly shown Islam and were hypocrites, and some men among the Muslims were close friends with them. So God revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as a mockery and a game﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And God knows best what they were concealing﴾. (p-٣٨٢) Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿And when you call to prayer, they take it as a mockery and a game﴾, that he said: The caller of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to call to prayer, and when the Muslims stood up for prayer, the Jews and Christians would say: "They have stood up; may they never stand!" And when they saw them bowing and prostrating, they would mock them and laugh at them. He said: A Jewish merchant, when he heard the caller calling the adhan, would say: "May God burn the liar!" He said: While he was like that, his servant girl came in with a flame of fire, and a spark flew from it into the house and burned it down. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, who said: There was a man from the Christians, and he mentioned something similar to the story of the Jewish man.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: A group of Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about which messengers he believed in. He said: "I believe in God, and in what was sent down to Ibrahim (Abraham), Isma'il (Ishmael), Ishaq (Isaac), Ya'qub (Jacob) and the al-Asbat (the tribes), and in what was given to Musa (Moses), 'Isa (Jesus) and the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submissive." When he mentioned 'Isa, they denied his prophethood and said: "We do not believe in 'Isa, nor in anyone who believes in him." So God revealed about them: ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, do you resent us only because we believe in God...﴾ up to His words: (fasiqun, defiant transgressors).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid, concerning God's words ﴿And He made some of them apes and swine﴾, that he said: "They were transformed from among the Jews."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Malik that he was asked: "Were the apes and swine in existence before they were transformed?" He said: "Yes, and they were among the nations that had been created."

Muslim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about the apes and swine: are they among those whom God transformed? He said: 'God does not destroy a people,' or he said, 'does not transform a people, so as to give them offspring or a descendant (aqibah). The apes and swine existed before that.'"

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, concerning God's words ﴿When they come to you, they say, "We believe"﴾ and the rest of the verse, that he said: "They were some people from among the Jews who used to enter upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and inform him that they were believers, content with what he had brought, while they were holding fast to their misguidance and disbelief. So they would enter with that and leave with that from the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi concerning the verse, that he said: "These were people from among the hypocrites who were Jews. The meaning is: they entered as disbelievers and left as disbelievers."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Zayd, concerning God's words ﴿You see many of them racing toward sin and aggression﴾, that he said: "These are the Jews" (﴿Wretched is what they used to do﴾) up to His words (﴿Wretched is what they used to produce﴾). He said: "Yasna'un (produce) and ya'malun (do) are one and the same. He spoke to these when they did not desist, just as He spoke to those when they committed (the sins)."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning God's words ﴿Why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them?﴾, that he said: "Then why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them? They are the jurists (fuqaha') and the learned ('ulama')."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more severe in rebuke than this verse: ﴿Why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them?﴾" Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated a similar report from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim.

Many hadiths have been transmitted on enjoining good (al-amr bi al-ma'ruf) and forbidding evil (al-nahy 'an al-munkar), but there is no need for us to expand on them here.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 57–63 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as a mockery and a game﴾. This is a prohibition on allying with those who make the religion a mockery and a game. It covers everyone from whom this occurs, whether from the polytheists, the People of the Book, or the people of innovation (ahl al-bida') who ascribe themselves to Islam. The explanation in His saying ﴿from those who were given the Book﴾ to the end of the verse does not preclude others from falling under the prohibition when the stated reason (al-'illa), which is the motive for the prohibition, is found in them.

His saying: (wa-l-kuffar, "and the disbelievers"). Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it in the genitive (bi-l-jarr), on the assumption of the preposition (min), meaning "and of the disbelievers." Al-Kisa'i said: "In the reading of Ubayy it is (wa-min al-kuffar)." The rest read it in the accusative (bi-l-nasb). Al-Nahhas said: "This is clearer and more explicit." Makki said: "Were it not for the consensus of the community (ijma'') on the accusative, I would have chosen the genitive for its strength in i'rab (grammatical inflection) and in meaning." Here "the disbelievers" means the polytheists, and it has been said that it means the hypocrites. ﴿And fear God﴾, by abandoning what He has forbidden you from this and other things, ﴿if you are believers﴾, for faith requires that.

The nida' (ندَاء, call) is calling out with a raised voice. One says nadahu, munadah and nida', meaning he cried out to him. (wa-tanadaw): meaning some of them called out to one another. (Tanadaw) also means they sat in the nadi (assembly). The pronoun in (ittakhadhuha, "they took it") refers to the prayer, meaning they took your prayer as a mockery and a game. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the call (al-munadah), which is implied by (nadaytum, "you called"). It has been said that the Book of God mentions the adhan (call to prayer) only in this passage. As for His saying concerning Friday: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday﴾, it is specific to the Friday call. The scholars have differed over whether the adhan is obligatory or not, and over its wording. This is expounded in its proper places.

His saying: ﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾. That is, that is because they are a people who do not reason, since mockery and play are the habit of people of foolishness, lightness and frivolity.

His saying: ﴿Say: "O People of the Book, do you find fault with us?"﴾. It is said: naqimtu 'ala al-rajul (with kasra, in the past tense) — fa-ana naqim, when you found fault with him.

Al-Kisa'i said: "Naqimtu (with kasra) is a dialectal form, and naqamtu al-amr (with fatha) also, and naqimtu means: when you disliked it. Allah took vengeance on him (intaqama Allahu minhu), that is, punished him. Its noun is al-niqmah, and its plural is niqamat, like kalimah and kalimat. If you wish, you may make the qaf sukun and transfer its vowel to the nun, and the plural is niqam, like ni'mah and ni'am." It has been said the meaning is "they are angered," and it has been said "they disapprove." 'Abd Allah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

"They found no fault with the Banu Umayyah, except that they are forbearing when they are angered."

So God revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as a mockery and a game﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And God knows best what they were concealing﴾. (p-٣٨٢) Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿And when you call to prayer, they take it as a mockery and a game﴾, that he said: The caller of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to call to prayer, and when the Muslims stood up for prayer, the Jews and Christians would say: "They have stood up; may they never stand!" And when they saw them bowing and prostrating, they would mock them and laugh at them. He said: A Jewish merchant, when he heard the caller calling the adhan, would say: "May God burn the liar!" He said: While he was like that, his servant girl came in with a flame of fire, and a spark flew from it into the house and burned it down. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, who said: There was a man from the Christians, and he mentioned something similar to the story of the Jewish man.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: A group of Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about which messengers he believed in. He said: "I believe in God, and in what was sent down to Ibrahim (Abraham), Isma'il (Ishmael), Ishaq (Isaac), Ya'qub (Jacob) and the al-Asbat (the tribes), and in what was given to Musa (Moses), 'Isa (Jesus) and the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submissive." When he mentioned 'Isa, they denied his prophethood and said: "We do not believe in 'Isa, nor in anyone who believes in him." So God revealed about them: ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, do you resent us only because we believe in God...﴾ up to His words: (fasiqun, defiant transgressors).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid, concerning God's words ﴿And He made some of them apes and swine﴾, that he said: "They were transformed from among the Jews."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Malik that he was asked: "Were the apes and swine in existence before they were transformed?" He said: "Yes, and they were among the nations that had been created."

Muslim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about the apes and swine: are they among those whom God transformed? He said: 'God does not destroy a people,' or he said, 'does not transform a people, so as to give them offspring or a descendant (aqibah). The apes and swine existed before that.'"

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, concerning God's words ﴿When they come to you, they say, "We believe"﴾ and the rest of the verse, that he said: "They were some people from among the Jews who used to enter upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and inform him that they were believers, content with what he had brought, while they were holding fast to their misguidance and disbelief. So they would enter with that and leave with that from the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Suddi concerning the verse, that he said: "These were people from among the hypocrites who were Jews. The meaning is: they entered as disbelievers and left as disbelievers."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Zayd, concerning God's words ﴿You see many of them racing toward sin and aggression﴾, that he said: "These are the Jews" (﴿Wretched is what they used to do﴾) up to His words (﴿Wretched is what they used to produce﴾). He said: "Yasna'un (produce) and ya'malun (do) are one and the same. He spoke to these when they did not desist, just as He spoke to those when they committed (the sins)."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning God's words ﴿Why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them?﴾, that he said: "Then why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them? They are the jurists (fuqaha') and the learned ('ulama')."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more severe in rebuke than this verse: ﴿Why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them?﴾" Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated a similar report from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim.

Many hadiths have been transmitted on enjoining good (al-amr bi al-ma'ruf) and forbidding evil (al-nahy 'an al-munkar), but there is no need for us to expand on them here.

**The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 64–66:**

His saying: (﴿The hand of God is chained﴾). In Arabic usage, *al-yad* (the hand) is used for the physical limb, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle of grass﴾. It is also used for blessing (*ni'mah*), as people say: "I have a hand (*yad*) with so-and-so," meaning a favour owed to him. It is used for power (*qudrah*), as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 73]. It is also used for support (*ta'yid*), as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The hand of God is with the judge while he judges." It is used in other meanings as well. This verse is by way of figurative expression (*tamthil*), like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ [Al-Isra': 29]. The Arabs use "the chaining of the hand" metaphorically for stinginess and "the spreading of the hand" for generosity, and they do not mean the physical limb. Thus they describe the stingy person as "one whose fingertips are tight" and "whose palm is closed." From this is the saying of the poet:

Khurasan was a land when Yazid was in it, and every gate of good things was open.

Then after him it was given to one whose fingers are tight, as if his face were sprinkled with vinegar.

So the intent of the Jews here, may the curses of God be upon them, is that God is stingy. God, glorified is He, answered them with His saying: (﴿Their hands are chained﴾), as a supplication against them for stinginess. Thus the answer against them corresponds exactly to what they intended by their saying: (﴿The hand of God is chained﴾). It is also permissible that what is meant is the actual chaining of their hands, by imprisonment in this world or by punishment in the Hereafter. The first meaning is strengthened by the fact that stinginess has clung to the Jews as the shadow clings to the sun, so that you will not find a Jew, however great his wealth, who is not among the stingiest of God's creatures. Also, the figurative reading is more suited to the context, because it corresponds to what precedes it.

His saying: (﴿And they are cursed for what they said﴾). It is coordinated with what precedes it, and the particle *ba'* (with) is causal; that is, they were removed from the mercy of God because of their saying: (﴿The hand of God is chained﴾). Then God, glorified is He, refuted them with His saying: (﴿Rather, both His hands are outspread﴾). That is: rather, He is in the utmost degree of generosity. He mentioned the two hands, although they had mentioned only one hand, for emphasis in refuting them, by affirming what indicates the utmost liberality, since attributing generosity to the two hands is more eloquent than attributing it to a single hand. This idrabi sentence (a sentence introduced by *bal*, "rather," which reverses or corrects what precedes) is coordinated with an implied sentence required by the context; that is: "No, the matter is not as they say, (﴿rather, both His hands are outspread﴾)." It has been said that what is meant by (﴿rather, both His hands are outspread﴾) is His outward worldly blessing and His inward blessing. It has been said: the blessing of rain and vegetation. It has been said: reward and punishment. Al-Akhfash related from Ibn Mas'ud that he read *bal yadahu basitatan*, meaning: freely moving, as He wills.

His saying: (﴿He spends as He wills﴾). This is a new sentence, emphasizing the completeness of His generosity, glorified is He. That is: His giving follows what His will requires. If He wills, He expands, and if He wills, He restricts. He is the Outspreader and the Restrainer. If He restricts, that is because of what His manifest wisdom requires, and not for anything else, since the treasuries of His dominion never run out and the sources of His generosity never end.

His saying: (﴿And surely many of them will increase in transgression and disbelief﴾), etc. The *lam* here is the *lam* of oath (*lam al-qasam*). That is: surely many of the Jews and Christians will increase in transgression and disbelief at what has been sent down to you of the Qur'an, which includes these good rulings. (﴿transgression and disbelief﴾) means: transgression added to their transgression, and disbelief added to their disbelief.

His saying: (And We cast among them) meaning among the Jews (enmity and hatred). Or among the Jews and Christians.

His saying: ﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it﴾. That is: every time they gather a force for war and prepare equipment for it, God scatters their gathering and removes their strength, so that they gain nothing and return with no benefit. Rather, they obtain from this only defeat. Thus they continue to stir up wars and gather for them, and then God nullifies that. The verse contains an eloquent metaphor (*isti'arah*) and a wonderful style. (﴿And they strive in the land to cause corruption﴾). That is: they strive to do what is corrupt, and among the greatest of it is what they intend, namely the nullification of Islam and the plotting against its people. It has been said that what is meant here by fire is anger. That is: every time they stir up anger in themselves, God extinguishes it by the terror He placed in their hearts, and by the humiliation and destitution imposed upon them.

His saying: (﴿And God does not love the corrupters﴾). If the *lam* is for the genus (*lam al-jins*), then they enter into this first and foremost. If it is for a specific known group (*lam al-'ahd*), then the placing of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun is to show the severity of their corruption and that they never cease from it.

His saying: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed and feared God﴾. That is: if those who hold fast to the Book, namely the Jews and Christians, (the definite article here being for the genus) (believed), the belief which God demanded of them, and among the most important of it is belief in what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought, as they were commanded in the Books of God that were revealed to them (and feared God), by avoiding the acts of disobedience, the greatest of which is what they are upon of associating partners with God and denying what the Messenger of God brought. (﴿We would have expiated from them their misdeeds﴾) which they committed, however many and varied they were. It has been said that the meaning is: We would have widened their provision.

﴿And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel﴾. That is: if they had upheld what is in them of rulings, among which is belief in what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought.

His saying: (﴿and what has been sent down to them from their Lord﴾). This refers to the rest of the Books of God, among which is the Qur'an, for all of them, even though they were revealed to others, are in the status of what was revealed to them, since they are obligated to act by what is in them. (﴿They would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾). He mentioned "above" and "beneath" for emphasis on the ease and abundance of the means of sustenance for them and the multiplicity of its kinds.

His saying: (﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾). This is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: Do all of them possess the attributes mentioned previously, or only some of them? The moderate among them are the believers, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and those who followed him, and a group of the Christians. (﴿And many of them—evil is what they do﴾) are those who persist in disbelief and rebel against accepting Muhammad (ﷺ) and believing in what he brought. Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir, and Ibn Mardawayh have related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: A man from the Jews called al-Nabbash ibn Qays said: "Indeed your Lord is stingy and does not spend." So God revealed: "And the Jews said: The hand of God is chained," to the end of the verse. Abu al-Shaykh related from him that it was revealed concerning Finhas the Jew. Ibn Jarir related the same from 'Ikrimah.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And the Jews said, the hand of God is chained﴾, that it means: stingy. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him something similar. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And surely many of them will increase in what has been sent down to you from your Lord in transgression and disbelief﴾, that he said: The envy of Muhammad and the Arabs drove them to abandon the Qur'an and to disbelieve in Muhammad and his religion, while they were finding it written with them. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war﴾, that he said: The war against Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi concerning the verse: Every time they unite their affair upon something, God scatters it and extinguishes their sharpness and their fire, and casts terror into their hearts. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed and feared God﴾, that he said: They believe in what was sent down to Muhammad and fear what God has forbidden.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel﴾, that he said: Acting by them both. As for (what has been sent down to them), it is Muhammad (ﷺ) and what was sent down to him. As for (﴿they would have eaten from above them﴾), it means: I would have sent down rain upon them. As for (from beneath their feet), he says: I would have made grow for them from the earth of My provision what would suffice them. (﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾) are the Muslims among the People of the Book. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas: (﴿They would have eaten from above them﴾) means: I would have sent the sky upon them in abundant rain, (﴿and from beneath their feet﴾), he said: the earth would have brought forth from its blessing. Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: The moderate community are those who neither transgress in religion nor exaggerate. He said: Exaggeration is excessive desire, and transgression is falling short of it.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi: (a moderate community) means: believing. Ibn Mardawayh said: 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far related to us, Ahmad ibn Yunus al-Dabbi related to us, 'Asim ibn 'Ali related to us, Abu Ma'shar related to us, from Ya'qub ibn Zayd ibn Talhah, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: We were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he mentioned a hadith. He said: Then the Prophet (ﷺ) related to them, saying: "The community of Moses split into seventy-two sects, one of which is in Paradise and seventy-one in the Fire. The community of Jesus split into seventy-two sects, one of which is in Paradise and seventy-one in the Fire. My community will exceed both groups together: one sect in Paradise and seventy-two in the Fire." They said: "Who are they, O Messenger of God?" He said: "The congregations, the congregations." Ya'qub ibn Zayd said: When 'Ali ibn Abi Talib related this hadith from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he would recite a Qur'an in it, saying: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed and feared God, We would have expiated from them their misdeeds﴾, to His saying: ﴿Among them is a moderate community; and many of them—evil is what they do﴾. (p-384) And he also recited: ﴿And among those We created is a community that guides by the truth and by it establishes justice﴾, meaning the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir, after mentioning this hadith, the following words: The hadith of the division of the nations into seventy-odd sects is narrated through many chains, which we have mentioned in another place. End of quote.

I say: As for the addition that all of them will be in the Fire except one, several of the scholars of hadith have declared it weak, and Ibn Hazm even said that it is fabricated (*mawdu'ah*).

My community will exceed both groups together: one sect in Paradise and seventy-two in the Fire." They said: "Who are they, O Messenger of God?" He said: "The congregations, the congregations." Ya'qub ibn Zayd said: When 'Ali ibn Abi Talib related this hadith from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he would recite a Qur'an in it, saying: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed and feared God, We would have expiated from them their misdeeds﴾, to His saying: ﴿Among them is a moderate community; and many of them—evil is what they do﴾. (p-384) And he also recited: ﴿And among those We created is a community that guides by the truth and by it establishes justice﴾, meaning the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir, after mentioning this hadith, the following words: The hadith of the division of the nations into seventy-odd sects is narrated through many chains, which we have mentioned in another place. End of quote.

I say: As for the addition that all of them will be in the Fire except one, several of the scholars of hadith have declared it weak, and Ibn Hazm even said that it is fabricated (*mawdu'ah*).

**The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 64–66:**

His saying: (﴿The hand of God is chained﴾). In Arabic usage, *al-yad* (the hand) is used for the physical limb, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle of grass﴾. It is also used for blessing (*ni'mah*), as people say: "I have a hand (*yad*) with so-and-so," meaning a favour owed to him. It is used for power (*qudrah*), as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 73]. It is also used for support (*ta'yid*), as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The hand of God is with the judge while he judges." It is used in other meanings as well. This verse is by way of figurative expression (*tamthil*), like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ [Al-Isra': 29]. The Arabs use "the chaining of the hand" metaphorically for stinginess and "the spreading of the hand" for generosity, and they do not mean the physical limb. Thus they describe the stingy person as "one whose fingertips are tight" and "whose palm is closed." From this is the saying of the poet:

Khurasan was a land when Yazid was in it, and every gate of good things was open.

Then after him it was given to one whose fingers are tight, as if his face were sprinkled with vinegar.

So the intent of the Jews here, may the curses of God be upon them, is that God is stingy. God, glorified is He, answered them with His saying: (﴿Their hands are chained﴾), as a supplication against them for stinginess. Thus the answer against them corresponds exactly to what they intended by their saying: (﴿The hand of God is chained﴾). It is also permissible that what is meant is the actual chaining of their hands, by imprisonment in this world or by punishment in the Hereafter. The first meaning is strengthened by the fact that stinginess has clung to the Jews as the shadow clings to the sun, so that you will not find a Jew, however great his wealth, who is not among the stingiest of God's creatures. Also, the figurative reading is more suited to the context, because it corresponds to what precedes it.

His saying: (﴿And they are cursed for what they said﴾). It is coordinated with what precedes it, and the particle *ba'* (with) is causal; that is, they were removed from the mercy of God because of their saying: (﴿The hand of God is chained﴾). Then God, glorified is He, refuted them with His saying: (﴿Rather, both His hands are outspread﴾). That is: rather, He is in the utmost degree of generosity. He mentioned the two hands, although they had mentioned only one hand, for emphasis in refuting them, by affirming what indicates the utmost liberality, since attributing generosity to the two hands is more eloquent than attributing it to a single hand. This idrabi sentence (a sentence introduced by *bal*, "rather," which reverses or corrects what precedes) is coordinated with an implied sentence required by the context; that is: "No, the matter is not as they say, (﴿rather, both His hands are outspread﴾)." It has been said that what is meant by (﴿rather, both His hands are outspread﴾) is His outward worldly blessing and His inward blessing. It has been said: the blessing of rain and vegetation. It has been said: reward and punishment. Al-Akhfash related from Ibn Mas'ud that he read *bal yadahu basitatan*, meaning: freely moving, as He wills.

His saying: (﴿He spends as He wills﴾). This is a new sentence, emphasizing the completeness of His generosity, glorified is He. That is: His giving follows what His will requires. If He wills, He expands, and if He wills, He restricts. He is the Outspreader and the Restrainer. If He restricts, that is because of what His manifest wisdom requires, and not for anything else, since the treasuries of His dominion never run out and the sources of His generosity never end.

His saying: (﴿And surely many of them will increase in transgression and disbelief﴾), etc. The *lam* here is the *lam* of oath (*lam al-qasam*). That is: surely many of the Jews and Christians will increase in transgression and disbelief at what has been sent down to you of the Qur'an, which includes these good rulings. (﴿transgression and disbelief﴾) means: transgression added to their transgression, and disbelief added to their disbelief.

His saying: (And We cast among them) meaning among the Jews (enmity and hatred). Or among the Jews and Christians.

His saying: ﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it﴾. That is: every time they gather a force for war and prepare equipment for it, God scatters their gathering and removes their strength, so that they gain nothing and return with no benefit. Rather, they obtain from this only defeat. Thus they continue to stir up wars and gather for them, and then God nullifies that. The verse contains an eloquent metaphor (*isti'arah*) and a wonderful style. (﴿And they strive in the land to cause corruption﴾). That is: they strive to do what is corrupt, and among the greatest of it is what they intend, namely the nullification of Islam and the plotting against its people. It has been said that what is meant here by fire is anger. That is: every time they stir up anger in themselves, God extinguishes it by the terror He placed in their hearts, and by the humiliation and destitution imposed upon them.

His saying: (﴿And God does not love the corrupters﴾). If the *lam* is for the genus (*lam al-jins*), then they enter into this first and foremost. If it is for a specific known group (*lam al-'ahd*), then the placing of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun is to show the severity of their corruption and that they never cease from it.

His saying: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed and feared God﴾. That is: if those who hold fast to the Book, namely the Jews and Christians, (the definite article here being for the genus) (believed), the belief which God demanded of them, and among the most important of it is belief in what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought, as they were commanded in the Books of God that were revealed to them (and feared God), by avoiding the acts of disobedience, the greatest of which is what they are upon of associating partners with God and denying what the Messenger of God brought. (﴿We would have expiated from them their misdeeds﴾) which they committed, however many and varied they were. It has been said that the meaning is: We would have widened their provision.

﴿And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel﴾. That is: if they had upheld what is in them of rulings, among which is belief in what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought.

His saying: (﴿and what has been sent down to them from their Lord﴾). This refers to the rest of the Books of God, among which is the Qur'an, for all of them, even though they were revealed to others, are in the status of what was revealed to them, since they are obligated to act by what is in them. (﴿They would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾). He mentioned "above" and "beneath" for emphasis on the ease and abundance of the means of sustenance for them and the multiplicity of its kinds.

His saying: (﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾). This is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: Do all of them possess the attributes mentioned previously, or only some of them? The moderate among them are the believers, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and those who followed him, and a group of the Christians. (﴿And many of them—evil is what they do﴾) are those who persist in disbelief and rebel against accepting Muhammad (ﷺ) and believing in what he brought. Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir, and Ibn Mardawayh have related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: A man from the Jews called al-Nabbash ibn Qays said: "Indeed your Lord is stingy and does not spend." So God revealed: "And the Jews said: The hand of God is chained," to the end of the verse. Abu al-Shaykh related from him that it was revealed concerning Finhas the Jew. Ibn Jarir related the same from 'Ikrimah.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And the Jews said, the hand of God is chained﴾, that it means: stingy. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him something similar. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And surely many of them will increase in what has been sent down to you from your Lord in transgression and disbelief﴾, that he said: The envy of Muhammad and the Arabs drove them to abandon the Qur'an and to disbelieve in Muhammad and his religion, while they were finding it written with them. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war﴾, that he said: The war against Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi concerning the verse: Every time they unite their affair upon something, God scatters it and extinguishes their sharpness and their fire, and casts terror into their hearts. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed and feared God﴾, that he said: They believe in what was sent down to Muhammad and fear what God has forbidden.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel﴾, that he said: Acting by them both. As for (what has been sent down to them), it is Muhammad (ﷺ) and what was sent down to him. As for (﴿they would have eaten from above them﴾), it means: I would have sent down rain upon them. As for (from beneath their feet), he says: I would have made grow for them from the earth of My provision what would suffice them. (﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾) are the Muslims among the People of the Book. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas: (﴿They would have eaten from above them﴾) means: I would have sent the sky upon them in abundant rain, (﴿and from beneath their feet﴾), he said: the earth would have brought forth from its blessing. Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: The moderate community are those who neither transgress in religion nor exaggerate. He said: Exaggeration is excessive desire, and transgression is falling short of it.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi: (a moderate community) means: believing. Ibn Mardawayh said: 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far related to us, Ahmad ibn Yunus al-Dabbi related to us, 'Asim ibn 'Ali related to us, Abu Ma'shar related to us, from Ya'qub ibn Zayd ibn Talhah, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: We were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he mentioned a hadith. He said: Then the Prophet (ﷺ) related to them, saying: "The community of Moses split into seventy-two sects, one of which is in Paradise and seventy-one in the Fire. The community of Jesus split into seventy-two sects, one of which is in Paradise and seventy-one in the Fire. My community will exceed both groups together: one sect in Paradise and seventy-two in the Fire." They said: "Who are they, O Messenger of God?" He said: "The congregations, the congregations." Ya'qub ibn Zayd said: When 'Ali ibn Abi Talib related this hadith from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he would recite a Qur'an in it, saying: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed and feared God, We would have expiated from them their misdeeds﴾, to His saying: ﴿Among them is a moderate community; and many of them—evil is what they do﴾. (p-384) And he also recited: ﴿And among those We created is a community that guides by the truth and by it establishes justice﴾, meaning the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir, after mentioning this hadith, the following words: The hadith of the division of the nations into seventy-odd sects is narrated through many chains, which we have mentioned in another place. End of quote.

I say: As for the addition that all of them will be in the Fire except one, several of the scholars of hadith have declared it weak, and Ibn Hazm even said that it is fabricated (*mawdu'ah*).

The general wording of "what has been sent down" (ma unzila) indicates that it is obligatory for the Messenger (ﷺ) to convey all that Allah sent down to him, concealing nothing of it. It is also evidence that he did not confide any part of what relates to what Allah sent down to him in secret to anyone. For this reason it is established in the two Sahihs, from Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her), that she said: "Whoever claims that Muhammad (ﷺ) concealed any part of the revelation has lied." In Sahih al-Bukhari, from the narration of Abu Juhayfa Wahb ibn Abd Allah al-Suwa'i, he said: I said to Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him): "Do you have anything of the revelation that is not in the Qur'an?" He said: "No, by the One who split the grain and created the soul, except for an understanding that Allah gives a man concerning the Qur'an, and what is in this sheet." I said: "What is in this sheet?" He said: "The blood-money (al-'aql), the freeing of captives, and that a Muslim is not to be killed for a disbeliever."

(﴿And if you do not do so﴾) meaning: if you do not convey all that you were commanded to convey, but conceal even part of it, (﴿then you have not conveyed His message﴾).

Abu Amr and the people of Kufa, except Shu'ba, read "risalatahu" (His message) in the singular. The people of Medina and the people of Syria read "risalatihi" (His messages) in the plural. (The recitation variants, qira'at, are the different authorized readings of the Qur'an.) Al-Nahhas said: "The plural is clearer, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) received the revelation gradually, piece by piece, and then explained it." End of quote. But there is room for scrutiny here: negating conveyance from a single message is more emphatic than negating it from messages, as the scholars of rhetoric (ulama al-bayan) have stated, though there is disagreement on this. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conveyed to his community what was sent down to them, and on more than one occasion he said to them: "Have I conveyed?" and they would testify to him that he had made it clear. May Allah reward him on behalf of his community with good. Then Allah, glorified is He, promised him protection from the people, to remove what might be thought to drive him to conceal the explanation, namely fear of harm from people. This was, praise be to Allah, realized, for he made clear to the servants of Allah what was sent down to them in full. Then he compelled those who refused to enter the religion to enter it, willingly or unwillingly; he killed the leaders of polytheism, scattered their hosts and dispersed their gathering, and the Word of Allah became supreme. Everyone who opposed him embraced Islam, except those whom the sword had not yet reached, until on the day of the Conquest he said to the leaders and nobles of Quraysh: "What do you think I will do with you?" They said: "A noble brother and the son of a noble brother." He said: "Go, for you are the freed ones (al-Tulaqa')."

Likewise, whoever among the scholars of this community has been granted divine care, Allah protects him from the people if he stands forth to make clear the proofs of Allah and to demonstrate His evidences, and proclaims among those who oppose Allah and defy Him and do not submit to His law, such as the sects of innovators. We have seen this in ourselves and heard of it in others, something that increases the believer in faith, firmness in the religion of Allah, and steadfastness in standing up for the proof of Allah. Everything that those of unsteady feet and agitated hearts imagine of harm befalling them or trials descending upon them is baseless fancy and false supposition, for every trial that appears to be a trial is in reality not so, since it brings nothing but good in this world and the next: (﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while he is a witness﴾) [Qaf: 37].

His saying (﴿Indeed Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾) is a sentence that serves to explain the preceding protection; that is, Allah does not grant them any way to harm you, so do not fear, and convey what you were commanded to convey.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid, who said: When (﴿Convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾) was revealed, he said: "My Lord, I am only one person, how can I do it? The people will gather against me." Then (﴿And if you do not do so, then you have not conveyed His message﴾) was revealed.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Hasan that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah sent me with His message, and I was distressed by it, and I knew that the people would deny me. Then He promised me that I would convey it or else He would punish me, and so (﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾) was revealed."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying (﴿And if you do not do so, then you have not conveyed His message﴾): meaning, if you conceal a single verse of what has been sent down to you, you have not conveyed His message. Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: This verse (﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you﴾) was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Ghadir Khumm concerning Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him).

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "We used to recite in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): (O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord, that Ali is the protector (mawla) of the believers; and if you do not do so, then you have not conveyed His message, and Allah will protect you from the people)." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Antara, who said: I was with Ibn Abbas when a man came to him and said: "People come to us and inform us that you have something that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not disclose to the people." He said: "Do you not know that Allah said: (O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord)? By Allah, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not bequeath to us a black spot on white (i.e., anything hidden)."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya in al-Mukhtara narrated from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: "Which verse sent down from heaven was the hardest on you?" He said: "I was in Mina during the days of the season, when the polytheists of the Arabs and the various groups of people gathered at the season, and Jibril came down to me and said: (O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you), to the end of the verse." He said: "I stood at the Aqaba and called out: 'O people, who will support me so that I may convey the message of my Lord, and for him is Paradise? O people, say: There is no god but Allah, and I am the Messenger of Allah to you; you will prosper and succeed, and for you is Paradise.'" He said: "No man, woman or child remained but that they threw dust and stones at me, spat in my face and said: 'A liar, a sabian (apostate).' Then a figure appeared before me and said: 'O Muhammad, if you are the Messenger of Allah, it is time for you to invoke against them as Nuh invoked destruction upon his people.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Allah, guide my people, for they do not know.' Then his uncle al-Abbas came, rescued him from them and drove them away from him." Al-A'mash said: "For this reason the Bani al-Abbas boast and say: 'It was concerning them that this was revealed: (Indeed you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills)' [al-Qasas: 56]. The Prophet (ﷺ) wished for Abu Talib, while Allah willed for Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib."

(p-385) Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi, both in al-Dala'il, narrated from Aisha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to be guarded until (﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾) was revealed, whereupon he put his head out of the tent and said: 'O people, disperse, for Allah has protected me.'" Al-Hakim said in al-Mustadrak: "Its chain is sound, but they (al-Bukhari and Muslim) did not narrate it." Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from the hadith of Abu Sa'id. Hadiths with this meaning have been narrated in several forms.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raided the Bani Anmar, he stopped at Dhat al-Riqa' under a palm tree. While he was sitting on the edge of a well with his legs dangling, a man from the Bani al-Najjar who was there said: 'I will surely kill Muhammad.' His companions said to him: 'How will you kill him?' He said: 'I will say to him: Give me your sword. When he gives it to me, I will kill him with it.' He came to him and said: 'O Muhammad, give me your sword so that I may look at it.' He gave it to him, and his hand trembled until the sword fell from his hand. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah has come between you and what you intended.' Then Allah, glorified is He, revealed: (O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you), to the end of the verse." Ibn Kathir said: "This hadith is gharib (rare) from this route." Ibn Hibban in his Sahih and Ibn Mardawayh narrated a similar story from Abu Hurayra, but did not name the man. Ibn Jarir narrated a similar account from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, and there are other narrations on this subject. The story of Ghawrath ibn al-Harith is established in the Sahih, and it is well known and famous.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verse 68–76 (part 1 of 2):

His words: (﴿on anything﴾) In this there is belittling and diminishing of what they are upon; that is: you are not upon anything worth considering until you establish the Torah and the Gospel, i.e., act upon what is in them of the commands and prohibitions of Allah, among which is your being commanded to follow Muhammad (ﷺ) and your being forbidden to oppose him. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: It is also possible that this refers to before their abrogation (naskh) of the two. His words: "and what has been sent down to you from your Lord." It has been said: this is the Qur'an, for the establishment of the two Books is not valid without establishing it. It is also possible that what is meant is what was sent down to them through the tongues of the prophets other than the two Books.

His words: ﴿And surely what has been sent down to you from your Lord will increase many of them in transgression and disbelief﴾: that is, disbelief added to their disbelief and transgression added to their transgression. What is meant by "many of them" is those who did not become Muslim and persisted in obstinacy. It has also been said that what is meant is their scholars. The opening of this sentence with an oath is to emphasize its content. His words: ﴿So do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾: that is, leave off grieving over these people, for the harm of that returns to them and descends upon them, and among those who follow you from the believers there is sufficiency for you in place of them. His words: (﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾) and so on, is a resumed sentence to encourage those among the believers other than them.

What is meant by "the believers" here are those who believed with their tongues, and they are the hypocrites. (﴿And those who became Jews﴾): that is, those who entered the religion of the Jews. (And the Sabians): it is in the nominative by way of inception, and its predicate is omitted; the estimated meaning is: "and the Sabians and the Christians likewise." Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: the nominative is taken as having been placed out of order, and the estimated meaning is: "Indeed, those who believed and those who became Jews, whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteous deeds, there is no fear for them nor will they grieve, and the Sabians and the Christians likewise." Sibawayh recited the verse of the poet:

"Otherwise, know that we and you are transgressors as long as we remain in schism."

That is: otherwise, know that we are transgressors and you likewise. Similar to it is the saying of Dabi al-Burjumi:

"Whoever has his dwelling in Medina by evening, then I and Qayyar in it are strangers."

That is: then I am a stranger, and Qayyar likewise. Al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash said: (al-Sabi'un) is in conjunction with the pronoun in (hadu). Al-Nahhas said: I heard al-Zajjaj say, when the saying of al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash was mentioned to him: "This is an error for two reasons: first, a pronoun in the nominative is not conjoined to unless it is emphasized. Second, the conjoined is a partner of the conjoined-to, so the meaning becomes: the Sabians have entered Judaism, and this is absurd."

Al-Farra' said: the nominative was permitted because "inna" is weak, so it affects only the subject and not the predicate. Thus, according to him, it is conjoined to the position (mahall) of the subject of inna, or to the whole of inna and its subject. It has also been said: the predicate of inna is omitted, and the following clause is the predicate of al-Sabi'un and al-Nasara, as in the saying of the poet:

"We are with what we have, and you are with what you have pleased, and opinions differ."

It has also been said: "inna" here means "na'am" (yes), so al-Sabi'un is in the nominative by inception, and similar to it is the saying of Qays ibn al-Ruqayyat:

"The blamers began in youth, so they blame me and I blame them,
And they say, 'Gray hair has risen over you, and you have grown old,' so I said, 'Innah.'"

Al-Akhfash said: "innah" means "na'am," and the ha' is for pausal (silence). The discussion of the Sabians and the Christians has already passed in al-Baqarah. It was read as al-Sabiyun with a clear ya', to ease the hamza, and it was read as al-Sabun without a ya'; it is from sabā yaṣbū, because they inclined (ṣabaw) toward following desire. (p-386) It was also read as wal-Sabi'in, in conjunction with the noun of inna.

His words: (﴿whoever believed in Allah﴾) is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿then no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾, and the subject with its predicate is the predicate of inna. The entry of the fa' is because the subject includes the meaning of a condition. The returning pronoun to the noun of inna is omitted; that is, whoever among them believed. It is also possible that "whoever believed" is a substitute for the noun of inna and what is conjoined to it, and the predicate of inna is "then no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve." The meaning, on the supposition that what is meant by "those who believed" are the hypocrites, as we have mentioned, is that whoever among these groups believed with sincere faith in the required manner and did righteous deeds, he is the one upon whom there is no fear nor grief. As for the supposition that what is meant by "those who believed" is all the people of Islam, both the sincere and the hypocrite, then what is meant by "whoever believed" is one who is characterized by sincere faith and persists in it, and whoever brings about sincere faith after his hypocrisy.

His words: ﴿Certainly We took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾: a new statement to explain some of their vile deeds. The meaning of the covenant (mithaq) has already been explained in al-Baqarah. (﴿And We sent to them messengers﴾) to inform them of the laws and to warn them. (﴿Every time a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire﴾): a conditional sentence which came as an answer to the question of some of the rabbis about the sending of the messengers, as if it was said: "What did they do with the messengers?" The answer of the condition is omitted; that is: they disobeyed him.

His words: ﴿a group they denied, and a group they kill﴾ is also a resumed sentence, an answer to the question of some people about the first answer, as if it was said: "How did they treat them?" So it was said: a group of them denied them and did not harm them, and another group of them killed them. He said "and a group they kill" only for the sake of observing the rhyme endings of the verses. Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari), Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Nafi' ibn Harithah, Sallam ibn Mishkam, Malik ibn al-Sayf and Rafi' ibn Harmalah came and said: 'O Muhammad, do you not claim that you are upon the religion (millah) and creed of Ibrahim, and that you believe in what we have of the Torah and testify that it is true from Allah?' So Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿Say: O People of the Book, you are not upon anything until you establish the Torah and the Gospel﴾, up to His saying: ﴿the disbelieving people﴾."

It has been said: this is the Qur'an, for the establishment of the two Books is not valid without establishing it. It is also possible that what is meant is what was sent down to them through the tongues of the prophets other than the two Books.

His words: ﴿And surely what has been sent down to you from your Lord will increase many of them in transgression and disbelief﴾: that is, disbelief added to their disbelief and transgression added to their transgression. What is meant by "many of them" is those who did not become Muslim and persisted in obstinacy. It has also been said that what is meant is their scholars. The opening of this sentence with an oath is to emphasize its content. His words: ﴿So do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾: that is, leave off grieving over these people, for the harm of that returns to them and descends upon them, and among those who follow you from the believers there is sufficiency for you in place of them. What is meant by "the believers" here are those who believed with their tongues, and they are the hypocrites. (﴿And those who became Jews﴾): that is, those who entered the religion of the Jews. Sibawayh recited the verse of the poet:

"Otherwise, know that we and you are transgressors as long as we remain in schism."

That is: otherwise, know that we are transgressors and you likewise. Similar to it is the saying of Dabi al-Burjumi:

"Whoever has his dwelling in Medina by evening, then I and Qayyar in it are strangers."

That is: then I am a stranger, and Qayyar likewise. Al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash said: (al-Sabi'un) is in conjunction with the pronoun in (hadu). It has also been said: "inna" here means "na'am" (yes), so al-Sabi'un is in the nominative by inception, and similar to it is the saying of Qays ibn al-Ruqayyat:

Al-Akhfash said: "innah" means "na'am," and the ha' is for pausal (silence). The discussion of the Sabians and the Christians has already passed in al-Baqarah.
