Ibn Jarir transmitted from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, concerning His words, exalted is He, ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you﴾: "Whatever it casts up dead, that is its food." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, as a mawquf (non-prophetic) report, something similar. Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq something similar.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from ʿIkrimah that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq said, regarding His words ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food﴾: "The game of the sea is what our hands catch, and its food is what the sea casts up." In another wording: "Everything in it." And in another wording: "Its food is its carrion."

This is supported by what is in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of the ʿanbarah (ambergris-like whale carcass) which the sea cast up, and the Companions ate from it, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) approved of that. Also the hadith: "Its water is pure and its carrion is lawful." And the hadith: "Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful for you."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿Allah made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of establishment for mankind﴾, that he said: "A means of establishment for their religion and the markers of their pilgrimage." Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, who said: "Its establishment is that whoever turns toward it is safe."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Shihab who said: Allah made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, and the Sacred Month a means of establishment for mankind, by which they were secure in the first Jahiliyyah, such that some of them did not fear others when they met them at the House, or in the Haram, or in the Sacred Month. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿Allah made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of establishment for mankind, and the Sacred Month, and the offering, and the garlands﴾, that he said: "They are barriers which Allah preserved among people in the Jahiliyyah. A man who had committed every crime and then took refuge in the Haram would not be seized or approached. A man who met the slayer of his father in the Sacred Month would not confront him or approach him. A man who met a garlanded offering while he was eating the leaves of trees out of hunger would not confront it or approach it. When a man wanted to go to the House, he would wear a garland of hair, which protected him and kept him from people; and when he returned, he would wear a garland of idhkhir or samur, which kept him from people until he reached his family. These were barriers which Allah preserved among people in the Jahiliyyah." Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam, regarding ﴿a means of establishment for mankind﴾, that he said: "Security."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 94–100 (part 1 of 2):

His words: ﴿Allah will surely test you﴾, meaning: He will surely try you. The lam is the answer to an omitted oath. Hunting (al-sayd) was one of the means of livelihood of the Arabs, so Allah tested them by its prohibition during ihram and within the Sacred Precinct (al-haram), just as He tested the Children of Israel that they should not transgress on the Sabbath. The verse was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. Some of them were in ihram and some were not, so when game appeared their circumstances differed regarding it. The scholars have differed concerning who is addressed by this verse: are they those who are not in ihram (al-muhillun) or those who are in ihram (al-muhrimun)? Malik held the first view, and Ibn 'Abbas the second. The preferred view is that the address is to all of them, and there is no basis for restricting it to some and not others. The "min" in ﴿of the game﴾ is partitive (lil-tab'id), and it refers to land game, as stated by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari and others. It has also been said that "min" is explanatory (bayaniyyah), meaning: a small/insignificant thing of the game, and the indefiniteness of "shay'" (thing) is for belittling.

His words: ﴿that your hands and your spears can reach﴾.
Ibn Wathhab read (yanaluhu) with a ya' (third person). This clause implies the generality of game, and that there is no difference between what is taken by the hand, which cannot flee, such as young animals and eggs, and what the spears reach, which can flee. He singled out the hands for mention because they are what the hunter most uses to take game, and he singled out the spears for mention because they were the greatest hunting instruments among the Arabs.

His words: ﴿that Allah may make evident who fears Him unseen﴾, meaning: that there may be distinguished before Allah who among you fears Him, by reason of His punishment in the Hereafter, for He is unseen and not present before you. ﴿So whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment﴾, meaning: after this clarification by which Allah has tested you, because transgression after knowledge of the prohibition is defiance of Allah, glorified is He, and audacity against Him.

His words: ﴿Do not kill game while you are in ihram﴾. He forbade them from killing game while in the state of ihram. Its meaning is also ﴿not hunting game while you are in ihram﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1]. This prohibition includes everyone among the believing men and women, because it is said: rajul haram (a man in ihram) and imra'ah haram (a woman in ihram), and the plural is hurum. And ahrama al-rajul means he entered the Sacred Precinct.

His words: ﴿And whoever of you kills it intentionally﴾. The one who acts intentionally (al-muta'ammid) is the one who aims at something while knowing he is in ihram. The mistaken one (al-mukhti') is the one who aims at something and hits game. The forgetful one (al-nasi) is the one who deliberately hunts game and does not remember his ihram.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ahmad in one narration, and Dawud from him, argued from the Almighty's restriction of the ruling to the intentional person that there is no expiation (kaffarah) for others; rather, it is obligatory only upon him alone. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Tawus and Abu Thawr said likewise. It has also been said that expiation is obligatory upon the mistaken and the forgetful just as it is upon the intentional, and they took the condition of intention as coming in the form of what is usual. This is narrated from 'Umar, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i and al-Zuhri, and Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and their companions said likewise, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. It has also been said that expiation is obligatory upon one who intentionally kills game while forgetting his ihram; Mujahid said this, and he said: if he was mindful of his ihram, then he has exited ihram and has no valid hajj, because he has committed what is forbidden in his ihram, so it is nullified for him, just as if he spoke during prayer or broke his wudu' during it.

His words: ﴿then the penalty is an equivalent of what he killed of the livestock﴾, meaning: then upon him is a penalty equivalent to what he killed, and ﴿of the livestock﴾ is an explanation of the equivalent penalty. It has been said: the intended meaning is equivalence in value, and it has been said: in form.

Abu Hanifah took the first view, while Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and the majority took the second, and it is the truth, because the explanation of the equivalent as livestock indicates that. Likewise, the phrase "as an offering reaching the Ka'bah" indicates it. It is narrated from Abu Hanifah that it is permissible to give the value even if the equivalent is found, and that the muhrim has a choice.

It is read ﴿fa-jaza'uhu mithlu ma qatala﴾ and it is read ﴿fa-jaza'u mithli﴾ with the construct of jaza' to mithl, and it is read with both in the accusative, on the assumption of "then let him give a penalty equal to what he killed". Al-Hasan read ﴿al-na'mi﴾ with a sukun on the ayn for lightness.

﴿judged by it﴾, meaning by the penalty or by the equivalent of what he killed, two just men from among you, meaning two men well known for justice among the Muslims. If the two judge something, it is binding; if they disagree, the matter is referred to others. It is not permissible for the offender to be one of the two judges. It has been said that it is permissible. The first view is that of Abu Hanifah, and the second is that of al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions. The apparent meaning of the verse requires two judges other than the offender.

His words: ﴿as an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾. "Hadyan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) or as an apposition (badal) to "mithl". "Baligha al-ka'bah" is an attribute of "hadyan", because the construction is not a true (genitive) construction. The meaning is that if the two judge the penalty, then it is treated as an offering is treated: sent to Makkah, slaughtered there, marked (ish'ar) and garlanded (taqlid). The intended meaning is not the Ka'bah itself, for an offering does not reach it; rather the Sacred Precinct is meant, and there is no disagreement on this.

His words: ﴿or an expiation﴾ is conjoined to the position (mahall) of "of the livestock", which is nominative, since it is the predicate of an omitted subject. ﴿food for the needy﴾ is an explanatory apposition to "expiation", or a substitute for it, or the predicate of an omitted subject. ﴿or its equivalent in fasting﴾ is conjoined to "food". It has been said that it is conjoined to "penalty", but that is weak. So the offender has a choice among these mentioned types. "'Adl" of a thing is what equals it from a different kind. ﴿fasting﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). The scholars have established the equivalent of each game in terms of feeding and fasting. The majority of scholars held that the offender is given the choice among the mentioned types. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the muhrim is not excused by feeding or fasting unless he does not find an offering. "'Adl" with a fath and a kasra on the ayn are two dialects, both meaning equivalence; this is said by al-Kisa'i.

Al-Farra' said: "'idl" with a kasra on the ayn means its like of the same kind, and with a fath on the ayn means its like of a different kind. The Basrans said likewise to what al-Kisa'i said.

His words: ﴿that he may taste the bad consequence of his deed﴾. "'Ala" (upon him) is for imposing the penalty; meaning: We imposed that upon him so that he may taste the bad consequence of his deed. Tasting is used figuratively for experiencing hardship, and similar to it is ﴿Taste; indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49]. Wabal means evil outcome; a wabil pasture is one that causes harm after it is eaten, and wabil food is that which is heavy.

His words: ﴿Allah has pardoned what has passed﴾, meaning in your pre-Islamic time, from your killing of game. It has been said: what passed before the revelation of the expiation. ﴿And whoever returns﴾ to what you were forbidden from, killing game after this clarification, ﴿Allah will take retribution from him﴾: this is the predicate of an omitted subject; meaning: he, Allah takes retribution from him. It has been said: the meaning is that Allah will take retribution from him in the Hereafter, punishing him for his sin; and it has been said: He takes retribution from him by the expiation. Shurayh and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he is judged upon the first occurrence, and if he returns he is not judged, but it is said to him: "Go, Allah will take retribution from you," meaning: your sin is too great to be expiated.

His words: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea﴾. The address is to every Muslim, or to those in ihram specifically. The game of the sea is what is hunted in it, and what is meant by "sea" here is every water in which sea game is found, even if it is a river or a pool.

His words: ﴿and its food as provision for you and for the travelers﴾. "Ta'am" is for everything that is eaten, and it has been mentioned before. It has been disputed what is meant by it here. It has been said: it is what the sea casts up and what floats upon it; this was said by many of the Companions and the Successors. It has been said: its food is what is salted out of it and remains; this was said by a group, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. It has been said: its food is its salt, which crystallizes from its water, and all other plants and the like in it; this was said by some people. It has been said: what is meant by it is what is eaten of the game, that is, what is lawful to eat, which is fish only; this is what the Hanafis said.

The meaning is: the use of everything hunted in the sea is lawful for you, and what is lawful to eat from it, which is fish, is lawful for you; so the specification follows the generalization, which is a forced interpretation with no basis. "Mata'an" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: you are given enjoyment of it as enjoyment. It has been said: it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) specific to the food; meaning: the food of the sea is lawful for you as provision. This is a forced reading offered by whoever held the last view. Rather, if it is an object of purpose, it applies to all: meaning, the hunted game of the sea and its food are lawful for you as enjoyment for you; that is, for those of you who are resident, who eat it fresh, and for the "sayyarah" (travelers) among you, who take it as provision and make it dried meat. It has been said: the "sayyarah" are specifically those who ride it.

His words: ﴿And the game of the land has been forbidden for you as long as you are in ihram﴾. Meaning: what is hunted on land has been forbidden for you as long as you are in ihram. Its apparent meaning is the prohibition of hunting it for the muhrim, even if the hunter is not in ihram. The majority held this, provided the non-muhrim hunted it on behalf of the muhrim, not if he did not hunt it for his sake; and this is the preferred view, and by it the hadiths are reconciled. It has been said that it is lawful for him absolutely, and this was held by a group. It has been said that it is forbidden for him absolutely, and this was held by others. We have expanded on this in our commentary on al-Muntaqa.

His words: ﴿And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered﴾, meaning: fear Allah regarding what He has forbidden you, the One to whom you will be gathered and not to other than Him. In this is emphasis and exaggeration in warning. It is read ﴿and the game of the land has been forbidden for you﴾ with the active voice, and it is read "ma dimtum" with a kasra on the dal.

His words: ﴿Allah has made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of establishment for the people﴾. "Ja'ala" here means "khalaqa" (created). The Ka'bah was named Ka'bah because it is square, and "takh'ib" means squaring, while most Arab houses are round, not square. It has been said it was named Ka'bah for its protrusion and prominence, and every prominent thing is a ka'b, whether round or not; from this comes "ka'b" of the foot, "ku'ub" of spears, and Ka'b as a woman's breast. "Al-Bayt al-Haram" is an explanatory apposition; it has been said it is a second object, but there is no basis for this. It was called a house (bayt) because it has roofs and walls, which is the real meaning of a house, even if no one dwells in it; and it was called sacred (haram) because Allah, glorified is He, made it sacred. His words: ﴿a means of establishment for the people﴾ is how the majority read it, while Ibn 'Amir read ﴿qiyaman﴾ (qayyaman). It is in the accusative either as the second object if "ja'ala" is transitive to two objects, or as a circumstantial state if it means "khalaqa" as stated before. The meaning of it being a means of establishment is that it is the axis of their livelihood and their religion; that is, they stand in it with what sets right their religion and their worldly life: whoever is afraid is safe in it, the weak among them are supported in it, their merchants profit in it, and their worshippers worship in it.

His words: ﴿and the sacred month﴾ is conjoined to the Ka'bah. It is Dhu al-Hijjah, and it was singled out from among the sacred months because it is the time of performing hajj. It has been said it is a generic noun, and what is meant is the sacred months: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram and Rajab, for they did not seek blood in them, did not fight an enemy in them, and did not violate their sanctity; so from this aspect they were a means of establishment for the people. ﴿and the offerings and the garlands﴾: that is, Allah made the offerings and the garlands a means of establishment for the people.

By "the garlands" is meant the animals bearing garlands from among the offerings, and there is no objection to meaning the garlands themselves. The reference of "that" is to the making: that making ﴿so that you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth﴾, that is, so that you may know that Allah knows the details of the affairs of the heavens and the earth, and knows your religious and worldly interests, for these are among what is in them; so everything He has legislated for you is a bringing in of your benefit and a repelling of what harms you. ﴿and that Allah is Knowing of all things﴾: this is generalization after specification.

Then He commanded them to know that Allah is severe in punishment for whoever violates His prohibitions and does not repent from that, and that He is Forgiving and Merciful to whoever repents and turns back. Then He informed them that the duty of His Messenger is only the conveying to them; so if they do not comply and obey, they harm only themselves, and they have committed no offense except against themselves. As for the Messenger, peace be upon him, he has done what was incumbent upon him and fulfilled what Allah commanded him.

Al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir, on surah 5, verses 94–100 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿And whoever among you kills it intentionally﴾, that he said: If he kills it intentionally, or forgetfully, or by mistake, a judgment is passed upon him. If he returns to it intentionally, the punishment is hastened for him, unless Allah pardons him. And regarding His words ﴿then a penalty equivalent to what he killed of the livestock﴾, he said: When the muhrim (one in the state of ihram) kills any game, a judgment is passed upon him concerning it. If he kills a gazelle or the like, then upon him is a sheep to be slaughtered in Makkah. If he does not find one, then feeding six poor people. If he does not find that, then fasting three days. If he kills an oryx (ayl) or the like, then upon him is a cow. If he does not find one, he feeds twenty poor people. If he does not find that, he fasts twenty days. And if he kills an ostrich, a wild ass or the like, then upon him is a camel (badanah). If he does not find one, he feeds sixty poor people. If he does not find that, he fasts thirty days. The food is a mudd for each person, enough to satisfy them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hakam that ʿUmar wrote that a judgment be passed upon him in the case of error and in the case of intention. They also transmitted something similar from ʿAta'. Something similar to this has been related from groups of the early generations (al-salaf), without distinguishing between the one who acts intentionally, the one who errs, and the one who forgets. It has also been related from others that this ruling applies only to the one who acts intentionally. The early scholars have extensive statements on determining the equivalent penalty and on determining its value, in their appropriate places.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said concerning the egg of the ostrich: "A day's fast or feeding a poor person." Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted from ʿAbd Allah ibn Dhakwan, from the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar. He also transmitted from ʿAʾishah, from him (ﷺ), something similar. Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through the route of Abu al-Muhazzim, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "For the egg of the ostrich, its price."

The Prophet (ﷺ) has exempted five creatures from the animals of the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), the fawasiq (harmful creatures), as is reported in the hadiths. It is therefore permissible for the muhrim to kill them, and there is nothing upon him. Ibn Jarir transmitted from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, concerning His words, exalted is He, ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you﴾: "Whatever it casts up dead, that is its food." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, as a mawquf (non-prophetic) report, something similar. Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq something similar.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from ʿIkrimah that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq said, regarding His words ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food﴾: "The game of the sea is what our hands catch, and its food is what the sea casts up." In another wording: "Everything in it." And in another wording: "Its food is its carrion."

This is supported by what is in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of the ʿanbarah (ambergris-like whale carcass) which the sea cast up, and the Companions ate from it, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) approved of that. Also the hadith: "Its water is pure and its carrion is lawful." And the hadith: "Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful for you."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿Allah made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of establishment for mankind﴾, that he said: "A means of establishment for their religion and the markers of their pilgrimage." Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, who said: "Its establishment is that whoever turns toward it is safe."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Shihab who said: Allah made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, and the Sacred Month a means of establishment for mankind, by which they were secure in the first Jahiliyyah, such that some of them did not fear others when they met them at the House, or in the Haram, or in the Sacred Month. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿Allah made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of establishment for mankind, and the Sacred Month, and the offering, and the garlands﴾, that he said: "They are barriers which Allah preserved among people in the Jahiliyyah. A man who had committed every crime and then took refuge in the Haram would not be seized or approached. A man who met the slayer of his father in the Sacred Month would not confront him or approach him. A man who met a garlanded offering while he was eating the leaves of trees out of hunger would not confront it or approach it. When a man wanted to go to the House, he would wear a garland of hair, which protected him and kept him from people; and when he returned, he would wear a garland of idhkhir or samur, which kept him from people until he reached his family. These were barriers which Allah preserved among people in the Jahiliyyah." Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam, regarding ﴿a means of establishment for mankind﴾, that he said: "Security."

The apparent meaning of the verse requires two judges other than the offender.

His words: ﴿as an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾. "Hadyan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) or as an apposition (badal) to "mithl". "Baligha al-ka'bah" is an attribute of "hadyan", because the construction is not a true (genitive) construction. The meaning is that if the two judge the penalty, then it is treated as an offering is treated: sent to Makkah, slaughtered there, marked (ish'ar) and garlanded (taqlid). The intended meaning is not the Ka'bah itself, for an offering does not reach it; rather the Sacred Precinct is meant, and there is no disagreement on this.

His words: ﴿or an expiation﴾ is conjoined to the position (mahall) of "of the livestock", which is nominative, since it is the predicate of an omitted subject. ﴿food for the needy﴾ is an explanatory apposition to "expiation", or a substitute for it, or the predicate of an omitted subject. ﴿or its equivalent in fasting﴾ is conjoined to "food". It has been said that it is conjoined to "penalty", but that is weak. So the offender has a choice among these mentioned types. "'Adl" of a thing is what equals it from a different kind. ﴿fasting﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). The scholars have established the equivalent of each game in terms of feeding and fasting. The majority of scholars held that the offender is given the choice among the mentioned types. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the muhrim is not excused by feeding or fasting unless he does not find an offering. "'Adl" with a fath and a kasra on the ayn are two dialects, both meaning equivalence; this is said by al-Kisa'i.

Al-Farra' said: "'idl" with a kasra on the ayn means its like of the same kind, and with a fath on the ayn means its like of a different kind. The Basrans said likewise to what al-Kisa'i said.

His words: ﴿that he may taste the bad consequence of his deed﴾. "'Ala" (upon him) is for imposing the penalty; meaning: We imposed that upon him so that he may taste the bad consequence of his deed. Tasting is used figuratively for experiencing hardship, and similar to it is ﴿Taste; indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49]. Wabal means evil outcome; a wabil pasture is one that causes harm after it is eaten, and wabil food is that which is heavy.

His words: ﴿Allah has pardoned what has passed﴾, meaning in your pre-Islamic time, from your killing of game. It has been said: what passed before the revelation of the expiation. ﴿And whoever returns﴾ to what you were forbidden from, killing game after this clarification, ﴿Allah will take retribution from him﴾: this is the predicate of an omitted subject; meaning: he, Allah takes retribution from him. It has been said: the meaning is that Allah will take retribution from him in the Hereafter, punishing him for his sin; and it has been said: He takes retribution from him by the expiation. Shurayh and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he is judged upon the first occurrence, and if he returns he is not judged, but it is said to him: "Go, Allah will take retribution from you," meaning: your sin is too great to be expiated.

His words: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea﴾. The address is to every Muslim, or to those in ihram specifically. The game of the sea is what is hunted in it, and what is meant by "sea" here is every water in which sea game is found, even if it is a river or a pool.

His words: ﴿and its food as provision for you and for the travelers﴾. "Ta'am" is for everything that is eaten, and it has been mentioned before. It has been disputed what is meant by it here. It has been said: it is what the sea casts up and what floats upon it; this was said by many of the Companions and the Successors. It has been said: its food is what is salted out of it and remains; this was said by a group, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. It has been said: its food is its salt, which crystallizes from its water, and all other plants and the like in it; this was said by some people. It has been said: what is meant by it is what is eaten of the game, that is, what is lawful to eat, which is fish only; this is what the Hanafis said.

The meaning is: the use of everything hunted in the sea is lawful for you, and what is lawful to eat from it, which is fish, is lawful for you; so the specification follows the generalization, which is a forced interpretation with no basis. "Mata'an" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: you are given enjoyment of it as enjoyment. It has been said: it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) specific to the food; meaning: the food of the sea is lawful for you as provision. This is a forced reading offered by whoever held the last view. Rather, if it is an object of purpose, it applies to all: meaning, the hunted game of the sea and its food are lawful for you as enjoyment for you; that is, for those of you who are resident, who eat it fresh, and for the "sayyarah" (travelers) among you, who take it as provision and make it dried meat. It has been said: the "sayyarah" are specifically those who ride it.

His words: ﴿And the game of the land has been forbidden for you as long as you are in ihram﴾. Meaning: what is hunted on land has been forbidden for you as long as you are in ihram. Its apparent meaning is the prohibition of hunting it for the muhrim, even if the hunter is not in ihram. The majority held this, provided the non-muhrim hunted it on behalf of the muhrim, not if he did not hunt it for his sake; and this is the preferred view, and by it the hadiths are reconciled. It has been said that it is lawful for him absolutely, and this was held by a group. It has been said that it is forbidden for him absolutely, and this was held by others. We have expanded on this in our commentary on al-Muntaqa.

His words: ﴿And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered﴾, meaning: fear Allah regarding what He has forbidden you, the One to whom you will be gathered and not to other than Him. In this is emphasis and exaggeration in warning. It is read ﴿and the game of the land has been forbidden for you﴾ with the active voice, and it is read "ma dimtum" with a kasra on the dal.

His words: ﴿Allah has made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of establishment for the people﴾. "Ja'ala" here means "khalaqa" (created). The Ka'bah was named Ka'bah because it is square, and "takh'ib" means squaring, while most Arab houses are round, not square. It has been said it was named Ka'bah for its protrusion and prominence, and every prominent thing is a ka'b, whether round or not; from this comes "ka'b" of the foot, "ku'ub" of spears, and Ka'b as a woman's breast. "Al-Bayt al-Haram" is an explanatory apposition; it has been said it is a second object, but there is no basis for this. It was called a house (bayt) because it has roofs and walls, which is the real meaning of a house, even if no one dwells in it; and it was called sacred (haram) because Allah, glorified is He, made it sacred. His words: ﴿a means of establishment for the people﴾ is how the majority read it, while Ibn 'Amir read ﴿qiyaman﴾ (qayyaman). It is in the accusative either as the second object if "ja'ala" is transitive to two objects, or as a circumstantial state if it means "khalaqa" as stated before. The meaning of it being a means of establishment is that it is the axis of their livelihood and their religion; that is, they stand in it with what sets right their religion and their worldly life: whoever is afraid is safe in it, the weak among them are supported in it, their merchants profit in it, and their worshippers worship in it.

His words: ﴿and the sacred month﴾ is conjoined to the Ka'bah. It is Dhu al-Hijjah, and it was singled out from among the sacred months because it is the time of performing hajj. It has been said it is a generic noun, and what is meant is the sacred months: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram and Rajab, for they did not seek blood in them, did not fight an enemy in them, and did not violate their sanctity; so from this aspect they were a means of establishment for the people. ﴿and the offerings and the garlands﴾: that is, Allah made the offerings and the garlands a means of establishment for the people.

By "the garlands" is meant the animals bearing garlands from among the offerings, and there is no objection to meaning the garlands themselves. The reference of "that" is to the making: that making ﴿so that you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth﴾, that is, so that you may know that Allah knows the details of the affairs of the heavens and the earth, and knows your religious and worldly interests, for these are among what is in them; so everything He has legislated for you is a bringing in of your benefit and a repelling of what harms you. ﴿and that Allah is Knowing of all things﴾: this is generalization after specification.

Then He commanded them to know that Allah is severe in punishment for whoever violates His prohibitions and does not repent from that, and that He is Forgiving and Merciful to whoever repents and turns back. Then He informed them that the duty of His Messenger is only the conveying to them; so if they do not comply and obey, they harm only themselves, and they have committed no offense except against themselves. As for the Messenger, peace be upon him, he has done what was incumbent upon him and fulfilled what Allah commanded him.

Al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir, on surah 5, verses 94–100 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿And whoever among you kills it intentionally﴾, that he said: If he kills it intentionally, or forgetfully, or by mistake, a judgment is passed upon him. If he returns to it intentionally, the punishment is hastened for him, unless Allah pardons him. And regarding His words ﴿then a penalty equivalent to what he killed of the livestock﴾, he said: When the muhrim (one in the state of ihram) kills any game, a judgment is passed upon him concerning it. If he kills a gazelle or the like, then upon him is a sheep to be slaughtered in Makkah. If he does not find one, then feeding six poor people. If he does not find that, then fasting three days. If he kills an oryx (ayl) or the like, then upon him is a cow. If he does not find one, he feeds twenty poor people. If he does not find that, he fasts twenty days. And if he kills an ostrich, a wild ass or the like, then upon him is a camel (badanah). If he does not find one, he feeds sixty poor people. If he does not find that, he fasts thirty days. The food is a mudd for each person, enough to satisfy them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hakam that ʿUmar wrote that a judgment be passed upon him in the case of error and in the case of intention. They also transmitted something similar from ʿAta'. Something similar to this has been related from groups of the early generations (al-salaf), without distinguishing between the one who acts intentionally, the one who errs, and the one who forgets. It has also been related from others that this ruling applies only to the one who acts intentionally. The early scholars have extensive statements on determining the equivalent penalty and on determining its value, in their appropriate places.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said concerning the egg of the ostrich: "A day's fast or feeding a poor person." Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted from ʿAbd Allah ibn Dhakwan, from the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar. He also transmitted from ʿAʾishah, from him (ﷺ), something similar. Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through the route of Abu al-Muhazzim, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "For the egg of the ostrich, its price."

The Prophet (ﷺ) has exempted five creatures from the animals of the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), the fawasiq (harmful creatures), as is reported in the hadiths. It is therefore permissible for the muhrim to kill them, and there is nothing upon him. Ibn Jarir transmitted from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, concerning His words, exalted is He, ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you﴾: "Whatever it casts up dead, that is its food." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, as a mawquf (non-prophetic) report, something similar. Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq something similar.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from ʿIkrimah that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq said, regarding His words ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food﴾: "The game of the sea is what our hands catch, and its food is what the sea casts up." In another wording: "Everything in it." And in another wording: "Its food is its carrion."

This is supported by what is in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of the ʿanbarah (ambergris-like whale carcass) which the sea cast up, and the Companions ate from it, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) approved of that. Also the hadith: "Its water is pure and its carrion is lawful." And the hadith: "Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful for you."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿Allah made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of establishment for mankind﴾, that he said: "A means of establishment for their religion and the markers of their pilgrimage." Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, who said: "Its establishment is that whoever turns toward it is safe."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Shihab who said: Allah made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, and the Sacred Month a means of establishment for mankind, by which they were secure in the first Jahiliyyah, such that some of them did not fear others when they met them at the House, or in the Haram, or in the Sacred Month. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿Allah made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of establishment for mankind, and the Sacred Month, and the offering, and the garlands﴾, that he said: "They are barriers which Allah preserved among people in the Jahiliyyah. A man who had committed every crime and then took refuge in the Haram would not be seized or approached. A man who met the slayer of his father in the Sacred Month would not confront him or approach him. A man who met a garlanded offering while he was eating the leaves of trees out of hunger would not confront it or approach it. When a man wanted to go to the House, he would wear a garland of hair, which protected him and kept him from people; and when he returned, he would wear a garland of idhkhir or samur, which kept him from people until he reached his family. These were barriers which Allah preserved among people in the Jahiliyyah." Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam, regarding ﴿a means of establishment for mankind﴾, that he said: "Security."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 94–100 (part 1 of 2):

His words: ﴿Allah will surely test you﴾, meaning: He will surely try you. The lam is the answer to an omitted oath. Hunting (al-sayd) was one of the means of livelihood of the Arabs, so Allah tested them by its prohibition during ihram and within the Sacred Precinct (al-haram), just as He tested the Children of Israel that they should not transgress on the Sabbath. The verse was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. Some of them were in ihram and some were not, so when game appeared their circumstances differed regarding it. The scholars have differed concerning who is addressed by this verse: are they those who are not in ihram (al-muhillun) or those who are in ihram (al-muhrimun)? Malik held the first view, and Ibn 'Abbas the second. The preferred view is that the address is to all of them, and there is no basis for restricting it to some and not others. The "min" in ﴿of the game﴾ is partitive (lil-tab'id), and it refers to land game, as stated by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari and others. It has also been said that "min" is explanatory (bayaniyyah), meaning: a small/insignificant thing of the game, and the indefiniteness of "shay'" (thing) is for belittling.

His words: ﴿that your hands and your spears can reach﴾.
Ibn Wathhab read (yanaluhu) with a ya' (third person). This clause implies the generality of game, and that there is no difference between what is taken by the hand, which cannot flee, such as young animals and eggs, and what the spears reach, which can flee. He singled out the hands for mention because they are what the hunter most uses to take game, and he singled out the spears for mention because they were the greatest hunting instruments among the Arabs.

His words: ﴿that Allah may make evident who fears Him unseen﴾, meaning: that there may be distinguished before Allah who among you fears Him, by reason of His punishment in the Hereafter, for He is unseen and not present before you. ﴿So whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment﴾, meaning: after this clarification by which Allah has tested you, because transgression after knowledge of the prohibition is defiance of Allah, glorified is He, and audacity against Him.

His words: ﴿Do not kill game while you are in ihram﴾. He forbade them from killing game while in the state of ihram. Its meaning is also ﴿not hunting game while you are in ihram﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1]. This prohibition includes everyone among the believing men and women, because it is said: rajul haram (a man in ihram) and imra'ah haram (a woman in ihram), and the plural is hurum. And ahrama al-rajul means he entered the Sacred Precinct.

His words: ﴿And whoever of you kills it intentionally﴾. The one who acts intentionally (al-muta'ammid) is the one who aims at something while knowing he is in ihram. The mistaken one (al-mukhti') is the one who aims at something and hits game. The forgetful one (al-nasi) is the one who deliberately hunts game and does not remember his ihram.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ahmad in one narration, and Dawud from him, argued from the Almighty's restriction of the ruling to the intentional person that there is no expiation (kaffarah) for others; rather, it is obligatory only upon him alone. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Tawus and Abu Thawr said likewise. It has also been said that expiation is obligatory upon the mistaken and the forgetful just as it is upon the intentional, and they took the condition of intention as coming in the form of what is usual. This is narrated from 'Umar, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i and al-Zuhri, and Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and their companions said likewise, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. It has also been said that expiation is obligatory upon one who intentionally kills game while forgetting his ihram; Mujahid said this, and he said: if he was mindful of his ihram, then he has exited ihram and has no valid hajj, because he has committed what is forbidden in his ihram, so it is nullified for him, just as if he spoke during prayer or broke his wudu' during it.

His words: ﴿then the penalty is an equivalent of what he killed of the livestock﴾, meaning: then upon him is a penalty equivalent to what he killed, and ﴿of the livestock﴾ is an explanation of the equivalent penalty. It has been said: the intended meaning is equivalence in value, and it has been said: in form.

Abu Hanifah took the first view, while Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and the majority took the second, and it is the truth, because the explanation of the equivalent as livestock indicates that. Likewise, the phrase "as an offering reaching the Ka'bah" indicates it. It is narrated from Abu Hanifah that it is permissible to give the value even if the equivalent is found, and that the muhrim has a choice.

It is read ﴿fa-jaza'uhu mithlu ma qatala﴾ and it is read ﴿fa-jaza'u mithli﴾ with the construct of jaza' to mithl, and it is read with both in the accusative, on the assumption of "then let him give a penalty equal to what he killed". Al-Hasan read ﴿al-na'mi﴾ with a sukun on the ayn for lightness.

﴿judged by it﴾, meaning by the penalty or by the equivalent of what he killed, two just men from among you, meaning two men well known for justice among the Muslims. If the two judge something, it is binding; if they disagree, the matter is referred to others. It is not permissible for the offender to be one of the two judges. It has been said that it is permissible. The first view is that of Abu Hanifah, and the second is that of al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions. The apparent meaning of the verse requires two judges other than the offender.

By "the garlands" is meant the animals bearing garlands from among the offerings, and there is no objection to meaning the garlands themselves. The reference of "that" is to the making: that making ﴿so that you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth﴾, that is, so that you may know that Allah knows the details of the affairs of the heavens and the earth, and knows your religious and worldly interests, for these are among what is in them; so everything He has legislated for you is a bringing in of your benefit and a repelling of what harms you. ﴿and that Allah is Knowing of all things﴾: this is generalization after specification.

Then He commanded them to know that Allah is severe in punishment for whoever violates His prohibitions and does not repent from that, and that He is Forgiving and Merciful to whoever repents and turns back. Then He informed them that the duty of His Messenger is only the conveying to them; so if they do not comply and obey, they harm only themselves, and they have committed no offense except against themselves. As for the Messenger, peace be upon him, he has done what was incumbent upon him and fulfilled what Allah commanded him.

Al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir, on surah 5, verses 94–100 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿And whoever among you kills it intentionally﴾, that he said: If he kills it intentionally, or forgetfully, or by mistake, a judgment is passed upon him. If he returns to it intentionally, the punishment is hastened for him, unless Allah pardons him. And regarding His words ﴿then a penalty equivalent to what he killed of the livestock﴾, he said: When the muhrim (one in the state of ihram) kills any game, a judgment is passed upon him concerning it. If he kills a gazelle or the like, then upon him is a sheep to be slaughtered in Makkah. If he does not find one, then feeding six poor people. If he does not find that, then fasting three days. If he kills an oryx (ayl) or the like, then upon him is a cow. If he does not find one, he feeds twenty poor people. If he does not find that, he fasts twenty days. And if he kills an ostrich, a wild ass or the like, then upon him is a camel (badanah). If he does not find one, he feeds sixty poor people. If he does not find that, he fasts thirty days. The food is a mudd for each person, enough to satisfy them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hakam that ʿUmar wrote that a judgment be passed upon him in the case of error and in the case of intention. They also transmitted something similar from ʿAta'. Something similar to this has been related from groups of the early generations (al-salaf), without distinguishing between the one who acts intentionally, the one who errs, and the one who forgets. It has also been related from others that this ruling applies only to the one who acts intentionally. The early scholars have extensive statements on determining the equivalent penalty and on determining its value, in their appropriate places.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said concerning the egg of the ostrich: "A day's fast or feeding a poor person." Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted from ʿAbd Allah ibn Dhakwan, from the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar. He also transmitted from ʿAʾishah, from him (ﷺ), something similar. Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through the route of Abu al-Muhazzim, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "For the egg of the ostrich, its price."

The Prophet (ﷺ) has exempted five creatures from the animals of the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), the fawasiq (harmful creatures), as is reported in the hadiths. It is therefore permissible for the muhrim to kill them, and there is nothing upon him. Ibn Jarir transmitted from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, concerning His words, exalted is He, ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you﴾: "Whatever it casts up dead, that is its food." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, as a mawquf (non-prophetic) report, something similar. Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq something similar.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from ʿIkrimah that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq said, regarding His words ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food﴾: "The game of the sea is what our hands catch, and its food is what the sea casts up." In another wording: "Everything in it." And in another wording: "Its food is its carrion."

This is supported by what is in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of the ʿanbarah (ambergris-like whale carcass) which the sea cast up, and the Companions ate from it, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) approved of that. Also the hadith: "Its water is pure and its carrion is lawful." And the hadith: "Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful for you."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿Allah made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of establishment for mankind﴾, that he said: "A means of establishment for their religion and the markers of their pilgrimage." Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, who said: "Its establishment is that whoever turns toward it is safe."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Shihab who said: Allah made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, and the Sacred Month a means of establishment for mankind, by which they were secure in the first Jahiliyyah, such that some of them did not fear others when they met them at the House, or in the Haram, or in the Sacred Month. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿Allah made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of establishment for mankind, and the Sacred Month, and the offering, and the garlands﴾, that he said: "They are barriers which Allah preserved among people in the Jahiliyyah. A man who had committed every crime and then took refuge in the Haram would not be seized or approached. A man who met the slayer of his father in the Sacred Month would not confront him or approach him. A man who met a garlanded offering while he was eating the leaves of trees out of hunger would not confront it or approach it. When a man wanted to go to the House, he would wear a garland of hair, which protected him and kept him from people; and when he returned, he would wear a garland of idhkhir or samur, which kept him from people until he reached his family. These were barriers which Allah preserved among people in the Jahiliyyah." Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam, regarding ﴿a means of establishment for mankind﴾, that he said: "Security."

It was said: what is meant by "the bad" and "the good" is the unlawful and the lawful. It was also said: the believer and the disbeliever. It was said: the disobedient and the obedient. And it was said: the inferior and the excellent.

The more appropriate view is that the consideration is the generality of the wording, so it includes these things mentioned and others that are described as bad or good, among persons, deeds and statements. The bad is not equal to the good in any state whatsoever.

His saying: ﴿Even if the abundance of the bad should impress you﴾. It was said: the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it was also said: it is to every addressee who is fit to be addressed with this. What is meant is the negation of equality in all states, even in the state where the bad impresses the beholder because of its abundance. For this abundance, together with the bad, is considered non-existent, because the badness of a thing nullifies its benefit, erases its blessing, and removes its usefulness. The waw is either for the circumstantial state (hal) or for coordination with an implied antecedent. That is: the bad and the good are not equal, even if the abundance of the bad does not impress you; and even if the abundance of the bad impresses you, as in your saying, "Be kind to so-and-so even if he wrongs you," meaning: be kind to him if he does not wrong you, and even if he wrongs you. The answer of "even if" (law) is omitted, meaning: even if the abundance of the bad impresses you, they are still not equal.

His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you﴾. That is, do not ask about things for which you have no need to ask and which are not among what concerns you in the matter of your religion. So His saying ﴿if they are disclosed to you, they will distress you﴾ is in the place of a genitive as an attribute of "things": that is, do not ask about things characterized by this attribute, namely that if they become manifest to you and you are obligated by them, they will distress you. God forbade them from frequently questioning the Messenger of God (ﷺ), for asking about what does not concern you and what no need calls for may be a cause of its being made obligatory upon the questioner and upon others.

His saying: ﴿And if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you﴾. This sentence is part of the attributive clause of "things." The meaning is: do not ask about things which, if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, [will be disclosed to you]. This is while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is among you and revelation is descending upon him. ﴿They will be disclosed to you﴾, that is, they will become manifest to you through what the Prophet (ﷺ) answers you with, or what revelation brings down, and that will be a cause of burdensome obligations, making obligatory what was not obligatory and forbidding what was not forbidden. This is in contrast to asking about them after revelation has ceased with the death of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), for then there is no obligation or prohibition that results from the question.

Some of the exegetes thought that the second conditional clause in it permits asking while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is present and revelation is descending upon him. So he said: the first conditional clause indicated the impermissibility of asking, and the second indicated its permissibility. He said the meaning is: "And if you ask about other things, of which there is need, they will be disclosed to you by the answer of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about them." He took the pronoun in "about them" to refer to things other than the things mentioned, and he likened this to His saying: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12], meaning Adam, then He said: ﴿Then We made him a sperm-drop﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 13], meaning the son of Adam.

His saying: ﴿God has pardoned that﴾, that is, He has pardoned what has passed of your questioning, so do not return to that.

It was also said: the meaning is that those things about which you asked are among what God has pardoned and has not made obligatory upon you. So how can you cause, by asking, the making obligatory of what God has pardoned and is not binding? The pronoun in "about them" refers, according to the first view, to the earlier question, and according to the second, to things. In that case the clause "God has pardoned that" is a third attribute of "things." The first view is more appropriate, because the second entails that the thing asked about had been legislated by God and then He pardoned it. It is possible to say that pardon here means leaving aside: that is, God left them and did not mention them with anything, so do not search after them. This is a sound meaning which does not entail that false consequence. Then He, glory be to Him, used the intensive form in describing Himself as Forgiving and Forbearing, to indicate that He does not hasten punishment upon the one who disobeys Him, because of the abundance of His forgiveness and the vastness of His forbearance.

His saying: ﴿A people before you did ask about them, then became disbelievers because of them﴾. The pronoun refers to the question understood from ﴿Do not ask﴾, but it is not this same question; rather it is like it in being something for which there is no need and which religious necessity does not require, and then they did not act upon it, but rather became disbelievers in it, that is, they concealed it and abandoned acting upon it. This is like the people of Salih asking for the she-camel, and the companions of Jesus asking for the table spread with food. The prohibition in this verse must be restricted to what no need calls for, as we have previously stated, because a matter for which need calls in the affairs of religion and of the world, God has permitted asking about, as He said: ﴿So ask the people of the reminder, if you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 43]. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May God fight them! Why did they not ask? For the cure of ignorance is asking."

His saying: ﴿God did not ordain any bahira﴾. This is an independent statement which includes a refutation of the people of ignorance regarding what they innovated, and here "ordain" (ja'ala) is in the sense of "name," as He said: ﴿Indeed We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 3]. The bahira (a she-camel dedicated and marked as forbidden, a sacred name for a practice of the pre-Islamic Arabs) is a form (fa'ila) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ula), like nati'a and dhabiha, and it is derived from bahr, which is slitting the ear.

Ibn Sida said: the bahira is the one that is left unherded. It was said: it is the one whose milk is dedicated to the idols, so no one among people milks it, and slitting its ear was made a sign of that. Al-Shafi'i said: when a she-camel gave birth to five females in succession, its ear was slit and it was forbidden. It was also said: when a she-camel gave birth to five offspring, if the fifth was male, they slit its ear and men and women ate it; and if the fifth was female, they slit its ear and its meat and milk were forbidden to women. It was also said: when a she-camel gave birth to five offspring without restriction to females, they slit its ear, forbade its riding and its milk.

The sa'iba (a freed animal dedicated to a deity or vow) is the she-camel that is set free, or the camel that is set free by a vow made by a man, if God delivers him from an illness or brings him to a station; so it is not held back from pasture or water, and no one rides it. This was said by Abu 'Ubayd. A poet said:

"And a sa'iba for God grows, out of gratitude, if God has granted health to 'Amir and Mujashi'."

It was also said: it is the one left free for God, with no restraint upon it and no herdsman for it. From this is the saying of the poet:

"You slaughtered a she-camel that was for my Lord, left free, so rise up for the retribution."

It was also said: it is the one that followed ten females in succession with no male among them; then its back is not ridden, its wool is not shorn, and only a guest drinks its milk. It was also said: they used to set free the slave, so he would go wherever he wished, with no one having authority over him.

The wasila: it was said that it is the she-camel when she gives birth to a female after a female. It was also said: it is the sheep which, when it gave birth to a female, was for them, and if it gave birth to a male, it was for their gods, and if it gave birth to a male and a female, they said it "joined" its brother, so they did not slaughter the male for their gods. It was also said: when the sheep gave birth to seven offspring, they examined: if the seventh was male, it was slaughtered and men and women ate of it; if it was female, it was left among the sheep; and if it was male and female, they said it "joined" its brother, so it was not slaughtered on its account, and its meat was forbidden to women, unless it died, in which case men and women ate it.

The ham: the stallion that protects its back from being ridden. When a young one rode the stallion, they said he has protected his back, so it is not ridden. A poet said:

"Abu Qabus protected them in the glory of his kingdom, as the stallion protects the offspring of its offspring."

It was also said: it is the stallion when it sired ten from its loins; they said: he has protected his back, so he is not ridden, nor prevented from pasture or water.

Then God, glory be to Him, described them: they did not say that except as a fabrication against God and a lie, neither by a legislation God legislated for them nor by an intellect that guided them to it. Glory be to God the Mighty, how weak and feeble are the minds of these people, who commit these deeds which are pure foolishness and the very essence of stupidity. ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what God has sent down and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon."﴾ These are the deeds of their forefathers and the customs they established for them. God spoke the truth, glory be to Him, when He said: ﴿Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?﴾, that is, even though they were ignorant and astray. The waw is for the circumstantial state, and the interrogative hamza entered upon it. It was also said it is for coordination with an implied sentence: that is, do they suppose that, even if their fathers...? The discussion of a similar verse has already occurred in al-Baqarah.

This saying which the people of ignorance uttered has become the object of the eyes of the blind followers (muqallidah) and their staff upon which they lean, if the caller of truth calls them and the crier of the Book and the Sunnah cries out to them. Their argument from one they follow, who is like them in being bound by God's legislation, while his statement contradicts the Book of God or the Sunnah of His Messenger, is like the saying of these people. There is no difference except in the mere verbal expression, not in the meaning upon which the conveying and receiving of knowledge revolves. O God, forgive us.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi concerning the verse: "The bad are the polytheists, and the good are the believers."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Anas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) delivered a sermon the like of which I had never heard. A man said, 'Who is my father?' He said, 'So-and-so.' Then this verse was revealed: 'Do not ask about things...'" Al-Bukhari and others narrated something similar from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas. In other narrations, this questioner was identified as 'Abd Allah ibn Hudhafah, and that he said, "Who is my father?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Your father is Hudhafah."

Ibn Hibban narrated from Abu Hurayrah that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) delivered a sermon and said: 'O people, God has made the Hajj obligatory upon you.' A man stood up and said, 'Every year, O Messenger of God?' He remained silent, and the man repeated it three times. He said: 'If I had said yes, it would have become obligatory, and if it had become obligatory you would not have performed it. Leave me as I leave you, for those before you perished through their abundance of questioning and their disagreement with their prophets. So when I forbid you from something, avoid it, and when I command you with something, do of it what you are able.'" This verse, namely "Do not ask about things," was revealed concerning that. Something similar was narrated from him by Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated something similar from Ibn 'Abbas. Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar from 'Ali, and all of them stated explicitly in their narrations that the verse was revealed concerning that.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "They used to ask about a thing which was lawful for them, and they kept asking until it became forbidden to them; and when it became forbidden to them, they fell into it." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The greatest of the Muslims in crime against the Muslims is the one who asks about a thing that was not forbidden, so it becomes forbidden because of his question."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God has set limits, so do not transgress them; He has imposed obligations, so do not neglect them; He has forbidden things, so do not violate them; and He has left things, not out of forgetfulness but out of mercy for you, so accept them and do not search after them." Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Do not ask about things﴾, that he said: "The bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab that he said: The *bahirah* (a she-camel whose milk was withheld from the *tawaghit*, idols, so that no one among the people would milk her). The *sa'ibah* (the animal they released for their gods, on which nothing was carried). The *wasilah* (the virgin she-camel that gave birth first to a female at the beginning of the camels' offspring, and then gave birth to a female again after that). They used to release these for their idols if one of the two was joined to the other with no male between them. The *ham* (the stallion camel that services the counted number of mares). When he had finished his service, they left him for the idols and exempted him from burden, so nothing was carried on him, and they called him the *ham*.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, through the chain of Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas that he said: The *bahirah* is the she-camel which, when she had given birth to five offspring, they looked at the fifth. If it was a male, they slaughtered it, and only the men ate it, not the women. If it was a female, they slit its ears and said: "This is a *bahirah*." As for the *sa'ibah*, they used to release some of their livestock for their gods, not riding them, not milking them for milk, not shearing their wool for anything, and not carrying anything on them. As for the *wasilah*, it is the sheep which, when it had given birth to seven offspring, they looked at the seventh. If it was a male or a female, and it was dead, the men shared in eating it, not the women. If it was a female, they spared it. If it was a male or a female in one birth, they spared both and said: "Its sister has joined it, so she has forbidden it to us." As for the *ham*, it is the stallion camel when it has fathered offspring from his offspring. They said: "This one has protected his back." So they did not carry anything on him, did not shear his wool, and did not prevent him from pasture or from a watering place from which he drinks, even if the water-place belonged to someone other than its owner.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related something similar from him through the chain of al-Awfi.

[p. 399]

The pronoun refers to the question understood from ﴿Do not ask﴾, but it is not this same question; rather it is like it in being something for which there is no need and which religious necessity does not require, and then they did not act upon it, but rather became disbelievers in it, that is, they concealed it and abandoned acting upon it. This is like the people of Salih asking for the she-camel, and the companions of Jesus asking for the table spread with food. The prohibition in this verse must be restricted to what no need calls for, as we have previously stated, because a matter for which need calls in the affairs of religion and of the world, God has permitted asking about, as He said: ﴿So ask the people of the reminder, if you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 43]. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May God fight them! Why did they not ask? For the cure of ignorance is asking."

His saying: ﴿God did not ordain any bahira﴾. This is an independent statement which includes a refutation of the people of ignorance regarding what they innovated, and here "ordain" (ja'ala) is in the sense of "name," as He said: ﴿Indeed We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 3]. The bahira (a she-camel dedicated and marked as forbidden, a sacred name for a practice of the pre-Islamic Arabs) is a form (fa'ila) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ula), like nati'a and dhabiha, and it is derived from bahr, which is slitting the ear.

Ibn Sida said: the bahira is the one that is left unherded. It was said: it is the one whose milk is dedicated to the idols, so no one among people milks it, and slitting its ear was made a sign of that. Al-Shafi'i said: when a she-camel gave birth to five females in succession, its ear was slit and it was forbidden. It was also said: when a she-camel gave birth to five offspring, if the fifth was male, they slit its ear and men and women ate it; and if the fifth was female, they slit its ear and its meat and milk were forbidden to women. It was also said: when a she-camel gave birth to five offspring without restriction to females, they slit its ear, forbade its riding and its milk.

The sa'iba (a freed animal dedicated to a deity or vow) is the she-camel that is set free, or the camel that is set free by a vow made by a man, if God delivers him from an illness or brings him to a station; so it is not held back from pasture or water, and no one rides it. This was said by Abu 'Ubayd. A poet said:

"And a sa'iba for God grows, out of gratitude, if God has granted health to 'Amir and Mujashi'."

It was also said: it is the one left free for God, with no restraint upon it and no herdsman for it. From this is the saying of the poet:

"You slaughtered a she-camel that was for my Lord, left free, so rise up for the retribution."

It was also said: it is the one that followed ten females in succession with no male among them; then its back is not ridden, its wool is not shorn, and only a guest drinks its milk. It was also said: they used to set free the slave, so he would go wherever he wished, with no one having authority over him.

The wasila: it was said that it is the she-camel when she gives birth to a female after a female. It was also said: it is the sheep which, when it gave birth to a female, was for them, and if it gave birth to a male, it was for their gods, and if it gave birth to a male and a female, they said it "joined" its brother, so they did not slaughter the male for their gods. It was also said: when the sheep gave birth to seven offspring, they examined: if the seventh was male, it was slaughtered and men and women ate of it; if it was female, it was left among the sheep; and if it was male and female, they said it "joined" its brother, so it was not slaughtered on its account, and its meat was forbidden to women, unless it died, in which case men and women ate it.

The ham: the stallion that protects its back from being ridden. When a young one rode the stallion, they said he has protected his back, so it is not ridden. A poet said:

"Abu Qabus protected them in the glory of his kingdom, as the stallion protects the offspring of its offspring."

It was also said: it is the stallion when it sired ten from its loins; they said: he has protected his back, so he is not ridden, nor prevented from pasture or water.

Then God, glory be to Him, described them: they did not say that except as a fabrication against God and a lie, neither by a legislation God legislated for them nor by an intellect that guided them to it. Glory be to God the Mighty, how weak and feeble are the minds of these people, who commit these deeds which are pure foolishness and the very essence of stupidity. ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what God has sent down and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon."﴾ These are the deeds of their forefathers and the customs they established for them. God spoke the truth, glory be to Him, when He said: ﴿Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?﴾, that is, even though they were ignorant and astray. The waw is for the circumstantial state, and the interrogative hamza entered upon it. It was also said it is for coordination with an implied sentence: that is, do they suppose that, even if their fathers...? The discussion of a similar verse has already occurred in al-Baqarah.

This saying which the people of ignorance uttered has become the object of the eyes of the blind followers (muqallidah) and their staff upon which they lean, if the caller of truth calls them and the crier of the Book and the Sunnah cries out to them. Their argument from one they follow, who is like them in being bound by God's legislation, while his statement contradicts the Book of God or the Sunnah of His Messenger, is like the saying of these people. There is no difference except in the mere verbal expression, not in the meaning upon which the conveying and receiving of knowledge revolves. O God, forgive us.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi concerning the verse: "The bad are the polytheists, and the good are the believers."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Anas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) delivered a sermon the like of which I had never heard. A man said, 'Who is my father?' He said, 'So-and-so.' Then this verse was revealed: 'Do not ask about things...'" Al-Bukhari and others narrated something similar from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas. In other narrations, this questioner was identified as 'Abd Allah ibn Hudhafah, and that he said, "Who is my father?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Your father is Hudhafah."

Ibn Hibban narrated from Abu Hurayrah that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) delivered a sermon and said: 'O people, God has made the Hajj obligatory upon you.' A man stood up and said, 'Every year, O Messenger of God?' He remained silent, and the man repeated it three times. He said: 'If I had said yes, it would have become obligatory, and if it had become obligatory you would not have performed it. Leave me as I leave you, for those before you perished through their abundance of questioning and their disagreement with their prophets. So when I forbid you from something, avoid it, and when I command you with something, do of it what you are able.'" This verse, namely "Do not ask about things," was revealed concerning that. Something similar was narrated from him by Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated something similar from Ibn 'Abbas. Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar from 'Ali, and all of them stated explicitly in their narrations that the verse was revealed concerning that.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "They used to ask about a thing which was lawful for them, and they kept asking until it became forbidden to them; and when it became forbidden to them, they fell into it." Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The greatest of the Muslims in crime against the Muslims is the one who asks about a thing that was not forbidden, so it becomes forbidden because of his question."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God has set limits, so do not transgress them; He has imposed obligations, so do not neglect them; He has forbidden things, so do not violate them; and He has left things, not out of forgetfulness but out of mercy for you, so accept them and do not search after them." Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Do not ask about things﴾, that he said: "The bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab that he said: The *bahirah* (a she-camel whose milk was withheld from the *tawaghit*, idols, so that no one among the people would milk her). The *sa'ibah* (the animal they released for their gods, on which nothing was carried). The *wasilah* (the virgin she-camel that gave birth first to a female at the beginning of the camels' offspring, and then gave birth to a female again after that). They used to release these for their idols if one of the two was joined to the other with no male between them. The *ham* (the stallion camel that services the counted number of mares). When he had finished his service, they left him for the idols and exempted him from burden, so nothing was carried on him, and they called him the *ham*.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, through the chain of Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas that he said: The *bahirah* is the she-camel which, when she had given birth to five offspring, they looked at the fifth. If it was a male, they slaughtered it, and only the men ate it, not the women. If it was a female, they slit its ears and said: "This is a *bahirah*." As for the *sa'ibah*, they used to release some of their livestock for their gods, not riding them, not milking them for milk, not shearing their wool for anything, and not carrying anything on them. As for the *wasilah*, it is the sheep which, when it had given birth to seven offspring, they looked at the seventh. If it was a male or a female, and it was dead, the men shared in eating it, not the women. If it was a female, they spared it. If it was a male or a female in one birth, they spared both and said: "Its sister has joined it, so she has forbidden it to us." As for the *ham*, it is the stallion camel when it has fathered offspring from his offspring. They said: "This one has protected his back." So they did not carry anything on him, did not shear his wool, and did not prevent him from pasture or from a watering place from which he drinks, even if the water-place belonged to someone other than its owner.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related something similar from him through the chain of al-Awfi.

[p. 399]

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verse 105:

Meaning: "Keep yourselves" (alzamū anfusakum), or "guard them," as you say: "ʿalayka Zaydan," i.e., "Keep to Zayd" (alzamhu). It was recited as lā yaḍurrukum with the jazm (apocopate, ending in sukun), on the basis that it is the answer (jawāb) to the imperative implied by the verbal noun (ism al-fiʿl) ʿalaykum (ism al-fiʿl: a noun functioning as a verb, here meaning "keep to").

Nāfiʿ and others read it with rafʿ (ḍamma), on the basis that it is a new sentence (mustaʾnaf), like the words of the poet:

"Then their guide said: Cast anchor, let us try it (nuzāwiluhā)"

Or on the basis that the ḍamma on the rāʾ is for ease of pronunciation (li-l-ittibāʿ). It was also recited as lā yaḍirrukum with a kasra on the ḍād, and as lā yaḍīrukum. The meaning is: the misguidance of those among people who go astray does not harm you when you are guided to the truth yourselves. There is nothing in the verse indicating that enjoining good and forbidding evil is dropped, for whoever abandons it, although it is among the greatest of religious duties, is not rightly guided. Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿if you are guided﴾. The Qur'anic verses and the abundant ḥadīths indicate the obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil as a binding, immediate duty.
