Therefore this verse is understood as applying to one who is unable to carry out the duty of enjoining good and forbidding evil, or for whom influence is not expected in any circumstance, or who fears that harm will befall him such that abandoning it becomes permissible for him. ﴿To Allah is your return on the Day of Resurrection, and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾ in this world, so He will reward the doer of good for his good and the doer of evil for his evil.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī (who graded it ṣaḥīḥ), al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Dāraquṭnī, al-Ḍiyāʾ in al-Mukhtārah, and others narrated from Qays ibn Abi Ḥāzim who said: Abū Bakr stood up, praised Allah and extolled Him, and said: "O people, you recite this verse: ﴿O you who believe, keep to yourselves; whoever goes astray will not harm you if you are guided﴾, and you place it in other than its proper place. I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'When people see the wrong and do not change it, Allah is about to encompass them with punishment.'" In a wording of Ibn Jarīr from him: "By Allah, you must enjoin good and forbid evil, or Allah will surely encompass you with punishment from Him."

al-Tirmidhī (who graded it ṣaḥīḥ), Ibn Mājah, Ibn Jarīr, al-Baghawī in his Muʿjam, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī, Abū al-Shaykh, al-Ḥākim (who graded it ṣaḥīḥ), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab narrated from Abū Umayyah al-Shaʿthānī who said: "I came to Abū Thaʿlabah al-Khushanī and said to him: How do you act regarding this verse? He said: Which verse? I said: His saying: ﴿O you who believe, keep to yourselves; whoever goes astray will not harm you if you are guided﴾. He said: By Allah, you have asked about it one who is well-informed. I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it and he said: 'Rather, enjoin good and forbid evil, until you see miserliness obeyed, desire followed, the world preferred, and every person of opinion pleased with his own opinion; then keep to your own self and leave aside the affair of the common people, for behind you are days in which patience is like grasping a coal; the one who acts in them has the reward of fifty men who act like your deeds.' In another wording it was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the reward of fifty men from us or from them?' He said: 'Rather, the reward of fifty from you.'"

Aḥmad, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Mardawayh narrated ("from ʿĀmir al-Ashʿarī: that there was a blind man among them, who delayed coming to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then came to him and said: What kept you? He said: O Messenger of Allah, I recited this verse: ﴿O you who believe, keep to yourselves; whoever goes astray will not harm you if you are guided﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: Where did you go? It is only: ﴿whoever goes astray will not harm you if you are guided﴾.")

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ṭabarānī and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from al-Ḥasan that a man asked Ibn Masʿūd about His saying: ﴿keep to yourselves﴾, and he said: "O people, it is not its time; rather, it is now accepted. But a time is about to come when you will enjoin good and it will be done to you thus and thus," or he said: "then it will not be accepted from you. At that time, keep to yourselves; whoever goes astray will not harm you if you are guided."

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from him concerning the verse: "Enjoin good and forbid evil so long as it does not go beyond the whip and the sword; when it is like that, then keep to yourselves."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that he said about this verse: "It is for people who will come after us; if they speak, it will not be accepted from them."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Ibn Jarīr narrated from a man who said: "I was in the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb in Medina, in a circle with the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and among them was an elder whom I think was Ubayy ibn Kaʿb. He recited ﴿keep to yourselves﴾ and said: Its interpretation is only at the end of time."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Abū Mazin who said: "I set out in the time of ʿUthmān to Medina, and there were people sitting, and one of them recited ﴿keep to yourselves﴾, and most of them said: The interpretation of this verse has not come today."

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Jubayr ibn Nufayr who said: "I was in a circle in which were Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), and I was the youngest of the people. They discussed enjoining good and forbidding evil, and I said: Does not Allah say: ﴿keep to yourselves﴾? They turned to me with one tongue and said: You bring up a verse of the Qur'an we do not know and do not understand its interpretation! Until I wished I had not spoken. Then they turned to talking among themselves, and when it was time for them to rise, they said: You are a young lad, and you have brought up a verse we do not know what it is. Perhaps you will live to see that time: when you see miserliness obeyed, desire followed, and every person of opinion pleased with his own opinion, then keep to yourself; whoever goes astray will not harm you if you are guided."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Muʿādh ibn Jabal, from the Prophet (ﷺ), a report similar to the ḥadīth of Abū Thaʿlabah al-Khushanī mentioned earlier, and at its end: "like the reward of fifty men from you."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī who said: "I mentioned this verse in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: Its interpretation has not come; its interpretation will not come until ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (peace be upon him) descends."

The narrations on this subject are numerous, and what we have mentioned is sufficient. In it is what guides to what we put forward regarding reconciling this verse with the verses and ḥadīths that come concerning enjoining good and forbidding evil.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 106–108 (part 1 of 2):

Makki said: "These three verses are, according to the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani), among the most difficult passages of the Qur'an in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis), meaning, and legal ruling." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is the statement of one who did not grasp their tafsir (exegesis), and this is clear from his book, may God have mercy on him", meaning from the book of Makki. Al-Qurtubi said: "What Makki mentioned, Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas also mentioned before him." Al-Sa'd said in his glosses on the Kashshaf: "They agreed that these are the most difficult verses of the Qur'an in i'rab, composition, and ruling."

His saying: ﴿shahadatu baynikum﴾ ("the testimony between you"). He attributed the testimony (shahada) to "between" (bayn) figuratively, because it takes place among them. It has been said that the original form is "the testimony of what is between you," so "ma" was deleted and the noun was made to be attributed to the adverbial expression, as in God's saying: ﴿Rather, the plotting of the night and the day﴾ [Saba: 33]. From this is the verse of the poet:

"You shake hands with whoever you meet of mine, who holds enmity, with open palms, while my hostility is hidden between your two eyes."

He meant "what is between your two eyes." Similar to it is the saying of another:

"And a day we witnessed it, Sulaym and 'Amir..."

That is, "we witnessed in it." From this is God's saying: ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. It has been said: the testimony here means the bequest (wasiyya), and it has been said: it means presence for the bequest. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: here it means the oath (yamin), so the meaning is: the oath of what is between you, that two should swear. He based what he said on the fact that God has no ruling in which an oath is obligatory upon a witness. Al-Qaffal chose this view, but Ibn 'Atiyya weakened it and chose that the testimony here is the testimony that is given by witnesses.

His saying: ﴿idha hadara ahadakumu al-mawt﴾ ("when death approaches one of you") is an adverbial clause (zarf) for the testimony. The intended meaning is: when its signs appear, because one who has died cannot call for witness. The fronting of the object is for emphasis and because of the complete control of the agent over the soul. His saying: ﴿hina al-wasiyya﴾ ("at the time of the bequest") is an adverbial clause for "hadara" or for "al-mawt," or a substitute (badal) for the first adverbial.

His saying: "ithnan" is the predicate of "shahada" with an implied element, that is: the testimony of two, or it is the subject of "shahada," with its predicate omitted, that is: concerning what has been prescribed for you, the testimony between you is two, on the assumption that two witnesses testify. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi mentioned both possibilities.

His saying: ﴿dhawa 'adlin minkum﴾ ("two persons of justice from among you") is a description of "ithnan," and likewise "minkum," meaning: they are from among you, that is, from your relatives, or "akharan" ("two others") is conjoined to "ithnan," and ﴿min ghayrikum﴾ ("from other than you") is a description of it, meaning: they are from outsiders. It has been said that the pronoun in "minkum" refers to the Muslims, and in "ghayrikum" to the disbelievers, and this is the most suitable to the context of the verse. This is the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, and others. Accordingly, the verse contains evidence for the permissibility of the testimony of people of the dhimma (protected non-Muslims) against Muslims while traveling, specifically in the matter of bequests, as the Qur'anic wording indicates, and the occasion of revelation supports this, as will come. So if there is no Muslim with the testator who can testify to his bequest, then two men from the people of disbelief should testify. When they arrive and give testimony about his bequest, they swear after the prayer that they did not lie or alter, and that what they testified to is true, and then their testimony is judged valid at that point.

If afterwards it is found ﴿that they both﴾ lied or betrayed, then two men from the guardians (awliya') of the testator take an oath, and the two disbelieving witnesses must pay what was found due to betrayal or the like. This is the meaning of the verse according to those previously mentioned, and this is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Mijlaz, al-Nakha'i, Shurayh, 'Ubayda al-Salmani, Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Thawri, Abu 'Ubayd, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. The first view, namely the interpretation of the pronoun in "minkum" as "by kinship or clan" and the interpretation of "min ghayrikum" as "outsiders," was held by al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, and 'Ikrima.

Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, and other jurists held that the verse is abrogated (mansukh), and they argued with God's saying: ﴿from among those whom you approve as witnesses﴾ [al-Baqara: 282], and His saying: ﴿and call to witness two persons of justice from among you﴾ [al-Talaq: 2]. These two are general in persons, times, and circumstances, whereas this verse is specific to the situation of travel, to the bequest, and to the situation of the absence of Muslim witnesses, and there is no contradiction between the general and the specific.

His saying: ﴿in antum﴾ ("if you are") is the subject of a verb that is omitted and explained by "darabtum" (you travel), or it is a subject-predicate sentence where what follows is its predicate. The first is the position of the majority of grammarians, and the second is the position of al-Akhfash and the Kufans. "Darb fi al-ard" (striking in the land) means travel.

His saying: ﴿fa-asabatkum musibatu al-mawt﴾ ("then the affliction of death befalls you") is conjoined to what precedes it, and its answer (jawab) is omitted, meaning: if you travel in the land and death befalls you and you wish to make a bequest and you do not find Muslim witnesses to it, then they (the two) go to your heirs with your bequest and with what you left, and they doubt their affair and the heirs claim that they betrayed. The ruling is that you detain them. It is also permissible that this be a resumptive sentence answering an implied question, as if they had said: "What should we do if we doubt the testimony?" So He said: "You detain them after the prayer, if you doubt their testimony." He specified "after the prayer," meaning the 'Asr prayer, as most scholars said, because it is the time at which God is angry with one who swears falsely during it, as in the authentic hadith. It has also been said: it is because it is the time when people gather and the judges sit for judgment. It has been said: it is the Zuhr prayer. It has been said: any prayer.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "Tahbisunahuma" ("you detain them") is a description of "akharan," and it is interrupted between the description and the described by His saying: ﴿if you travel in the land﴾. The meaning of detention is holding the two witnesses at that time in order to make them swear. This contains evidence for the permissibility of detention in its general sense, and for the permissibility of making the oath more binding by time, place, and the like. His saying: ﴿fa-yuqsimani billah﴾ ("then they both swear by God") is conjoined to "tahbisunahuma," meaning: the two witnesses to the bequest, or the two executors (wasiyyan), swear by God.

Ibn Abi Layla used this as evidence for making two witnesses swear in every case where doubt arises about their testimony. But this is open to question, because the oath of the two witnesses here is only because the claim of betrayal or the like has been made against them.

His saying: ﴿in irtabtum﴾ ("if you doubt") — the answer to this condition is omitted, indicated by what came before it, as already mentioned. His saying: ﴿la nashtri bihi thamanan﴾ ("we will not sell it for a price") is the answer to the oath, and the pronoun in "bihi" refers to God, the Exalted.

The meaning is: we will not sell our share from God, the Exalted, for this paltry goods, so that we swear falsely by Him for the sake of the wealth which you have claimed against us. It has been said that it refers to the oath, that is: we will not exchange the validity of the oath by God for some worldly goods. It has been said that it refers to the testimony, and the pronoun is used because testimony means speech, that is: we will not exchange our testimony for a price. The Kufans said: the meaning is "one with a price," so the modified noun was deleted and the modifier was put in its place. This is based on the view that goods are not called a price, whereas for the majority, goods are called a price just as they are called merchandise.

His saying: ﴿wa-law kana dha qurba﴾ ("even if he were a relative") means: even if the one for whom the oath is sworn, or the one for whom testimony is given, were a relative, we would still prefer the truth and honesty, and we would not prefer worldly goods nor kinship. The answer to "law" (even if) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, that is: even if he were a relative, we will not sell it for a price.

His saying: ﴿wa-la naktumu shahadata Allah﴾ ("nor will we conceal the testimony of God") is conjoined to "la nashtri" and is included with it under the ruling of the oath. The testimony is attributed to God, glorified is He, because He is the one who commands its establishment and forbids its concealment.

His saying: ﴿fa-in 'uthira 'ala annahuma istahaqqa ithman﴾ ("then if it is discovered that the two deserved sin"). "'Athara 'ala kadha" means: he became aware of it. One says: "I came upon a betrayal from him" (athartu minhu 'ala khiyana), that is, I became aware, and I made others aware of it. From this is God's saying: ﴿And thus We made them known﴾ [al-Kahf: 21]. The original meaning of "'uthur" is falling upon or stumbling over something, and from this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"With a she-camel with a limp, which we squeezed when she stumbled; so ruin is more fitting for her than that I say 'la'a' (may she perish)."

The meaning is: if after the oath it becomes apparent that the two witnesses or the two executors deserved sin, that is, they became liable to sin, either by lying in the testimony or the oath, or by the manifestation of betrayal. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "ithm" here is the name of the thing taken, because the one who takes it sins by taking it, so it was called "ithm," just as what is taken unjustly is called "mazlama" (wrongful seizure). Sibawayh said: "mazlama" is the name of what is taken from you, so likewise this taken thing was named by the name of the verbal noun.

His saying: ﴿fa-akharani yaqumani maqamahuma﴾ ("then two others shall stand in their place") means: then two other witnesses, or two other oath-takers, shall stand in the place of the two who were found to have deserved sin, and they shall testify or swear to what is the truth. It is not meant that they stand in their place in delivering the testimony that the two who deserved sin had given.

His saying: ﴿min alladhina istahaqqa 'alayhimu al-awliyan﴾ ("from among those against whom the two nearest have a claim"). "Istahaqqa" is in the passive voice in the reading of the majority. 'Ali, Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas, and Hafs read it in the active voice. "Al-awliyan," in the first reading, is in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: they are the two nearest, as if it were said: "who are they?" and it was answered: "they are the two nearest." It has also been said it is a substitute for the pronoun in "yaqumani" or for "akharan." Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and Hamza read "al-awwalin" (the first ones), the plural of "awwal," as a substitute for "alladhina" or for the "hum" in "'alayhim." al-Hasan read "al-awwalan" (the first two).

The meaning with the passive voice is: from among those upon whom sin has been inflicted, that is, the people of the deceased and his clan, for they have the greater right to testimony or oath than others. Thus "al-awliyan" is the dual of "awla" (more worthy). The meaning with the active reading is: from among those against whom the two nearest, from among them, by testimony, have a right, that they should bring them forward to stand as witnesses and expose by them the lying of the liars, because the two are the closest to the deceased. Thus "al-awliyan" is the subject of "istahaqqa," and its object is that they bring them forward to stand as witnesses. It has been said that the object is omitted, and the meaning is: from among those against whom the two nearest have a right, by the deceased, the bequest that he made.

His saying: ﴿fa-yuqsimani billah﴾ ("then they both swear by God") is conjoined to "yaqumani" ("they stand"), meaning: they swear by God, "our testimony is truer than their testimony," that is, our oath is truer. The testimony here means the oath, as in God's saying: ﴿so the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by God﴾ [al-Nur: 6], meaning: they swear that "our testimony is more deserving than their testimony," that is, more deserving than their oath that they are truthful and trustworthy. "And we have not transgressed" means: we have not exceeded the truth in our oath. ﴿Indeed, then we would be among the wrongdoers﴾, if we had sworn to falsehood.

His saying: ﴿dhalika adna an ya'tu bi-l-shahadati 'ala wajhiha﴾ ("That is more likely to bring the testimony in its proper form"): that is, that explanation which God, glorified is He, has given in this story, and we have learned how one who wishes to make a bequest while traveling should act, when none of his family or clan is with him and there are disbelievers with him. "Adna" means: closer to, that the witnesses who bear the testimony of the bequest will give testimony in its proper form, so they will not distort, alter, or betray. This is a new statement that contains mention of the benefit and the advantage in this ruling which God legislated in this place of His Book. The pronoun in "ya'tu" refers to the witnesses to the bequest from among the disbelievers. It has been said that it refers to the Muslims addressed by this ruling.

The intention is to warn them against betrayal and to command them to testify to the truth. His saying: ﴿aw yakhafu an turadda aymanun ba'da aymanihim﴾ ("or they fear that oaths will be repeated after their oaths"): that is, that oaths will be turned back to the heirs, so that they swear contrary to what the witnesses to the bequest testified, and then the witnesses to the bequest are exposed. This is conjoined to his saying "an ya'tu" (that they bring), so the benefit in God's legislation of this ruling, glorified is He, is one of two things: either the witnesses to the bequest are restrained from lying and betrayal, so they bring the testimony in its proper form.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 106–108 (part 2 of 2):

or they fear that the oaths will be repudiated after they are taken on the kinsmen of the deceased, and so they swear by something that implies their lying or their betrayal. Thus that will be a means of the witnesses to the bequest giving their testimony in its proper form, without lying (p-402) or betrayal.

It was also said: "or they fear" is joined to an implied clause after the first clause, and the sense is: "That is closer to their giving testimony in its proper form and their fearing the punishment of the Hereafter for lying and betrayal, or their fearing exposure through the rejection of the oath." Whichever of the two fears occurs, the purpose is achieved. ﴿And fear Allah in opposing His commands.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾, those who depart from His obedience in any sin, among which is lying in an oath or in testimony.

The sum of what this passage of the Mighty Book contains is that whoever is visited by the signs of death should call two just men from among the just Muslims to witness his bequest. If he does not find Muslim witnesses, and he is traveling, and finds non-Muslims, he may call two men from among them to witness his bequest. If the heirs of the testator doubt them, the two shall swear by Allah that they testified truthfully, and that they concealed nothing of the testimony and betrayed nothing of what the deceased left behind. If afterward it becomes clear that what they swore to was false, through a flaw in the testimony or the appearance of some part of the estate of the deceased which they claimed had come into their possession in some way, then two men from the heirs shall swear, and the ruling is applied accordingly.

Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it and graded it weak, as did Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Nahhas in his History, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Ma'rifa, through the route of Abu al-Nadr, who is al-Kalbi, from Baadhan, the freedman of Umm Hani, who said: "From Ibn Abbas, concerning Tamim al-Dari regarding this verse: ﴿O you who have believed, let there be [a] testimony among you when death approaches one of you﴾ He said: 'People were absolved of it except for me and Adi ibn Baddaa. The two of them were Christians who used to travel to Syria before Islam. They came to Syria for their trade, and a freedman of Banu Sahm called Budayl ibn Abi Maryam came to them with merchandise, carrying a silver cup which he intended for the king, and it was the greatest of his merchandise. He fell ill and made them his executors, and he instructed them to deliver what he had left to his family.' Tamim said: 'When he died, we took that cup and sold it for a thousand dirhams, then Adi ibn Baddaa and I divided it between us. When we came to his family, we handed over to them what we had with us, and they missed the cup and asked us about it. We said: "He left nothing other than this," or "He gave us nothing other than this."' Tamim said: 'When I embraced Islam after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived in Madina, I felt guilty about that. So I went to his family and informed them of the matter, and I paid them five hundred dirhams, and I told them that my companion had the same amount. They brought it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he asked them for evidence, but they found none. So he commanded them to have him swear by that which is held in reverence among the people of his religion. He swore, and Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, let there be [a] testimony among you﴾ to His saying ﴿that oaths be repudiated after their oaths﴾. Then Amr ibn al-As and another man stood and swore, and the five hundred dirhams were taken from Adi ibn Baddaa.'"

In its isnad (chain of transmission) is Abu al-Nadr, who is Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi, the author of the tafsir (exegesis). Al-Tirmidhi said: "The people of hadith abandoned him."

Al-Bukhari transmitted it in his History, and al-Tirmidhi graded it good, as did Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Nahhas, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "A man from Banu Sahm went out with Tamim al-Dari and Adi ibn Baddaa, and the Sahmi died in a land where there was no Muslim. He made them his executors. When they brought back his estate, they missed a silver cup decorated with gold. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ made them swear by Allah that they had not concealed it and had not taken it. Then they found the cup in Makka, and it was said: 'We bought it from Tamim and Adi.' Two men from the Sahmi's guardians stood and swore by Allah: 'Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and the cup belongs to our companion.' And they took the cup." He said: "And concerning them was revealed ﴿O you who have believed, let there be [a] testimony among you﴾, the verse."

In its isnad is Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim al-Kufi. Al-Tirmidhi said: "It was said that he is good in hadith (salih al-hadith)." Abu Dawud also transmitted it through his route. A group of the Successors (tabi'un) transmitted that this story is the cause of the revelation of the verse, and the exegetes mentioned it in their tafsirs.

Al-Qurtubi said: "The exegetes unanimously agreed that this story is the cause of the revelation of the verse." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Nahhas transmitted, through the route of Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas, concerning ﴿O you who have believed, let there be [a] testimony among you﴾, the verse. He said: "This is for one who dies while Muslims are present; Allah commanded him to call two just Muslim men to witness his bequest." Then He said: ﴿or two others from other than you, if you are traveling through the land﴾. "This is for one who dies while no Muslim is with him; Allah commanded [him to call] the testimony of two men from among non-Muslims. If their testimony is doubted, they shall swear by Allah after the prayer that they did not sell their testimony for a small price. If the guardians discover that the two unbelievers lied in their testimony, and there are two men among the guardians who swear by Allah that the testimony of the two unbelievers is false, that is His saying: ﴿then if it becomes known that they both deserved sin﴾, meaning: if it is discovered that the two unbelievers lied, that is closer to ﴿their giving testimony in its proper form, or fearing that oaths will be repudiated after their oaths﴾, so that the testimony of the two unbelievers is rejected and judgment is made on the testimony of the guardians. There is no oath upon the testimony of Muslims; oaths are only required when the two are unbelievers."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that he was asked about this verse and said: "This is a man who set out on a journey with wealth, and his appointed time overtook him. If he finds two Muslim men, he hands his estate over to them and calls two just Muslim men to witness it. If he does not find two just Muslim men, then two men from the People of the Book. If they deliver it, then that is their way. If they deny it, they shall be made to swear by Allah, besides whom there is no god, after the prayer: 'Indeed this which was handed to me, I have not concealed anything from it.' When he swears, he is cleared. Then if the two companions from the People of the Book come afterward and testify against him, and then the people make a claim against him regarding what they named, the oaths of the heirs are imposed together with their testimony, and then they take his right. That is what Allah means by: ﴿two men of justice from among you or two others from other than you﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿or two others from other than you﴾, that he said: "From other than Muslims, from the People of the Book."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "This verse is abrogated (mansukha)." Ibn Jarir transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning the verse, who said: "That was for a man who died while no one from the people of Islam was with him, and that was at the beginning of Islam, when the land was at war and the people were unbelievers except for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his companions in Madina. People used to inherit by bequest. Then the bequest was abrogated, the obligatory shares were established, and the Muslims acted accordingly."

Ibn Jarir also transmitted from al-Zuhri, who said: (p-403) "The sunna has been established that the testimony of an unbeliever is not valid, whether in residence or on a journey; it is only [valid] among Muslims."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ubayda, concerning His saying ﴿you detain both of them after the prayer﴾, that he said: "The afternoon prayer (salat al-asr)." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Zayd, concerning His saying ﴿we will not exchange it for a price﴾, that he said: "We will not take a bribe for it." ﴿Nor will we conceal the testimony of Allah﴾, even if its owner is distant.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Qatada, concerning His saying ﴿then if it becomes known that they both deserved sin﴾, that is, it became known from them that they had betrayed by lying or concealing. Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Zayd, concerning His saying "the two nearest", that he said: "[It refers] to the deceased."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatada, concerning His saying ﴿that is closer to their giving testimony in its proper form﴾, that he said: "That is more likely that they will be truthful in their testimony," ﴿or they fear that oaths will be repudiated after their oaths﴾, that he said: "And that they fear reproach." Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Zayd, concerning His saying ﴿or they fear that oaths will be repudiated after their oaths﴾, that he said: "Then their oaths will be nullified and the oaths of these others will be taken."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 106–108 (part 1 of 2):

Makki said: "These three verses are, according to the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani), among the most difficult passages of the Qur'an in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis), meaning, and legal ruling." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is the statement of one who did not grasp their tafsir (exegesis), and this is clear from his book, may God have mercy on him", meaning from the book of Makki. Al-Qurtubi said: "What Makki mentioned, Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas also mentioned before him." Al-Sa'd said in his glosses on the Kashshaf: "They agreed that these are the most difficult verses of the Qur'an in i'rab, composition, and ruling."

His saying: ﴿shahadatu baynikum﴾ ("the testimony between you"). He attributed the testimony (shahada) to "between" (bayn) figuratively, because it takes place among them. It has been said that the original form is "the testimony of what is between you," so "ma" was deleted and the noun was made to be attributed to the adverbial expression, as in God's saying: ﴿Rather, the plotting of the night and the day﴾ [Saba: 33]. From this is the verse of the poet:

"You shake hands with whoever you meet of mine, who holds enmity, with open palms, while my hostility is hidden between your two eyes."

He meant "what is between your two eyes." Similar to it is the saying of another:

"And a day we witnessed it, Sulaym and 'Amir..."

That is, "we witnessed in it." From this is God's saying: ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. It has been said: the testimony here means the bequest (wasiyya), and it has been said: it means presence for the bequest. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: here it means the oath (yamin), so the meaning is: the oath of what is between you, that two should swear. He based what he said on the fact that God has no ruling in which an oath is obligatory upon a witness. Al-Qaffal chose this view, but Ibn 'Atiyya weakened it and chose that the testimony here is the testimony that is given by witnesses.

His saying: ﴿idha hadara ahadakumu al-mawt﴾ ("when death approaches one of you") is an adverbial clause (zarf) for the testimony. The intended meaning is: when its signs appear, because one who has died cannot call for witness. The fronting of the object is for emphasis and because of the complete control of the agent over the soul. His saying: ﴿hina al-wasiyya﴾ ("at the time of the bequest") is an adverbial clause for "hadara" or for "al-mawt," or a substitute (badal) for the first adverbial.

His saying: "ithnan" is the predicate of "shahada" with an implied element, that is: the testimony of two, or it is the subject of "shahada," with its predicate omitted, that is: concerning what has been prescribed for you, the testimony between you is two, on the assumption that two witnesses testify. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi mentioned both possibilities.

His saying: ﴿dhawa 'adlin minkum﴾ ("two persons of justice from among you") is a description of "ithnan," and likewise "minkum," meaning: they are from among you, that is, from your relatives, or "akharan" ("two others") is conjoined to "ithnan," and ﴿min ghayrikum﴾ ("from other than you") is a description of it, meaning: they are from outsiders. It has been said that the pronoun in "minkum" refers to the Muslims, and in "ghayrikum" to the disbelievers, and this is the most suitable to the context of the verse. This is the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, and others. Accordingly, the verse contains evidence for the permissibility of the testimony of people of the dhimma (protected non-Muslims) against Muslims while traveling, specifically in the matter of bequests, as the Qur'anic wording indicates, and the occasion of revelation supports this, as will come. So if there is no Muslim with the testator who can testify to his bequest, then two men from the people of disbelief should testify. When they arrive and give testimony about his bequest, they swear after the prayer that they did not lie or alter, and that what they testified to is true, and then their testimony is judged valid at that point.

If afterwards it is found ﴿that they both﴾ lied or betrayed, then two men from the guardians (awliya') of the testator take an oath, and the two disbelieving witnesses must pay what was found due to betrayal or the like. This is the meaning of the verse according to those previously mentioned, and this is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Mijlaz, al-Nakha'i, Shurayh, 'Ubayda al-Salmani, Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Thawri, Abu 'Ubayd, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. The first view, namely the interpretation of the pronoun in "minkum" as "by kinship or clan" and the interpretation of "min ghayrikum" as "outsiders," was held by al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, and 'Ikrima.

Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, and other jurists held that the verse is abrogated (mansukh), and they argued with God's saying: ﴿from among those whom you approve as witnesses﴾ [al-Baqara: 282], and His saying: ﴿and call to witness two persons of justice from among you﴾ [al-Talaq: 2]. These two are general in persons, times, and circumstances, whereas this verse is specific to the situation of travel, to the bequest, and to the situation of the absence of Muslim witnesses, and there is no contradiction between the general and the specific.

His saying: ﴿in antum﴾ ("if you are") is the subject of a verb that is omitted and explained by "darabtum" (you travel), or it is a subject-predicate sentence where what follows is its predicate. The first is the position of the majority of grammarians, and the second is the position of al-Akhfash and the Kufans. "Darb fi al-ard" (striking in the land) means travel.

His saying: ﴿fa-asabatkum musibatu al-mawt﴾ ("then the affliction of death befalls you") is conjoined to what precedes it, and its answer (jawab) is omitted, meaning: if you travel in the land and death befalls you and you wish to make a bequest and you do not find Muslim witnesses to it, then they (the two) go to your heirs with your bequest and with what you left, and they doubt their affair and the heirs claim that they betrayed. The ruling is that you detain them. It is also permissible that this be a resumptive sentence answering an implied question, as if they had said: "What should we do if we doubt the testimony?" So He said: "You detain them after the prayer, if you doubt their testimony." He specified "after the prayer," meaning the 'Asr prayer, as most scholars said, because it is the time at which God is angry with one who swears falsely during it, as in the authentic hadith. It has also been said: it is because it is the time when people gather and the judges sit for judgment. It has been said: it is the Zuhr prayer. It has been said: any prayer.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "Tahbisunahuma" ("you detain them") is a description of "akharan," and it is interrupted between the description and the described by His saying: ﴿if you travel in the land﴾. The meaning of detention is holding the two witnesses at that time in order to make them swear. This contains evidence for the permissibility of detention in its general sense, and for the permissibility of making the oath more binding by time, place, and the like. His saying: ﴿fa-yuqsimani billah﴾ ("then they both swear by God") is conjoined to "tahbisunahuma," meaning: the two witnesses to the bequest, or the two executors (wasiyyan), swear by God.

Ibn Abi Layla used this as evidence for making two witnesses swear in every case where doubt arises about their testimony. But this is open to question, because the oath of the two witnesses here is only because the claim of betrayal or the like has been made against them.

His saying: ﴿in irtabtum﴾ ("if you doubt") — the answer to this condition is omitted, indicated by what came before it, as already mentioned. His saying: ﴿la nashtri bihi thamanan﴾ ("we will not sell it for a price") is the answer to the oath, and the pronoun in "bihi" refers to God, the Exalted.

The meaning is: we will not sell our share from God, the Exalted, for this paltry goods, so that we swear falsely by Him for the sake of the wealth which you have claimed against us. It has been said that it refers to the oath, that is: we will not exchange the validity of the oath by God for some worldly goods. It has been said that it refers to the testimony, and the pronoun is used because testimony means speech, that is: we will not exchange our testimony for a price. The Kufans said: the meaning is "one with a price," so the modified noun was deleted and the modifier was put in its place. This is based on the view that goods are not called a price, whereas for the majority, goods are called a price just as they are called merchandise.

His saying: ﴿wa-law kana dha qurba﴾ ("even if he were a relative") means: even if the one for whom the oath is sworn, or the one for whom testimony is given, were a relative, we would still prefer the truth and honesty, and we would not prefer worldly goods nor kinship. The answer to "law" (even if) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, that is: even if he were a relative, we will not sell it for a price.

His saying: ﴿wa-la naktumu shahadata Allah﴾ ("nor will we conceal the testimony of God") is conjoined to "la nashtri" and is included with it under the ruling of the oath. The testimony is attributed to God, glorified is He, because He is the one who commands its establishment and forbids its concealment.

His saying: ﴿fa-in 'uthira 'ala annahuma istahaqqa ithman﴾ ("then if it is discovered that the two deserved sin"). "'Athara 'ala kadha" means: he became aware of it. One says: "I came upon a betrayal from him" (athartu minhu 'ala khiyana), that is, I became aware, and I made others aware of it. From this is God's saying: ﴿And thus We made them known﴾ [al-Kahf: 21]. The original meaning of "'uthur" is falling upon or stumbling over something, and from this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"With a she-camel with a limp, which we squeezed when she stumbled; so ruin is more fitting for her than that I say 'la'a' (may she perish)."

The meaning is: if after the oath it becomes apparent that the two witnesses or the two executors deserved sin, that is, they became liable to sin, either by lying in the testimony or the oath, or by the manifestation of betrayal. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "ithm" here is the name of the thing taken, because the one who takes it sins by taking it, so it was called "ithm," just as what is taken unjustly is called "mazlama" (wrongful seizure). Sibawayh said: "mazlama" is the name of what is taken from you, so likewise this taken thing was named by the name of the verbal noun.

His saying: ﴿fa-akharani yaqumani maqamahuma﴾ ("then two others shall stand in their place") means: then two other witnesses, or two other oath-takers, shall stand in the place of the two who were found to have deserved sin, and they shall testify or swear to what is the truth. It is not meant that they stand in their place in delivering the testimony that the two who deserved sin had given.

His saying: ﴿min alladhina istahaqqa 'alayhimu al-awliyan﴾ ("from among those against whom the two nearest have a claim"). "Istahaqqa" is in the passive voice in the reading of the majority. 'Ali, Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas, and Hafs read it in the active voice. "Al-awliyan," in the first reading, is in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: they are the two nearest, as if it were said: "who are they?" and it was answered: "they are the two nearest." It has also been said it is a substitute for the pronoun in "yaqumani" or for "akharan." Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and Hamza read "al-awwalin" (the first ones), the plural of "awwal," as a substitute for "alladhina" or for the "hum" in "'alayhim." al-Hasan read "al-awwalan" (the first two).

The meaning with the passive voice is: from among those upon whom sin has been inflicted, that is, the people of the deceased and his clan, for they have the greater right to testimony or oath than others. Thus "al-awliyan" is the dual of "awla" (more worthy). The meaning with the active reading is: from among those against whom the two nearest, from among them, by testimony, have a right, that they should bring them forward to stand as witnesses and expose by them the lying of the liars, because the two are the closest to the deceased. Thus "al-awliyan" is the subject of "istahaqqa," and its object is that they bring them forward to stand as witnesses. It has been said that the object is omitted, and the meaning is: from among those against whom the two nearest have a right, by the deceased, the bequest that he made.

His saying: ﴿fa-yuqsimani billah﴾ ("then they both swear by God") is conjoined to "yaqumani" ("they stand"), meaning: they swear by God, "our testimony is truer than their testimony," that is, our oath is truer. The testimony here means the oath, as in God's saying: ﴿so the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by God﴾ [al-Nur: 6], meaning: they swear that "our testimony is more deserving than their testimony," that is, more deserving than their oath that they are truthful and trustworthy. "And we have not transgressed" means: we have not exceeded the truth in our oath. ﴿Indeed, then we would be among the wrongdoers﴾, if we had sworn to falsehood.

His saying: ﴿dhalika adna an ya'tu bi-l-shahadati 'ala wajhiha﴾ ("That is more likely to bring the testimony in its proper form"): that is, that explanation which God, glorified is He, has given in this story, and we have learned how one who wishes to make a bequest while traveling should act, when none of his family or clan is with him and there are disbelievers with him. "Adna" means: closer to, that the witnesses who bear the testimony of the bequest will give testimony in its proper form, so they will not distort, alter, or betray. This is a new statement that contains mention of the benefit and the advantage in this ruling which God legislated in this place of His Book. The pronoun in "ya'tu" refers to the witnesses to the bequest from among the disbelievers. It has been said that it refers to the Muslims addressed by this ruling.

The intention is to warn them against betrayal and to command them to testify to the truth. His saying: ﴿aw yakhafu an turadda aymanun ba'da aymanihim﴾ ("or they fear that oaths will be repeated after their oaths"): that is, that oaths will be turned back to the heirs, so that they swear contrary to what the witnesses to the bequest testified, and then the witnesses to the bequest are exposed. This is conjoined to his saying "an ya'tu" (that they bring), so the benefit in God's legislation of this ruling, glorified is He, is one of two things: either the witnesses to the bequest are restrained from lying and betrayal, so they bring the testimony in its proper form.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 106–108 (part 2 of 2):

or they fear that the oaths will be repudiated after they are taken on the kinsmen of the deceased, and so they swear by something that implies their lying or their betrayal. Thus that will be a means of the witnesses to the bequest giving their testimony in its proper form, without lying (p-402) or betrayal.

It was also said: "or they fear" is joined to an implied clause after the first clause, and the sense is: "That is closer to their giving testimony in its proper form and their fearing the punishment of the Hereafter for lying and betrayal, or their fearing exposure through the rejection of the oath." Whichever of the two fears occurs, the purpose is achieved. ﴿And fear Allah in opposing His commands.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾, those who depart from His obedience in any sin, among which is lying in an oath or in testimony.

The sum of what this passage of the Mighty Book contains is that whoever is visited by the signs of death should call two just men from among the just Muslims to witness his bequest. If he does not find Muslim witnesses, and he is traveling, and finds non-Muslims, he may call two men from among them to witness his bequest. If the heirs of the testator doubt them, the two shall swear by Allah that they testified truthfully, and that they concealed nothing of the testimony and betrayed nothing of what the deceased left behind. If afterward it becomes clear that what they swore to was false, through a flaw in the testimony or the appearance of some part of the estate of the deceased which they claimed had come into their possession in some way, then two men from the heirs shall swear, and the ruling is applied accordingly.

Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it and graded it weak, as did Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Nahhas in his History, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Ma'rifa, through the route of Abu al-Nadr, who is al-Kalbi, from Baadhan, the freedman of Umm Hani, who said: "From Ibn Abbas, concerning Tamim al-Dari regarding this verse: ﴿O you who have believed, let there be [a] testimony among you when death approaches one of you﴾ He said: 'People were absolved of it except for me and Adi ibn Baddaa. The two of them were Christians who used to travel to Syria before Islam. They came to Syria for their trade, and a freedman of Banu Sahm called Budayl ibn Abi Maryam came to them with merchandise, carrying a silver cup which he intended for the king, and it was the greatest of his merchandise. He fell ill and made them his executors, and he instructed them to deliver what he had left to his family.' Tamim said: 'When he died, we took that cup and sold it for a thousand dirhams, then Adi ibn Baddaa and I divided it between us. When we came to his family, we handed over to them what we had with us, and they missed the cup and asked us about it. We said: "He left nothing other than this," or "He gave us nothing other than this."' Tamim said: 'When I embraced Islam after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived in Madina, I felt guilty about that. So I went to his family and informed them of the matter, and I paid them five hundred dirhams, and I told them that my companion had the same amount. They brought it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he asked them for evidence, but they found none. So he commanded them to have him swear by that which is held in reverence among the people of his religion. He swore, and Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, let there be [a] testimony among you﴾ to His saying ﴿that oaths be repudiated after their oaths﴾. Then Amr ibn al-As and another man stood and swore, and the five hundred dirhams were taken from Adi ibn Baddaa.'"

In its isnad (chain of transmission) is Abu al-Nadr, who is Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi, the author of the tafsir (exegesis). Al-Tirmidhi said: "The people of hadith abandoned him."

Al-Bukhari transmitted it in his History, and al-Tirmidhi graded it good, as did Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Nahhas, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "A man from Banu Sahm went out with Tamim al-Dari and Adi ibn Baddaa, and the Sahmi died in a land where there was no Muslim. He made them his executors. When they brought back his estate, they missed a silver cup decorated with gold. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ made them swear by Allah that they had not concealed it and had not taken it. Then they found the cup in Makka, and it was said: 'We bought it from Tamim and Adi.' Two men from the Sahmi's guardians stood and swore by Allah: 'Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and the cup belongs to our companion.' And they took the cup." He said: "And concerning them was revealed ﴿O you who have believed, let there be [a] testimony among you﴾, the verse."

In its isnad is Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim al-Kufi. Al-Tirmidhi said: "It was said that he is good in hadith (salih al-hadith)." Abu Dawud also transmitted it through his route. A group of the Successors (tabi'un) transmitted that this story is the cause of the revelation of the verse, and the exegetes mentioned it in their tafsirs.

Al-Qurtubi said: "The exegetes unanimously agreed that this story is the cause of the revelation of the verse." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Nahhas transmitted, through the route of Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas, concerning ﴿O you who have believed, let there be [a] testimony among you﴾, the verse. He said: "This is for one who dies while Muslims are present; Allah commanded him to call two just Muslim men to witness his bequest." Then He said: ﴿or two others from other than you, if you are traveling through the land﴾. "This is for one who dies while no Muslim is with him; Allah commanded [him to call] the testimony of two men from among non-Muslims. If their testimony is doubted, they shall swear by Allah after the prayer that they did not sell their testimony for a small price. If the guardians discover that the two unbelievers lied in their testimony, and there are two men among the guardians who swear by Allah that the testimony of the two unbelievers is false, that is His saying: ﴿then if it becomes known that they both deserved sin﴾, meaning: if it is discovered that the two unbelievers lied, that is closer to ﴿their giving testimony in its proper form, or fearing that oaths will be repudiated after their oaths﴾, so that the testimony of the two unbelievers is rejected and judgment is made on the testimony of the guardians. There is no oath upon the testimony of Muslims; oaths are only required when the two are unbelievers."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that he was asked about this verse and said: "This is a man who set out on a journey with wealth, and his appointed time overtook him. If he finds two Muslim men, he hands his estate over to them and calls two just Muslim men to witness it. If he does not find two just Muslim men, then two men from the People of the Book. If they deliver it, then that is their way. If they deny it, they shall be made to swear by Allah, besides whom there is no god, after the prayer: 'Indeed this which was handed to me, I have not concealed anything from it.' When he swears, he is cleared. Then if the two companions from the People of the Book come afterward and testify against him, and then the people make a claim against him regarding what they named, the oaths of the heirs are imposed together with their testimony, and then they take his right. That is what Allah means by: ﴿two men of justice from among you or two others from other than you﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿or two others from other than you﴾, that he said: "From other than Muslims, from the People of the Book."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "This verse is abrogated (mansukha)." Ibn Jarir transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning the verse, who said: "That was for a man who died while no one from the people of Islam was with him, and that was at the beginning of Islam, when the land was at war and the people were unbelievers except for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his companions in Madina. People used to inherit by bequest. Then the bequest was abrogated, the obligatory shares were established, and the Muslims acted accordingly."

Ibn Jarir also transmitted from al-Zuhri, who said: (p-403) "The sunna has been established that the testimony of an unbeliever is not valid, whether in residence or on a journey; it is only [valid] among Muslims."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ubayda, concerning His saying ﴿you detain both of them after the prayer﴾, that he said: "The afternoon prayer (salat al-asr)." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Zayd, concerning His saying ﴿we will not exchange it for a price﴾, that he said: "We will not take a bribe for it." ﴿Nor will we conceal the testimony of Allah﴾, even if its owner is distant.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Qatada, concerning His saying ﴿then if it becomes known that they both deserved sin﴾, that is, it became known from them that they had betrayed by lying or concealing. Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Zayd, concerning His saying "the two nearest", that he said: "[It refers] to the deceased."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatada, concerning His saying ﴿that is closer to their giving testimony in its proper form﴾, that he said: "That is more likely that they will be truthful in their testimony," ﴿or they fear that oaths will be repudiated after their oaths﴾, that he said: "And that they fear reproach." Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Zayd, concerning His saying ﴿or they fear that oaths will be repudiated after their oaths﴾, that he said: "Then their oaths will be nullified and the oaths of these others will be taken."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 106–108 (part 1 of 2):

Makki said: "These three verses are, according to the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani), among the most difficult passages of the Qur'an in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis), meaning, and legal ruling." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is the statement of one who did not grasp their tafsir (exegesis), and this is clear from his book, may God have mercy on him", meaning from the book of Makki. Al-Qurtubi said: "What Makki mentioned, Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas also mentioned before him." Al-Sa'd said in his glosses on the Kashshaf: "They agreed that these are the most difficult verses of the Qur'an in i'rab, composition, and ruling."

His saying: ﴿shahadatu baynikum﴾ ("the testimony between you"). He attributed the testimony (shahada) to "between" (bayn) figuratively, because it takes place among them. It has been said that the original form is "the testimony of what is between you," so "ma" was deleted and the noun was made to be attributed to the adverbial expression, as in God's saying: ﴿Rather, the plotting of the night and the day﴾ [Saba: 33]. From this is the verse of the poet:

"You shake hands with whoever you meet of mine, who holds enmity, with open palms, while my hostility is hidden between your two eyes."

He meant "what is between your two eyes." Similar to it is the saying of another:

"And a day we witnessed it, Sulaym and 'Amir..."

That is, "we witnessed in it." From this is God's saying: ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. It has been said: the testimony here means the bequest (wasiyya), and it has been said: it means presence for the bequest. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: here it means the oath (yamin), so the meaning is: the oath of what is between you, that two should swear. He based what he said on the fact that God has no ruling in which an oath is obligatory upon a witness. Al-Qaffal chose this view, but Ibn 'Atiyya weakened it and chose that the testimony here is the testimony that is given by witnesses.

His saying: ﴿idha hadara ahadakumu al-mawt﴾ ("when death approaches one of you") is an adverbial clause (zarf) for the testimony. The intended meaning is: when its signs appear, because one who has died cannot call for witness. The fronting of the object is for emphasis and because of the complete control of the agent over the soul. His saying: ﴿hina al-wasiyya﴾ ("at the time of the bequest") is an adverbial clause for "hadara" or for "al-mawt," or a substitute (badal) for the first adverbial.

His saying: "ithnan" is the predicate of "shahada" with an implied element, that is: the testimony of two, or it is the subject of "shahada," with its predicate omitted, that is: concerning what has been prescribed for you, the testimony between you is two, on the assumption that two witnesses testify. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi mentioned both possibilities.

His saying: ﴿dhawa 'adlin minkum﴾ ("two persons of justice from among you") is a description of "ithnan," and likewise "minkum," meaning: they are from among you, that is, from your relatives, or "akharan" ("two others") is conjoined to "ithnan," and ﴿min ghayrikum﴾ ("from other than you") is a description of it, meaning: they are from outsiders. It has been said that the pronoun in "minkum" refers to the Muslims, and in "ghayrikum" to the disbelievers, and this is the most suitable to the context of the verse. This is the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, and others. Accordingly, the verse contains evidence for the permissibility of the testimony of people of the dhimma (protected non-Muslims) against Muslims while traveling, specifically in the matter of bequests, as the Qur'anic wording indicates, and the occasion of revelation supports this, as will come. So if there is no Muslim with the testator who can testify to his bequest, then two men from the people of disbelief should testify. When they arrive and give testimony about his bequest, they swear after the prayer that they did not lie or alter, and that what they testified to is true, and then their testimony is judged valid at that point.

If afterwards it is found ﴿that they both﴾ lied or betrayed, then two men from the guardians (awliya') of the testator take an oath, and the two disbelieving witnesses must pay what was found due to betrayal or the like. This is the meaning of the verse according to those previously mentioned, and this is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Mijlaz, al-Nakha'i, Shurayh, 'Ubayda al-Salmani, Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Thawri, Abu 'Ubayd, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. The first view, namely the interpretation of the pronoun in "minkum" as "by kinship or clan" and the interpretation of "min ghayrikum" as "outsiders," was held by al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, and 'Ikrima.

Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, and other jurists held that the verse is abrogated (mansukh), and they argued with God's saying: ﴿from among those whom you approve as witnesses﴾ [al-Baqara: 282], and His saying: ﴿and call to witness two persons of justice from among you﴾ [al-Talaq: 2]. These two are general in persons, times, and circumstances, whereas this verse is specific to the situation of travel, to the bequest, and to the situation of the absence of Muslim witnesses, and there is no contradiction between the general and the specific.

His saying: ﴿in antum﴾ ("if you are") is the subject of a verb that is omitted and explained by "darabtum" (you travel), or it is a subject-predicate sentence where what follows is its predicate. The first is the position of the majority of grammarians, and the second is the position of al-Akhfash and the Kufans. "Darb fi al-ard" (striking in the land) means travel.

His saying: ﴿fa-asabatkum musibatu al-mawt﴾ ("then the affliction of death befalls you") is conjoined to what precedes it, and its answer (jawab) is omitted, meaning: if you travel in the land and death befalls you and you wish to make a bequest and you do not find Muslim witnesses to it, then they (the two) go to your heirs with your bequest and with what you left, and they doubt their affair and the heirs claim that they betrayed. The ruling is that you detain them. It is also permissible that this be a resumptive sentence answering an implied question, as if they had said: "What should we do if we doubt the testimony?" So He said: "You detain them after the prayer, if you doubt their testimony." He specified "after the prayer," meaning the 'Asr prayer, as most scholars said, because it is the time at which God is angry with one who swears falsely during it, as in the authentic hadith. It has also been said: it is because it is the time when people gather and the judges sit for judgment. It has been said: it is the Zuhr prayer. It has been said: any prayer.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "Tahbisunahuma" ("you detain them") is a description of "akharan," and it is interrupted between the description and the described by His saying: ﴿if you travel in the land﴾. The meaning of detention is holding the two witnesses at that time in order to make them swear. This contains evidence for the permissibility of detention in its general sense, and for the permissibility of making the oath more binding by time, place, and the like. His saying: ﴿fa-yuqsimani billah﴾ ("then they both swear by God") is conjoined to "tahbisunahuma," meaning: the two witnesses to the bequest, or the two executors (wasiyyan), swear by God.

Ibn Abi Layla used this as evidence for making two witnesses swear in every case where doubt arises about their testimony. But this is open to question, because the oath of the two witnesses here is only because the claim of betrayal or the like has been made against them.

His saying: ﴿in irtabtum﴾ ("if you doubt") — the answer to this condition is omitted, indicated by what came before it, as already mentioned. His saying: ﴿la nashtri bihi thamanan﴾ ("we will not sell it for a price") is the answer to the oath, and the pronoun in "bihi" refers to God, the Exalted.

The meaning is: we will not sell our share from God, the Exalted, for this paltry goods, so that we swear falsely by Him for the sake of the wealth which you have claimed against us. It has been said that it refers to the oath, that is: we will not exchange the validity of the oath by God for some worldly goods. It has been said that it refers to the testimony, and the pronoun is used because testimony means speech, that is: we will not exchange our testimony for a price. The Kufans said: the meaning is "one with a price," so the modified noun was deleted and the modifier was put in its place. This is based on the view that goods are not called a price, whereas for the majority, goods are called a price just as they are called merchandise.

His saying: ﴿wa-law kana dha qurba﴾ ("even if he were a relative") means: even if the one for whom the oath is sworn, or the one for whom testimony is given, were a relative, we would still prefer the truth and honesty, and we would not prefer worldly goods nor kinship. The answer to "law" (even if) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, that is: even if he were a relative, we will not sell it for a price.

His saying: ﴿wa-la naktumu shahadata Allah﴾ ("nor will we conceal the testimony of God") is conjoined to "la nashtri" and is included with it under the ruling of the oath. The testimony is attributed to God, glorified is He, because He is the one who commands its establishment and forbids its concealment.

His saying: ﴿fa-in 'uthira 'ala annahuma istahaqqa ithman﴾ ("then if it is discovered that the two deserved sin"). "'Athara 'ala kadha" means: he became aware of it. One says: "I came upon a betrayal from him" (athartu minhu 'ala khiyana), that is, I became aware, and I made others aware of it. From this is God's saying: ﴿And thus We made them known﴾ [al-Kahf: 21]. The original meaning of "'uthur" is falling upon or stumbling over something, and from this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"With a she-camel with a limp, which we squeezed when she stumbled; so ruin is more fitting for her than that I say 'la'a' (may she perish)."

The meaning is: if after the oath it becomes apparent that the two witnesses or the two executors deserved sin, that is, they became liable to sin, either by lying in the testimony or the oath, or by the manifestation of betrayal. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "ithm" here is the name of the thing taken, because the one who takes it sins by taking it, so it was called "ithm," just as what is taken unjustly is called "mazlama" (wrongful seizure). Sibawayh said: "mazlama" is the name of what is taken from you, so likewise this taken thing was named by the name of the verbal noun.

His saying: ﴿fa-akharani yaqumani maqamahuma﴾ ("then two others shall stand in their place") means: then two other witnesses, or two other oath-takers, shall stand in the place of the two who were found to have deserved sin, and they shall testify or swear to what is the truth. It is not meant that they stand in their place in delivering the testimony that the two who deserved sin had given.

His saying: ﴿min alladhina istahaqqa 'alayhimu al-awliyan﴾ ("from among those against whom the two nearest have a claim"). "Istahaqqa" is in the passive voice in the reading of the majority. 'Ali, Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas, and Hafs read it in the active voice. "Al-awliyan," in the first reading, is in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: they are the two nearest, as if it were said: "who are they?" and it was answered: "they are the two nearest." It has also been said it is a substitute for the pronoun in "yaqumani" or for "akharan." Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and Hamza read "al-awwalin" (the first ones), the plural of "awwal," as a substitute for "alladhina" or for the "hum" in "'alayhim." al-Hasan read "al-awwalan" (the first two).

The meaning with the passive voice is: from among those upon whom sin has been inflicted, that is, the people of the deceased and his clan, for they have the greater right to testimony or oath than others. Thus "al-awliyan" is the dual of "awla" (more worthy). The meaning with the active reading is: from among those against whom the two nearest, from among them, by testimony, have a right, that they should bring them forward to stand as witnesses and expose by them the lying of the liars, because the two are the closest to the deceased. Thus "al-awliyan" is the subject of "istahaqqa," and its object is that they bring them forward to stand as witnesses. It has been said that the object is omitted, and the meaning is: from among those against whom the two nearest have a right, by the deceased, the bequest that he made.

His saying: ﴿fa-yuqsimani billah﴾ ("then they both swear by God") is conjoined to "yaqumani" ("they stand"), meaning: they swear by God, "our testimony is truer than their testimony," that is, our oath is truer. The testimony here means the oath, as in God's saying: ﴿so the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by God﴾ [al-Nur: 6], meaning: they swear that "our testimony is more deserving than their testimony," that is, more deserving than their oath that they are truthful and trustworthy. "And we have not transgressed" means: we have not exceeded the truth in our oath. ﴿Indeed, then we would be among the wrongdoers﴾, if we had sworn to falsehood.

His saying: ﴿dhalika adna an ya'tu bi-l-shahadati 'ala wajhiha﴾ ("That is more likely to bring the testimony in its proper form"): that is, that explanation which God, glorified is He, has given in this story, and we have learned how one who wishes to make a bequest while traveling should act, when none of his family or clan is with him and there are disbelievers with him. "Adna" means: closer to, that the witnesses who bear the testimony of the bequest will give testimony in its proper form, so they will not distort, alter, or betray. This is a new statement that contains mention of the benefit and the advantage in this ruling which God legislated in this place of His Book. The pronoun in "ya'tu" refers to the witnesses to the bequest from among the disbelievers. It has been said that it refers to the Muslims addressed by this ruling.

The intention is to warn them against betrayal and to command them to testify to the truth. His saying: ﴿aw yakhafu an turadda aymanun ba'da aymanihim﴾ ("or they fear that oaths will be repeated after their oaths"): that is, that oaths will be turned back to the heirs, so that they swear contrary to what the witnesses to the bequest testified, and then the witnesses to the bequest are exposed. This is conjoined to his saying "an ya'tu" (that they bring), so the benefit in God's legislation of this ruling, glorified is He, is one of two things: either the witnesses to the bequest are restrained from lying and betrayal, so they bring the testimony in its proper form.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 106–108 (part 2 of 2):

or they fear that the oaths will be repudiated after they are taken on the kinsmen of the deceased, and so they swear by something that implies their lying or their betrayal. Thus that will be a means of the witnesses to the bequest giving their testimony in its proper form, without lying (p-402) or betrayal.

It was also said: "or they fear" is joined to an implied clause after the first clause, and the sense is: "That is closer to their giving testimony in its proper form and their fearing the punishment of the Hereafter for lying and betrayal, or their fearing exposure through the rejection of the oath." Whichever of the two fears occurs, the purpose is achieved. ﴿And fear Allah in opposing His commands.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾, those who depart from His obedience in any sin, among which is lying in an oath or in testimony.

The sum of what this passage of the Mighty Book contains is that whoever is visited by the signs of death should call two just men from among the just Muslims to witness his bequest. If he does not find Muslim witnesses, and he is traveling, and finds non-Muslims, he may call two men from among them to witness his bequest. If the heirs of the testator doubt them, the two shall swear by Allah that they testified truthfully, and that they concealed nothing of the testimony and betrayed nothing of what the deceased left behind. If afterward it becomes clear that what they swore to was false, through a flaw in the testimony or the appearance of some part of the estate of the deceased which they claimed had come into their possession in some way, then two men from the heirs shall swear, and the ruling is applied accordingly.

Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it and graded it weak, as did Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Nahhas in his History, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Ma'rifa, through the route of Abu al-Nadr, who is al-Kalbi, from Baadhan, the freedman of Umm Hani, who said: "From Ibn Abbas, concerning Tamim al-Dari regarding this verse: ﴿O you who have believed, let there be [a] testimony among you when death approaches one of you﴾ He said: 'People were absolved of it except for me and Adi ibn Baddaa. The two of them were Christians who used to travel to Syria before Islam. They came to Syria for their trade, and a freedman of Banu Sahm called Budayl ibn Abi Maryam came to them with merchandise, carrying a silver cup which he intended for the king, and it was the greatest of his merchandise. He fell ill and made them his executors, and he instructed them to deliver what he had left to his family.' Tamim said: 'When he died, we took that cup and sold it for a thousand dirhams, then Adi ibn Baddaa and I divided it between us. When we came to his family, we handed over to them what we had with us, and they missed the cup and asked us about it. We said: "He left nothing other than this," or "He gave us nothing other than this."' Tamim said: 'When I embraced Islam after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ arrived in Madina, I felt guilty about that. So I went to his family and informed them of the matter, and I paid them five hundred dirhams, and I told them that my companion had the same amount. They brought it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he asked them for evidence, but they found none. So he commanded them to have him swear by that which is held in reverence among the people of his religion. He swore, and Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, let there be [a] testimony among you﴾ to His saying ﴿that oaths be repudiated after their oaths﴾. Then Amr ibn al-As and another man stood and swore, and the five hundred dirhams were taken from Adi ibn Baddaa.'"

In its isnad (chain of transmission) is Abu al-Nadr, who is Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi, the author of the tafsir (exegesis). Al-Tirmidhi said: "The people of hadith abandoned him."

Al-Bukhari transmitted it in his History, and al-Tirmidhi graded it good, as did Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Nahhas, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "A man from Banu Sahm went out with Tamim al-Dari and Adi ibn Baddaa, and the Sahmi died in a land where there was no Muslim. He made them his executors. When they brought back his estate, they missed a silver cup decorated with gold. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ made them swear by Allah that they had not concealed it and had not taken it. Then they found the cup in Makka, and it was said: 'We bought it from Tamim and Adi.' Two men from the Sahmi's guardians stood and swore by Allah: 'Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and the cup belongs to our companion.' And they took the cup." He said: "And concerning them was revealed ﴿O you who have believed, let there be [a] testimony among you﴾, the verse."

In its isnad is Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim al-Kufi. Al-Tirmidhi said: "It was said that he is good in hadith (salih al-hadith)." Abu Dawud also transmitted it through his route. A group of the Successors (tabi'un) transmitted that this story is the cause of the revelation of the verse, and the exegetes mentioned it in their tafsirs.

Al-Qurtubi said: "The exegetes unanimously agreed that this story is the cause of the revelation of the verse." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Nahhas transmitted, through the route of Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas, concerning ﴿O you who have believed, let there be [a] testimony among you﴾, the verse. He said: "This is for one who dies while Muslims are present; Allah commanded him to call two just Muslim men to witness his bequest." Then He said: ﴿or two others from other than you, if you are traveling through the land﴾. "This is for one who dies while no Muslim is with him; Allah commanded [him to call] the testimony of two men from among non-Muslims. If their testimony is doubted, they shall swear by Allah after the prayer that they did not sell their testimony for a small price. If the guardians discover that the two unbelievers lied in their testimony, and there are two men among the guardians who swear by Allah that the testimony of the two unbelievers is false, that is His saying: ﴿then if it becomes known that they both deserved sin﴾, meaning: if it is discovered that the two unbelievers lied, that is closer to ﴿their giving testimony in its proper form, or fearing that oaths will be repudiated after their oaths﴾, so that the testimony of the two unbelievers is rejected and judgment is made on the testimony of the guardians. There is no oath upon the testimony of Muslims; oaths are only required when the two are unbelievers."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that he was asked about this verse and said: "This is a man who set out on a journey with wealth, and his appointed time overtook him. If he finds two Muslim men, he hands his estate over to them and calls two just Muslim men to witness it. If he does not find two just Muslim men, then two men from the People of the Book. If they deliver it, then that is their way. If they deny it, they shall be made to swear by Allah, besides whom there is no god, after the prayer: 'Indeed this which was handed to me, I have not concealed anything from it.' When he swears, he is cleared. Then if the two companions from the People of the Book come afterward and testify against him, and then the people make a claim against him regarding what they named, the oaths of the heirs are imposed together with their testimony, and then they take his right. That is what Allah means by: ﴿two men of justice from among you or two others from other than you﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿or two others from other than you﴾, that he said: "From other than Muslims, from the People of the Book."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "This verse is abrogated (mansukha)." Ibn Jarir transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning the verse, who said: "That was for a man who died while no one from the people of Islam was with him, and that was at the beginning of Islam, when the land was at war and the people were unbelievers except for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his companions in Madina. People used to inherit by bequest. Then the bequest was abrogated, the obligatory shares were established, and the Muslims acted accordingly."

Ibn Jarir also transmitted from al-Zuhri, who said: (p-403) "The sunna has been established that the testimony of an unbeliever is not valid, whether in residence or on a journey; it is only [valid] among Muslims."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ubayda, concerning His saying ﴿you detain both of them after the prayer﴾, that he said: "The afternoon prayer (salat al-asr)."
