Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Zayd, concerning His saying ﴿we will not exchange it for a price﴾, that he said: "We will not take a bribe for it." ﴿Nor will we conceal the testimony of Allah﴾, even if its owner is distant.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Qatada, concerning His saying ﴿then if it becomes known that they both deserved sin﴾, that is, it became known from them that they had betrayed by lying or concealing. Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Zayd, concerning His saying "the two nearest", that he said: "[It refers] to the deceased."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatada, concerning His saying ﴿that is closer to their giving testimony in its proper form﴾, that he said: "That is more likely that they will be truthful in their testimony," ﴿or they fear that oaths will be repudiated after their oaths﴾, that he said: "And that they fear reproach." Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Zayd, concerning His saying ﴿or they fear that oaths will be repudiated after their oaths﴾, that he said: "Then their oaths will be nullified and the oaths of these others will be taken."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 5, verses 109–111:

His saying: ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the Messengers﴾. The word governing the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is an implied verb, meaning: "listen," or "remember," or "beware." Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative case governed by his saying "and fear Allah," mentioned in the first verse. It was also said that it is a substitute (badal) for the object of "fear Allah," a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal). It was said that it is an adverbial phrase of time (zarf) for his saying "does not guide" [al-Ma'idah: 109], mentioned before it. It was also said that it is in the accusative case governed by a delayed implied verb, its sense being: ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the Messengers﴾, [and] there will be such-and-such circumstances.

His saying: ﴿What was the response you received?﴾ That is: what response did your nations, to whom Allah sent you, give you? Or: what answer did they give you? In both interpretations, the word "what" (ma) is in the accusative case, governed by the verb mentioned after it. The question is directed at the Messengers in order to rebuke their peoples. Their answer, "We have no knowledge," although they know what their peoples responded, is a committing of the matter to Allah and a display of helplessness and inability, especially since they know that the question is one of rebuke. Committing the answer to Allah is more effective in achieving this. It was said that the meaning is: "We have no knowledge of what they innovated after us." It was said: "We have no knowledge of what their inner selves harbored." It was said: the meaning is: "We have no knowledge except what You know better than us." It was also said that they were overcome with confusion about what their peoples had answered, because of the terror of the place of gathering.

His saying: ﴿When Allah said: "O Jesus, son of Mary﴾. "When" (idh) is a substitute for "the Day when He will gather." This is specification after generalization. The specification of Jesus, peace be upon him, among the Messengers is due to the disagreement of the two groups, the Jews and the Christians, concerning him, in excess and in deficiency: this group makes him a god, and that group makes him a liar. It was also said: it is in the accusative case by the implied "remember."

His saying: ﴿Remember My favor upon you and upon your mother﴾. He, glory be to Him, reminded him of His favor upon him and upon his mother, while He is the One who remembers them and knows of Allah's bestowal of grace upon them. [This is] for the purpose of informing the nations of what Allah singled them out with, of the honor and the elevated status that He distinguished them with. Or [it is] to confirm the proof and to rebuke the denier, [showing] that their station with Allah is this station, and to rebuke whoever took them as two gods, by clarifying that this favor upon them is entirely from Allah, glory be to Him, and that they are two servants among His servants, blessed with the favors of Allah, glory be to Him, having no share in the affair whatsoever.

His saying: ﴿When I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit﴾. "When" (idh) is an adverbial phrase of time for "favor," because the word "favor" carries the sense of a verbal noun. That is: remember My favor upon you at the time of My strengthening you. Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) for "favor," meaning: [this favor] being at that time, when I strengthened you. "Strengthened" (ayyadtuka) means "I gave you strength," derived from "al-ayd," which is strength.

Regarding the Holy Spirit (ruh al-qudus), there are two views. One is that it is the pure spirit with which Allah specially favored him. It was said that it is Gabriel, peace be upon him. It was said that it is the speech by which He gives life to souls. "Al-qudus" means purity, and its attribution to the spirit is because it is its cause. The clause ﴿you speak to the people﴾ explains the meaning of the strengthening. "In the cradle" (fi al-mahd) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, you speak to the people whether you are a child or an adult, your speech not differing in the two states, whereas the speech of others differs between these two states with clear difference.

His saying: ﴿And when I taught you the Book﴾ is coordinated with ﴿When I strengthened you﴾, meaning: and remember My favor upon you at the time of My teaching you the Book, that is, the kind of Book, or the intended meaning of "the Book" is writing. According to the first view, the mention of the Torah and the Gospel is the mention of the particular after the general, and their specific mention is for the greater particularity of his connection to them. As for the Torah, it was used as proof against the Jews in most of what passed between him and them in debate, as is explicitly stated in the Gospel. As for the Gospel, it is because it was revealed to him from Allah, glory be to Him. The intended "wisdom" is the kind of wisdom. It was said: it is firm speech.

﴿And when you created from clay the likeness of a bird﴾: that is, you shaped [it] into a form like the form of a bird, by My permission to you for that and My facilitation of it for you, so you breathed into the shaped form and it became a bird, moving and alive like the rest of birds. ﴿And you healed the blind and the leper by My permission﴾ — by My permission to you and My facilitation of it for you and My making it easy for you. The explanation of this has been mentioned at length in al-Baqarah, so we will not repeat it. ﴿And when you brought forth the dead﴾ from their graves, and that was a great sign for you by My permission. The repetition of "by My permission" in the four places is for the emphasis that all of that was from Allah's side; Jesus, peace be upon him, had no action in it except the mere obedience to the command of Allah, glory be to Him.

His saying: ﴿And when I restrained the Children of Israel from you﴾ is coordinated with "when you brought forth." "Kaffa" means: I repelled and turned away. ﴿The Children of Israel from you﴾ — when they intended to kill you, ﴿when you came to them with clear proofs﴾, with the manifest miracles, ﴿and those who disbelieved among them said: "This is nothing but clear magic"﴾. That is: what you have brought is nothing but clear magic. When this matter became great in their breasts (p. 404) and they were dazzled by it, they could not deny it entirely, so they attributed it to magic.

His saying: ﴿And when I inspired the disciples to believe in Me and My Messenger﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it, and its explanation has already been mentioned.

In the language of the Arabs, "wahy" (inspiration) means "ilham" (divine inspiration): that is, I inspired the disciples and cast it into their hearts. It was said that its meaning is: I commanded them through the tongues of the Messengers to believe in Me with monotheism and sincerity, and to believe in the mission of My Messenger.

His saying: ﴿They said: "We have believed"﴾ is a new sentence, as if it were said: "What did they say?" So he said: they said, "We have believed." ﴿And bear witness that we are Muslims﴾, that is, sincere in faith. That is: bear witness, O Lord, or bear witness, O Jesus.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujahid regarding his saying: ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the Messengers, and say: "What was the response you received?"﴾ — they will be terrified and will say, ﴿"We have no knowledge"﴾, so their hearts will be returned to them and they will know.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Suddi regarding the verse, he said: That is because they will stop at a station where minds are bewildered, and when they are asked they will say, "We have no knowledge." Then they will stop at another station and bear witness against their peoples.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn Abbas, he said: They will say, "We have no knowledge," out of terror that will numb their minds. Then Allah will return their minds to them, and they will be the ones who are questioned, according to Allah's saying: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [al-A'raf: 6].

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir transmitted from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, the Prophets and their nations will be summoned. Then Jesus will be summoned, and He will remind him of His favor upon him, and he will acknowledge it. He will say: 'O Jesus, son of Mary, ﴿Remember My favor upon you and upon your mother﴾,' and so on. Then He will say: 'Did you say to the people: "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?' He will deny that he said that. Then the Christians will be brought and questioned, and they will say, 'Yes, he commanded us to do that.' Jesus's hair will grow long until every angel takes hold of a hair from his head and body, and he will kneel before them in the presence of Allah for a period of a thousand years, until He establishes the proof against them, the cross will be raised for them, and they will be taken to the Fire."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And when I restrained the Children of Israel from you, when you came to them with clear proofs﴾: that is, with the signs that were manifested at his hands, of bringing the dead to life, creating from clay the likeness of a bird, healing ailments, and informing of many unseen matters. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Suddi regarding His saying: ﴿And when I inspired the disciples﴾, he said: "I cast it into their hearts." Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Qatada something similar.

His saying: ﴿And when I taught you the Book﴾ is coordinated with ﴿When I strengthened you﴾, meaning: and remember My favor upon you at the time of My teaching you the Book, that is, the kind of Book, or the intended meaning of "the Book" is writing. According to the first view, the mention of the Torah and the Gospel is the mention of the particular after the general, and their specific mention is for the greater particularity of his connection to them. As for the Torah, it was used as proof against the Jews in most of what passed between him and them in debate, as is explicitly stated in the Gospel. As for the Gospel, it is because it was revealed to him from Allah, glory be to Him. The intended "wisdom" is the kind of wisdom. It was said: it is firm speech.

﴿And when you created from clay the likeness of a bird﴾: that is, you shaped [it] into a form like the form of a bird, by My permission to you for that and My facilitation of it for you, so you breathed into the shaped form and it became a bird, moving and alive like the rest of birds. ﴿And you healed the blind and the leper by My permission﴾ — by My permission to you and My facilitation of it for you and My making it easy for you. The explanation of this has been mentioned at length in al-Baqarah, so we will not repeat it. ﴿And when you brought forth the dead﴾ from their graves, and that was a great sign for you by My permission. The repetition of "by My permission" in the four places is for the emphasis that all of that was from Allah's side; Jesus, peace be upon him, had no action in it except the mere obedience to the command of Allah, glory be to Him.

His saying: ﴿And when I restrained the Children of Israel from you﴾ is coordinated with "when you brought forth." "Kaffa" means: I repelled and turned away. ﴿The Children of Israel from you﴾ — when they intended to kill you, ﴿when you came to them with clear proofs﴾, with the manifest miracles, ﴿and those who disbelieved among them said: "This is nothing but clear magic"﴾. That is: what you have brought is nothing but clear magic. When this matter became great in their breasts (p. 404) and they were dazzled by it, they could not deny it entirely, so they attributed it to magic.

His saying: ﴿And when I inspired the disciples to believe in Me and My Messenger﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it, and its explanation has already been mentioned.

In the language of the Arabs, "wahy" (inspiration) means "ilham" (divine inspiration): that is, I inspired the disciples and cast it into their hearts. It was said that its meaning is: I commanded them through the tongues of the Messengers to believe in Me with monotheism and sincerity, and to believe in the mission of My Messenger.

His saying: ﴿They said: "We have believed"﴾ is a new sentence, as if it were said: "What did they say?" So he said: they said, "We have believed." ﴿And bear witness that we are Muslims﴾, that is, sincere in faith. That is: bear witness, O Lord, or bear witness, O Jesus.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujahid regarding his saying: ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the Messengers, and say: "What was the response you received?"﴾ — they will be terrified and will say, ﴿"We have no knowledge"﴾, so their hearts will be returned to them and they will know.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Suddi regarding the verse, he said: That is because they will stop at a station where minds are bewildered, and when they are asked they will say, "We have no knowledge." Then they will stop at another station and bear witness against their peoples.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn Abbas, he said: They will say, "We have no knowledge," out of terror that will numb their minds. Then Allah will return their minds to them, and they will be the ones who are questioned, according to Allah's saying: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [al-A'raf: 6].

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir transmitted from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, the Prophets and their nations will be summoned. Then Jesus will be summoned, and He will remind him of His favor upon him, and he will acknowledge it. He will say: 'O Jesus, son of Mary, ﴿Remember My favor upon you and upon your mother﴾,' and so on. Then He will say: 'Did you say to the people: "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?' He will deny that he said that. Then the Christians will be brought and questioned, and they will say, 'Yes, he commanded us to do that.' Jesus's hair will grow long until every angel takes hold of a hair from his head and body, and he will kneel before them in the presence of Allah for a period of a thousand years, until He establishes the proof against them, the cross will be raised for them, and they will be taken to the Fire."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And when I restrained the Children of Israel from you, when you came to them with clear proofs﴾: that is, with the signs that were manifested at his hands, of bringing the dead to life, creating from clay the likeness of a bird, healing ailments, and informing of many unseen matters. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Suddi regarding His saying: ﴿And when I inspired the disciples﴾, he said: "I cast it into their hearts." Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Qatada something similar.

**Al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir: commentary on Surah al-Ma'ida (5), verses 112–115**

His words, ﴿When the disciples said﴾: the adverbial clause (al-zarf, a temporal phrase) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, meaning "remember" or something similar, as explained earlier. It is said that the address is to Muhammad (ﷺ).

Al-Kisa'i read (هَلْ تَسْتَطِيعُ, "Is your Lord able") with the feminine second-person form (al-fawqiyya, "with the upper dot" in recitation terminology), and with (رَبَّكَ, "your Lord") in the accusative. Ali, Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid also read it this way. The rest of the readers read it with the masculine third-person form (al-tahtiyya, "with the lower dot") and (رَبُّكَ, "your Lord") in the nominative. The second reading raises a difficulty, because Allah has described the disciples as saying: ﴿We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾, and questioning their ability to do so contradicts what they said about themselves. This was answered by saying that this happened at the beginning of their knowledge, before their knowledge of Allah had become firm. For this reason Jesus, in answer to this question coming from them, said: ﴿Fear Allah, if you are believers﴾, meaning: do not doubt the power of Allah. It was also said that they claimed faith and Islam falsely, but this is refuted by the fact that the disciples (al-hawariyyun) were the sincere companions and helpers of Jesus, as he said: ﴿Who are my helpers in the cause of Allah? The disciples said: We are the helpers of Allah﴾ (Al 'Imran 52). It was also said that this statement came from someone who was with them. It was said too that they did not doubt the ability of the Creator, for they were believers who knew this, and the phrase is like a man saying: "Is so-and-so able to come?", while knowing that he is able and capable of it. So the meaning is: will he do it, and will he be inclined to it? It was said also that they sought reassurance, as Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ (al-Baqara 260), and their later words ﴿and that our hearts may be reassured﴾ support this. As for the first reading, the meaning is: Are you able to ask your Lord? Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "Will you request your Lord's obedience in what you ask of Him?", so it is of the same type as ﴿and ask the town﴾ (Yusuf 82). Al-Ma'ida is the table (al-khiwan) when food is on it, from the root (madda), meaning to give and to provide, as if it extends (tumid) to whoever approaches it. This was said by Qutrub and others. It was also said that it is an active participle with the meaning of a passive, like ﴿a pleasing life﴾ (al-Haqqa 21). This was said by Abu Ubayda. Jesus, peace be upon him, answered them with his words: ﴿Fear Allah, if you are believers﴾, meaning: fear Him from this request and the like, if you are truthful in your faith, for the nature of the believer is to refrain from making demands of his Lord in this manner. It was also said that he commanded them to fear Allah so that this would be a means to achieving what they asked for.

His words, ﴿They said: We wish to eat from it﴾: by this they stated the purpose of their request for the table to be sent down. Likewise what is joined to it in their words: ﴿and that our hearts may be reassured, and that we may know that you have told us the truth, and that we may be witnesses to it﴾. The meaning: our hearts will be reassured by the perfect power of Allah, or by the fact that you are a messenger sent to us from Him, or by the fact that Allah has answered what we asked; and we will know with certain knowledge that you have told us the truth about your prophethood; and we will be witnesses to it before those of the Children of Israel who were not present, or before the rest of mankind, or we will be witnesses to Allah's oneness, or we will be among the witnesses, meaning those present, not merely the listeners. When Jesus saw what they had said about their own purpose in sending down the table, he said: ﴿O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table from heaven﴾, meaning: existing or descending from heaven. According to Sibawayh and his followers, the original form of (اللَّهُمَّ, "O Allah") is (يَا اللَّهُ, "O Allah"), and the letter (م, m) was made a substitute for the vocative particle. (رَبُّنا, "our Lord") is a second vocative, and is not an adjective. And ﴿that it may be a feast for us﴾ is an adjective of (مائِدَة, "table").

Al-A'mash read (يَكُونُ لَنا عِيدًا, "it may be a feast for us"), meaning the day of its descent will be a feast for us. Its descent took place on a Sunday, which was a feast day for them. (العِيد, "feast") is the singular of (الأعْياد, "feasts"). Its plural is formed with the letter ya', while its original root is with waw, because the waw is fixed in the singular. It was also said that this is to distinguish it from (أعْواد, "sticks"), the plural of (عُود, "stick"). Al-Jawhari mentioned this meaning. It was also said that its root is from (عادَ يَعُودُ, "to return, to recur"), meaning he returned, so it is (عَوْد) with waw, which changes to ya' because the letter before it is kasra, like (المِيزان, "the balance"), (المِيقات, "the appointed time"), and (المِيعاد, "the appointment"). Thus the festivals of the Breaking of the Fast and of the Sacrifice are called two feasts, because they return every year. Al-Khalil said: the feast is every day of gathering, as if they return to it.

His words, ﴿for the first of us and the last of us﴾: this is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in (لَنا, "for us"), with the governing verb repeated. The meaning: for those in our era and for those who come after us, from our descendants and others. His words, ﴿and a sign from You﴾, are conjoined to (عِيدًا, "a feast"). The meaning: a proof and a clear evidence of Your perfect power and the truth of Your sending the one You sent. ﴿Provide for us﴾, meaning give us this desired table, or provide us with sustenance that will help us in Your worship. ﴿And You are the best of providers﴾: in reality there is no provider other than You, and no giver besides You.

Allah, glorified is He, answered the request of Jesus, peace be upon him, and said: ﴿I am sending it down﴾, meaning the table, ﴿upon you﴾. The people of knowledge have differed over whether the table was actually sent down to them or not. The majority held the first view, which is the truth, because of His words, glorified is He: ﴿I am sending it down upon you﴾. His promise is true, and He does not break His promise.

Mujahid said: it was not sent down; rather, it is a parable that Allah set forth for His creation, forbidding them to ask the prophets for signs. Al-Hasan said: He promised them that it would be granted. Then when He said: ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves after this﴾, they asked Allah's forgiveness and said: "We do not want it."

His words, ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves after this﴾, meaning after its descent, ﴿I will punish him with a punishment﴾, meaning a punishment such that ﴿I will not punish anyone of the worlds with it﴾. The phrase (لا أُعَذِّبُهُ, "I will not punish him") is an adjective of (عَذابًا, "a punishment"), and the pronoun refers to (العَذاب, "the punishment") in the sense of (التَّعْذِيب, "punishing"). The meaning: I will not punish anyone with the like of that punishment. ﴿Anyone of the worlds﴾: it was said the intended meaning is the worlds of their time; it was also said it is the plural of "the worlds". In this there is threat and warning beyond measure.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Aisha, who said: "The disciples were too knowing of Allah to say: ﴿Can your Lord...?﴾ They only said: Are you able to ask your Lord to...?" This is supported by what al-Hakim transmitted and declared sound, as did al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited to me: (هَلْ تَسْتَطِيعُ رَبَّكَ, "Are you able, your Lord...")", with the letter ta' (in the second-person form), meaning the upper-dot form. Abu Ubayd, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he recited it in the same way.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "The ma'ida is the khiwan, and (تَطْمَئِنَّ, "be reassured") means to be certain." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi concerning His words ﴿be a feast for us﴾: he said: "We take the day on which it was sent down as a feast, which we and those after us honour." Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he used to narrate from Jesus son of Mary that he said to the Children of Israel: "Would you fast for Allah for thirty days, then ask Him, and He will give you what you ask? For the reward of the worker is due from the one for whom he works." They did so, then they said: "O teacher of goodness, you told us that the reward of the worker is due from the one for whom he works, and you commanded us to fast for thirty days, and we did. We never worked for anyone for thirty days without him feeding us." ﴿Can your Lord send down to us a table...﴾ up to His words ﴿anyone of the worlds﴾. Then the angels came flying with a table from heaven, on which were seven fishes and seven loaves, until they placed it before them, and the last of the people ate from it as the first of them did.

At-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ammar ibn Yasir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The table was sent down from heaven as bread and meat, and they were commanded not to betray (the trust) and not to store up for the next day. But they were afraid and stored up and kept (food) for the next day, so they were transformed into monkeys and pigs." This has also been transmitted as a statement of Ammar (mawquf). At-Tirmidhi said: "The stopping (at Ammar) is more sound."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The ma'ida was a fish and loaves." Ibn Jarir transmitted through al-Awfi from him, who said: "There came down upon Jesus son of Mary and the disciples a table upon which were fish and bread, which they ate from wherever they turned, whenever they wished." Ibn Jarir transmitted something similar from him through Ikrima. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Abdullah ibn Amr, who said: "Indeed, the most severely punished people on the Day of Resurrection will be those who disbelieved among the people of the table, the hypocrites, and the family of Pharaoh."

The rest of the readers read it with the masculine third-person form (al-tahtiyya, "with the lower dot") and (رَبُّكَ, "your Lord") in the nominative. The second reading raises a difficulty, because Allah has described the disciples as saying: ﴿We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾, and questioning their ability to do so contradicts what they said about themselves. This was answered by saying that this happened at the beginning of their knowledge, before their knowledge of Allah had become firm. For this reason Jesus, in answer to this question coming from them, said: ﴿Fear Allah, if you are believers﴾, meaning: do not doubt the power of Allah. It was also said that they claimed faith and Islam falsely, but this is refuted by the fact that the disciples (al-hawariyyun) were the sincere companions and helpers of Jesus, as he said: ﴿Who are my helpers in the cause of Allah? The disciples said: We are the helpers of Allah﴾ (Al 'Imran 52). It was also said that this statement came from someone who was with them. It was said too that they did not doubt the ability of the Creator, for they were believers who knew this, and the phrase is like a man saying: "Is so-and-so able to come?", while knowing that he is able and capable of it. So the meaning is: will he do it, and will he be inclined to it? It was said also that they sought reassurance, as Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ (al-Baqara 260), and their later words ﴿and that our hearts may be reassured﴾ support this. As for the first reading, the meaning is: Are you able to ask your Lord? Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "Will you request your Lord's obedience in what you ask of Him?", so it is of the same type as ﴿and ask the town﴾ (Yusuf 82). Al-Ma'ida is the table (al-khiwan) when food is on it, from the root (madda), meaning to give and to provide, as if it extends (tumid) to whoever approaches it. This was said by Qutrub and others. It was also said that it is an active participle with the meaning of a passive, like ﴿a pleasing life﴾ (al-Haqqa 21). This was said by Abu Ubayda. Jesus, peace be upon him, answered them with his words: ﴿Fear Allah, if you are believers﴾, meaning: fear Him from this request and the like, if you are truthful in your faith, for the nature of the believer is to refrain from making demands of his Lord in this manner. It was also said that he commanded them to fear Allah so that this would be a means to achieving what they asked for.

His words, ﴿They said: We wish to eat from it﴾: by this they stated the purpose of their request for the table to be sent down. Likewise what is joined to it in their words: ﴿and that our hearts may be reassured, and that we may know that you have told us the truth, and that we may be witnesses to it﴾. The meaning: our hearts will be reassured by the perfect power of Allah, or by the fact that you are a messenger sent to us from Him, or by the fact that Allah has answered what we asked; and we will know with certain knowledge that you have told us the truth about your prophethood; and we will be witnesses to it before those of the Children of Israel who were not present, or before the rest of mankind, or we will be witnesses to Allah's oneness, or we will be among the witnesses, meaning those present, not merely the listeners. When Jesus saw what they had said about their own purpose in sending down the table, he said: ﴿O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table from heaven﴾, meaning: existing or descending from heaven. According to Sibawayh and his followers, the original form of (اللَّهُمَّ, "O Allah") is (يَا اللَّهُ, "O Allah"), and the letter (م, m) was made a substitute for the vocative particle. (رَبُّنا, "our Lord") is a second vocative, and is not an adjective. And ﴿that it may be a feast for us﴾ is an adjective of (مائِدَة, "table").

Al-A'mash read (يَكُونُ لَنا عِيدًا, "it may be a feast for us"), meaning the day of its descent will be a feast for us. Its descent took place on a Sunday, which was a feast day for them. (العِيد, "feast") is the singular of (الأعْياد, "feasts"). Its plural is formed with the letter ya', while its original root is with waw, because the waw is fixed in the singular. It was also said that this is to distinguish it from (أعْواد, "sticks"), the plural of (عُود, "stick"). Al-Jawhari mentioned this meaning. It was also said that its root is from (عادَ يَعُودُ, "to return, to recur"), meaning he returned, so it is (عَوْد) with waw, which changes to ya' because the letter before it is kasra, like (المِيزان, "the balance"), (المِيقات, "the appointed time"), and (المِيعاد, "the appointment"). Thus the festivals of the Breaking of the Fast and of the Sacrifice are called two feasts, because they return every year. Al-Khalil said: the feast is every day of gathering, as if they return to it.

His words, ﴿for the first of us and the last of us﴾: this is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in (لَنا, "for us"), with the governing verb repeated. The meaning: for those in our era and for those who come after us, from our descendants and others. His words, ﴿and a sign from You﴾, are conjoined to (عِيدًا, "a feast"). The meaning: a proof and a clear evidence of Your perfect power and the truth of Your sending the one You sent. ﴿Provide for us﴾, meaning give us this desired table, or provide us with sustenance that will help us in Your worship. ﴿And You are the best of providers﴾: in reality there is no provider other than You, and no giver besides You.

Allah, glorified is He, answered the request of Jesus, peace be upon him, and said: ﴿I am sending it down﴾, meaning the table, ﴿upon you﴾. The people of knowledge have differed over whether the table was actually sent down to them or not. The majority held the first view, which is the truth, because of His words, glorified is He: ﴿I am sending it down upon you﴾. His promise is true, and He does not break His promise.

Mujahid said: it was not sent down; rather, it is a parable that Allah set forth for His creation, forbidding them to ask the prophets for signs. Al-Hasan said: He promised them that it would be granted. Then when He said: ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves after this﴾, they asked Allah's forgiveness and said: "We do not want it."

His words, ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves after this﴾, meaning after its descent, ﴿I will punish him with a punishment﴾, meaning a punishment such that ﴿I will not punish anyone of the worlds with it﴾. The phrase (لا أُعَذِّبُهُ, "I will not punish him") is an adjective of (عَذابًا, "a punishment"), and the pronoun refers to (العَذاب, "the punishment") in the sense of (التَّعْذِيب, "punishing"). The meaning: I will not punish anyone with the like of that punishment. ﴿Anyone of the worlds﴾: it was said the intended meaning is the worlds of their time; it was also said it is the plural of "the worlds". In this there is threat and warning beyond measure.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Aisha, who said: "The disciples were too knowing of Allah to say: ﴿Can your Lord...?﴾ They only said: Are you able to ask your Lord to...?" This is supported by what al-Hakim transmitted and declared sound, as did al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited to me: (هَلْ تَسْتَطِيعُ رَبَّكَ, "Are you able, your Lord...")", with the letter ta' (in the second-person form), meaning the upper-dot form. Abu Ubayd, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he recited it in the same way.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "The ma'ida is the khiwan, and (تَطْمَئِنَّ, "be reassured") means to be certain." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi concerning His words ﴿be a feast for us﴾: he said: "We take the day on which it was sent down as a feast, which we and those after us honour." Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he used to narrate from Jesus son of Mary that he said to the Children of Israel: "Would you fast for Allah for thirty days, then ask Him, and He will give you what you ask? For the reward of the worker is due from the one for whom he works." They did so, then they said: "O teacher of goodness, you told us that the reward of the worker is due from the one for whom he works, and you commanded us to fast for thirty days, and we did. We never worked for anyone for thirty days without him feeding us." ﴿Can your Lord send down to us a table...﴾ up to His words ﴿anyone of the worlds﴾. Then the angels came flying with a table from heaven, on which were seven fishes and seven loaves, until they placed it before them, and the last of the people ate from it as the first of them did.

At-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ammar ibn Yasir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The table was sent down from heaven as bread and meat, and they were commanded not to betray (the trust) and not to store up for the next day. But they were afraid and stored up and kept (food) for the next day, so they were transformed into monkeys and pigs." This has also been transmitted as a statement of Ammar (mawquf). At-Tirmidhi said: "The stopping (at Ammar) is more sound."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The ma'ida was a fish and loaves." Ibn Jarir transmitted through al-Awfi from him, who said: "There came down upon Jesus son of Mary and the disciples a table upon which were fish and bread, which they ate from wherever they turned, whenever they wished." Ibn Jarir transmitted something similar from him through Ikrima. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Abdullah ibn Amr, who said: "Indeed, the most severely punished people on the Day of Resurrection will be those who disbelieved among the people of the table, the hypocrites, and the family of Pharaoh."

His saying: ﴿And when Allah said﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and it is in the accusative position by its governing verb, or by a governing verb implied here, meaning: remember. The majority of the exegetes (mufassirun) held that this saying of His, glorified is He, will be on the Day of Resurrection. The point is to rebuke the worshippers of the Messiah and his mother from among the Christians.

Al-Suddi (al-Suddi) and Qutrub (Qutrub) said: He said this statement to him when He raised him up to the heaven, when the Christians said about him what they said. The first view is preferable. It has been said: "idh" (when) here carries the meaning of "idha" (whenever), as in His saying: ﴿If only you could see when they are terrified﴾ [Saba: 51], meaning, whenever they are terrified; and as in the saying of Abu al-Najm:

*Then may Allah reward you on my behalf, when He rewarded*
*The Gardens of Eden in the high heavens*

meaning, whenever He rewarded; and as in the saying of al-Aswad ibn Ja'far al-Asadi:

*Now, when I jest with them, for they say*
*"Has the old man not gone a way?"*

meaning, whenever I jest with them. This is an expression of a future event in the past tense, to affirm that it will certainly occur. It has been said, regarding the purpose of this interrogation from Him, exalted is He, that it is for the purpose of rebuke, as has preceded. It has also been said that it is for the purpose of informing the Messiah that his people changed after him and attributed to him what he did not say. (p-406) His saying: ﴿besides Allah﴾ is connected to His saying "take me," in the sense of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: transgressing the limit. It is also permissible that it be connected to an omitted element that serves as a description of "two gods," meaning: existing apart from Allah.

His saying: "Glory be to You" is an affirmation of His transcendence, glorified is He, meaning: I declare You far above such things. ﴿It is not for me to say what is not mine by right﴾, meaning: it is not proper for me to claim for myself what is not rightfully mine. ﴿If I had said it, You would surely have known it﴾: he referred that to His knowledge, glorified is He, and He knew that he had not said it, and thereby the non-occurrence of that saying from him is established.

His saying: ﴿You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Your soul﴾: this sentence serves as a causal explanation of what came before it, meaning: You know what is known to me, and I do not know what is known to You. This speech is of the type of mushakala (mushakala, a rhetorical device of matching one term with another for its sake), as is well known among the scholars of meanings and eloquence (ʿulamaʾ al-maʿani wa al-bayan). It has been said that the meaning is: You know what is in my unseen, and I do not know what is in Your unseen. It has also been said: You know what I conceal, and I do not know what You conceal. It has been said: You know what I intend, and I do not know what You intend.

His saying: ﴿I said to them only what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord."﴾ This sentence confirms the content of what preceded it, meaning: I only commanded them with what You commanded me. ﴿Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord﴾ is an explanation of the meaning of ﴿I said to them﴾, meaning: I commanded them. It has been said that it is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to the pronoun in "bihi" (with it), and it has also been said that it is a substitute (badal) for it. ﴿And I was a witness over them﴾, meaning: a guardian and an observer, watching over their conditions and preventing them from opposing Your command. ﴿As long as I remained among them﴾, meaning: for the duration of my stay among them.

﴿Then when You took me up﴾: it has been said that this indicates that Allah, glorified is He, caused him to die before raising him. This is not correct, because the reports have multiply confirmed that he did not die, and that he remains alive in the heaven in the life he had in this world until he descends to the earth at the end of time. The meaning is: when You raised me up to the heaven. It has been said that "al-wafat" (taking, death) in the Book of Allah, glorified is He, has come in three aspects: in the meaning of death, as in His saying: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [al-Zumar: 42]; in the meaning of sleep, as in His saying: ﴿It is He who takes you at night﴾ [al-An'am: 60], meaning: He puts you to sleep; and in the meaning of raising, as in: ﴿Then when You took me up﴾, and ﴿When Allah said: "O Jesus, I will take you up"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 55].

﴿You were the Watcher over them﴾: the origin of al-muraqaba (watching) is observing, meaning: You were the Guardian over them, the One who knows them, and the Witness over them.

﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants﴾: You do with them what You will and judge them as You wish. ﴿And if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾, meaning: the One able to do that, the Wise in His actions. It has been said that he said this in the manner of seeking compassion, as a master seeks compassion from his servant. For this reason he did not say, "If You punish them, they have disobeyed You." It has also been said that he said it in the manner of submitting to Allah's command and yielding to Him, and for this reason he turned away from "the Most Forgiving, the Most Merciful" to "the Exalted in Might, the Wise."

His saying: ﴿Allah said: "This is a day on which the truthful benefit from their truthfulness"﴾, meaning: their truthfulness in this world. It has been said: in the Hereafter, and the first is preferable. Nafi' and Ibn Muhaysin (Ibn Muhaysin) read "yawma" (the day) with a fatha (accusative), and the rest read it with a damma (nominative). The reasoning for the fatha is that it is an adverbial complement (zarf) of the speech, meaning: Allah said this statement on the day on which the truthful benefit. The reasoning for the damma is that it is the predicate of the subject, which together with what is added to it forms the sentence.

Al-Kisa'i (al-Kisa'i) said: "yawma" is in the accusative here because it is attached (mudaf) to a clause, and he cited:

*At a time when I rebuked gray hair for youth*
*And I said: "Shall I not yet be sober while gray hair restrains?"*

Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj) also held this view. The Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun) do not permit what those two said, except when the adverbial noun is attached to a past tense verb. Al-A'mash read "hadha yawmun yanfa'u" (this is a day that benefits) with tanwin on "yawmin," as in His saying: ﴿And fear a day when no soul will avail another soul at all﴾. Both readings are detached from the genitive construction by means of tanwin.

*The Gardens of Eden in the high heavens*

meaning, whenever He rewarded; and as in the saying of al-Aswad ibn Ja'far al-Asadi:

*Now, when I jest with them, for they say*
*"Has the old man not gone a way?"*

meaning, whenever I jest with them. This is an expression of a future event in the past tense, to affirm that it will certainly occur. It has been said, regarding the purpose of this interrogation from Him, exalted is He, that it is for the purpose of rebuke, as has preceded. It has also been said that it is for the purpose of informing the Messiah that his people changed after him and attributed to him what he did not say. It is also permissible that it be connected to an omitted element that serves as a description of "two gods," meaning: existing apart from Allah.

It has been said: You know what I intend, and I do not know what You intend.

His saying: ﴿I said to them only what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord."﴾ This sentence confirms the content of what preceded it, meaning: I only commanded them with what You commanded me. ﴿Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord﴾ is an explanation of the meaning of ﴿I said to them﴾, meaning: I commanded them. The reasoning for the damma is that it is the predicate of the subject, which together with what is added to it forms the sentence.

*At a time when I rebuked gray hair for youth*
*And I said: "Shall I not yet be sober while gray hair restrains?"*

His saying: ﴿And when Allah said﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it, and it is in the accusative position by its governing verb, or by a governing verb implied here, meaning: remember. The majority of the exegetes (mufassirun) held that this saying of His, glorified is He, will be on the Day of Resurrection. The point is to rebuke the worshippers of the Messiah and his mother from among the Christians.

Al-Suddi (al-Suddi) and Qutrub (Qutrub) said: He said this statement to him when He raised him up to the heaven, when the Christians said about him what they said. The first view is preferable. It has been said: "idh" (when) here carries the meaning of "idha" (whenever), as in His saying: ﴿If only you could see when they are terrified﴾ [Saba: 51], meaning, whenever they are terrified; and as in the saying of Abu al-Najm:

*Then may Allah reward you on my behalf, when He rewarded*
*The Gardens of Eden in the high heavens*

meaning, whenever He rewarded; and as in the saying of al-Aswad ibn Ja'far al-Asadi:

*Now, when I jest with them, for they say*
*"Has the old man not gone a way?"*

meaning, whenever I jest with them. This is an expression of a future event in the past tense, to affirm that it will certainly occur. It has been said, regarding the purpose of this interrogation from Him, exalted is He, that it is for the purpose of rebuke, as has preceded. It has also been said that it is for the purpose of informing the Messiah that his people changed after him and attributed to him what he did not say. (p-406) His saying: ﴿besides Allah﴾ is connected to His saying "take me," in the sense of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: transgressing the limit. It is also permissible that it be connected to an omitted element that serves as a description of "two gods," meaning: existing apart from Allah.

His saying: "Glory be to You" is an affirmation of His transcendence, glorified is He, meaning: I declare You far above such things. ﴿It is not for me to say what is not mine by right﴾, meaning: it is not proper for me to claim for myself what is not rightfully mine. ﴿If I had said it, You would surely have known it﴾: he referred that to His knowledge, glorified is He, and He knew that he had not said it, and thereby the non-occurrence of that saying from him is established.

His saying: ﴿You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Your soul﴾: this sentence serves as a causal explanation of what came before it, meaning: You know what is known to me, and I do not know what is known to You. This speech is of the type of mushakala (mushakala, a rhetorical device of matching one term with another for its sake), as is well known among the scholars of meanings and eloquence (ʿulamaʾ al-maʿani wa al-bayan). It has been said that the meaning is: You know what is in my unseen, and I do not know what is in Your unseen. It has also been said: You know what I conceal, and I do not know what You conceal. It has been said: You know what I intend, and I do not know what You intend.

His saying: ﴿I said to them only what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord."﴾ This sentence confirms the content of what preceded it, meaning: I only commanded them with what You commanded me. ﴿Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord﴾ is an explanation of the meaning of ﴿I said to them﴾, meaning: I commanded them. It has been said that it is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to the pronoun in "bihi" (with it), and it has also been said that it is a substitute (badal) for it. ﴿And I was a witness over them﴾, meaning: a guardian and an observer, watching over their conditions and preventing them from opposing Your command. ﴿As long as I remained among them﴾, meaning: for the duration of my stay among them.
